1. The firm has to state why SE-HPLC is not one of the parameter for purity and
impurities - aggregates.
2. 2. The firm is required to submit APQR for last three years (2021, 2022 and 2023) for
DS and DP
Answer:
The assay is a Reverse Phase High Performance Liquid Chromatography (RP-HPLC) 
method that uses fluorescence detection. Damoctocog Alfa Pegol is a heterodimer 
composed of a heavy chain (HC) and a PEGylated light chain (LC). This procedure uses 
RP-HPLC separation on a non-porous polymeric column to separate the principle 
components of Damoctocog Alfa Pegol preparations according to their hydrophobic 
properties. Fluorescence detection is used and the percent peak area of LC and HC 
proteins is determined. All other protein peaks are integrated as impurities. 
Damoctocog Alfa Pegol purity, LC/HC ratio and identity are reported.
The requested APQRs are provided with the response.

Question:

A) In the process validation of Regeneron Ireland, Justification of acceptance criteria of
protein concentration in UF/DF process

Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (3.2.S.2.5):
A) In the FDS process validation of Regeneron Ireland, Justification of acceptance
criteria of protein concentration in UF/DF process
During manufacturing process development, the acceptable manufacturing range for the target 
final concentrated pool (FCP) protein concentration was established based on development 
and characterization studies, and historical manufacturing experience. A high protein 
concentration in the FCP would be diluted through the sucrose adjustment and formulation 
unit operations to acceptable levels. A low protein concentration at the FCP stage could cause 
over-dilution during formulation, potentially leading to a formulated drug substance (FDS) 
that is below the specified range. The established range for commercial manufacturing (165-
184 g/L) is considered a non-critical process condition to be met during routine manufacture 
to ensure process consistency.
Typically in Biotech processes, the final concentrated pool after ultrafiltration/diafiltration, is 
set clearly higher than the actual minimal needed concentration.

In addition to the target FCP protein concentration, the lower limit for the FCP protein 
concentration was then set and classified as a critical quality attribute (CQA).
The CQA (≥ 128.8 g/L) is the minimum FCP protein concentration necessary to ensure that 
the material produced will have a concentration that is compatible with further product 
dilution and formulation steps. Additional details are provided in Table 1 below.
Following the ultrafiltration/diafiltration (UF/DF) unit operation, during the formulation step, 
there is a dilution due to the addition of the sucrose buffer, excipient buffer and dilution 
buffer. The acceptance criteria (≥ 128.8 g/L) was established as the minimal concentration 
needed at the FCP stage to ensure that the FDS will be within the final release specifications 
(103 - 126 g/L) after the addition of the three buffers.

Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 19 (3.2.S.2; 3.2.P.1):
Aflibercept solution 40 mg/ml and Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL share the same drug 
substance intermediate (DSI) and the manufacturing process until the DSI stage is identical 
(as described in S.2.2.02_022971469_03).
The subsequent manufacturing steps are similar but there are differences related to the higher 
protein concentration and different composition as summarized below:
• More DSI is used as starting material for Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL FDS
compared to Aflibercept solution 40 mg/ml drug substance (DS)/formulated bulk (FB) 
due to higher concentration of protein in the new strength. The amount of DSI used 
during process validation for Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL FDS is included in 
S.2.5.01_022972866_02.
• The size exclusion column is run for more cycles (as there is more material to
process) as shown in S.2.6.01_022972998_01.
• The tangential flow filter concentrates the product to a higher concentration (160 –
200 g/L vs. 55 g/L) due to the higher protein concentration for Aflibercept solution 
114.3 mg/mL FDS  as described in S.2.2.02_022972987_02.
• The final drug substance concentration is different (114.3 g/L vs. 40 g/L) as described
in the product composition in P.1.01_022982760_01.
• The formulation uses different excipient buffer due to differences in the composition
(P.1.01_022971855_01).
• There is no isolated unformulated DS in the Aflibercept solution 114.3. mg/mL
process which corresponds to the Aflibercept 40 mg/mL drug substance, only a direct 
formulation from DSI to FDS, and the formulation process is described in Module 
3.2.S.2.2 (S.2.2.02_022972987_02). However, for the approved Aflibercept solution 
40 mg/mL the unformulated DS is described in Module 3.2.S and considered the final

S7: Stability
a. Please explain why endotoxin content, bioburden, polysorbate content and osmolality
are not tested for stability study.

a) Endotoxin content, bioburden, polysorbate content, and osmolality are not included in the 
stability studies as those are not stability-indicating parameters and do not change at real time

content was observed until end of shelf life.
c) As aggregation and fragmentation are the main degradation pathways it is expected that 
those impurities will specifically increase under the accelerated condition. The real time 
storage condition is -80°C and no meaningful change was observed for these parameter until 
end of shelf life.

Question:

P5.4 Batch analyses
a. It is noted that the acceptance criteria for colour is Not > BY2, but the results for all
three batches reports as Not > BY6. Please confirm if these are the same.
b. It is noted in the P5.1 Specification for Release that the Purity by Reduced CE-SDS
for % LMW species is ≤ 8% LMW species. However, this is not reflected in the batch 
analyses. Please clarify.
c. It is noted in the P5.1 Specification for Release that the Purity by SE-UPLC for % %
Aggregate is ≤ 3.5 % aggregate. However, this is not reflected in the batch analyses. 
Please clarify.
d. Please explain why Isoaspartate content is not tested in the batch analyses

batch analyses are for the filling process. Please provide batch analyses for the 
manufacturing process.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 34 (3.2.P.5.4):
a) The compendial method for color testing is based on the comparison of the drug product 
solution against a defined reference solution. The reference solution is getting more diluted 
from BY1 to BY7 and resultantly, less intensively colored. Therefore, the result “Not > BY6” 
reported for the batches in P.5.4.01-01 is more stringent and complies with the acceptance 
criterion of “Not > BY2”.
b) The acceptance criteria in P.5.4.01-01 reflect the specification that was valid at the time of 
testing of 8345600001, 8345600002 and 8345600003 which was conducted during the 
development of the new Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in vial presentation. This is also 
indicated in footnote “a” of P.5.4.01-01.  
With more batch data becoming available and a deeper product knowledge the applicant 
updated the acceptance criterion for the commercial product testing for CE-SDS %LMW 
from ≤ 8% to ≤ 7.5% as shown in P.5.1.01-01 and justified in P.5.6.01-01.  
The data demonstrates that the batches 8345600001, 8345600002 and 8345600003 also 
comply with the tighter limit of ≤ 7.5% as established for the commercial product testing.
c) Similar to the explanation given above for CE-SDS, also for Purity by SE-UPLC the

Question: (iv) the visual inspection is not included as part the QC testing, please clarify and justify the alternative sites.
Answer:
Visual inspection is a GMP required step to provide a 100% control in order to eliminate all damaged or defective PFS, which shares similar characteristics with a quality control testing.
During the steps conventionally summarized under “Manufacturing”, there is direct access to the medicinal product itself as long as it is not yet in its primary packaging. An error (e.g. mixing up excipients) could have massive impact on the composition of the medicinal product.
In contrast, visual inspection concerns the primary packaged medicinal product without direct access to the product. The visual inspection is a control measure which eliminates damaged or broken PFS. In this respect it is similar to quality control testing which collects information about the product without altering it.
Vetter Pharma Fertigung GmbH is a highly skilled contact manufacturing organization (CMO) with a large number of clients and a high workload. To ensure the uninterrupted manufacturing and associated testing, it is required to establish redundant capacities in case of non-availability of resources at one site. Non-availability can be the result of planned maintenance or unexpected equipment failure.
Especially biotech products need rapid processing due to the sensitivity of the protein and the resulting need of reduced time out of refrigeration (TOR). The visual inspection is a time-consuming process and cannot be pushed out arbitrarily but requires rapid execution. Therefore, the establishment of alternative sites is mandatory. Once a manufacturing process is started, it must be guaranteed that the final product is not jeopardized by the failure of any device or apparatus. It must be made sure the process and all its required tests can be completed as the limited availability of resources would have a high impact on safe market supply. This is why Vetter Pharma Fertigung GmbH as a CMO has contractual obligations to keep alternative sites available for these cases to ensure robust supply continuity at all times, and all sites are governed by the same Quality Assurance system to make sure a change of sites would still warrant the same result.

A forced degradation study was conducted for Levonorgestrel implant 75 mg and during the 
study  levonorgestrel micronized ( API), placebo (sample matrix without API) and drug 
product were subjected to stress tests, such as thermal, humidity, photolytic, oxidative, 
hydrolytic and metal ions conditions. In addition, the study included reference samples 
(unstressed samples)
The stress test conditions were established with the aim of achieving a 10% to 30% reduction 
of levonorgestrel peak area. The stress test conditions are listed in the following table. The 
samples were analyzed with validated assay and impurity methods.

Test

Question:

Query:
Firm has stated that the synthesis impurities that are not potential degradation products are 
controlled at levonorgestrel drug substance QC testing are omitted in the drug product test 
results according to ICH Q3B guidance. Further, The acceptance limit for the sum of all 
impurities is based on the USP monograph on Levonorgestrel>>>> However, selected any 
individual impurities limit i.e. 0.5% of the applied product Levonorgestrel implant 75 mg is 
not found in line with IP-2022. Therefore, if agreed, we may ask the firm to submit impurity

product are required to meet the standard as prescribed under second schedule of Drugs and 
Cosmetic Act. Also submit the comparative specification at the time release and during the 
shelf life and acceptance criteria thereof for each parameters of the specification.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2 :
The acceptance limit for the sum of all impurities is based on the USP monograph on 
Levonorgestrel in the related substances test of Jadelle implant.
European Pharmacopoeia has published a compendial HPLC purity method, Related 
substances A, in the <Levonorgestrel> 01/2014: 0926 monograph and this method has been 
implemented for Levonorgestrel drug substance quality control (QC) testing. Therefore, also 
the proposed drug product HPLC purity method of Jadelle applies the Ph. Eur. method. The 
extraction procedure and HPLC method has been validated for use in the analysis of the drug 
product. The synthesis impurities that are not potential degradation products are controlled at 
levonorgestrel drug substance QC testing are therefore omitted in the drug product test results 
according to ICH Q3B guidance. The potential known and unidentified levonorgestrel 
degradation products above 0.1% reporting threshold are included in the test results.
The impurities test, and the applied specifications, follow the available monographs 
(European and US Pharmacopoeias) for Levonorgestrel drug substance, and additionally it is 
based on principles in ICH Q3B. The proposed specifications are not following the Indian 
Pharmacopoeia 2022, as Ph. Eur. and USP Levonorgestrel monographs are applied, as well as

Question 1:
3.2.P.2.2 – Dissolution method (initial Q1): The use of prior knowledge of the development
of a dissolution method should correlate with the pharmaceutical form being developed. Film-
coated tablet formulation and granules for oral suspension of Riociguat differ. Thus, the full
dissolution development method with justification of choice where appropriate should be
presented for granules for oral suspension as an immediate release formulation in 3.2.P.2.2.

3.2.P.2.02-01 (with data presented in Tables 4-2 to 4-6), showing an average drug release
between 93 – 100% in 15 minutes using the current QC method (Phosphate buffer pH 6.8
with 0.1% SLS), the dissolution acceptance criterion of Q = 80% in 15 minutes is considered
too widely when the principles of “Reflection paper on the dissolution specification for
generic solid oral immediate release products with systemic action” are considered. You are
thus requested to tighten the dissolution acceptance criteria to Q = 85% in 15 minutes.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (P.2.2.01, P.2.2.02, P.5.1.01, P.5.1.02, P.5.2.01, P.5.2.02,
P.5.3.02, P.5.3.21, P.5.4.01, P.5.6.01, & P.8.3.01):
Based on Bayer AG history of the dossier’s granularity, the dissolution method development
of the granules is described in section P.5 and identified as P.5.3.21. The reason why we
provide this information here is because it was performed during the pharmaceutical
development and, at the same time, it also supports the validation of the dissolution test
P.5.3.02.
By reviewing P.2.2.02 approved by Swissmedic for other Bayer products, we found that
P.5.3.21 was also referenced here. Therefore, we have amended the P.2.2.02 document from

Question:
Question 2:
3.2.P.2.2.1 – Viscosity of xanthan gum (initial Q7): It can be seen that the highest viscosity
grade of Xanthan gum (1850 mPa s) shows a lag in dissolution at all points until 30 minutes
compared to the medium (1600 mPa s) and low viscosity (1440 mPa s) grades of Xanthan
gum containing granules. Considering a proposed specification of Q = 80% in 15 minutes, the
grade of Xanthan gum should be specified, unless it can unambiguously be demonstrated
(with for example, the testing of several batches) that the variation in grade of Xanthan gum
in the formulated granules does not significantly affect dissolution. Please specify in 3.2.P.1
the viscosity range and / or grades of Xanthan gum that can be used to ensure consistent drug
release or please provide additional data to show that high viscosity grades of Xanthan gum
do not affect the dissolution of the formulated product.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2 (P.2.2.01):
The dissolution profiles using different viscosities of the excipient Xanthan gum were
measured with two different time profiles. The dissolution of the batch with the highest
viscosity of Xanthan gum (1850 mPa s) was only measured after 15, 30, 45 and 60 minutes,
whereas the other two batches were measured with additional timepoints after 5 and 10
minutes. This might give the impression of a lag time. Even though the dissolution of the
highest viscosity grade is slightly slower than the others (89.2 % compared to 96.7 and 97.7%
at 15 min), the dissolution is still very rapid (≥ 85% after ≤ 15 minutes), but well within the
specification at time of testing, and would likely comply with stage 2 with the tighter
specification, for example be considered comparable without the calculation of an f2 value.
Due to the fact that the dissolution of the final drug product has been tightened and specified
with Q = 85% after 15 minutes, the viscosity of the excipient Xanthan gum does not need to
be specified.

0.3 % for oral suspension (#022990878, amended)

Question:
Question 3:
3.2.P.2.2.1 – Robustness test (initial Q8): In the absence of measured data: viscosity
measurement over time, thixotropic behaviour (e.g. yield point determination) of the
suspension, the determination of a deflocculated or flocculated system of the suspension,
please provide ten (10) drug product bottles as samples, the proposed measuring device and
Liquid Dose Dispenser (LDD) along with the most up to date instructions for use to
Swissmedic in order to enable evaluation of the initial suspendability, the re-suspendability,
the sedimentation of the suspension and the usability of the syringes.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 3 (P.2.2.10 (Homogeneity, LDD and Sediment) &
STED.7.3.02):
It is appreciated that Swissmedic wants to familiarize themselves with the Adempas pediatric
kit. Ten (10) samples of drug product in bottles, and four (4) kits labelled as placebo with
empty bottles together with the proposed measuring device, Liquid Dosing Devices (LDD),
along with the initial instructions for use (IFU) booklet have been shipped to your laboratory
facilities. The IFU included in the kits is only a sample to demonstrate the appearance of the
complete kit, but it should not be followed. Instead, the submitted IFU, which has also been
added to the kits (4 copies) shall be used.
Due to the absence of measured data on viscosity over time, thixotropic behaviour (such as
yield point determination), and the classification of the suspension as either deflocculated or
flocculated, the applicant provides the following justification:
To ensure optimal availability of the drug product for patients, it is essential to prepare a
homogeneous suspension. The procedures for achieving this taking into account potential user
errors are detailed in several test reports. These include evaluations of shaking time (see
P.2.2.10 Homogeneity) and assessments of oral syringe performance when used with the
suspension at the end of its in-use period (see P.2.2.10 LDD)
Regarding the usability of the medical devices and the re-suspension process – including
visibility of clumps or sediments in the suspension, these were assessed during usability
studies which were executed under simulated use conditions. (Reference is made to the report
of the Human Factor test STED.7.3.02 and the “Guideline on quality documentation for
medicinal products when used with a medical device”
EMA/CHMP/QWP/BWP/259165/2019).
The applicant also would like to share with the agency that during the Day 180 review by
EMA, formation of sediment (cake) was observed by the Health Authority (HA) during the
preparation of the suspension. An additional sedimentation test was conducted by the
applicant (see P.2.2.10 Sediment) to develop user handling instructions in the event of cake
formation. As a result, the IFU have been updated.
The applicant has proposed the following adaptations to the Package Leaflet (PL) and the
IFU, which have already been approved by the Committee for Medicinal Products for Human
Use (CHMP). Consequently, it is now at the discretion of Swissmedic to accept or reject the
proposed changes outlined below:
a) Adding pictogram to text in the IFU
To further mitigate the risk of cake formation, the applicant suggests introducing a
pictogram showing the activity which corresponds to the text in the IFU “Gently tap
the bottle on your hand”.

b) Adding information to the IFU showing how to remove clumps or sediment (cake).
The applicant proposes to adapt section “Preparing the oral suspension” of the IFU as
shown below, to provide guidance on what the caretaker/user should do when clumps
or sediment are noticed. The proposed revision is outlined below.

c) Include Contact Information in the IFU for Clarification of questions regarding
Preparation and Usage of Adempas Oral Suspension.
It is suggested to add information at the beginning of the IFU regarding whom to contact
if a caregiver or patient has any questions about the preparation or use of Adempas oral
suspension. The proposed revision is outlined below.

d) Adding information to the PL.
In addition to the revisions to the IFU, the applicant proposes enhancement of the PL by
including additional information on how to address potential issues that may arise during the
preparation of the suspension. See the highlighted text in red shown below:
“Before you use
-
Make sure the correct dose is written on the carton. If not, ask your pharmacist or doctor
to provide it. Keep the carton until the granules for oral suspension are used up.
-
Follow the “Instructions for Use” included in the carton on how to prepare and use
Adempas oral suspension carefully to avoid handling problems e.g., clumps or
sediments in the suspension “.
In addition, in case of any product technical complaints (PTC) e.g. sediment (cake) formation,
patients have the possibility to report these to the Representative of Marketing Authorization
Holder via contact information provided in the PL. There is a standard system in place to
monitor all PTCs / medication errors on a regular basis. The established procedure covers
handling, processing and reporting of PTC and PTC associated with adverse events.

Question 5:
3.2.P.3.5 - Design space verification (initial Q22): The hybrid approach is acknowledged.
However, in accordance with section 5.4 of EMA/CHMP/CVMP/QWP/BWP/70278/2012-
Rev1, please submit the continuous process verification protocol.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 5:
The applicant acknowledges the HA request. For the validation of the manufacturing process
a hybrid approach according to section 5.3 of EMA “Guideline on process validation for
finished products” (EMA/CHMP/CVMP/QWP/BWP/70278/2012-Rev1) was used. The
granulation DoE in lab scale was used to gain general process knowledge and to select
process parameters for commercial scale. The design space for the granulation process was
then developed with the help of DoE runs on a commercial scale.
A continuous process verification is currently not planned. The routine production will only
take place in the validated ranges. If the operating ranges will be enlarged or moved within
the design space, respective changes will be validated.
We apologize for the misunderstanding regarding the wording continuous vs. continued
(ongoing) process verification.
Before starting commercial production, a protocol for the ongoing (continued) process
verification will be compiled. The CPPs and CQAs will be evaluated risk based. In routine
production the ongoing (continued) process verification will be conducted to monitor the
product quality and process performance. This ensures that a state of control is maintained
throughout the commercial manufacture of the product lifecycle.

Question 7:
3.2.P.8.3 (and 3.2.P.5.3) – Stress tests -mass balance (initial Q47):
While peak purity is confirmed for thermal conditions (3.2.P.8.3.11-01) and for other stressed
conditions 3.2.P.8.3.04-02), no mass balance calculation is presented discussing the decrease
in assay under all stressed conditions (thermal, oxidative, acid, alkaline) in relation to the
increase in degradation products in module 3.2.P.8.3 – Stress tests.
Table 19 of the response to Q47 presents the mass balance calculation under various stress
conditions. Significance difference in assay loss (17.2% for temperature, 7.4% for humidity,
14.0% for alkaline hydrolysis and 29.4% for oxidative degradation) is indicated as being
possible due to the use of two wavelengths (260 nm and 342 nm). The degradation products
are not accounted for, with respect to the loss in assay. This leads to the conclusion that the
current method is not stability indicating and therefore not considered suitable. The method
should be updated / re-developed and validated as necessary. Please updated 3.2.P.8.3 – Stress
tests accordingly to include the mass balance calculation, an explanation for any difference
observed between the loss in assay and the degradation products (as reported in the response
document) along with the updated analytical method (3.2.P.5.3) demonstrating the stability
indicating capabilities of the chosen method.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 7 ( S.1.3.01, P.5.1.01, P.5.1.02, P.5.2.01, P.5.3.01 & P.8.3.04):
a)
Chosen wavelengths
To ensure correct quantitation of all components, different wavelengths were selected.
Besides the assay of riociguat and its degradation products, the assay for sodium benzoate
must be determined, as it is used as a preservative in the formulation.
As shown in Figure 1 below, the UV spectrum of riociguat presents the most prominent
absorption maxima at 210, 260 and 326 nm.
The determination of riociguat and sodium benzoate is carried out at a wavelength of 260 nm,
guaranteeing baseline separation between the two peaks. Since this wavelength is not an
absorption maximum of sodium benzoate, this procedure allows for parallel quantitation of
both components despite the approximately 12-fold higher concentration of sodium benzoate
in the formulation.
For the determination of degradation products of riociguat, a wavelength of 324 nm was
selected. This wavelength is a good compromise between the absorption maxima of known
riociguat impurities and degradation products as exemplified by the spectra of
Methoxycarbonyltrisamine, Dihydropurinone, Methyldihydropurinone, Mono-methyl
compound, Isopropyl carbamate and 4-Amino-6-hydroxy riociguat. At the same time, sodium
benzoate shows only negligible UV absorption at 324 nm, thus allowing for sufficiently
sensitive and reproducible detection and quantitation of the relevant riociguat degradation
products.
Both quantitation of riociguat and its degradation products are performed using a riociguat
reference standard only, since the main component is generally considered a suitable
surrogate for the quantitation of its unknown degradation products. As documented in
3.2.P.5.3.01, relative response factors (RRF) have been determined for all degradation
products, which are relevant for product stability under accelerated conditions (40 °C / 75%
RH) and stable enough for isolation, namely Dihydropurinone and 4-Amino-6-hydroxy-
riociguat. For discussion of the influence of these RRFs on quantitation, please refer to the
section “Evaluation of mass balances”.

Source:  P.5.3.01-02 Validation of Test for Assay and Impurities / Riociguat granules
0.3%for oral suspension (#022974277; amended)

b) Evaluation of mass balances
The applicant acknowledges the absence of plausible mass balances in the presented stress
study data set. The gap between the loss in Assay and Sum of all Degradation Products is
found to be as high as 15%, apparently suggesting that the HPLC method for Assay and
Degradation Products is not qualified for detecting and / or quantitating all potential API
degradation products.
However, the following points need to be taken into consideration.

Study design and sample appearance
The data presented in section P.8.3.04 (Stress test stability data for drug product) were
obtained applying generic stress conditions with the primary goal of evaluating the impact on
drug product quality, which may not only be compromised by the formation of degradation
products but also through changes in physico-chemical properties. Consequently, the
experimental setup was not designed to necessarily prove the analytical capabilities, i.e.
stability-indicating properties of the HPLC-UV method for Assay and Degradation Products.
Indeed, certain stress conditions resulted in obvious changes in granule properties that
rendered the samples unfit for HPLC analysis. Please find a more detailed discussion of the
applied stress conditions and their impact on the drug product properties below.
Sample preparation
Samples of granules subjected to alkaline, acidic and oxidative stress were prepared in
solvents similar to the solvent described in P.5.2.01 (Water pH 1.6 / Acetonitrile 4+1), but
substituting water pH 1.6 with 0.1 N NaOH, 0.1 N HCl or 3% H2O2, respectively. The
consequences of this approach are discussed in the following sections on the individual stress
conditions.
I.1. Evaluation of thermal stress
Thermal stress at 60°C for 6 months results in a loss of approximately 14% in riociguat assay.
This strong decrease in assay values is likely related to the formation of sticky and discolored
lumps, which could not be dissolved by using the sample preparation according to the test
procedure. Such a change in sample appearance from free-flowing white granules to brownish
agglomerates clearly indicates the formation of polymeric degradation products of higher
molecular mass. The potential formation of polymeric degradation products was also found to
be a plausible degradation pathway based on theoretical calculations. Due to their limited
solubility, discrimination in the course of filtration and / or strong adherence to reversed-
phase HPLC column materials, such compounds usually evade HPLC detection, contributing
to an implausible mass balance. The document P.8.3.04 was revised in order to more clearly
describe the consequences of the change in sample appearance on the mass balance obtained
by HPLC.
In a realistic setting, sample material of obvious discoloration and aggregation would not be
subjected to HPLC analysis, but already rejected due to its violation of the specification for
product appearance (P.5.1.01 and P.5.1.02: Formulation, Color (visual), Color of suspension
(visual)). Concludingly, batches not discriminated by the HPLC analysis are still safely
recognized as not complying to the P.5.1 specification.

Source:  P.5.1.01-06 Release Specification / Riociguat granules 0.3% for oral
suspension (#022974253; amended)
P.5.1.02-06 Shelf Life Specification / Riociguat granules 0.3% for oral
suspension (#0022974254; amended)
P.8.3.04-03 Stability Data - Stress Tests / Riociguat granules 0.3% for oral
suspension (#022974495; amended)

I.2. Evaluation of alkaline stress
For alkaline stress conditions, an unstressed sample was listed in the respective P.8.3.04,
reflecting an assay value of 100%. At the same time, the prepared alkaline stress sample was
analyzed at the beginning of the experiment testing at a significantly lower assay value of
87.7%. This lower assay value does not reflect a degradation in riociguat but rather the
known, considerably lower solubility of riociguat in basic media (please also refer to
S.1.3.01-01 General Information – General Properties / Riociguat micronized substance).
In order to correctly judge the mass balance under basic stress conditions, the results obtained
after 3 days of stress need to be compared to the initial value of 87.7 %, which reflect an
identical composition of sample solution. After 3 days, the loss in assay is approximately 1%
(87.7% vs. 86.8%) which complements the detected sum of degradation products of 1.1%.
Concludingly, NaOH leads to moderate degradation of riociguat while a gap in mass balance
could not be observed. The document P.8.3.04 was revised in order to provide an
unambiguous explanation of the obtained data.

Source:  S.1.3.01-01 General Information - General Properties/ Riociguat micronized
drug substance (#006607609; unchanged)
P.8.3.04-03 Stability Data - Stress Tests / Riociguat granules 0.3% for oral
suspension (#022974495; amended)

II.
Influence of unknown relative response factors
Evaluation of Oxidative Stress:
Oxidative stress applied through H2O2-containing solutions results in considerable
degradation of riociguat in the granules. All peaks resulting from the respective degradation
products are well separated from riociguat. As previously demonstrated, the purity plot of the
riociguat peak confirms the absence of co-eluting components. This holds true for riociguat
both in the reference standard as well as the stressed sample. Following 7 days of stress
application by H2O2, degradation of riociguat to an extent of approximately 28 % is observed
as judged by the loss in assay. However, the sum of all observed degradation products
amounts to 18.9 % only, among which the compound at RRT=0.77 accounts for approx. 17 %.
In total, there is a difference between loss in assay and sum of degradation products of 10 %.
A potential root cause for this gap is found in absorption coefficients which might differ
between the drug substance riociguat and its unknown degradation products. While it is
common practice to quantitate unknown degradation products using the main component as
surrogate and applying a relative response factor (RRF) of 1.0, it is acknowledged that this
procedure might not be optimal in this specific case. As documented in 3.2.P.5.3, RRFs have
been determined for two of the specified degradation products relevant for product stability
(40 °C / 75 % RH), namely Dihydropurinone and 4-Amino-6-hydroxy-riociguat. Considering
the obtained RRFs for these degradation products, it is found that they are considerably higher
than the default value of 1.0 (RRF=1.4 for Dihydropurinone and RRF=1.5 for 4-Amino-6-
hydroxy-riociguat).
Based on these limited data, it could be concluded that an RRF of 1.5 is more representative
of the majority of observed degradation products of riociguat. In order to validate this
hypothesis, the obtained oxidative stress data was re-evaluated with respect to surrogate
quantitation of unknown degradation products. The general application of an RRF=1.5 for all
such degradation products increases the sum of all degradation products from 18.9 % to 28.3
%, thus effectively closing the observed gap in mass balance (remaining difference: approx.
1 %).

Conclusion
▪ The validated setup of the analytical method, including the chosen wavelengths, was
proven to allow for the accurate and reproducible quantitation of the main components
(riociguat and sodium benzoate), as well as two known degradation products of
riociguat based on validated RRFs.
▪ The peak purity of riociguat in all reference standards and relevant samples of the
stress study was shown to meet the acceptance criteria across the wavelength range of
200 – 400 nm, confirming sufficient selectivity of the analytical method, even in the
presence of a multitude of degradation products.
▪ Owing to the setup of the presented stress study focusing on drug product stability,
certain stress conditions were found to induce changes in the drug product which are
not compatible with HPLC analysis. These stress conditions, namely thermal and
alkaline stress, either led to visible chemical degradation (discoloration) or inhibited
full dissolution of the sample material. Considering the generally lowered solubility in
alkaline media and comparing the stress test results to the correct reference, it is found
that mass balance is obtained under all conditions relating to changes in pH value
(acidic and alkaline media).
▪ The results of the oxidative stress study suggest that RRFs higher than 1.0 may be
applicable not only to known degradation products (Dihydropurinone and 4-Amino-6-
hydroxy-riociguat), but also to further unknown degradation products.
Considering the above listed findings, the applicant is convinced that the presented stress
study does not question the stability-indicating properties of the analytical method. However,
it is acknowledged that the chosen experimental setup did not allow for the evaluation of the
HPLC analytical performance under all relevant stress conditions.
The general application of an RRF = 1.5 for all unknown degradation products effectively
closes the observed gap in mass balance. In order to resolve an identical objection regarding
the stability-indicating properties of the analytical method raised by EMA before, the
applicant has amended the P.5.2.01 to incorporate the revised procedure of quantitation.

Source:  P.8.3.04-03 Stability Data - Stress Tests / Riociguat granules 0.3% for oral
suspension (#022974495; amended)
P.5.2.01-05 Test Procedure / Riociguat granules 0.3 % for oral suspension
(#022974261; amended)

Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 12 (3.2.P.2.2):
The comparison study presented in P.2.2.02-IQMS-256250_1.0 (P.2.2.02_022983259_01) 
provided in variation documentation follows the ICH guideline M9, as applicable to the 
product in question. Bayer considers ICH M9 to be equivalent to the relevant sections of 
Decision No. 85 of the EEC council.
12.1 – number of batches
The process validation at the newly introduced production site Delpharm Milano S.r.l., Italy 
included 3 batches per dose strength, as explained in section 3.2 of the above-mentioned 
P.2.2.02_1.0. The same number of comparison batches were selected from the current site 
Bayer AG, Kaiser-Wilhelm-Allee, Leverkusen, Germany. This approach means that the 
complete set of process validation batches from Delpharm Milano S.r.l., Italy is assessed for 
comparability between the two sites, using sufficient batches from the Bayer AG, Kaiser-
Wilhelm-Allee, Leverkusen, Germany site. This study design exceeds the EEC requirements
of comparing only 2 of the validation batches against a single batch from the Bayer AG, 
Kaiser-Wilhelm-Allee, Leverkusen, Germany site.

12.2 – values for coefficient of variation (RSD, %) at the 5th and 10th minute in dissolution 
media at pH 1.2 and pH 4.5.
It is explained in section 3.3 of the document that “ICH M9 states that not more than one 
mean value of ≥ 85% is included in an f2 test. To ensure that two data points at < 85% mean 
dissolution are available, t = 5 min is included for the QC medium alone. This measure is not 
required or meaningful for the other test conditions and has been determined for information 
only.”
In other words, dissolution results at t = 5 min at pH 1.2 were collected but for information 
only. Since the t = 5 min data points are part of the raw data of this study, they were presented 
in the above-mentioned P.2.2.02_1.0 of the sake of completeness only.
Each single profile overlay (e.g. Fig 5-1) shows a table (e.g. Table 5-1) in which the data 
points are stated that were used in the f2 test of the profiles shown in the overlay. None of the 
comparisons at pH 1.2 use the t = 5 min data point. The RSD values > 20% at this data point 
are therefore not relevant for the data analysis and the purpose of the study. Likewise, none of 
the comparisons at pH 4.5 use the t = 5 min data point.
A few t = 10 min data points show RSD values > 10%, while a single t = 15 min time point 
shows an RSD value > 15%. In all cases, all time points with a mean dissolution < 85% were 
included in the respective f2 tests, since it offers the most stringent case for the purpose of the 
test, as explained below.
Excluding the t = 5 min data point, as explained above, the largest difference in mean 
dissolution, in any medium, between any set of profiles of LEV and DEL batches is observed 
between 10 and 20 min. All profiles, in all media, show highly similar results once the mean 
dissolution exceeds 85%. The f2 test reflects the difference in mean dissolution between two 
profiles, as shown in section 3.3 of the above mentioned P.2.2.02_1.0. Therefore, selecting 
data points with lower mean differences automatically reduces the stringency of the f2 test. 
For that reason, the ICH M9 requires not more than one data points with a mean dissolution ≥ 
85% to be included in the f2 test, while two data points with a mean dissolution < 85% are 
included, if possible.
Both the ICH M9 and the EEC guideline (No. 85) set a limit for the RSD value per time point, 
because a high variability per unit (high RSD) is evened out in the mean result (n = 12). 
Therefore, high RSD values in the selected data points can reflect genuine differences 
between batches that are masked by the mean results. The limits for the RSD values (max 
20% up to t = 10 min and max 10% for t = 10 min and further) are general benchmarks to 
limit the impact of this effect on the comparison. In summary, the RSD limits serve to 
maximize the stringency of the f2 test.
In this study, the maximum stringency for the f2 test is achieved by including all data points 
at t = 10, 15 and 20 min or at t = 10, 15, 20 and 30 min, depending on the dissolution medium. 
As a result, the lowest (most stringent) f2 values are presented that can be obtained from the 
data presented. It was confirmed that using other (later) time points yield higher (less 
stringent) f2 values. Overall, varying the selected data points does not change the outcome of 
the study. It was thus decided to only present the most stringent approach in the above-
mentioned P.2.2.02_1.0.
12.3 – stirring speed
Section 3.3 of the above-mentioned P.2.2.02_1.0 contains the following statement:
Agitation: all profiles were collected with an agitation speed of 75 rpm, in accordance with 
the QC method (…).
Finerenone tablets are known to show coning in the dissolution vessel at 50 rpm, leading to 
higher tablet-to-tablet variability and lower discriminatory power. This effect at 50 rpm 
would introduce a laboratory artefact into the equivalence assessment of the two 
manufacturing sites. Using 75 rpm is therefore considered optimal for the purpose of this 
study.
A lower agitation speed typically increases the discriminatory power of the dissolution test. 
However, coning is a known effect at low speeds for immediate release drugs. Coning negates 
any potential benefit that a lower speeds may have regarding discriminatory power. ICH M9 
sets 50 rpm as the default speed. If an effect such as coning occurs however, the default is not 
suitable for the drug in question. This case applies to this study.

12.4 – less than 85% mean dissolution at pH 1.2 and 6.8
Only the 20 mg dose strength shows < 85% mean dissolution at t = 60 and t = 120 min in 
dissolution medium pH 6.8. All batches from the newly introduced production site Delpharm 
Milano S.r.l., Italy site and Bayer AG, Kaiser-Wilhelm-Allee, Leverkusen, Germany site 
show essentially the same behavior. In line with ICH M9, all data points were used in the f2 
tests. All pairwise comparisons shows f2 values > 50.
There is no specific reason not to use the f2 test for this condition. Furthermore, similarity of 
the profiles can be judged visually from the presented overlays of the profiles. The level of 
similarity is comparable to the other test conditions. Using other means of statistical 
comparison does not offer more informative value for this test condition.

12.5 - statistical software
The only quantitative analysis presented in the above-mentioned P.2.2.02_1.0 is the 
calculation of the f2 values. A validated Microsoft Excel sheet was used for this purpose.
The correctness of the f2 value of a given profile pair can be verified using the mean 
dissolution values at the given data points for each profile. All data (single as well as mean 
results) are presented in full in the above-mentioned P.2.2.02_1.0.
12.6 CDKT results
The study design and performance is described in detail in section 3 of the above-mentioned 
P.2.2.02_1.0. As stated in Tables 3-3 and 3-4, quantitation was done by HPLC, according to 
the registered P.5.2.02_IQMS-247514_3.0 (P.5.2.02_022974879_03) and P.5.2.02_IQMS-
247513_3.0 (P.5.2.02_022974878_03) test procedures. The latter documents contains 
representative chromatograms of the dissolution method.

12.7 quality certificates
The batches from Delpharm Milano S.r.L. are presented in the corresponding 
P.3.5.01_IQMS-252511_1.0 (P.3.5.01_022982751_01) and P.5.4.01_IQMS-252763_1.0 
(P.5.4.01_022982792_01) and P.5.4.01_IQMS-252764_1.0 (P.5.4.01_022982825_01) all 
provided in variation documentation.. The batches from Bayer AG, Kaiser-Wilhelm-Allee, 
Leverkusen, Germany were selected from commercial production, intended for global market 
supply. Relevant release test results for all batches are presented and evaluated in section 4.1 
of the above-mentioned P.2.2.02_1.0.

12.8 intervals between sample collections
The number and intervals between data points meet the ICH M9 requirements. Collecting 
additional data points will not yield any information that would affect the outcome of the 
study.

12.9 120 minutes sampling time
The profiles were only extended to 120 min for the 20 mg dose strength in dissolution 
medium pH 6.8. This option was foreseen in the study design, as explained in section 3.1 of 
the above-mentioned P.2.2.02_1.0.
Finerenone is a weak base (pK ca. 4.4), which means that its solubility decreases rapidly 
above pH 3. At pH 6.8 without surfactant, the maximum solubility is ca. 24 mg / 1000 mL at 
37 °C. The 20 mg dose is therefore not expected to fully dissolve within 60 min. To ensure 
that the dissolution profile is as close to a plateau as possible within technical constraints, the 
sampling time was extended to 120 min. A further extension, e.g. to t = 360 min, is not 
considered meaningful for the purpose of this study.

Question:
Question 1.1.1.1
Establish a validated requirement for the signal-to-noise ratio for the main peak on the
electropherogram of the monoclonal IgG solution to assess system sensitivity (reduced
conditions);
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1.1.1.1:
The Applicant proposes a system sensitivity criterion based on the IgG standard for reduced
conditions consistent with that previously proposed for non-reduced conditions. Monoclonal
IgG is the established system suitability standard for the method and supports the existing
criteria.

During method validation, the limit of quantitation (LOQ) of the aflibercept CE-SDS test
method was determined through the analysis of the signal/ noise (S/N) of the main peak of a
monoclonal IgG system suitability standard under non-reduced conditions. The monoclonal
IgG system suitability standard was chosen since the heavy chain peak of IgG standard has
better resolution than aflibercept sample under electrophoresis, which makes the S/N
evaluation more accurate. Also, the migration time of the main peak of IgG standard is similar
to the typical size variants observed for aflibercept. The LOQ is the lowest amount of analyte
in a sample that can be determined with acceptable precision and accuracy under the stated
experimental conditions.

In answer to the response by the Expert Institution, the Applicant proposes to add a sensitivity
standard and system suitability criterion based on the similarity in response of the IgG
standard under reduced and non-reduced conditions, and the validated LOQ for the diluted
monoclonal IgG standard under non-reduced CE-SDS conditions.

This sensitivity standard solution should be prepared from the monoclonal IgG standard at a
concentration of 0.01 mg/ml and analyzed under reducing conditions.

Therefore, the following system suitability criterion and preparation of solutions are proposed
and added to the normative document.:
-
The signal-to-noise ratio calculated for the main peak of the Monoclonal IgG solution
for system sensitivity assessment electropherogram under reducing conditions should
be not less than 10.**
Preparation of solutions:

Monoclonal IgG stock solution for system sensitivity assessment (0.05 mg/mL) (to be used in
preparation of reduced and non-reduced Monoclonal IgG solutions for system sensitivity
assessment):

Add 40 µL of monoclonal IgG SST stock solution (2.5 mg/mL) to 1960 µL of MiliQ-water
and mix thoroughly.
Use the solution freshly prepared.

Reduced monoclonal IgG solution for system sensitivity assessment (0.01 mg/mL):

In a separate tube, make a single preparation by combining 40 µL of the Monoclonal IgG
stock solution for system sensitivity assessment (0.05 mg/mL) with 160 μL of Dilution Buffer
(Reducing) for a final concentration of 0.01 mg/mL.

Record all dilutions.

Source: Normative Document (VV-REGQUAL-065844, amended)

Answer:

The operation “visual inspection” is formally classified as a manufacturing step and is applied 
to 100% of all filled prefilled syringes. Within the available options for manufacturing 
activities/role, it is categorized under “manufacturer of dosage form”.
Nonetheless, Bayer would like to point out that the purpose of this “manufacturing step” is 
not any kind of manipulation of the intermediate drug product, but only a visual check of 
every single prefilled syringes to ensure that any prefilled syringes with visible defects are 
rejected. In this respect it is similar to quality control testing which collects information about 
the product without altering it.

reduced time out of refrigeration (TOR), rapid processing is needed for biological product.

for intravitreal injection in pre-filled syringe 40mg/ml, and we urge that this could be 
maintained.

Question:
Question 1
(i) Please clarify how the data for real-time storage conditions in Table 4-1 to 4-4 can support 
the in-use stability. Should provide cycling studies/stress tests.
(ii) Please clarify how the TOR was determined.
(iii) Please clarify how to determine 24 hours despite the TOR proposed.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (3.2.P.8.3):
The applicant would like to highlight that the proposed allowable storage of the unopened 
blister outside of the refrigerator for up to 24 hours does not present an in-use scenario of the 
drug product. The drug product remains within its protective packaging and is not exposed to 
the environment as would be the case for multi-dose products or products that require 
constitution/dilution for which actual in-use stability studies are conducted. Resultantly, the 
storage of the unopened blister is rather similar to a short-term temperature excursion from 
the long-term storage conditions and is therefore also investigated with respective real-time 
data after maximal exposure to 25°C.
To define the maximum exposure of the drug product to up to 25°C an end-to-end Time Out 
of Refrigeration (TOR) concept for Aflibercept 114.3 mg/mL in prefilled syringe (PFS) was 
established. This concept covers all TOR occurring throughout the lifecycle of a batch of 
Aflibercept 114.3 mg/mL in PFS from the start of manufacture, over distribution until 
handling by healthcare professionals (HCP). The maximum total TOR defined for Aflibercept 
solution 114.3 mg/mL in PFS was defined as 226.5 h, respectively 237.5 h for the extended 
sterilization batch (see CTD section (P.8.3.11-03).
Table 1 provides further details of the allocation of maximum allowable TOR for each step, 
along with the criteria applied to define the TOR for each stage. As indicated in the table, the 
TOR concept reserves 24 hours for handling by HCP. This forms the basis for the label claim: 
“Prior to usage, the unopened blister may be stored outside the refrigerator below 25 °C for 
up to 24 hours.”. 24 hours for HCP handling were defined based on requirements from several 
global markets and as established for the approved Aflibercept 40 mg/mL strength and the 
Aflibercept 114.3 mg/mL vial presentation.
The real-time storage data presented in Tables 4-1 to 4-4 of CTD section P.8.3.11-03 were 
sourced from Process Performance Qualification (PPQ) batches that were cycled at 25 °C and 
exceeding the defined maximum end-to-end TOR shown in Table 1. Consequently, the 
applicant has provided data demonstrating the stability of the product after being exposed to 
the maximum end-to-end TOR. Up to date, 18 months real-time stability data are available. 
The data are projected to meet the shelf-life specification limits after 24 months of storage.

Question: Please confirm that you are claiming Design Space for the granulation spray rate, product temperature and moisture factor, and film coating spray rate and outlet air temperature process parameters, and clarify whether the QbD processes applied during pharmaceutical development and the resulting Design Space fully meet the requirements defined in ICH Q8(R2) Pharmaceutical Development and ICH Q10: Pharmaceutical Quality System.
Answer:
We confirm that we are claiming Design Spaces for the process parameters spray rate and product temperature in granulation and spray rate and inlet air temperature in film-coating.
Multivariate process understanding was generated for the respective unit operations in accordance with ICH Q8(R2) using statistically designed experiments. Initially, a quality target product profile (QTPP) was generated from which the critical quality attributes (CQAs) were derived.
Subsequently, a comprehensive initial risk assessment was conducted to identify process parameters that might have an impact on the CQAs (please refer to the technical registration document P.2.3.01_022988084_02). The identified process parameters were then investigated at laboratory scale. Fractional factorial designs (26−1 and 25−1 with respectively 4 center points) were conducted, both allowing for estimation of all two-factor interactions. Based on these prior investigations, which showed no relevant impact of interaction effects on the CQAs, the risk assessment was updated accordingly and the commercial-scale design was deliberately optimized for models including main effects only.
Specifically, for granulation and tableting a D-optimal design comprising 7 runs was performed.
For the film-coating step, a full factorial 22design was carried out, supplemented by two center points and an additional run at increased spray rate. This experimental setup supported the development of multivariate process understanding for the film-coating step.
The distance of the CQAs from their acceptance criteria was quantified using the process capability index (Cpk). For all CQAs, the Cpk was greater than 1.8, which corresponds to more than 5 standard deviations.
We therefore confirm the claim of a Design Space for the process parameters spray rate and product temperature in granulation and spray rate and outlet air tempereture in film-coating.
Furthermore, in line with the recommendation of ICH Q8(R2) section 2.4.4 Relationship of Design Space to Scale and Equipment, we claim a scale-independent Design Space for the moisture factor in the granulation step which was calculated based on the process parameters product temperature and spray rate. The identified Design Spaces were included into the control strategy (please refer to the technical registration document P.2.3.01_022988084_02).
The applied Quality by Design approach and the resulting Design Spaces are managed within our pharmaceutical quality system in accordance with ICH Q10. This includes integration of process knowledge, lifecycle-based control strategies, and appropriate systems for change management and continued process verification.

Question:
Please provide a forced degradation study for the assay and degradation products method used for the drug product that considers the overall mass balance. Ideally samples should be stored under stress conditions (e.g., light, heat, humidity, acid/base hydrolysis and oxidation) to give a 5 to 15% drop in assay compared to the untreated sample.
Each stressed sample should be analysed for assay and degradation products and the quantitative results for the individual and total related substances should be reported. Any lack of mass balance (<95%) should be justified.
Mass balance calculation in its simplest form i.e. Assay + Total impurities should be calculated for each stressed condition, OR preferably using the following equation  (Assay(post-stress) + Impurities(post stress) )/ (Assay(pre-stress) + Impurities(pre-stress)) x 100 = Mass balance (%)
Answer:
Although forced degradation studies are not explicitly required with regard to ICH guidelines, ICH Q1A (R2) recommends stress testing to help identifying likely degradation products which can in turn help establish the intrinsic stability of the molecule and validate the stability indicating power of the analytical procedures used. As thermal and hydrolytic stress conditions, as well as photolytic stability revealed a high stability of Finerenone (P.8.3.04_022987142_01 and P.8.3.05_022987143_01), i.e. only minor degradation was observed, additional chemical stress conditions were applied.
Samples of Finerenone micronized drug substance and Finerenone coated tablet 40 mg were subjected to extended stress tests (thermal, hydrolytic, photolytic and chemical) as summarized in Table 1 in order to investigate the formation of potential degradation products and to demonstrate the assay and degradation products method is selective and accurate regarding potential degradation products.

The mass balance has been calculated as well (see Table 2 and Table 3) according to the recommended equation:
(Assay (post-stress) + Impurities (post stress))/ (Assay (pre-stress) + Impurities (pre-stress)) x 100 = Mass balance (%)
The additional chemical stress test conditions are well suited to obtain assay drop in the range from 5 to 15% and no lack of mass balance (< 95%) was observed, neither for the Finerenone micronized drug substance nor for Finerenone coated tablets 40 mg.
Thus, the methods were shown to be stability indicating and are suitable for determination of assay and degradation products.

Ensure the revised frequency matches those found in the proposed commercial Manufacturing Product Documents (MPD).
Answer:
In-process testing is performed at the beginning, middle, and end of the batch process, to confirm that the process meets the specification.
As outlined in the document “Finerenone coated tablet 40 mg - Process Controls” (previously P.3.3.02_022983913_01, now P.3.3.01_IQMS-398583_1.0), the following in-process controls (IPCs) are measured during batch processing:
• Loss on drying
• Uniformity of mass
• Breaking load
• Disintegration
• Friability
The results from the process validation (see P.3.5.01_022988781_01) indicated that all IPCs were well within the acceptance criteria. Additionally, further tests including blend uniformity of the ready-to-press mixture and content uniformity of the tablets were conducted during the process validation. For the determination of the content uniformity of the tablets, samples were withdrawn from 20 evenly distributed time points during the tablet compression. The results of these additional tests along with the results of quality control testing (see P.5.4.01_022987430_01) demonstrate that the manufacturing process is well under control and fulfils all predefined quality attributes. Therefore, the applicant deems the IPC frequency as sufficient.
The sampling frequency was accordingly included in the document “Finerenone coated tablet 40 mg - Process Controls” (see Table 4 and Table 5 below as well as adapted P.3.3.01_IQMS-398583_1.0). Accordingly, Section 2.3.P.3.3 of the CPID has been updated with the additional information. See Module 1.3.6 Annotated CPID.

Question: Based on your executed Manufacturing Product Documents and the batch data provided in your process validation report, you are requested to remove the specifications of ‘Mean tablet weight ± 15 % (100 %) for the in-process ‘Uniformity of mass’ test. Therefore, the uniformity of mass should be 200 mg ± 7.5 % only.
Answer:
The consistency of the manufacturing process is, among other items, controlled by a regular determination of the tablet weight throughout the whole tableting process. The limit for this IPC test is set in accordance with Ph. Eur. 2.9.5 uniformity of mass +/- 7.5% (90% of the tablets) and +/- 15% (100% of the tablets). The applicant’s internal procedure ensures that not more than 2% (α = 0.05) of the whole batch size is outside the T1 limit (± 7.5%).
The appropriateness of this concept was proven during process validation (see P.3.5.01_022988781_01). All predefined IPCs, additional tests and CQAs fulfilled the acceptance criteria. Particularly, the content uniformity test of the uncoated tablets during the tableting showed narrowly distributed results and very low variability. Consequently, based on the results of the process validation, it was demonstrated that the manufacturing process is well under control with the current IPC methodology (also refer to the response above).
A footnote referring to the internal procedure was added to the document “Finerenone coated tablet 40 mg - Process Controls” (see adapted P.3.3.01_IQMS-398583_1.0).

Question:
Question 1
Difference between the Jivi and Kovaltry
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 ( CTD section):
Jivi and Kovaltry are both recombinant Factor VIII (rFVIII) therapies for the treatment of 
Hemophilia A. Kovaltry contains octocog alfa, a standard half-life recombinant Factor VIII. 
Jivi contains damoctocog alfa pegol, which is PEGylated (polyethylene glycol-modified) 
octocog alfa. This modification extends the half-life of the molecule in the bloodstream. In 
general, Damoctocog Alfa Pegol lyophilizate specifications are based on regulatory 
requirements (ICH-Q3B/Q6B, USP, Ph. Eur., JP), alignment with the Bayer rFVIII marketed 
products (Kogenate (Antihemophilic Factor (recombinant) Formulated with Sucrose (rFVIII-
FS)) and Kovaltry (BAY 81-8973)), historical range and/or statistical analysis of release and 
stability data where appropriate. Specifications based on statistical analysis were initially 
established using Phase 3 clinical and conformance batch results. Subsequently, specifications 
for select attributes (total protein, specific activity, and osmolality) were re-evaluated based 
on conformance and commercial batches, with adjustments to specification ranges when 
appropriate. Specific activity specifications are later adjusted to reflect an optimized method 
implemented for determination of rFVIII activity (potency). Refer to P.3.5.50 “Process 
Validation and/or Evaluation - Bulking/Filling – Media Fills, “Process Validation and/or 
Evaluation - Bulking/Filling” and P.3.5.60 “Process Validation and/or Evaluation - Freeze 
Drying” for the details of the validation studies.

Question:
Question 2
Source of active ingredient , name and address
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2 ( CTD section):
DNA clones encoding the complete human Factor VIII sequence were isolated by (a) 
chemical synthesis of a 36 nucleotide DNA probe corresponding to the known amino acid 
sequence of a tryptic fragment derived from purified human plasma Factor VIII, (b) screening 
a human lymphoblastoid cell line genomic DNA library, and (c) isolating cDNA clones from 
cellular messenger RNA shown to encode Factor VIII. Several of the cDNA clones and one 
genomic clone were assembled into a single transcription unit encoding the full-length Factor 
VIII protein, and the sequence of the coding region was confirmed. A detailed description of 
the cloning process as described in the source document has also been published (References 
1, 2, 3 in the source document). Standard molecular cloning techniques were utilized to 
generate a B-domain deleted (BDD) recombinant FVIII molecule from the above-described 
full length FVIII coding sequence. The BDD recombinant FVIII is a truncated factor VIII in 
which the majority of the B domain is deleted. The first four amino acids at the amino end of 
the B-domain (SFSQ) were fused to the last 10 amino acids at the carboxyl end of the B 
domain(NPPVLKRHQR) representing a native SQ junction. Essentially the BDD 
recombinant FVIII has the 90-kD and 80-kD chains linked by a SQ linker consisting of 14 
amino acids (SFSQNPPVLKRHQR). The cell line development medium used in the 
transfection and clone selection process contained Human Plasma Protein Solution (HPPS), 
cholesterol, recombinant insulin and was supplemented with Fetal Bovine Serum (FBS). Once 
the cell clone was selected, the cells were adapted into a serum-free and animal protein-free 
medium. All subsequent cell banking activities, including final accession cell bank, MCB and 
WCB, were performed using this serum-free and animal protein-free medium. 
Direct and indirect sources of materials of animal/human origin used during the 
manufacturing process are presented in further detail and evaluated for product risk in 
Module 3.2.A.2 
 
 
An individual vial from the Master Cell Bank (MCB) batch 2709NR8 was used for Working 
Cell Bank (WCB) production. One vial from the MCB was thawed on 2009-03-19 and 
expanded in cell bank medium prepared without materials derived of human or animal origin, 
as described in S.2.3.50 “Cell Banking System, Characterization, and Testing – Master Cell 
Bank”. Cell viability on thaw was 98%. Cells were then expanded through 7 passages over 
14 days to a volume of 12 L for WCB creation. The culture viability in all passages was 
between 90 and 99%. 
WCB cryopreservation was performed on 2009-04-02. The cell culture was centrifuged, and 
the cell pellet re-suspended in a smaller volume of fresh cell bank medium containing 7.5% 
dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) to obtain high cell density in the cell suspension for 
cryopreservation. The age of the WCB is calculated from this cryopreservation date. The 
average viable cell density of the cell suspension prior to cryopreservation was 20.5 x 106 
cells/mL with a cell viability of 97%. The target viable cell density in the cryopreserved vials 
was 20 x 106 cells/mL. 1 mL of the DMSO-containing culture was then dispensed into 2 mL 
cryovials. A total of 441 vials were created for the WCB (batch number 270CCRP). After 
the dispensing was complete, viable cell density and cell viability measurements were taken 
from the remaining cell suspension and the values were 22.2 x 106 cells/mL and 96%, 
respectively. The vials were then transferred to a 70°C freezer for 18 hours and were 
transferred afterwards to the vapor phase of the liquid nitrogen freezer.

All WCB preparation activities were conducted in a GMP area following the procedure 
summarized above and with suitable controls to avoid microbial contamination and cross 
contamination with other cell lines. The WCB was manufactured and stored in the clinical 
manufacturing facility on site (Bayer Berkeley) and transferred to the commercial 
manufacturing facility also on site (Bayer Berkeley) during launch activities. WCB vials 
used for conformance and initial launch lots originated from the clinical manufacturing 
facility. WCB vials are stored on site and in an off-site location at BioReliance, 9610 
Medical Center Drive, Rockville, MD, USA. 
The projected WCB vial consumption rate is approximately 10 vials per year. Based on this 
rate, the current inventory of the WCB will support more than 40 years of continuous 
production. Therefore, no plan or procedure for the routine qualification of new WCBs is 
included.
Source:  S.2.3.54_011684960_02 Source, History and Generation of Cell Substrate

products. (Antihemophilic Factor Recombinant Factor VIII)
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 3 (3.2.A):
BAY 81-8973 can be regarded as safe with respect to TSE according to the European guideline 
“Note for guidance on minimising the risk of transmitting animal spongiform encephalopathy 
agents via human and veterinary medicinal products” (EMEA/410/01, current version).
The starting materials used for the BAY 81-8973 drug product have been investigated to assess 
TSE risk as outlined in the “Note for guidance on minimising the risk of transmitting animal 
spongiform encephalopathy agents via human and veterinary medicinal products - 
EMEA/410/01 current version ” (hereafter referred to as Note for Guidance). Materials that fall 
in the scope of the Note for Guidance are provided in Table 1-1. The raw materials used for 
manufacturing of BAY 81-8973 are free from animal or human origin. However, some animal 
or human origin materials were used in the early stage of cell line development and cell banking 
(Table 1-1). The TSE risk from these materials is considered to be minimal as discussed below.
During cell line development, the host cell passaging, transfection, and clone selection were 
performed with culture media containing fetal bovine serum (FBS) from HyClone™ 
Laboratories. Adherent cells were passaged with Trypsin-EDTA solution from Life 
Technologies (formerly GIBCO, Invitrogen Coorporation). The master cell bank (MCB) and 
working cell bank (WCB) were grown in culture media containing recombinant human insulin 
(Eli Lilly No. ID4034 or Novo Nordisk No. 4502), human plasma protein solution (HPPS) and 
cholesterol (See S.2.3.53 “Control of Source and Starting Materials of Biological Origin - Cell 
bank”).

BAY 81-8973 drug product is manufactured using raw materials containing no ingredients of 
animal or human origin. The raw materials of animal or human origin used at early stage of cell 
line development and cell bank production had been treated so that the risk of TSE transmission 
was minimized. 
Demonstrated robust removal of hamster scrapie agent by the manufacturing process for 
preparing plasma derivatives suggests that transmission of CJD/vCJD infectivity from HPPS 
during the cell line development and banking is highly unlikely.

Question:
Question 3
Section 1.0.4 (Page 2)
As noted in the Stability Data (T.04.02-06), the dissolution parameters for some samples were 
85 or below for the batches BT10U31, BT10U81, & BT10UG1 (Acceptance criterion: Q = 
80%). Please clarify if S2 has been conducted for these samples.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 3 (CTD section P.8):
Please note that S1 and S2 have been conducted for 24 months timepoint for dissolution tests 
during stability studies for batch BT10U31. The results are documented in technical 
registration document T.04.02.

The test is performed according to the harmonized method of USP 711 and Ph.Eur. 2.9.3 for 
immediate-release dosage forms.
The USP (United States Pharmacopeia) dissolution acceptance criteria are based on the 
amount of drug substance dissolved from a dosage form within a specific time frame. These 
criteria typically involve three stages (S1, S2, S3) with increasing numbers of units 
tested. The acceptance criteria are expressed as a percentage of the labeled amount of drug 
substance, denoted as "Q". And Q is  80 %.
Three Stages: 
The USP dissolution test proceeds through three stages: 
S1: 6 units are tested. Acceptance criteria are usually Q+5% or greater.  
S2: If S1 is not met, 6 more units are tested. The average of the combined S1 and S2 results 
must meet Q or greater.  
S3: If S1 and S2 are not met, 6 more units are tested (total of 12). The average of the 
combined S1, S2, and S3 results must be Q or greater. 
Consequently Q=80% resolves in (S1) as 6 single units with a min. average of 85%

Please find below the dissolution data of batches BT10U31, BT10U81, & BT10UG1. As seen

Finerenone is a poorly soluble drug substance in aqueous solution. This is demonstrated in 
3.2.S.1.3.01_022285635_01 (Finerenone micronized drug substance – General information) 
and 3.2.P.5.3.21_022994232_02 (Finerenone coated tablet 40 mg – Method Development – 
Dissolution) documents.
In accordance with general requirements on dissolution testing, i.e. described in USP <1092>, 
dissolution conditions should consider the solubility of the drug substance and the addition of 
surfactant is allowed to improve solubility.
USP <1092> suggests that “when developing a dissolution procedure, one goal is to have sink 
conditions which are defined as having a volume of medium at least three times the volume 
required to form a saturated solution of drug substance…”. Maintaining sink conditions 
increases the likelihood that dissolution results will accurately reflect the properties of the 
dosage form. Sink conditions help in effectively distinguishing between acceptable and 
unacceptable batches. In accordance to USP<1092>, Bayer conducted several experiments on 
solubility and dissolution to justify the choice and concentration of Tween 20 for Finerenone 
40 mg coated tablets.

• 
Selection of the surfactant based on drug substance solubility data (sink 
conditions)
As recommended, Bayer tested the solubility of the drug substance Finerenone in a stepwise 
approach with increasing levels of surfactant in the dissolution medium (see Table 1, the same 
information is also provided in  Table 2-2 of 3.2.P.5.3.21_022994232_02). The test was 
performed using the qualitative same dissolution medium applied for the approved lower 
dosage strengths (Finerenone coated tablet 10 mg and 20 mg), i.e. acetate buffer pH 4.5 and 
Tween 20 (Polysorbate 20).
Sink conditions for 40 mg were only achieved in acetate buffer pH 4.5 with the addition of 
0.6% Tween 20. Using this level of surfactant in the dissolution medium, the solubility of the
drug substance is 113 mg/900 mL dissolution medium (corresponding to 125 mg/L, see Table 
1, the same information is also provided in Table 2-2 of 3.2.P.5.3.21_022994232_02). This 
concentration is even slightly below the recommended threefold sink conditions of 
120 mg/900 mL for the 40 mg dose strength.

A concentration of 0.1% Tween 20 appears to be sufficient to dissolve 40 mg Finerenone drug 
substance within the duration of the dissolution test. This is consistent with the solubility data 
given in Table 1, however sink conditions are not achieved at this surfactant concentration.
Further experiments with the same batch as above (batch number KM60385) were performed 
to investigate sink conditions during the dissolution test of the drug product Finerenone 
coated tablet 40 mg by testing dissolution of three tablets per vessel (900 mL in acetate buffer 
pH 4.5) with the addition of different concentrations of Tween 20 (see Figure 2). Three tablets 
were added per vessel because the dissolution medium should be able to dissolve at least 3 
times the amount of Finerenone drug substance. The complete dissolution data (individual, 
n=6, mean, COV) are reported in 3.2.P.5.3.21_022994232_02 section 4, Table 4-15 to Table 
4-20.

The dissolution profile of 3 tablets per vessel in the dissolution media with different Tween 
20 concentrations is presented in Figure 2.
Figure 2: Finerenone coated tablet 40 mg, batch no. KM60385, acetate buffer pH 4.5 
with different concentrations of Tween 20, 3 Tablets / 900 mL, 75 rpm, n=6

The solubility data presented in Table 1, which demonstrates that sink conditions are only 
reached with a Tween 20 concentration of 0.6% are confirmed with the dissolution 
experiment described above. More specifically, the dissolution profiles depicted in Figure 2 
clearly demonstrate that the use of 0.6% Tween 20 results in a plateau of approx. 92% drug 
substance dissolved. In addition, these results indicate that Tween 20 concentrations below 
0.6% are not sufficient to achieve an acceptable dissolution (at least 85%).
The data obtained from this experiment are in alignment with the data from the drug 
substance solubility test (see Table 1).
When sink conditions are met, the dissolution process is primarily controlled by the 
dissolution rate of the solid dosage form rather than by the solubility characteristics of the 
drug substance. This allows for a more reliable assessment of the drug product's release 
profile. Maintaining sink conditions is essential to achieve the level of consistency and 
reliability needed for robust methods, particularly for BCS Class II compounds such as 
Finerenone.

Based on the results presented above, a dissolution medium with 0.6% Tween 20 is proposed 
to avoid artificial, over discriminatory effects and ensures sink conditions are met.
According to USP <1092> “when the V/Vsat ratio is too large the dissolution test may not 
detect critical changes in the formulation and manufacturing process”. However, this is not 
the case for the surfactant concentration of 0.6% revealing the recommended V/Vsat ratio of 3.
In conclusion, Bayer believes that the selected dissolution medium acetate buffer pH 4.5 with 
addition of 0.6% Tween 20, provides acceptable sink conditions and has shown 
discriminatory power (see P.5.3.21_022994232_02 section 2.6) and robustness 
(P.5.3.21_022994232_02 section  3).

Question:
Question 1
In order to be able to assess the D-optimal design of the Design of Experiments (DoE) the
applicant is requested to provide the design matrix and verify the matrix orthogonality by quality
measures like condition number and/or G-efficiency.
Answer:
Applicant’s response:
To ensure both operational efficiency and statistical robustness, the number of experimental runs
was predefined at seven, reflecting the practical conditions of the commercial setting. This design
size was considered sufficient to support meaningful conclusions while maintaining feasibility.

Within this framework, the goal was to identify the most statistically efficient design possible,
based on established design evaluation criteria.
The design matrix, applied for the DoE study in commercial scale (granulation and tableting
process), is shown in Table 1 in coded coordinates.
