The selected experimental design includes two center points (DoE runs 1 and 3). This is in line with
standard recommendations in the design of experiments literature, as center points provide
valuable information about potential curvature in the response surface and contribute to a more
reliable estimation of the pure error. Including center points also supports model adequacy checks,
which are essential in the context of regulatory submissions.
All candidate designs were exhaustively evaluated, as the number of possible combinations for five
non-center point runs across three factors remains computationally manageable. The final design
was identified as optimal based on this comprehensive assessment, according to the following well-
established statistical criteria:
• 
D-efficiency (related to the precision of parameter estimation)
• 
G-efficiency (related to prediction accuracy over the design space)

The selected design achieved the best possible values across both criteria simultaneously—a
combination that underscores the high quality of the design. This result was verified using a
dedicated R script that systematically assessed all possible alternatives.
The D-efficiency is 74.4%, which is considered excellent, especially considering the inclusion of
two center points. While center points slightly reduce D-efficiency, their inclusion is important from
a modeling and validation perspective, and this trade-off has been well managed in the selected
design.
The G-efficiency is 62.6%, well above the commonly recommended minimum of 50% following
(Stat-Ease, 2019). This reflects uniformly high prediction accuracy across the entire experimental
region, which is particularly relevant for risk minimization.
Moreover, the design’s condition number is 1.64. This is a very low value, indicating near-
orthogonality of the design matrix. According to (Montgomery, 2012) and (Stat-Ease, 2019),
condition numbers below 100 are generally considered acceptable. A value as low as 1.64 provides
strong assurance of numerical robustness and absence of multicollinearity.

Taken together, these metrics show that the employed design is not only statistically optimal, but
also well suited to support robust, reliable, and regulatorily sound conclusions. It offers a balanced
compromise between model quality, prediction accuracy, and numerical stability.

Question:
Question 2
Figure 6-9 makes no sense since no validated model was obtained for the response coating defects
class 3 – the predicting ability is non-existent. If critical, a root cause analysis is recommended to
identify the reason for the defects. Are there any other unknown factors, material attributes of
coating solution or other process factors still not investigated?
Answer:
Applicant’s response:
In the context of the DoE performed in commercial scale for the coating process, the applicant
would like to highlight that all critical quality attributes (appearance, assay, drug dissolution after
15 min and 30 min, respectively) that may be influenced by the coating process were well within
the specified range while exhibiting a low variability under all investigated process parameters.
Consequently, the entire range of the process parameters spray rate and outlet air temperature
was shown to be suitable to fulfill the critical quality attributes.
On top of that, additional tests for E, surface roughness and coating defects (AQL testing) were
performed to gain further knowledge. The coating defects identified by the AQL testing within the
DoE batches do not impact the overall performance, patient safety or efficacy. This test serves as
an internal quality standard. The limits of the AQL testing are based on what the applicant
considers acceptable, for example in terms of minor defects (e.g. sticking or picking). Once the
internal limit is exceeded, the coated tablets undergo a sorting where the coated tablets exhibiting
certain defects will be separated and discarded.

While the predictive R-2 of the defect class 3 model is moderate at 19%, both main effects are
statistically significant, and the adjusted R-2 reaches a strong 82%. This suggests that, despite
limited predictive power, the model captures a meaningful portion of the systematic variation in the
data and provides valuable insights into the underlying factor relationships.
The originally submitted Figure 6-9 of the technical registration document P.2.3.01_022988084_02
has been replaced by the more informative Figure 1 (in the response document, updated Figure 6-
10 of P.2.3.01_IQMS-265199_3.0). While the previous Figure 6-9 visualized the model using
contour lines, the new Figure 6-10 presents the defect class 3 counts for each of the 7 runs. For
clarity, it highlights only the critical contour line corresponding to the threshold of 61 defect counts.
In addition, the explanatory text to Figure 6-10 as well as some typos and wording of section 6.4
“Design of Experiments (DoE) at Commercial Scale - Coating Process” have been revised to
improve the overall comprehensibility.
The findings described are supported by galenic subject matter expertise, which strengthens the
plausibility of the above findings. For instance, (Toshev, 2023) describe in their paper
“Optimization study of aqueous film-coating process in the industrial scale using design of
experiments” that “the spray rate had the highest influence on all responses” amongst others
coating defects. This is also confirmed by (Pandey, Bindra, & Felton, 2014) in their study “Influence
of process parameters on tablet bed microenvironmental factors during pan coating” where it is
stated that “The spray rate is one of the most important coating process parameters. At one
extreme, a high spray rate may cause coating defects such as twinning, picking and sticking, and
logo bridging…”. As a third example the paper from (Yoshino, et al., 2018) “A Scale-up Approach
for Film Coating Process Based on Surface Roughness as the Critical Quality Attribute” can be
mentioned, clearly recognizing that “two process parameters, the inlet air temperature and the
spray rate, significantly affect the surface roughness” and with that the appearance of the tablets.
In accordance with the galenic subject matter expertise, both experiments revealing defect rates
above the upper AQL limit of 61 occurred at high spray rates and low to moderate outlet air
temperatures and the claimed design space illustrated by the blue square in Figure 1 is placed with
a huge safety margin of 100 kg/min in spray rate direction to those experiments which resulted in
defects of 72 and 119 (experimental DoE runs 1 and 6).
In conclusion, it is important to emphasize that, despite the moderate predictive capability of the
model, the applicant considers it acceptable to restrict the design spaces as outlined. This
restriction is solely driven by responses that are not classified as critical quality attributes (CQA)
but enables a more targeted and effective optimization of the coating process. Comprehensive data
analysis, combined with insights from relevant scientific literature, supports the soundness of the
chosen process parameter ranges, ensuring that the overall quality of the coated tablets is
maintained.

Question:
Question 3
How is the limit for coating defect (error class 3) established? Please, justify this limit.
Answer:
Applicant’s response:
Finerenone tablets are film-coated to provide a homogeneous appearance, to add a color for
product identification and to facilitate swallowing. Defect evaluation is performed to assess the
occurrence of defects of tablets.
Defects are classified in different categories based on their impact: Critical defects affect the
usability or functionality of the product in an extent that may lead to severe consequences,
including significant impact on the patient safety, the processability of the drug product or a
significant increase in market complaints. Major defects have a low to negligible impact on the
usability or functionality of the product or the patient's safety but are associated with a higher-
than-expected number of market complaints. Minor defects do not affect the usability or
functionality of the product. They include issues that may reduce the desired product appearance
but do not impact the overall performance, patient safety of efficacy or lead to a significant
increase in market complaints. Cosmetic defects pose no risk to the patient. The usability and
functionality of the product remains unaffected, and no market complaints are expected.
Coating defects < 2 mm are classified as minor defects (defect class 3).
The acceptance limit for defect class 3 (minor defects) is determined in reference to DIN ISO 2859.
Defect evaluation is performed on a sample size of 1,250 tablets (representative sample for a
batch size > 500,000 tablets). Defects with minor impact are assigned to an AQL of 4.0. To
determine the allowed absolute number of defects, this AQL is statistically linked to a 95%
probability of acceptance of the lot. This means that with an AQL of 4.0, lots with 4% defects will
be accepted with a 95% probability. Using the cumulative binomial probability equation with given
sample size, defective numbers and lot percent defective, the corresponding probability of
acceptance can be calculated resulting in an acceptance number of 61 for defect class 3.

Question:
Question 4
Since the film-coating step has been listed as a critical step, the need for including in-process
controls to monitor the outcome of this step should be further discussed and if no in-process
control is considered needed, this should be justified.
Answer:
Applicant’s response:
The coating step was evaluated as critical process step that may have an influence on dissolution,
assay and appearance. Nevertheless, in the context of the DoE performed in commercial scale for
the coating process, all critical quality attributes (appearance, assay, drug dissolution after 15 min
and 30 min, respectively) that may be influenced by the coating process were well within the
specified range while exhibiting a low variability under all investigated process parameters.
In addition, the coating is a non-functional coating that is only added to ensure a homogeneous
appearance, to add a color for product identification and to facilitate swallowing. As shown in
Figure 6-11 of the updated P.2.3.01_IQMS-265199_3.0, uncoated and coated tablets have
comparable dissolution profiles (please refer to Figure 6–11: Drug dissolution - comparison of
uncoated tablet batches produced within the commercial DoE).

The film-coating step is the last step regarding the manufacturing of coated tablets. Samples,
potentially withdrawn during the coating process to enable an in-process control, do not reflect the
final appearance of the coated tablets, e.g. the color will change and become homogeneous with
increasing film-coat application. Therefore, investigations carried out during the still proceeding
coating process have only limited validity regarding the characteristics of the final product.
Furthermore, a DoE investigation in commercial scale was carried out to identify the process
parameter ranges which lead to a product with none or a neglectable number of coating defects.
For this purpose, spray rate and outlet air temperature were varied as described in P.2.3.01_IQMS-
265199_3.0 and each batch was evaluated concerning possible coating defects. With this
procedure, process parameter ranges could be identified which led to none or only small numbers
of coating defects. Additionally, the safety margin concerning the process parameter ranges of the
coating process was chosen huge as described in the answer to question 2.
Moreover, to ensure that the final product will comply with the specification, the coated tablets
undergo quality testing according to the release specification. Release will only take place when all
analyses comply with the specification.
Therefore, the applicant maintains that the implementation of additional IPCs is not necessary to
ensure the quality of the final product

Question:
Question 6
Any hold times used during manufacture of commercial batches should be stated in section P.3.3
Description of manufacturing process and be supported by data.
Answer:
Applicant’s response:
The manufacturing process of Finerenone film-coated tablets is the same for all dose strengths. In
addition, the all strengths have the same qualitative composition except for the colors of the film-
coat. The pre-blend components are weighed into a container, followed by a mixing step. Fluid-bed
granulation is carried out by spraying a granulation suspension containing the active ingredient
onto the mixed pre-blend. The granules are then dried to a specified moisture content. The dried
granules are sieved and collected in the product container. After the addition of the post-blend,
another mixing step takes place in the container. The ready-to-press mixture is compressed to
tablets on a rotary tablet press. In the final step, the tablets are film-coated.
Holding times were validated in commercial scale for the dose strengths 10/20 mg resulting in:
Intermediate product 
Dose strengths 10/20 mg
Ready-to-press mixture 
≤ 42 days
Uncoated tablet 
≤ 30 days
(for further information please refer to the technical registration document
P.3.5.01_022978386_03)

To evaluate the holding times for the 40 mg dose strength a risk assessment was carried out
considering the following aspects:
Regarding the ready-to-press mixture
• 
Stored in a closed, light-tight container
• 
Stored in a temperature-controlled area
• 
Storage area subject to particle contamination monitoring
• 
Quality control testing of the final product: assay, degradation products, uniformity of
dosage, dissolution, and microbial purity against the requirements of the specification
• 
Considerations of the results of all holding time evaluations independent of scale
Concerning the uncoated tablets
• 
Storage in closed, light-tight containers
• 
Storage in a temperature-controlled area
• 
Storage area is subject to particle contamination monitoring
• 
Storage area is subject to microbiological monitoring
• 
In-process controls: mass uniformity, breaking load, disintegration time, and friability
• 
Quality control testing of the final product: assay, degradation products, uniformity of
dosage, dissolution, and microbial purity against the requirements of the specification
• 
Consideration of the results of all holding time evaluations independent of scale

Supported by data gathered in pilot scale when manufacturing Finerenone coated tablets 40 mg
justifying holding times of even ≤ 56 days for the intermediates ready-to-press mixture and
uncoated tablet (for further information please refer to the technical registration document
P.2.2.10_022987636_01) the holding time of ≤ 42 days for the ready-to-press mixture and ≤ 30
days for the uncoated tablets of Finerenone coated tablets 10/20 mg was transferred to Finerenone
coated tablets 40 mg. Product quality is assured by compliance with the release tests.
Both holding times of the intermediates produced in commercial scale are added in the

Question:
Question 2
Section 1.0.7.1 – It was previously commented that the product is not included in the scope of 
the GMP certificate of Eurofins and justification was pending. In this reply, GMP evidence 
from a different country was provided. The supporting evidence that product is included in the 
scope of the GMP certificate of Eurofins is still pending.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2:
For pharmaceutical sites in the USA, the US GMP status can be accessed in a US database - 
Drug Establishments Current Registration Site (Link: https://dps.fda.gov/decrs).

In the past, GMP certificates from EU inspections could be issued and provided to 
demonstrate the successful outcome of GMP inspections of pharmaceutical sites in the USA. 
This became challenging after the entering into force of the U.S.-EU Mutual Recognition 
Agreement (MRA) Sectoral Annex for Pharmaceutical Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) 
on November 1, 2017 for human medicines. This MRA between the USA and EU allows 
mutual recognition of GMP inspections and sharing of information on inspections and quality 
defects. Therefore, EU authorities can rely on US GMP evidence and have no further need to 
perform their own inspections for active substances/medicinal products covered by this MRA.

One of the product groups covered by this MRA from the very beginning are marketed 
biological products, e.g. therapeutic biotechnology-derived biological products such as 
aflibercept (active pharmaceutical ingredient of the marketed biological product – Eylea). 
Manufacturing sites or laboratories for the QC testing/analysis of Eylea are therefore covered
by this MRA and do not need to be inspected separately by EU authorities. This explains why 
Eylea (aflibercept) was not included in the scope of the Italian GMP certificate of Eurofins 
(Cert. No.: IT/GMP/E/08/2023).

The Italian GMP certificate only covered products that are excluded from or currently not 
included in the MRA scope as listed below because the US GMP evidence was not 
recognized and could not be used in EU.
Excluded from the MRA scope are:
• human blood and plasma
• human tissues and organs
• veterinary immunologicals
• advanced therapy medicinal products

Currently not included in the MRA scope but maybe in the future:
• vaccines for human use and plasma-derived medicines: postponed due to the COVID-19
pandemic. A new date for a decision on a possible expansion of the scope needs to be 
agreed between the EU and the US. However, the parties have agreed to start technical 
cooperation with a view to a future decision on possible expansion of the scope.
• products intended for use in clinical trials (investigational medicinal products): discussion
at a later stage.

Source:  EMA website on Mutual Recognition Agreement (MRA) at Mutual recognition
agreements (MRA) | European Medicines Agency (EMA)
FDA website on Mutual Recognition Agreement (MRA) at European Union 
(EU) Mutual Recognition Agreement | FDA

Question:
Question 1
In the draft regulatory document on quality (in the Specification and in the text) include 
control of the indicator ‘Residual organic solvents’, which provides for control of residual 
content of the solvent of toxicity class 2 of cyclohexane used in the process of manufacturing 
of the medicinal product (during manual assembly of systems) in accordance with the 
Requirements for study conducting (testing) of medicinal products in terms of assessment and 
control of the content of impurities (Decision of the Board of the Eurasian Economic 
Commission of 04 October 2022 No. 138); the relevant information should be reflected in the 
associated sections of module 3 of the registration dossier (where applicable).
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1:
We acknowledge the query from the Russian Health Authority requesting inclusion of a 
control for the residual organic solvent cyclohexane, classified as a Class 2 solvent, in 
accordance with the EAEU requirements (Decision of the Board of the Eurasian Economic 
Commission dated 04 October 2022, No. 138). 
 
We would like to provide the following justification:
• The Mirena intrauterine delivery system is currently assembled exclusively by a
mechanical process. The manual assembly process, which historically involved the use 
of cyclohexane, has not been used for over 10 years and is no longer part of the 
manufacturing process.
• Consequently, the manual assembly method is not described in the current version of
the regulatory dossier, as it is obsolete.
• As detailed in TRD P.3.3.01_005823293_02 of the dossier, in cases where
cyclohexane was used, it was allowed to evaporate in a fume hood for two hours to 
overnight, thereby ensuring no residual solvent in the final product.
• Based on the current manufacturing process and historical data, cyclohexane is not
present in the finished product, and therefore, it is not included in the release or shelf-
life specifications.
• Furthermore, we plan to formally delete the obsolete manual assembly method and
associated procedures from the dossier via a variation submission (REC 32848-
(Deletion of manual assembly including in-process control (IPC) parameters for 
manual assembly and usage of cyclohexane)), which is planned for submission by the 
end of 2025 in the EAEU region.

Given the above, Bayer Oy believes that inclusion of cyclohexane as a residual solvent in the 
specification is not scientifically justified, as it is neither used in the current process nor 
present in the final product.

Source:  P.3.3.01__02 Manufacturing Process/ Levonorgestrel intrauterine delivery
system 52 mg with inserter (MIRENA) (#005823293; unchanged)

Question:
Question 1
We acknowledge your proposed dissolution method (USP 2 (paddle)/ 75 rpm, in 900 mL of 
Acetate buffer pH 4.5 with 0.6% Tween 20) for the dissolution testing of your proposed drug 
product, Finerenone Tablets, 40 mg. However, the proposed dissolution method is not 
acceptable due to an unjustified high level of surfactant (0.6% Tween 20). Based on the 
information/data submitted, greater than 85% of finerenone is released in 15 minutes with 
only 0.1% Tween 20 added to the dissolution medium. Excessive surfactant concentration 
may mask potential formulation issues and lead to unreliable quality control results. 
Therefore, we recommend the following dissolution method and acceptance criterion for your 
drug product Finerenone Tablets, 40 mg:
Method: 900 mL of Acetate buffer pH 4.5 with 0.1% Tween 20, 37°C, USP Apparatus II 
(Paddle), 75 RPM.
Acceptance Criterion: NLT 80% (Q) of finerenone is dissolved in 15 minutes
Update all relevant sections of your submission, including drug product specification tables 
for release and stability, to reflect the recommended dissolution method and acceptance 
criterion.
We request a response by Thursday, June 5, 2025.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (P.5):
Bayer acknowledges FDA’s proposed dissolution method and agrees to implement the new 
method and specifications as proposed.  (900 mL of Acetate buffer pH 4.5 with 0.1% Tween 
20, 37°C, USP Apparatus II (Paddle), 75 RPM).
Several sections of the NDA will require updating based on this change.  The updated 
specifications and test methods reflecting this change can be submitted to the NDA by June 
11, 2025.  Additional time will be needed to perform the necessary analytical work to adapt 
the method validation and other sections of the NDA to the new test method and we would 
like to further agree on the submission strategy that will satisfy FDA requirements and not 
impact the PDUFA date of July 13, 2025.

𝑊𝑒𝑖𝑔ℎ (𝑆1)×𝑅𝑒𝑠𝑝𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑒(𝑆2)

Adults

Question:
Question 1
In the cover letter, it is necessary to describe the method used for the “Sterility” test and provide data confirming the suitability of the method.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 ( CTD section):
We acknowledge the comments from the authority and providing below the test procedure for Sterility test and TRD for suitability of the method.
Source: P.5.3.922-01 Validation - Other Methods/ Iopromide solution for parenteral use (SH L00414A SH L00414B SH L00414C SH L00414G) (ULTRAVIST) (DocID#004448239/new)
We acknowledge the comments from the authority and providing below the test procedure for Sterility test:
Sterility test is performed according to harmonized pharmacopeial method (USP < 71>, PharmEur 2.6.1, JP 4.06)

Sterility Test Procedure for Ultravist 300:
Sterility (membrane filtration)
Principle of the method:
Membrane filtration using disposable elements (MILLIPORE Steritest system for two culture media). The sample solutions are filtered using the Steritest system. The membrane filter (mean pore size ≤ 0.45 μm) retains any microorganisms present. The membrane filter is covered with culture medium and the entire assembly is incubated. Turbidity is evidence of microbial growth and possibly of contamination of the sample solution.

Reagents:
- casein peptone + soybean peptone digest medium (CSB)
- thioglycolate medium
Consumables:
Merck (Millipore): Steritest™ Container Type TZHA

Test procedure:
Note:
Samples can be used directly for sterility test. No preparation necessary.
Conduct the test under aseptic conditions (laminar-flow bench). The composition of the culture media and buffer solutions meet the requirements of Ph.Eur. and USP. Likewise follow the USP and Ph.Eur. stipulations on preparatory tests to establish:
- the sterility of the culture media, solutions and apparatus employed
- the growth-promoting qualities of the culture media employed
- any antimicrobial activity of the test substance in the culture media

Conduct of the test:
The determination is conducted depending on the filling volume of the vessels.

Number of product samples for for testing for
5 ml solution for injection, ampoule 20 containers
10 ml solution for injection, vial 20 containers
20 ml solution for infusion, vial 20 containers
30 ml solution for infusion, vial 20 containers
50 ml solution for infusion, bottle 20 containers
75 ml solution for infusion, 100 ml bottle 20 containers
100 ml solution for infusion, bottle 20 containers
125 ml solution for infusion, 150-ml bottle 20 containers
150 ml solution for infusion, bottle 20 containers
200 ml solution for infusion, 250-ml bottle 20 containers
500 ml solution for infusion, bottle 20 containers
1000 ml solution for infusion, bottle 20 containers

For the extractable volumes of 125, 150 and 200 ml conduct the test in two runs with 10 containers each.
For the extractable volumes of 500 ml conduct the test in five runs with 4 containers each.
For the extractable volumes of 1000 ml conduct the test in ten runs with 2 containers each.

Distribute the contents of the relevant containers evenly between the two filter assemblies of the Steritest system, then filter (sample pool). The samples are transferred directly into the sterility test containers via injection needle. The maximum volume permitted through one membrane is 1000 ml. No rinsing fluid is used, since no antimicrobial properties of the product could be detected which would require rinsing of the membrane (see P.5.3.922#004448239.
Cover one membrane filter with 100 ml CSB and the other with 100 ml thioglycolate medium.
Incubation:
14 days at 20°C to 25°C (CSB)
14 days at 30°C to 35°C (thioglycolate medium)

Evaluation of initial test:
On every work day after incubation, examine the filter units for growth visible to the naked eye (turbidity).
The sterility requirement is met, if the culture media remain clear after being shaken for a moment.

Question:
Question 1
Section 1.0.4 - Long term stability Report
For stability tests at accelerated storage condition for sterilized PFS (Tables 4-12 to 4-15 of 
“P.8.3.01_022980339_05 Stability Data.pdf”), please justify the out-of-specification result for 
the purity tests and test on isoaspartate content toward the end of the test (month 6 and/or 3). 
Please justify why 24 months of shelf life can be claimed.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (3.2.P.8.3):
Out-of-specification (OOS) results observed in the course of accelerated stability studies 
(25 ± 2 °C, 60 ± 5% relative humidity) performed for Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/ml in 
prefilled syringe (PFS) are within expectation and in-line with the known degradation profile 
of Aflibercept drug product.
OOS results are known to occur after 3 and/or 6 months of storage for the tests “Purity by SE-
UPLC”, “Isoaspartate Content” and “Purity by reduced CE-SDS”. OOS results at the 
accelerated stability condition therefore do not reflect any adverse impact on the product 
quality. Instead, the purpose of those studies is to confirm that the degradation profile of 
Aflibercept at this storage condition is within expectation after changes in manufacturing, like 
e.g. the comparison between the drug product in vial and the drug product in PFS.
The available data confirms that the degradation profile is comparable for vial and PFS under 
accelerated condition. The OOS results at the accelerated stability condition do not correlate 
with a risk of not meeting the shelf-life specification acceptance criteria after 24 months at the 
recommended storage condition of 2-8 °C and it is not utilized to extrapolate the shelf life. 
Analytical comparability data demonstrates that the Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/ml in vial 
and PFS are highly similar also in term of behavior during long term storage at 2-8 °C. 
Therefore, based on the 24 months stability data available for the vial, the same shelf life is 
justified for the PFS.
Note that the sterilized PFS batches in P.8.3.01-05 are currently under testing after 24 months 
and there is no indication that any batch will not meet the shelf-life specification acceptance 
criteria. We will provide the 24 months data once available.
Source:  P.8.3.01-05 TRD code title / Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in prefilled
syringe for intravitreous injection (#022980339; unchanged)

Question:
Question 3
Section 1.1.0-P3 & 1.1.1 – item 40 - Elemental impurities
(i). Please clarify how the AET and concentration of elemental impurities in the migration and 
extraction studies are related to the “Threshold for Additional Controls” and “PDE” in 
3.2.P.5.5.01-01 and ICH Q3D.
(ii). In page 6 of 3.2.P.5.5.01-01, section 2.1 mentioned that “based on ICH Q3D a risk 
scoring describing the likelihood and amount of elemental impurities in the DP (with respect 
to permitted daily exposure (PDE) was established.”. Please clarify if the scoring is available 
for assessment. The purpose if for us to assess if the classes of elemental impurities, testing 
methods/studies and control are appropriate.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 3 (3.2.P.5.5):
(i) The analytical evaluation threshold (AET) is always defined by using a safety threshold, 
and in these studies the safety concern threshold (SCT)/threshold of toxicological concern 
(TTC) of 1.5 µg/d for potentially genotoxic and mutagenic compounds has been applied. 
From that daily safety limit, study specific AET values have been derived as presented in 
P.2.4.06-01 and P.2.4.07-01.
SCT of 1.5 µg/d is lower than any of the element specific permitted daily exposure (PDE) 
values for parenteral route, the lowest PDE being 2 µg/d for Cd. Therefore, elemental 
impurities, as a part of all studied substances, are reported in extractable and leachable studies 
by using safety based AET , which is sufficiently low for all elemental impurities in relation 
to safety.
When extractable and leachable study results are evaluated in regard of toxicological safety, 
safety of potentially detected elemental impurities is assessed by using administration route 
related PDE limits for defining whether reported element may require some additional 
control.
Thresholds for additional controls (P.5.5.01-01) are theoretical limits related to the 
administration route specific PDE values and defining 30% of the respective PDE value as the 
limit for additional controls.
In summary, for reporting results from extractable and leachable studies the AET is used. 
Considering the toxicologic safety for elemental impurities, 30% of the respective PDE value 
is used as reference to determine whether additional analytical control is required. None of the 
elemental impurities requires additional analytical control for Aflibercept solution 
114.3 mg/ml in PFS.
(ii) Risk scoring mentioned in 3.2.P.5.5. in page 6 refers to ICH Q3D classification of 
elements to different risk classes 1, 2A, 2B, and 3, which then have different administration 
route dependent PDE values, please refer to Appendix 2 Established PDEs for Elemental 
Impurities - Table A.2.1: Permitted Daily Exposures for Elemental Impurities of the ICH
Q3D guideline (see attachment below). These ICH Q3D classes for elements are described in 
Table 2-2 in P.5.5.01-01.

Question:
Question 1
Module 3.2.2.3 applicant provided a report with results demonstrating that identification of 
RXM12 and RXM1J media feed by UPLC is specific, precise and robust but did not provide 
the results for RXM12 and RXM1J media feed identification by HPLC. Therefore, applicant 
is requested to comply with SAHPRA biological guideline (SAHPGL-PEM-BIO-05_v6) to 
provide comparative results demonstrating that the approved and proposed analytical 
procedures are equivalent.ext of Question in Bayer Body Text Full
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (S.2.3):
The Sponsor would like to clarify that both the HPLC and UPLC methods are used to confirm 
the identity of the feeds prior to inclusion in the aflibercept manufacturing process. These 
liquid chromatography methods were determined to be suitable for their intended use through 
method validation. Validation of the method ensures that the selected method can adequately 
identify the individual feeds. The proposed UPLC method was determined to be suitable for 
use through assay validation in accordance with ICH Q2 (results are summarized in 
S.2.3.12_022978999_01 (Regeneron validation report AV-SR-027120). While ICH only 
requires specificity for identification methods, further assessments were performed for the 
UPLC assay validation. The validation results demonstrate that the UPLC identity method is 
specific, precise, repeatable, and robust in the identification of RXM1J and RXM12 media 
feeds and suitable for use.
The current identification method uses HPLC parameters to reliably identify RXM12 or 
RXM1J media feed powder from other related amino acid media products. Because both 
RXM1J and RXM12 media feed contain similar amino acids, the specificity between the two 
media was assessed by comparing the peak area ratio of arginine/tyrosine (Arg/Tyr). To 
determine the method comparability between the HPLC and UPLC methods, the Arg/Tyr 
peak area ratio in RXM1J and RXM12 were compared between data generated using the 
UPLC method and the previously generated HPLC data. As part of the comparability study, 
16 lots (eight lots of RXM1J and eight lots of RXM12) were tested using UPLC, and the peak 
area ratio of Arg/Tyr for both RXM1J and RXM12 was used to determine the method 
comparability between the HPLC and UPLC methods.
As shown in Table 1 the peak area ratio for Arg/Tyr for both RXM1J and RXM12 HPLC and 
UPLC are not comparable. This is because the current HPLC method uses a fluorescence 
(FLR) detector while the UPLC method uses a photodiode array (PDA) detector, as a result, 
the amino acid response between the two detectors is different. Therefore, the observed 
differences between the two methods can be attributed to the different principles of the two 
types of detection. FLR requires the excitation and emission from fluorescent molecules and 
PDA measures the absorption of ultraviolet light. When amino acids are analyzed using the 
FLR detectors they have different fluorescence yields when compared to the response from 
the PDA detector, therefore due to this difference, the ratio criteria set for the HPLC method 
cannot be translated to the UPLC method.
The results of the comparability study between HPLC and UPLC methods demonstrate that 
the Arg/Tyr peak area ratio for RXM1J and RXM12 media powder tested by UPLC is not 
comparable by absolute numbers to the results generated by HPLC. This is expected due to 
the different responses originating from the two different detector types. Additional 
evaluation was performed to determine the appropriate acceptance criteria to differentiate the 
two media using the UPLC method.
Assessment of the UPLC validation data, summarized in S.2.3.12_022978999_01 (Regeneron 
validation report AV-SR-027120, identified that the aspartic acid/glycine (Asp/Gly) peak area 
ratio can be used to differentiate between the two media. The Asp and Gly peaks were 
identified to be stable, well-resolved peaks and consistent in terms of peak height area and 
shape; therefore, the ratio between the two peaks was chosen to be used to differentiate 
between the two media feeds.
The assessment was performed using 169 runs of RXM1J and 179 runs of RXM12 media, the 
results are summarized in Figure 1 below. Based on this assessment the newly proposed 
criteria for the Asp/Gly peak area ratio for RXM12 is Asp/Gly: ≥ 3.0, and the peak area ratio 
for RXM1J is Asp/Gly:< 3.0. As shown in Figure 1, since the tolerance interval for RXM12 
and RXM1J media do not overlap, the newly proposed criteria are suitable to distinguish 
between the two media feeds. Moreover, the difference between the upper tolerance intervals 
and lower tolerance intervals for the two media types and the two different amino acid ratios 
is larger for Asp/Gly (3.37 – 2.81 = 0.56) than for Arg/Tyr (2.43 – 2.06 = 0.37). This 
underscores the ability of the UPLC method to distinguish between the two media types, with 
the Asp/Gly ratio demonstrating a better ability to differentiate.  This new criterion will 
replace the criteria listed in the current specification.
A summary of the identified acceptance criteria for the UPLC is presented in Table 2 on the 
next page.
Furthermore, testing using the UPLC instruments allows for increased speed, heightened 
resolution, and heightened sensitivity when compared to HPLC. These benefits aided in the 
selection of the UPLC method as a replacement for the HPLC method.
In conclusion, there is no impact to product quality with the introduction of the UPLC method 
proposed to replace the HPLC method for identification testing of RXM1J media feed. The 
UPLC method met all assay validation criteria for specificity, repeatability, precision, 
robustness and is therefore considered equivalent to the HPLC method for the identification of 
RXM1J. Consequently, the UPLC method is suitable for identity testing of the RXM1J media 
feed.

Question:
Question 1
Recommended to provide:
- report on the revalidation of the manufacturing process of the finished product (data for 
2019 are presented). According to paragraph 146 of Appendix 3 of the Order of the Minister 
of Health of the Republic of Kazakhstan dated February 4, 2021 No. КР ДСМ-15 “On 
approval of good pharmaceutical practices”, processes and procedures are subject to periodic 
revalidation (repeated validation) to ensure that they remain suitable for achieving certain 
results;
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (P.3.5):
Bayer’s approach to validation and revalidation is in accordance with international guidelines 
e.g. EMA Guideline on Process Validation for Finished Products – Information and Data To 
Be Provided in Regulatory Submissions (November 2016) and the EU Annex 15: 
Qualification and Validation (October 2015) which outline the general principles and 
approaches for the appropriate elements of process validation for the manufacture of human 
drugs. These guidances align Process Validation activities with a product lifecycle concept as 
presented in the International Conference on Harmonization (ICH) Guidance for Industry, Q8 
(R2) Pharmaceutical Development, Q9 Quality Risk Management, and Q10 Pharmaceutical 
Quality System. The lifecycle concept links product and process development, validation of 
the commercial manufacturing process, and maintenance of the process in a state of control 
during routine commercial production. Specifically, process validation confirms that the 
control strategy is adequate to the process design and the quality of the product. Subsequently, 
ongoing process verification confirms that the process remains in a state of control during 
commercial manufacture and supports the validated status of the product. Whereas only 
significant changes to the production process, including any changes to equipment or starting 
and packaging materials that may affect the quality of the product and (or) the consistency of 
the process, need to be re-validated.
The initial process validation and defined control strategy was completed in 2019. Since that 
time, no major changes have been implemented for the product as registered in Kazakhstan. 
The annual product review has confirmed periodically that the manufacturing process has 
reproducibly yielded finished product meeting the specified quality and in-process controls. 
Hence, the validated control strategy has continuously been verified to be adequate and still 
valid.
In summary, in line with the above Bayer would consider the requirements, as requested 
based “On approval of good pharmaceutical practices”, for processes and procedures to be 
subject to periodic revalidation (repeated validation) to ensure that they remain suitable for 
achieving certain results as fulfilled.

Question:
Question 3
• Regarding container closure integrity testing by dye ingress, you are asked to provide a
summary of the study including the following information: 
a. The number of samples tested 
b. A summary of the dye ingress method 
c. Confirmation that positive control samples (i.e. vials that have been intentionally
compromised) were included in the study to verify that the test conditions were 
suitable, or that the dye ingress method has been suitably validated including positive 
controls.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 3a:
During validation runs 375 samples were tested in total. All tested samples met the 
requirements. Additionally, 50 samples are tested annually as part of the stability studies 
regarding CCIT over the shelf life.

Bayer Response to Question 3b:
The Dye Ingress Method is a destructive probabilistic CCIT method that assesses container 
closure integrity (CCI) by immersing the test containers in a dye solution (Eosin Y, 1%) and 
simultaneously applying three cycles of differential pressure (30 min each alternating normal 
pressure and vacuum at 500 mbar). After the challenge is completed, the test samples’ outer 
surfaces are rinsed thoroughly under running water and the content is checked for dye ingress 
via visual examination under suitable illumination.

Bayer Response to Question 3c:
The dye ingress CCIT is performed according to valid standard operating procedures and 
methods that were validated following the same approach as for testing.
Test units with injected dye solution (so called "positive samples"), are used to simulate 
leakage or damage to the primary packaging. All test units are immersed in a dye bath and 
subjected to an underpressure cycle.

Question:
Question 2
Based on the information provided why was tert-butanol not detected in the extractable study 
of the rubber stopper and detected in both the simulated and ongoing leachable studies? 
Further in the ongoing leachable study if the vial is stored in the upright orientation how is the 
tert-butanol leaching into the DP without direct contact?
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2 ( S.2.4.):
Tert-butanol (CAS 75-65-0) was detected in the extractable study, but the concentration was 
just below the analytical evaluation threshold (AET) and therefore, it was not reported as an 
extractable compound. Then in the leachable simulation study tert-butanol (CAS 75-65-0) 
exceeded the AET, but was unexpected as it was not earlier reported in the extractable study 
(P.2.4.01_022988846_02).
When extractable study data was re-examined it was observed that tert-butanol was released 
during the extraction of the stopper with both pH 5 phosphate buffer and in the thermal 
extraction at 80 C, but the amounts were slightly below the AET of the extractable study. As 
a part of this leachable simulation study the vial stopper was cut into pieces and subjected to 
HS-GC-MS analyses for volatile compounds. The vial stopper was confirmed to be the source 
of tert-butanol with an estimated amount of approximately 7 – 10 µg/stopper.
At the initial stability study timepoint tert-butanol was detected with approximately 4.0 
µg/mL, which corresponds to 0.28 µg/eye and 0.56 µg/treatment. At the timepoint T6 the 
amount of tert-butanol was 9.0 µg/mL, which corresponds to 0.63 µg/eye and 1.26 
µg/treatment. Leachable analyses at the next timepoint T12 are on-going and when reported 
development in the amount of tert-butanol will be clarified then. Final confirmation of the 
amount of tert-butanol released in real time and under temperature storage conditions will be 
obtained when the leachable stability study will progress to the end of shelf-life.
Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL vials are stored upright at 2 – 8C vial stopper not having a 
direct contact with drug solution. Nevertheless, volatile leachable compounds are known to 
migrate from container closure systems into drug product although leachable compounds are 
not in direct contact with the drug solution. It is also known that storage temperature affects 
migration efficiency of volatile leachable compounds. When considering the released amount 
of tert-butanol (7 – 10 µg/stopper) in stopper material in relation to filling volume of the vial, 
which is 0.263 mL, the estimated theoretical maximum concentrations of tert-butanol in 
Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL are 27 – 38 µg/mL.
From that perspective available timepoint T6 results for tert-butanol are well in line with the 
theoretical maximum concentrations estimated above..

Source:  P.2.4.01-02 Pharmaceutical Development - Container Closure
System / Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in vial for intravitreous injection 
(Bayer AG, Berlin) (#022988846; unchanged)

Question: Regarding the finished product specification, it is noted that the acceptance criteria of the sliding and static friction for this product (plastic PFS) is different from that stated in the specification of the glass PFS (HK-57330). Please justify the difference.
Answer:
Sliding Friction (also known as Gliding Force) refers to the force required to maintain continuous movement of the syringe plunger once initiated. Static Friction (also called Breakaway Force) is the force needed to overcome initial resistance and start the plunger’s movement from rest.
Measuring both static and sliding friction as part of the push-pull test method is critical for ensuring:
• 
Safe, smooth, and predictable syringe performance
• 
Optimized material compatibility and lubrication strategy
• 
Compliance with regulatory requirements governing functional device properties
The specifications for static and sliding friction differ between glass and plastic syringes due to inherent differences in:
• 
Material properties (rigidity, flexibility and elasticity)
• 
Surface texture and adhesion characteristics
• 
Manufacturing variability and tolerances
As outlined in P.5.6.01-01: Justification of Specification for Gadobutrol Solution 1 mol/L in Prefilled Plastic Syringe for Parenteral Use, the friction limits applied to plastic syringes were derived from experience with glass syringes.
However, plastic syringe barrels are inherently more flexible and less dimensionally rigid than glass, which increases variability in their interaction with the rubber plunger stopper. As a result, plastic syringes naturally exhibit higher and more variable friction forces, which justifies the application of broader acceptance criteria for both static and sliding friction values.

Source:  

P.5.6.01-01 Justification of Specification for Gadobutrol Solution 1 mol/L in Prefilled Plastic Syringe for Parenteral Use (GADOVIST)(#DocID; 015878159_ new)

Question:
Question 1
The viral clearance as presented cannot be evaluated due to insufficient description of the 
scale down process and incomplete or unclear viral clearance data. Provide all relevant 
parameters of the scale down process involved in the viral clearance study (ie. Column height, 
residence time, resin load etc.) and how they are representative of the production scale 
process or represent worst case. Provide a clear description of the viral clearance risk 
assessment and the calculations and justification for the calculations used to calculate the 
safety margin and theoretical RVLP exposure per maximum proposed dose.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (A.2):
A description and summary of the viral clearance studies are provided in 3.2.A.2.03, 
Virological Safety. The relevant parameters of the scale down process are described for the 
low pH hold of Protein A eluate, anion exchange chromatography (membrane adsorber), and 
filtration with Planova™ BioEX viral filter process steps (refer to 3.2.A.2.03 Table 3-4, Table 
3-6, and Table 3-8, respectively). Viral clearance by Protein A column chromatography 
process step was performed at production scale (2000 L, refer to Table 3-1). Additional 
details are in the study reports provided in 3.2.A.2.50, Study Reports of Virus Clearance 
Validation.

Each manufacturing process operation unit is representative of the production scale by 
proportionally scaling down while the critical operation parameters were kept consistent 
between the laboratory scale (the scaled-down test system) and the manufacturing scale. 
Accordingly, the results obtained by the scaled-down test system could be extrapolated to the 
manufacturing process at production scale. The suitability of each scaled-down test system 
was evaluated in the study by demonstrating acceptable recovery of the process intermediate 
and acceptable performance parameters, such as a chromatographic profile where applicable.  
All small scale viral clearance studies were performed using the worst-case scenarios of each 
step. For the low pH viral inactivation hold operation, the higher pH and lower incubation 
temperature values used for the scaled-down study were considered to cover the worst-case 
scenarios in the manufacturing process. For the anion exchange chromatography operation, 
the higher loading density, lower pH, and higher conductivity of the set range used for the 
scaled-down model were considered worst case scenarios. For the filtration with Planova™ 
BioEX viral filter operation, the higher filter loading density used for the scaled-down model 
was considered to cover the worst-case scenarios.

The viral clearance risk assessment includes an evaluation of the potential risk of virus 
contamination in BAY 3401016 production from the ERVLP present in the CHO cells that 
produce recombinant BAY 3401016 drug substance or from adventitious virus contaminants. 
The following measures are implemented to assess and mitigate the risk of virus 
contamination: determination of the level of CHO cell endogenous retrovirus particle in the 
unprocessed bulk; validation of sufficient virus clearance capacity achieved by the 
manufacturing process; evaluation of cell substrates and raw materials; monitoring and 
controlling of manufacturing environment. The viral clearance studies are designed and 
performed per guidance ICH Q5A. The removal of ERVLP (endogenous retrovirus-like 
particles) from the clarified harvest (i.e. the unprocessed bulk without the CHO cells) serves 
as a benchmark for retrovirus clearance capacity by the post-harvest purification process.

The calculation of estimated particles per dose follows ICH Q5A(R2) (Annex 4). The dose 
equivalent amount of ERVLP in the clarified harvest is estimated to be 9.51 log10 as described 
in 3.2.A.2.03 Table 4-1 (for convenience, Table 4-1 is reproduced below). The estimates in 
this table include worst case assumptions, including maximum daily dose. Determination of 
ERVLP concentration (6.79 log10 particles/mL) in the clarified harvest is described in 
3.2.A.2.50 Section 2.5 (Report ERVLP-24-02-3401016). The overall retrovirus clearance 
capacity, a summation of all demonstrated retroviral clearance results (≥ 18.72 ± 0.55 log10), 
provides ≥ 9.21 log10 (= 18.72 – 9.51) safety margin, which exceeds the 6.0 log10 general 
industry consensus safety margin described in ICH Q5A.

In summary, the lower value of Log10 Reduction Factor (LRF) is used as the worst case to 
determine virus clearance capacity for each operational step. The small-scale viral clearance 
studies conducted represent worst case scenario. Results from virus clearance validation 
studies with test articles of BAY 3401016 manufacturing intermediates have demonstrated 
that the process is highly effective and robust in virus inactivation and removal.

Question:
Question 1
The company was asked to confirm that positive control samples (i.e. vials that have been 
intentionally compromised) were included in the study to verify that the test conditions were 
suitable, or that the dye ingress method has been suitably validated including positive 
controls.
The response provided is not acceptable and has not demonstrated that the test method has 
been appropriately validated. A positive control is created by deliberately compromising a 
vial which is then immersed with the test vials. A direct inoculation of dye into a vial is not 
acceptable to demonstrate dye ingress under test conditions. For a response to be found 
acceptable, the company would need to confirm that they prepare a positive control vial by 
intentionally compromising a vial to demonstrate dye ingress into the vial under test 
conditions.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 ( 3.2.P.7):
The TGA’s request to incorporate deliberately compromised vials as a positive control in the 
Container Closure Integrity Testing (CCIT) method is acknowledged. While the CCIT test 
results presented to support this variation are based upon the method established in accordance 
with an earlier USP version <1207>, it is noted that current USP  <1207> is more specific with 
respect to the positive control expectations.
The Sponsor commits to completing and submitting the validation of the enhanced method, 
including deliberately compromised vials, within an agreed timeframe.
The proposal is to complete validation of the enhanced method for the Eylea 114.3mg/mL vial 
as part of a validation bracketing approach that will cover various combinations of drug 
products and container closure systems in different sizes and filling volumes.
Notwithstanding the commitment to undertake validation of the enhanced USP  <1207> 
method, the Sponsor considers that the CCIT results presented with this variation, in 
combination with the additional process validation data and manufacturing history illustrate the 
product is not at high risk of loss of integrity. The basis is as follows:
1. Sterility testing at multiple stability timepoints to highlight absence of contamination.
The sterility results obtained under the applied and already approved conditions for the 
current approved Catalent site provide evidence that the packaging system has 
performed as intended.
2. Scientific and Regulatory precedent – International guidance (e.g., ICH Q5C and USP
<1207>) – supports the use of sterility testing or container closure integrity testing at 
the beginning and end of shelf life. While CCIT is preferred for long-term assurance, 
sterility testing is an established standard and validation of the enhanced CCIT method 
is planned.
3. Risk mitigation:
- 
Process controls in place to ensure container integrity (e.g. validated process – 
stopper,  capping and checks)
- 
Historical data from Eylea vials from both 40mg/mL & 114.3mg/mL showing the 
closure system has a history of integrity
On this basis, it is proposed the current CCIT data and sterility results from stability studies 
provide reasonable assurance of product sterility during the whole life cycle. The Sponsor 
believes that this approach is scientifically justified and aligned with TGA expectations with 
provision that a re-validated CCIT method in accordance with the current USP <1207> is 
implemented within the proposed timeline. We respectfully request the TGA’s consideration of 
this variation with a post-approval commitment to complete validation of the CCIT method 
incorporating deliberately compromised vials as positive control, as per the Agency’s request.
Validation preparations are currently ongoing and will be implemented in Q4 2025. 
Consequently, a protocol will be shared by Q4 2025, and a report will be presented in Q2 2026.
Dye Ingress method validation will be performed, as requested, demonstrating the method’s 
effectiveness by comparing negative and positive controls. Positive controls will have laser-
drilled defects of different nominal leak sizes.

An assessment of Working cell bank (WCB) lot 8005700009 was completed by comparing it

evaluating the upstream cell culture performance and productivity from the seed train through 
the expansion to the production bioreactor, as well as all subsequent downstream purification

experience using a more stringent statistically derived comparability limit. The results of the 
comparability analysis are summarized in Tables 1 and Table 2. An explanation of how the 
comparability limits for release and extended characterization were determined is provided in

Question:
Question 1
Section 1.0.4:
[Long term stability report]:
(i). Please submit stability data once applicable and update the input for stability report accordingly (e.g. 18 months for duration for the time being).
(ii). Please clarify the lack of sterility tests for accelerated condition (whole planned duration – Table 4-12 to 4-15) and long term condition (initial to 12th months – Table 4-5 to 4-8).
(iii). Please clarify why there is no data for the first 2 time points (initial & 3rd months) for long term condition (Table 4-5 to 4-8).
(iv). Please clarify if the tests were conducted according to the test schedule in Table 2-5 as there is “NR” in so many timepoint for various tests (e.g. appearance, clarify, color, pH, particulate matter content, endotoxin and sterility).
(v). Please update the study start date to 01.10.2023 as far as only sterilized PFS is concerned.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (3.2.P.8.3):
(i) Updated stability data including 24 month long-term storge are provided in the sections P.8.1.01-06, P.8.3.01-7.0.
(ii) The sterility testing concept for Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in prefilled syringe (PFS) is compliant with ICH guidelines and provides adequate control over quality, safety and efficacy of the drug product.
ICH Q5C “Stability Testing of Biotechnological/Biological Products” states in section 5.4 “Other Product Characteristics”:
“Sterility testing or alternatives (e.g., container/closure integrity testing) should be performed at a minimum initially and at the end of the proposed shelf-life.”
Therefore, sterility testing is performed at release and at the end of the shelf-life for long-term stability studies, while it is not required at any timepoint before the current end of shelf-life of 24 months.
Sterility testing is not performed for accelerated studies, since the purpose of these studies is to investigate the degradation behavior of the product at this storage condition. The inclusion of sterility testing during accelerated stability is furthermore not considered to provide meaningful information since the commercial product will have a predefined maximum time out of refrigeration, which is in the order of magnitude of a few days only and covered by dedicated maximum TOR stability studies that include sterility testing (refer to P.8.3.11-6.0). A potential sterility out of specification result after 1, 3 or 6 months at 25 ± 2 °C, 60 ± 5% relative humidity could therefore not be transferred to a sterility issue at the real-time storage condition.
(iii) The manufacturing process of Aflibercept 114.3 mg/mL PFS consists of two parts: (i) aseptic filling of formulated drug substance into syringes (bulk PFS) at Vetter Pharma and (ii) Labeling, Assembly, Blistering and Sterilization (LABS) of the outer surface of the syringe at the Bayer AG, Berlin, Germany (BAG). The LABS process can occur several months after the filling process.
The shelf life of Aflibercept 114.3 mg/mL PFS starts with the time of filling and is controlled (see CTD sections P.5.6.01-01 and P.8.1.01-06). The time between the filling and LABS processing is already part of the overall shelf life and the total shelf life is not impacted by the date of LABS processing.
Resultantly and depending on the time difference between bulk PFS manufacturing (filling) and LABS process, data for several time points (e.g., 0, 3 and 6 months) can be missing for the sterilized batches as also explained in P.8.2.01-01.
(iv) It is confirmed that the long-term and accelerated stability studies are conducted in accordance with the schedule as provided in table 2-5 of P.8.3.01-7.0. This table only defines at which time points stability tests are performed and at which time points stability tests are not required as indicated with “--“, i.e., for accelerated studies all time points beyond the 6 months.
The individual tests that are performed for the long term and the accelerated study at each time point are defined in Table 3-1 and Table 3-2 in P.8.1.01-06. “NR” indicates that a test item is not required at a certain time point. The applicant defined this table based on the experience with the approved Aflibercept solution 40 mg/mL in vial and PFS as well as the Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in vial. Specification parameter that do not undergo any changes throughout the shelf life and are therefore not stability indicating, have been waived at certain time points. However, the full testing panel as per P.5.1.02-01 is conducted at least at the end of shelf life.
(v) As explained in the response to Question 1 (iii), the shelf life of the finished product starts with the filling of bulk syringes. The start date of the stability studies, however, is always set at 30 days after filling. This is to support the procedure applied at Bayer to set the expiration date of the finished product, which is usually the last date of a month two years (or the respective shelf life) after start of the shelf life. For Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in PFS this means that syringes which were filled on e.g. 01.10.2024 will have an expiration date of 30.10.2026 expressed as 10/2026 on the label and the secondary packaging.
To cover the maximum 30 days difference, the stability study start (T0) is set 30 days after the filling date of the PFS, meaning 30 days after the start of the shelf life. In total, the product will have 25 months of storage, while the stability study runs 24 months.
The most appropriate study start date of the finished product (PFS after LABS) presented in P.8.3.01-7.0 is therefore April 2023 (KT0KK7S, KT0KKC1 and KT0KKC3) or May 2023 (KT0KVBJ and KT0KVBJ-D), which is the study start date of the parent bulk PFS batches as shown in Table 2-1 of the aforementioned CTD section.
For Eylea solution for intravitreal injection in pre-filled syringe 114.3mg/ml in Hong Kong, shelf life calculation is in exact date, which means that syringes which were filled on e.g. 01.10.2024 will have an expiration date of 01.10.2026. The expiry date shown on outer secondary packaging consists of day-month-year (e.g. 01.10.2026). Exact date format presentation is subject to site’s setting.

Question:
Question 3
Section 1.1.0-P2:
[Item 15]:
Please justify the necessity of this amount of overfill.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 3 (3.2.P.2.4, 3.2.P.2.6):
The Aflibercept 114.3 mg/mL prefilled syringe was designed to deliver a 70 μL dose. An overfill is required for a prefilled syringe to ensure that the intended dose can consistently be delivered.
Overfilling is required to compensate variations in fill volume that occur during the filling process and for the dead volume within the injection needle and prefilled syringe. The dead volume is the drug solution remaining in the syringe and needle after injection.
Resultantly, the target fill volume of 0.184 mL was set considering dose preparation, void volume in syringe and needle, and variance of the fill volume within qualified limits as also explained in P.2.4.02-01.
Overfill must also compensate additional losses of drug that are associated with priming of the injection system. During the priming process, the air bubble in the syringe must be expelled. With that also some droplets of drug are expelled.
Overall, the capability of the Aflibercept 114.3 mg/mL prefilled syringe to precisely deliver a dose of 70 µL is shown in the dose accuracy results from design verification study and presented in P.2.6.01-01.

Question:
Question 4
Section 1.1.0-P3&1.1.1:
[Item 29]:
[Overall]:
(i). Please upload justification of specification.
(ii). For release and shelf-life specifications, please clarify why there is no test(s) on the device functionality (e.g. break out/sustaining forces) versus that of the vial previously approved (HK68359).
(iii). For release and shelf-life specifications, please clarify why the limits on Particulate Matter Content differ from that of the vial previously approved (HK68359).
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 4 (3.2.P.3.3, 3.2.P.5.6):
(i) Handled locally.
(ii) The Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in prefilled syringe (PFS) drug device combination product is a disposable, prefilled syringe with customized finger flange and plunger rod for single, fixed dose delivery. The drug device combination product has an integrated dosing mechanism that provides the delivery of a preselected dose. Manual dose setting by the user (e.g., healthcare professional) is not possible in contrast to the already approved Aflibercept solution 40 mg/mL PFS, where a dose line is applied.
In accordance with the design control processes applied to develop the PFS, priming and injection forces are defined as functional performance attributes for the drug device combination product and are tested following applicable sections of ISO11608-1 as part of the design verification (including end of shelf-life testing).
Those forces are equivalent to breakout/ sustain forces for a filled/stoppered bulk syringe. The priming and injection forces consider hydrodynamic and friction forces of the bulk PFS combined with the friction forces of the fully assembled Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL drug device combination product (including the customized finger flange and plunger rod).
As outlined in section P.3.3.01-01 the priming and injection forces are considered as In-Process Controls for the packaging process of the Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL PFS with an acceptance criterion of ≤ 30 N. These IPC tests will be performed during routine commercial production.
In combination with the additional performance tests this ensures that the drug device combination functions as intended. Therefore, the applicant considers it appropriate that breakout/ sustain forces are not included in the drug product’s release and shelf-life specification.
(iii) As pointed out in section P.5.6.01-01, the applicant harmonized the test procedure and acceptance criteria for sub-visible particles of the Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL prefilled syringe with the approved Aflibercept solution 40 mg/mL prefilled syringe. The limits of the 40 mg/mL prefilled syringe were defined based on available batch data and independently from the vial presentation when switching the sub-visible particles test of the PFS from Light-Obscuration (Method 1) to Microscopy (Method 2). The approved test method and acceptance criteria of the Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL vial are harmonized with the 40 mg/mL vial.
Table 1: Comparison of sub-visible particles test method and acceptance criteria
40 mg/mL PFS / 114.3 mg/mL PFS / 114.3 mg/mL vial / 40 mg/mL vial
Acceptance criteria (particles/mL):
a. Particles ≥ 10 μm; b. Particles ≥ 25 μm
PFS: a. ≤ 200; b. ≤ 20
Vial: a. ≤ 2000; b. ≤ 50
Test method:
PFS: Ph. Eur. 2.9.19 Method 2
Vial: Ph. Eur. 2.9.19 Method 1
The acceptance criteria of the PFS are based on, but more stringent than the Ph. Eur. 2.9.19 and are supported by the PFS process performance qualification batches.

Question:
Question 5
Section 1.1.0-P3&1.1.1:
[Item 29]:
[Release Specification]:
(i).The release specification mentioned that the test on sterility (Syringe in blister tray) follow in- house testing method but not Ph. Eur. 2.6.1 like the shelf-life spec. However, the COA provided mentioned following Ph. Eur. 2.6.1. Please explain the discrepancy.
(ii). Please explain why many steps of testing are on product after aseptic filling but not after blistering and outer surface sterilization?
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 5 (3.2.P.5.1, 3.2.P.5.2, 3.2.P.5.6):
(i) The standard method for testing the sterility (Syringe in blister tray) is the in-house method using bioindicators, which was also applied to the batch KT0S635 presented in the CoA. This method is therefore also reflected in the release specification in P.5.1.01-01 and in the testing procedure in P.5.2.01-01.
However, in case of deviations during the outer sterilization of the syringe in blister tray the method according to Ph. Eur. 2.6.1 can be applied to test the sterility. Both methods are suitable to show sterility of the finished product and are listed as alternatives in the CoA.
(ii). As already mentioned in the response to Question 1 (i), the labeling, assembly, blistering, and outer surface sterilization (LABS) process may occur several months after the filling process, whereas the shelf-life of the DP starts after the filling process. The bulk PFS batch size comprises approximately 60,000 syringes, while the sterilization batch size was validated between 3,200 and 12,800 PFS. Each bulk PFS batch (parent) will therefore yield several outer surface sterilized (daughter) batches.
To accommodate this aspect, it is intended to register a release testing approach where all tests, which are not affected by the outer surface sterilization process, are tested on bulk PFS batches (parent batch) only, especially since release specification acceptance criteria were derived from testing of Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in vial batches shortly after manufacturing, while labeling, assembly, blistering and sterilization of PFS can occur several months after filling. Such a release testing approach was approved and successfully introduced for the Aflibercept solution 40 mg/mL in prefilled syringe.
The results from the side-by-side analytical comparison of bulk and sterilized PFS batches, presented in P.5.6.01-01, demonstrate that the labeling, assembly, blistering and outer surface sterilization processes for Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in prefilled syringe for intravitreous injection (PFS) that is performed at Bayer AG, Berlin do not have a meaningful impact on any of the purity and potency quality attributes tested.
The data confirm that release testing for purity and potency of Aflibercept PFS before the LABS processes is appropriate for batch release and representative also for the product after LABS. The release test matrix in Table 2-1 of P.5.6.01-01 is therefore appropriate for maintaining control over the quality of the final drug product, i.e. the blistered and sterilized PFS.

Question:
Question 15
15. 3.2.S.3.2. MUTAGENIC IMPURITIES. Considering the use of p-toluenesulfonic acid and 
low molecular weight alcohols (ethanol and methanol) in the synthesis of API, discuss the 
formation and control of alkyl derivatives of p-toluenesulfonic acid, substances known to 
be mutagenic.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 15 ( CTD section):
Ethyl and methyl p-toluenesulfonate (tosylate) are class 2 compounds according to the 
classifications in ICH guideline M7. They are potential by-products from the condensation 
reaction between p-toluenesulfonic acid and the respective alcohol, ethanol and methanol. P-
toluenesulfonic acid and ethanol are employed in synthesis step 2b of the manufacturing process 
of BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance and methanol may be present as a residual 
solvent in the transiently isolated and dried product of step 2a, BAY 2927088 crude.
Yet, the risk of the formation of both ethyl and methyl p-toluenesulfonate in step 2b is 
considered negligible, as the following factors in that step impose substantial barriers for any 
such unwanted sulfonic acid esterification, which are well documented in a review from 2015 
[D. Snodin, A. Teasdale, Org. Process Res. Dev. 2015, 19, 1465−1485].
• Equimolar amounts of p-toluenesulfonic acid monohydrate and BAY 2927088 crude
are combined to form a salt solution of the drug substance, thus hampering the acid’s 
ability to protonate alcohols, as is a prerequisite for alkyl tosylate formation. Moreover, 
a superstoichiometric amount of sodium hydroxide, employed to generate and 
crystallize the drug substance in its free base form in the later part of the process 
diminishes the chances for such side reactions even further.
• A large fraction of 24% (w/w) of the solvent mixture comprises water, sufficient even
in unbuffered systems to reportedly put sulfonic acid esterification almost entirely to a 
halt.
• Due to its nature as a (pH-shift) recrystallization, step 2b lacks any prolonged holding
or reaction times and operates at mildly elevated temperatures, thus further reducing the 
likelihood of any notable alkyl tosylate formation.
Despite the above considerations, in order to further safeguard the absence of ethyl and methyl 
tosylate in the final drug substance, the fate and purge of ethyl tosylate was investigated by a 
spiking experiment. Of 10% of ethyl tosylate (with respect to the mass of BAY 2927088 crude) 
which were added at the beginning of step 2b, none was detected in isolated BAY 2927088 
purified intermediate (at a limit of quantification of 0.02%). With that purge alone, even 41% 
of ethyl tosylate, which would be the amount resulting from the esterification of the entire 
amount of subjected p-toluenesulfonic acid monohydrate, would be purged to no more than 
0.08% of ethyl tosylate in BAY 2927088 purified, which is already below the acceptable limit 
of max. 0.10%, in line with ICH guideline S9.
As for methyl tosylate, the fact that its precursor methanol may solely be introduced in small 
amounts into step 2b as a residual solvent in BAY 2927088 crude, as opposed to ethanol 
employed as solvent, renders its formation even less likely than that of ethyl tosylate.
In conclusion, the absence of alkyl tosylates in BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug 
substance is secured within step 2b, as neither the formation, nor retention of alkyl tosylates are 
expectable, based on applicable literature precedence and experimentation.

Source:  S.2.4.10-01/ Control of Critical Steps and Intermediates - Additional
Information/BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance/ S.2.4.10_IQMS-
400119_1.0/new

Question:
Question 16
16. 3.2.S.4.5 (SPECIFICATION JUSTIFICATION). We inform you that the approval of the 
DS-Pyridone impurity limit is subject to the approval of the impurity qualification study by the 
Safety and Efficacy Analysis Management (GESEF). Therefore, we request that the company 
request a specific amendment (subject: 12224 - RDC 359/2020 - Evaluation of the safety limit 
of impurities (ICH guides Q3A, Q3C, Q3D, M7 and their updates)), containing the 
documentation related to the qualification of the DS-Pyridone impurity.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 16 (3.2.S.4.5):
We would like to clarify that, according to Informative Item 1 of the amendment subject 12224 
in SOLICITA website and in the ‘Subject Consultation’ section of the ANVISA website: 
‘Informational Item 1: This amendment refers to situations where the impurities to be qualified 
are present only in the API. If impurities or degradation products are also found in the finished 
product (DP), please submit a single document using subject code 12380. The 12224 protocol 
is not required.

Since DS-Pyridone is present not only in the API but also in the DP, the 12224 protocol is not 
required. 
 
Additionally, we would like to clarify that Bayer has not submitted the amendment code 12380 
for the DP because in accordance with RDC 964/2025 (which establishes the general 
requirements for conducting Forced Degradation Studies on medicines containing synthetic and 
semi-synthetic active pharmaceutical ingredients and defines the parameters for the 
notification, identification and qualification of degradation products in these products):  
 
Art. 19 states that ‘A degradation product may be considered qualified when it meets at least 
one of the following conditions:  
I - the degradation product is a significant metabolite identified during studies in humans or 
animals.  
 
Considering that DS-pyridone is a major metabolite, it falls within the limits for toxicological 
qualification as stated in “S.4.5.01-02 - Justification of Specification and Skip Testing” and, 
according to the “NDA 219972 – Sevabertinib (BAY 2927088) – 2.6.6 Toxicology Written 
Summary” (presented on 12/May/2025, expedient nº 0637512250, during NDA submission): 
“The major human metabolite M1, BAY 3306572 (DS-pyridone), is also the major metabolite 
in the rat and cynomolgus monkey. M1 is produced at high levels in monkeys. The metabolite 
was also quantified in the 13-week repeated dose toxicity studies and in the reproductive 
toxicity studies in the rat.”  Therefore, we can conclude that DS-pyridone complies with Art. 
19, item I of RDC 964/2025, which, makes amendment 12380 inapplicable. 
 
In conclusion, we respectfully request the reconsideration of your request to perform the    
specific amendment “12224 - RDC 359/2020 - Evaluation of the impurity safety limit (ICH 
guides Q3A, Q3C, Q3D, M7 and their updates)” to GESEF, as it is not applicable to the API – 
Sevabertinib.”

Source:  
S.4.5.01-02 - Justification of Specification and Skip Testing/ / BAY 2927088 
hydrate micronized drug substance/ S.4.5.01_IQMS-263705_2.0/unchanged

million lux-hours) do not meet the content and color discounts. Therefore, we understand that 
the API is light sensitive. Therefore, we request that the company present justifications and a

amount of water detected 
In conclusion, a new photostability study will not be conducted and the API will be declared as

Question:
Comment 8
Long R3 IGF-1 was identified as a process related impurity found in the DS at ≤0.02 ppm. 
However, a risk assessment of the impact of Long R3 IGF-1 was not provided. Provide a risk 
assessment for worst case exposure of Long R3 IGF-1 to patient safety.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Comment 8 (S.3.2):
Bayer provides the below risk assessment for worst case exposure of Long R3 IGF-1 to 
patient safety.
The maximum amount of insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) in the drug was determined to 
be 0.02 ng/mg. This corresponds to a maximum amount of 0.02 µg when applying a dose of 
925 mg BAY 3401016 which would result from the loading and maintenance dose together. 
Basal levels of IGF-1 in serum differ significantly depending on age. IGF-1 values in the 
range of 100 to 400 ng/mL are reported normal for healthy adult subjects (Zhu et al. 2017, 
Chanson et al. 2016, Sabbah et al. 2021). Given a mean blood volume of 5 L per person, the 
total amount of IGF-1 in the circulation is in the range of 500 to 2000 µg / individual. It can 
be excluded that an additional entry of 0.02 µg IGF-1 by administration of the worst case dose 
of 925 mg should have an unintended pharmacological or toxicological effect. In the study,
after the initial loading dose of 700 mg, weekly administrations of 225 mg BAY 3401016 are 
planned thus even lower additional entry amounts are expected.

Source:  S.3.2.01-03 Impurities / BAY 3401016 (#022989733_03; unchanged)
References:
• Zhu et al. 2017, doi: 10.1371/journal.pone.0185561
• Chanson et al. 2016, doi: 10.1210/jc.2016-1257
• Sabbah et al. 2021, doi: 10.1530/EC-21-0175
