Question: You are requested to provide a detailed narrative description of the drug product manufacturing process (10 mg, 20 mg and 40 mg tablets and 3.4% granules) that includes equipment types and process parameters such as blend speed, blend time, spray rate, temperature, coating parameters, etc.
Answer:
Please note that the additional information to narrative description of the drug product manufacturing process for the tablet formulations as well as for the granules are for information only. The submitted IMPD-Q information reflects the current development status and was also submitted and approved by Health Canada for the other pediatric studies conducted by Bayer Inc. namely FIONA study (19920, e258048, Control#258048) and FIONA-OLE study (20186, e283357, Control#283357).

In the following section the additional information to manufacturing process for the granules are presented.

Manufacturing process BAY 94-8862 granules 3.4%
The drug product BAY-94-8862 granules 3.4% for oral suspension is currently still in the development phase and the process has not yet been validated, therefore changes to the process equipment and parameters are still feasible.

Screening and Optional Milling of Citric Acid Anhydrous and Sodium Citrate
All excipients are pre-screened through a sieve (e.g. Russell Finex 22). The excipients are sieved through a 500 µm sieve (e.g. Russell Finex 22).

Manufacture of Granulation Liquid
Hypromellose 5 cP is dispersed in purified water in bulk. BAY 94-8862 micronized is dispersed in the hypromellose dispersion by homogenization with a high-performance disperser (e.g. IKA Ultraturrax T65).

Manufacture of Premix
The components mannitol, methyl parahydroxybenzoate, microcrystalline cellulose, carmellose sodium, sucralose and xanthan gum are sieved and then mixed in the fluid-bed granulator.

Granulation
The premix is granulated with the granulation liquid in the fluid-bed granulator (e.g. Diosna CAP150) . Afterwards, the granules are dried. The granules are sieved through a 800 µm sieve (e.g. Russell Finex 22).

In Table 1 the current available process parameters are provided, which might be changed in the later development phase of this product.

Table 1: Overview of process parameters used for manufacturing process of BAY-94-8862 granules 3.4% for oral suspension
Phase
Preheating step: Inlet air volume 600 m3/h; Inlet air temperature 55 °C; Spray rate n/a; Atomizing air pressure n/a
Pre-blending and preheating: Inlet air volume 600 m3/h; Inlet air temperature 55 °C; Preheating time: Until product temperature reaches 35 °C
Granulation/Spraying phase: Inlet air volume 600 m3/h; Inlet air temperature 55 °C; Spray rate 100 g/min; Atomizing air pressure 2.5 bar; Target product temperature: 31 °C – 33 °C
Granulation/Drying phase: Inlet air volume 600 m3/h; Inlet air temperature 55 °C; Endpoint of drying: <2.5%

Blending
The blending is performed with a blender (e.g. Pharmatech LC400). The granules are blended with pre-screened citric acid anhydrous, flavor strawberry and sodium citrate.
Blending speed: 20 rpm
Blending time: 25 min

Packaging
Fill BAY 94-8862 granules 3.4% for oral suspension into glass bottles. Close the bottles with screw caps. The bottle filling is performed on a high speed filling line (e.g. All Fill Series 2 PIB bottle line). The filling is based on a volumetric principle. In addition a 100% mass control is implemented.

IPCs
Loss on drying is performed.

In the following section the additional information to manufacturing process for the tablets are presented.

Manufacturing process of Finerenone coated tablets 10 mg, 20 mg and 40 mg
In addition to the already given information in the section 3.3 of 2.1.P part of the IMPD-Q documents following details regarding to equipment and process parameters used in the production of tablet formulation are presented for information only.

For the manufacturing of pilot scale batches with 54.4 kg (for the 10 mg and 20 mg tablets) or 51.75 kg (for the 40 mg tablets) following equipment is used (see Table 2).

Table 2: Overview of equipment and equipment parameters used for the production of pilot scale batches of Finerenone coated tablets 10 mg, 20 mg and 40 mg
Mixing: fluidized bed granulator (e.g. FBG 60 (Glatt)); 220 L granulator volume; fluidized bed granulator; mixing
Granulation and drying: fluidized bed granulator (e.g. FBG 60 (Glatt)); 220 L granulator volume; fluidized bed granulator; automatic granulating, drying
Screening (granules): dry screen (e.g. Frewitt MG 636 oscillating); motor power 1.4 kW; oscillating beater granulator mill; screening
Mixing: mixer (e.g. Müller FTMH-300 MG 1); 300 L volume; drum blender; automatic mixing
Tablet compression: rotary tablet press (e.g. Korsch PH 230); max. 122400 tablets/hour; power assisted tablet press; automatic tableting
Manufacturing of coating suspension: homogenizer (e.g. IKA RW 16 Basic); 40 – 1,200 rpm speed range; electronic overhead laboratory stirrer; mixing
Film-coating: pan coater (e.g. Bohle BFC 50 Tripan Coater); max. 75 kg; perforated pan coating system; automatic coating

For the manufacturing of pilot scale batches with 54.4 kg (for the 10mg+20mg tablets) or 51.75 kg (for the 40mg tablets) following process parameters are used (see Table 3).

Table 3: Overview of process parameters used for the production of pilot scale batches of Finerenone coated tablets 10mg, 20mg and 40 mg
Mixing (Fluidized bed granulator): fluidization until 32 °C product temperature are reached; inlet air volume: 500-700 m³/h
Granulation (Granulation suspension vessel): time: min. 5 min; homogenization
Granulation (Fluid bed granulator): spray rate: 440 (400 – 480) kg/min; prod. temperature: 30 (28 – 32) °C; spray pressure: 4.5 (4.0 – 5.0) bar
Drying: end point of drying product temperature: up to 40 °C; humidity: 1-3 % (LoD)
Sieving and Blending: Screen (granules) screen size: equals 1.0 mm; Screen (lubricant) screen size: 0.5 mm; Tumble mixer with container time: approx. 5 min; speed: 15 (14-16 rpm)

Question: It was noted that black specks were observed during the stability testing of the granules. Therefore, you are requested to explain this observation (root cause analysis), its impact on overall safety/quality of the granules and the corrective/preventive actions taken.
Answer:
The black particles were detected during stability testing and analyzed by a particle lab, which concluded that the foreign particles observed were technically unavoidable particles (TUP) from the excipient microcrystalline cellulose (MCC) and carboxymethylcellulose. A supplier statement is attached to our response (see Module 3.2.P.8.3, Supplier statement to TUP dated Oct-2023). It provides a summary of the sources, formation and nature of TUP in various excipients and concludes that “low levels of visible particles can result from the excipient manufacturing, handling or packaging processes, which do not look like the rest of the batch but pose no risk to formulation and patient safety”.

On every occurrence of TUPs – either during manufacturing, release of a batch or during stability studies – the occurrence was documented including the size of the particles. There is the potential that TUPs will be determined in upcoming batches as well as they are unavoidable.

However, based on the information provided above it can be concluded that there is no impact on the overall safety/quality of the granules.

Source: Supplier statement to TUP dated Oct-2023

Question:
Question 1 a:
You stated that Calcobutrol is added in a 0.1% mol/mol ratio with regard to the total
gadolinium (bound in gadoquatrane) in the final formulation to chelate potential free
gadolinium, forming the gadobutrol complex. From drug product perspective, the
gadobutrol complex can be treated as impurity and therefore, it should be included in the
drug product specifications with appropriate acceptance criterion. Provide justification
for the established limits based on data.
Answer:
Bayer respectfully does not believe that considering gadobutrol as a drug product impurity is 
appropriate for the following reasons:
1. Calcobutrol is added as a scavenger to complex any amounts of free gadolinium.
Therefore there is a fixed upper limit to the amount of gadobutrol that can be formed 
in the drug product defined by the amount of calcobutrol   Higher amounts are not 
possible, and amounts of free gadolinium that would exceed the amount of available 
calcobutrol are unlikely and would be detected during release testing.  Gadobutrol  
should therefore not be considered a degradation product for purposes of specification 
setting.

2. The amount of gadobutrol present in the product is several orders of magnitude below
the amounts determined to be safe for use as a drug product in the approved product 
Gadavist.  Since the amount cannot increase above a fixed threshold, setting a 
specification for gadobutrol adds cost and complexity while not providing any 
additional level of control over safety.
Further details on our rationale for not setting a specification is provided below.
According to the guideline ICH Q6A, section 1.2 a specification “establishes the set of criteria 
to which a drug substance or drug product should conform to be considered acceptable for its 
intended use.” and that specification “...should focus on those characteristics found to be 
useful in ensuring the safety and efficacy of the drug substance and drug product”. Moreover, 
under section 2.4 Design And Development Consideration, ICH Q6A list several examples of 
when “It may be possible to propose excluding or replacing certain tests..” on the basis of 
experience and data accumulated during the development of a new drug product, e.g. 
“extractables from product containers where it has been reproducibly shown that either no 
extractables are found in the drug product or the levels meet accepted standards for safety;”.

The maximum amount of gadobutrol that can form is limited by the amount of calcobutrol in 
the formulation, which according to the specification may not exceed 0.235 mg/mL and which 
in turn limits gadobutrol to a maximum of 0.291 mg/mL (0.11% in terms of the nominal 
concentration of gadoquatrane in gadoquatrane solution). Gadobutrol being the active 
ingredient of Gadavist®, a contrast agent that has been approved and marketed in the United 
States for over a decade, is qualified in humans at much higher limits. As discussed in 
P.5.6.01 the human exposure to gadobutrol would be at least 2078-fold higher when using 
Gadavist® compared to the theoretically possible amount of gadobutrol in Gadoquatrane 
solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection. Therefore, the level of gadobutrol cannot exceed 
accepted standards and a specification would not contribute to ensuring safety or efficacy.
Moreover, there is a clear negative correlation between the amount of calcobutrol and 
gadobutrol, and a positive correlation between the formation of Mono-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane 
and gadobutrol in the formulation as can be seen from Figure 2-1 and Table 2.4 in P.5.6.01 
and as shown by experiments involving multiple sterilization cycles to force the formation of 
gadobutrol from calcobutrol. Thus, implicitly gadobutrol is controlled by the lower limit of 
calcobutrol and by the upper limits for Mono-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane Isomer 1 and 2.

Bayer believes that the conversion of calcobutrol to gadobutrol is a situation comparable to 
the conversion of the active form of an preservative or antioxidant agent to its inactive form in 
such formulations. For preservative or antioxidant agents it seems acceptable to ensure an 
effective concentration of the preservative agent or antioxidant only by monitoring their 
assay, as is done for calcobutrol, whereas it is not required to also track the reaction products 
of the preservative or antioxidant, as the use of such compounds is generally recognized as 
safe. As the conversion path for calcobutrol is fully understood and leads to gadobutrol, a 
compound with a known safety profile, for that human exposure will always be far below safe 
limits when administering Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection complying 
with the specifications that Bayer proposed. An additional specification of gadobutrol is not 
considered relevant to the quality, safety or efficacy of  Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol 
Gd/mL for injection as it should not be decisive for the acceptability of the product.

Source:  P.5.6.01_022992844-02 (IQMS-265606) Justification of
Specification/ Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection 
(unchanged)

Question:
Question 1b
In addition to the possible degradation product ‘Mono-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane’, it appears
that there are 2 more possible degradation products, i.e., Di-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane and
Tri-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane. Both degradation products should also be included in the
specifications with appropriate acceptance criteria. Provide justification for the
established limits based on data.
Answer:
It is accurate to state that Di-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane and Tri-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane are 
theoretical degradation products that would arise from the twofold or threefold loss of 
Gadolinium from the tetrameric complex, however the formation of relevant amounts of Di- 
and Tri-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane in Gadoquatrane solution can be excluded for the following 
reasons:
• 
The formation of Di-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane and Tri-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane from the 
tetrameric Gadoquatrane (Gd4L) only occurs under very harsh acidic conditions (e.g. pH 
1.2, 37°C, 5 weeks incubation) by proton assisted dissociation, and it follows a stepwise 
dissociation encompassing the following reactions:
Gd4L → Gd + Gd3L → 2 Gd + Gd2L → 3 Gd + GdL  
(reference 1)
At physiological pH and temperature, the proton concentration is low, and accordingly the 
dissociation of Gd3+ ions from macrocyclic gadolinium-based contrast agents could be 
shown to be extremely slow. See reference 1 at the end of the page 6. 
 
• 
Compared to the physiological conditions (37°C, pH 7.4, 15 days) used in reference 1, 
temperatures occurring during bulk manufacturing are typically not much higher than 
37°C or of only short duration and pH not lower than 7.2. Only for a short duration during 
terminal sterilization is the product exposed to higher temperatures.
(P.2.3.01, P.3.3.01)
• The value of the 4 complex formation constants of Gadoquatrane should be very
similar and the log k of about 20-21 clearly illustrates that thermodynamically the 
equilibrium clearly lies on side of the gadolinium complex. This means that the 
propensity for the formation of desgadolinium complexes will decrease if Gd3L 
increases as the back reaction to Gd4L will become more important. 
(S.1.3.01, section 7)
• The release and shelf-life specification require the pH of the solution to be between
6.9 and 7.9. 
(P.5.1.01 / P.5.1.02)
• Given the stepwise dissociation, the low propensity to dissociation and the large
excess of Gadoquatrane (Gd4L), Mono-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane (Gd3L ) can reasonably 
be expected to be the most abundant of the des-gadolinium compounds. The 
maximum amount of Mono-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane Isomer 1 and Isomer 2 allowed by 
the specification is 0.40% (in sum). Assuming that the same percentage of Di-Des-Gd-
Gadoquatrane (Gd2L ) forms from Mono-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane (Gd3L), this would 
correspond to only 0.0016% (in terms of the API), which is much lower than the 
reporting threshold. The amount of Tri-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane (GdL) would be 
0.000064%. This consideration confirms that these compounds are not expected to 
occur in Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection above the reporting 
threshold (0.05%).

1 
Gruendemann, Frenzel, Lohrke, Boyken, Jost, Berger, Ulbrich, Pietsch, Investigative
Radiology 2025, DOI: 10.1097/RLI.0000000000001195

then ramp up to xx Celsius, then xx hours ramp down to xx negative Celsius. The thermal

specifications. Also, data should be collected throughout the studies rather than only 2 time

Initial approval of parametric release at the Bayer AG site at Müllerstrasse (same as

Question:
Question 17
3.2.P.8.3 Stability Data
The ASEAN Guideline on Stability Study of Drug Product is applicable for products in 
Singapore which is in the ASEAN stability zone IVb condition of 30C/75%RH.
The general condition for long term stability testing condition of the drug product is therefore 
30C/75%RH, to demonstrate the complete stability profile of the drug product under this 
storage condition. For drug products packaged in semi-permeable containers, additional water 
loss studies at 30C/35%RH is required.
We note the pre-filled syringes is made from cycloolefin polymer material and is not 
completely impermeable to water vapour.
Please provide the long-term stability studies at 30C/75%RH and water loss studies at 
30C/35%RH for the pre-filled syringes presentation.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 17 (3.2.P.8.3 Stability Data):
Bayer confirms that the pre-filled syringes presentation is a semi-permeable container. Please 
find water loss studies at 30C/35%RH for the pre-filled syringes presentation enclosed 
(P.8.3.11).

Regarding long-term storage conditions we would like to make reference to ICH Q1A, 
chapter 2.2.7.3. Drug products packaged in semi-permeable containers which states the 
following for long term storage conditions for aqueous-based products packaged in semi-
permeable containers: 25°C ± 2°C/40% RH ± 5% RH or 30°C ± 2°C/35% RH ± 5% RH.
Furthermore, the guideline states “Alternative storage conditions can be used, if justified.”.
While recognizing that the ASEAN Guideline on Stability Study of Drug Product is 
applicable for products in Singapore which is in the ASEAN stability zone IVb condition of 
30C/75%RH, it is our understanding that also the ASEAN Guideline allows for “…other 
storage conditions … if justified…”.
Taking this into account we would like to ask you consider the justification for storage 
conditions for Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL in prefilled syringe for injection as an 
aqueous-based product packaged in semi-permeable containers which is provided in the 
following.
Justification for long-term study design:
Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL prefilled syringes is an aqueous solution. As 
opposed to other formulation types (e.g. tablets, granules, emulsions, etc.) contact with water 
or water vapor or small changes in water content are typically uncritical or not applicable for 
aqueous solutions, where the API and excipients are dissolved in water anyways, e.g. no 
change in degradation pathways or kinetics is expected.
Moreover, in a closed container, the water vapor in the headspace will be in equilibrium with 
the aqueous solution and a relative humidity of close to 100% RH can be assumed for the 
headspace volume. Independent from the outer humidity, the only risk is a change in the 
concentration of dissolved materials (e.g. API, excipients) due to water loss, that could result 
in changes of test attributes as assay gadoquatrane, osmolality or pH. Given the smaller 
gradient between inside and outside the syringe, the water loss will be much lower at 75%RH 
compared to 35%RH. Using 30°C/35%RH is therefore a worst case compared to 
30°C/75%RH. Bayer is convinced that deriving the stability profile of Gadoquatrane solution 
0.4 mmol Gd/mL at 30°C/35%RH is adequate to demonstrate stability of Gadoquatrane 
solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for climatic zone IVb conditions as well.
Moreover, Bayer commits to include Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL in prefilled 
syringe for injection into the ongoing stability program at 30°C/75%RH. Furthermore, the 
next batch manufactured of Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL 5 ml, 7.5. mL, 10 mL 
and 15 mL in prefilled syringe will be put on ongoing stability at 30°C/75%RH.

Question:
CMC Question 2
Supplementary Request Reason: Insufficient information and evidence for the master cell 
bank (S.2.3)
Supplementary Request:  ① Submit detailed information on the manufacturer of the master 
cell bank. ② Submit detailed data on the establishment of monoclonality for the master cell 
bank.
HA Comment : additional explanation is needed regarding point . ② Photos of the equipment used and the 
series of processes are required. While the photo for day 0 is confirmed in figure 2-2, request submission of 
photos for the subsequent days as well.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2 (S.2.3):
Part 1:
The MCB (master cell bank) was manufactured at the Bayer HealthCare LLC site in Berkeley, 
CA, USA.

Part 2:
Transfectant cell pool (CLI-724629) was single cell cloned by using a single cell printer 
(Cytena, Freiburg, Germany) into 384WPs (well plates). The device can eliminate droplets 
which contain more than one cell using parameters such as roundness and shape of the cells to 
prevent the deposition of cell doublets (or multiple cells) into each well. To further enhance 
the monoclonality, the 384WPs were imaged with Cell Metric (refer to Figure 7) before and 
after the single cell deposition into these plates. The printing process of the single cell 
containing droplet (CLI-732458, see Figure 8) is captured by pictures before, during and after 
printing (refer to Figure 9, Figure 10, Figure 11). In order to ensure all cells are in the focal 
plane of the imager, the 384WPs are centrifuged right after the single cell deposition prior to 
imaging, and again in the following days (day 0, 1, 4 and 7, see below) to track the growth of 
single cells into colonies. Only the colonies derived from a single cell on day 0 plus the 
respective single cell printer nozzle pictures from Cytena showing single cell deposition were 
considered for the top clones. With these processes and image verification a probability of 
monoclonality of 99.9% can be obtained based on the mixing studies performed internally and 
from the literature (Yim and Shaw, Biotechnol. Prog., 2018, Vol. 34, No. 6; doi: 
10.1002/btpr.2698).

Answer: Sample collection following compatibility testing is performed in a non-aseptic laboratory environment using standard containers. Due to the ubiquitous presence of fibrous particles (e.g., from lab coats or gloves), incidental fiber introduction into sample containers during handling cannot be entirely ruled out. Importantly, this type of contamination is not applicable in clinical use, where the product is administered directly to the patient without intermediate sampling. Therefore, no control measures are needed.

Question:
Question 1
Your current specifications propose to replace the existing HPLC and UV/VIS identity tests 
with Near-Infrared Spectroscopy (NIRS) as a single identification method. The proposed 
NIRS method may serve as one identification technique; however, you must retain or 
implement a second, fundamentally different analytical approach that provides independent 
confirmation of identity through a different analytical method.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (P.5):
The identification of Darolutamide drug product by NIRS spectroscopy contains two 
fundamentally separate identification models incorporated to the NIRS method.
The first is based on Euclidean distance of identification model, where specific threshold 
value (0.277) has been determined with verified samples (positive identification) by primary 
HPLC method (HPLC 1). The identification model was validated with 27 independent 
Darolutamide drug product tablets (on concentration range 60 – 140%) and one negative 
challenge sample. The sample mold is specific for Darolutamide drug product tablet size and 
negative challenge sample was selected as being the same size and form. In addition, the 
negative challenge sample contains three Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (API), which 
have similar functional groups and structures as Darolutamide. All known samples (positive) 
had hit quality values below the set threshold value (0.277) of the identification model. The 
negative challenge test sample had hit quality value of 0.717, well above the set threshold 
value for Darolutamide, and failed the identity test. Based on positive identification of known 
samples it can be extrapolated that the identification model (Euclidean distance) would reject 
a sample that is free of the Darolutamide compound.
The second identification is based on Mahalanobis distance of assay model (PLS algorithm) 
where specific threshold value (1.0) has been determined with verified samples (assay values) 
by primary HPLC method (HPLC 1). Assay model was validated with known samples of 
Darolutamide drug product and all Mahalanobis distance results were below the set threshold 
value (1.0).
In summary, the identification with NIRS method is conducted in two steps. At first samples 
need to pass the identification by Euclidean distance threshold (identification model). Second 
step is identification of assay model by Mahalanobis distance. Samples need to pass 
identification of both identification model and assay model to be released.

Source:  P.5.1.01-04 Release Specification / Darolutamide film-coated tablet 0.3 g
(#IQMS-406804; amended)

Question:
Question 3
Your application proposes to reduce the testing frequency for degradation products and 
microbial purity from every batch at release to testing at least one in every ten batches (skip-
lot testing). However, you have not provided adequate scientific justification or supporting 
data to demonstrate that this reduced testing frequency is appropriate and will not compromise 
product quality or patient safety. Provide comprehensive historical batch data and justification 
to support your proposal for skip-lot testing.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 3 (P.5):
Additional supporting data for reduced testing frequency for degradation product and 
microbial purity are provided in 3.2.P.5.6.02, Justification of Skip Testing. Historical data 
comprising 115 batches from Jan-2024 through Dec-2024 on degradation products and 
microbial purity are presented in Table 3-1 and Table 3-3, respectively. Additional batch 
analysis for every tenth batch (n=33) throughout the production history, excluding the year 
2024, on degradation products and microbial purity are presented in Table 3-2 and Table 3-4, 
respectively. Degradation products of the drug product, consisting of Keto-darolutamide, any 
unspecified degradation product, and sum of all degradation products, remain below limit-of-
quantitation in the batches analyzed. Microbial purity, consisting of Total aerobic microbial 
count, Total combined yeast/mould count, and Escherichia coli, also remain below limit-of-
quantitation in the batches analyzed.
The product has a very low water activity (Aw) which greatly assists in the prevention of 
microbiological proliferation and ensuring the quality of the product. Based on extensive 
experience, the manufacturing process is robust, consistently producing batches within the 
specifications, as demonstrated by the provided historical data. Furthermore, the product is 
very stable as proven by the various long-term, accelerated and stress condition stability 
studies.
Therefore, implementation of skip testing for degradation products and microbial purity, 
performed at release on every tenth batch, is considered justified for the Darolutamide film- 
coated tablet 0.3 g.

Source:  P.5.6.02-02 Justification of Skip Testing / Darolutamide film-coated tablet 0.3
g (Degradation Products and Microbial Purity) (#0IQMS-406925; amended)

Question:
Question 2-4:
Please provide relevant assessment reports or study data to demonstrate whether the TA strategy
and LOV monitoring are comparable (or if one is superior). Explain the rationale for classifying
LOV as an IPC parameter while the TA strategy is evaluated as a non-IPC parameter. Assess
whether the revised process control strategy can effectively monitor the manufacturing process.
It is recommended to consider including the TA strategy as an IPC parameter.
Answer:
Bayer response to Q2-4:
Chromatography Lift-off Volume (LOV) has previously been classified as a general (non-
critical) quality attribute by the applicant (see present / approved 3.2.S.2.4.01). It is employed
for the Protein A, Cation Exchange, Anion Exchange, Hydrophobic Interaction and Size
Exclusion chromatography steps as a potential indication of chromatography performance and
to signal potential deterioration of a given column.
As a result of a review of the control strategy, the single IPC parameter (LOV) to monitor the
column performance will be replaced by a more comprehensive and robust transition analysis
(TA). TA in combination with chromatogram review will be used outside of the IPC program
as part of a holistic strategy to continuously monitor column performance as part of the
company quality system.
The following long-term evaluation was performed and concluded that TA is equivalent or
more effective at detecting column deterioration:
Along with lift-off volume (LOV) monitoring, transition analysis (TA) data were used to
analyze the aflibercept lots processed between 25Jan2013 and 31Dec2020 (1,151 lots).
Regeneron routinely evaluates TA data with respect to unit operation-specific historically
accepted limits for non-gaussian height equivalent of a theoretical plate (NGHETP) and
skewness. Historical TA data were assessed for excursions from these historically accepted
limits. LOV and TA excursions were further categorized according to Table 2-4-1 to directly
compare efficacy and robustness of TA and LOV. A representative example from every
excursion category is detailed below.
Overview of the investigation data analyzed by both the LOV and TA methods:
Of the 1,151 lot investigations analyzed, there were 213 LOV and 20 TA excursions identified.
133 of these LOV investigations identified a root cause corresponding to Normal Process
Variability/IPC Monitoring whereas only 15 TA excursions were found in this same timeframe.
Therefore, the rate of false positives within this category was observed to be 88.7% lower for
the TA monitoring approach than for LOV.
TA is proven to have comparable robustness for detecting instances of column deterioration.
Of the 213 identified LOV excursions, three investigations were found to be attributed to
unacceptable chromatography Column Performance. TA excursions were also identified for the
three lots requiring an LOV investigation. TA identified two additional instances of column deterioration
for aflibercept which did not correspond to an observed LOV excursion. No instances of chromatography
column deterioration were identified from 25Jan2013 to 31Dec2020 that were not identified by TA.
Based on this assessment, significantly fewer false positive excursions have been historically identified
using TA and equal or superior monitoring is achieved with TA.
Examples are provided for: (1) Column Performance root cause categorization (including review and
mitigation by column repack and review of VI pool CHO HCP and step yield), (2) Normal Process
Variability/IPC Monitoring, and (3) Measurement Sensitivity.
The TA strategy is evaluated as a non-IPC parameter as multiple IPCs are monitored to ensure
proper column performance. Table 2-4-5 provides a summary of the current IPCs that ensure adequate
column performance (e.g., pool CHO protein/DNA, resin cycle number, step yield, pool SE-UPLC purity).

Question:
Question 3-3:
Please specify the involved DP strength affected by the SE-UPLC limit adjustment. It is
recommended to summarize the retrospective and monitoring stability data of multiple batches
related to the affected DP strength. Analyze and explain the reasons for the decrease in the SE-
UPLC main peak and the increase in aggregates, and justify the rationale for widening SE-
UPLC specification limit.
Answer:
Bayer response to Q3-3:
The SE-UPLC limit adjustment is only applicable to Eylea 2mg vial and PFS.
As mentioned in the change description, this change is made based on difference in testing
results between SE-HPLC and SE-UPLC due to methodological variations, no change of
current SE-UPLC method and change of product quality.
The shelf-life acceptance criteria for purity test of Eylea 2mg was initially set using SE-HPLC
data and supported by toxicological and clinical data, which was approved at the time of NDA.
Bayer applied method change from SE-HPLC to SE-UPLC in 2018, the acceptance criteria
were not changed based on the method equivalence shown in the initial method comparability
study containing a limited release data set from ten DP batches tested in parallel by SE-HPLC
and SE-UPLC. After analysis of a more comprehensive data set comprising reference standard
and 70 pairs of DP release and stability samples, measured in parallel with SE-HPLC and SE-
UPLC revealed a offset in the test results using different methods. The shelf-life acceptance
criteria shall be adjusted.
Retrospective Analysis of Reference Standard Data:
Reference standard results obtained at Bayer with both methods over a longer period of time
(SE-HPLC: 2017 to 2020; SE-UPLC: 2018 to 2020) reveal a 90% confidence interval for the
average offset of 0.34-0.37% (testing on reference standard RSVITV-5) for % aggregate (Table
3-3–1). The % main peak results display the same absolute offset in inverse direction.
Retrospective Analysis of DP Release and Stability Data:
DP release and stability samples tested in parallel (n = 70 pairs) reveal 90% confidence
intervals for the average offset of 0.29 to 0.34% aggregate and -0.25 to -0.30% main peak
(Table 3-3-2).
Based on this, Bayer concludes an SE-UPLC method offset of ~0.3% should be considered to
shift the SEC-UPLC limits at end of shelf-life to keep consistency with the previously
established method based on clinical study.
Representative Stability Data in the Past Years:
Bayer provided 20 batches of DP stability data for purity by SE-UPLC since 2018 (Tables 3-3-3
to 3-3-10). Bayer states there is no change of DP quality since all real-time stability data for
SE-UPLC purity can meet the current shelf-life specification (main peak ≥96.5%, aggregates
≤3.5%). Bayer proposes to adjust shelf-life specification with new SE-UPLC limit (main peak
≥96.2%, aggregates ≤3.8%) to reflect the observed methodological offset between SE-HPLC
and SE-UPLC.

Excerpt of Registration stability report P.8.3.01:

The main manufacturing steps, which include the high-shear wet granulation having a 
significant impact on the key quality attributes of the final product was done in the 
commercial scale of 300 kg (appr. 500,000 film-coated tablets). From this 300 kg commercial 
scale tableting mass 80 kg were used for tableting and coating of the respective primary 
stability batch (e.g. 1748671). This 80 kg tableting mass portion of the 300 kg commercial 
scale calculates to a theoretical number of 133,000 film-coated tablets (300 kg = 500,000; 80

tablets on stability was submitted in course of the NDA evaluation process (P.8.2.01-02 
submitted with response to COFEPRIS Official communication 213300404K0011).
The real-time results of these commitment batches (e.g. 1860672) - along with the data 
requested in below Question 2 - have been included in a variation to increase the shelf life of 
Nubeqal from 24 months to 36 months. Furthermore, this stability report (P.8.3.01 Stability 
Data) already contained the results for the increased batch size of 1,500,000 tablets as the 
threefold increase (309 kg to 927 kg) is considered a minor change which classifies for 
immediate implementation due to a batch size increase less than 10 times. Based on these 
stability data provided (for summary refer to Annex 3), the shelf-life extension was approved 
by COEFEPRIS early this year on 27 Jun 2025.

Question: 3.2.S.3.2: According to ICH M7, chapter 9.2 actual and potential degradation products likely to be present in the final drug substance or drug product and where the structure is known should be evaluated for mutagenic potential. The results and a description of the (Q)SAR systems used in silico are to be presented, as well as supporting information to conclude on class 4 and 5 classifications. Please submit this information for all impurities listed on tables 2-1 to 2-4 and 4-2 in tabular form with links to supporting information and the respective reports.
Answer:
Mutagenic impurities described in S.3.2.01 have been assessed using two different in silico methods: a rule-based system (DEREK Nexus, version 6.0.0) and a statistical system (Leadscope Model Applier, version: 2.4.1). Combining both approaches, the classification was concluded taking also into account potentially available experimental data for the structure itself or structurally related compounds stored in the toxicity database VITIC Nexus (version 2.6.1). In addition, experimental Ames Test data were generated and described in the Toxicology Written Summary 2.6.6. Overall results are described in S.3.2.01.
Furthermore, the underlying original report entitled NON GLP Report Version 1: Structure-based assessment of potentially mutagenic impurities, Study ID: T104685-4, Report ID: PH-41284 as well as Derek Nexus Report for fluorobisiminocarbamate from 26. January 2023 (DEREK Nexus, version 6.1.0) have been provided as well.
Based on above mentioned documents, for all impurities listed in tables 2-1 to 2-4 and 4-2 of S.3.2.01, the information justifying the classification of impurities from tables 2-1 to 2-4 and 4-2 are presented in the table below.

Name of impurity / Classification / Justification

- Fluorotrisamine; Fluorotrisamine-5-sulfoximine; 7H-Purincarbamate; Fluorobismethylcarbamate; 2-Phenyl-pyrido-carbamate; o-Semidinecarbamate; p-Semidinecarbamate; des-F-Fluoromethylcarbamate; 3-F-Fluoromethylcarbamate — Class 5 — inactive in DEREK; negative in Leadscope; A high structural similarity to the API that was negative in the Ames test
- Fluorobisiminocarbamate — Class 5 — The query structure does not match any structural alerts or examples for (bacterial in vitro) mutagenicity in Derek. Additionally, the query structure does not contain any unclassified or misclassified features and is consequently predicted to be inactive in the bacterial in vitro (Ames) mutagenicity test
- Fluorodihydropurinone — Class 5 — inactive in DEREK; positive in Leadscope (aromatic amine moiety leading to an indeterminate prediction); potential mutagenic impurity based on in silico analysis, negative Ames test data for fluorodihydropurinone

Question: Please assign a value to the Gd-GlyMe-DOTA impurity reference standard according to the mass balance method.
Answer:
The assay value of the Gd-GlyMe-DOTA impurity reference standard has been determined by mass balance according to the following formula:
A (%) = 100.0 – I – W – free Gd

A = Assay Gd-GlyMe-DOTA, as is
I = Impurities, sum (%)
W = Water (%)
Free Gd = free gadolinium

Question: The assay of impurity is low, please conﬁrm whether the assignment is accurate.
Answer: The assay of the Gd-GlyMe-DOTA impurity reference standard is 93.6%. Further components in the reference standard are water (5.7%) and organic impurities (sum of organic impurities: 0.7%). The reference standard complies to the specification of the drug substance synthesis intermediate Gd-GlyMe-DOTA. The high water content of 5.7% is due to the hygroscopic nature of the complex. Additionally, high purity is achieved through the control of organic impurities using HPLC, as well as monitoring free Gd levels. This control strategy ensures that the compound can be reliably used as a reference standard.

Question:
Question 1
1. Documents regarding the Drug Substance that comply with Article 7(2)(b) of the
regulation.
Answer:
Question 1a.
a. Related Regulation: Article 7(2)(b)
Reason for Supplement: 3.2.S.1.3. General Characteristics and 3.2.S.3.1 
Structure and Other Characteristics
1) Submission of detailed results of structural analysis on the non-quantified
hydrate form of the drug substance is required.
2) Molecular formula and molecular weight should be presented based on the
hydrated form of the drug substance.
3) Solubility data for non-polar solvents have not been submitted.
4) XRPD detailed numerical data (2Θ) for verification of the drug substance has
not been submitted and insufficient explanation of results based on the 
hydrated state.
Supplement Requirement: Please submit additional materials regarding the general 
characteristics of the drug substance considering the above matters.

Bayer Response to Question 1a. ( S.3.1):
a.1)
The drug substance in its crystalline form, Hydrate 1 Mod. A, has been fully characterized by 
thermoanalytical, spectroscopic, and X-ray diffractometric data (see S 3.1.01 Structure 
Elucidation and other Characteristics). In addition, the special non-stoichiometric character 
of this hydrate was clearly demonstrated by an X-ray single-crystal structure based on one 
single crystal. In the X-ray single-crystal analysis, it can be seen that the water molecules are 
randomly arranged between the layers of the active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) 
molecules. The crystal packing including the water molecules is shown in the following 
figures.

In addition to the interactions between the API molecule and the water molecules, 
intermolecular hydrogen bonds also occur between the water molecules, which supports the 
nonstoichiometric, variable character of Hydrate 1 Mod. A.

These different types of intermolecular interactions explain why this crystal lattice can 
implement varying numbers of water molecules without the actual lattice structure changing. 
The correlation of XRPD data to the X-ray single-crystal structure was achieved by 
comparing the calculated X-ray powder diffraction pattern with the measured X-ray powder 
diffraction pattern of the various batches of Hydrate 1 Mod. A.

Bayer acknowledges the Agency’s request to specify the amount of (x) based on the water 
content 1-4% specified for the drug substance and to include the range in the Korean 
application form.
Based on the nonstoichiometric, variable character of Hydrate 1 Mod. A with an undefined 
ratio of sevabertinib to water, a value for (x) cannot be specified.
The water content in the DS is ensured by the manufacturing process and is controlled by the 
DS specification (refer to Specification S.4.1.01). DS batches that do not comply with the 
specification will not be used to manufacture the drug product (DP). However, converting the 
acceptance criterion for water into a specified value for (x) in the structural formula would not 
be a correct representation of the DS physical structure.
The dose strength of the DP is based on the anhydrate form, specifying that each tablet 
contains 10 mg sevabertinib. The latter information is critical for ensuring the safety and 
efficacy of the drug, as it directly relates to correct dosing and is independent of the water 
content of the hydrate. In light of these considerations, Bayer proposes that no value or range 
should be specified for the water content (x) in the local application form.

a.2)
It is well-known that two kinds of hydrate formation exist[1]:
Stoichiometric hydrates have a crystal lattice based on an exact water content with a well-
defined mole ratio of water molecules and given API molecule.
Non-stoichiometric hydrates have a continuously variable composition (due to the water 
content) within a certain range without any significant changes in crystalline structure.
Hydrate 1 Mod. A belongs to the second class described above and thus exhibits variability in 
water content. This must be described by the following structural formula:
C24H25ClN4O5 · x H2O

The variable molar fraction of water in the crystal lattice of hydrate 1 Mod. A makes it 
impossible to name a molar mass based on the hydrated form. The molecular weight can only 
be provided for the anhydrous form.
In 2008 Newman, Reutzel-Edens and Zografi[2] described in their minireview the way to 
evaluate sorption data of a given pharmaceutical active ingredient by using the following 
flowchart (figure 4).

By using these criteria and based on the given definitions, Sevabertinib Hydrate (BAY 
2927088 hydrate) can be described as a non-stoichiometric hydrate, because its crystalline 
lattice is able to include variable numbers of water molecules without changes in the observed 
XRPD pattern and consequentially the crystalline structure. Water content in the drug 
substance will be controlled with the specification of 1.0 to 4.0 %.

a.3)
We have determined the requested solubility data of the solvents Tetrahydrofuran and 
Isopropyl acetate.
Solubility for Tetrahydrofuran was found to be 41.579 g/l (after 3 hours at 25°C).
Solubility for Isopropyl acetate was found to be 2.695 g/l (after 3 hours at 25°C).
This information is included in S.1.3.01 General Information - General Properties.

a.4)
Detailed numerical data (2Θ) of all technically relevant XRPD patterns of the different 
crystalline forms is provided in S.3.1.01 Structure Elucidation and other Characteristics / 
Additional Information on Polymorphism.
In RH XRPD experiments, the behavior of the crystalline lattice of Hydrate 1 Mod. A was 
examined under different humidity conditions (0 – 90% RH sorption and desorption in 10% 
steps) at a constant temperature of 25°C. In the sorption experiment, the substance (Hydrate 1 
Mod. A, Batch BXR9J78) was initially dried at 0% humidity and was present as Mod. IV at 
1% RH. This modification was retained up to 20% RH and converted in the next step to 
Hydrate 1 Mod. A. This crystal lattice then remained unchanged up to 90% RH. This effect 
was also observed in the desorption experiment: at 20% RH, Hydrate 1 Mod. A was 
converted to the anhydrous form Mod. IV. These experiments clearly demonstrate the 
behavior of Hydrate 1 Mod. A in a kinetic experimental design. It cannot be directly 
correlated with the results of the storage studies, as these are based on a thermodynamic 
approach.

The RH XRPD results perfectly match the data from the DVS measurements, which gives us 
information on the change of water amount in and on the sample BXR9J78 (Hydrate 1 Mod. 
A). Dynamic uptake (sorption) of water was observed between 0 and 10% RH, followed by a 
flatter curve up to 95% RH and a total water uptake of 4%. The desorption curve follows this 
curve in the opposite direction, not without exhibiting a slight hysteresis. This is due to the 
fact that even in a variable non-stoichiometric hydrate, intermolecular interactions must first 
be overcome to remove the water from the lattice. This process, as well as the formation of 
the crystal lattice of the metastable Mod. IV, slightly delays the kinetics of desorption 
compared to sorption.

Another technique for investigating the behavior of Hydrate 1 Mod. A upon loss of water are 
thermoanalytical methods. In this case, Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) and 
Thermogravimetry (TGA) techniques were used. The thermogram of the DSC measurement 
of sample BXR9J78 (Hydrate 1 Mod. A) initially shows a broad endothermic signal, which 
indicates the release of water. This is confirmed by the TGA measurement, which describes a 
mass loss. Unlike stoichiometric hydrates, this stage is somewhat soft and continuous, clearly 
highlighting the non-stoichiometric character of the hydrate.

After the water release, the sample fundamentally has the possibility to become amorphous or 
to convert into any of the crystal lattices of the anhydrous modifications, thereby slightly 
stabilizing the lattice. In this case, a further small endothermic process is observed at higher 
temperatures, followed by a similarly small exothermic process. This involves the melting and 
recrystallization of one of the formed anhydrous forms, followed by the melting process of 
Mod. I.
Compared to the previously described techniques, the DSC measurement is energetically non-
neutral for the applied sample and can thus significantly favor transformation processes, 
especially at higher temperatures. This leads to the observation of the melting point of Mod. I, 
while the kinetic experiments (RH XRPD and DVS) did not result in a transformation of 
Hydrate 1 Mod. A to Mod. I.

In summary, all available data support the assignment of sevabertinib hydrate as a non-
stoichiometric hydrate.
Source: S.1.3.01; S.3.1.01; S.4.1.01; [1] J.-R. Authelin, Int. J. Pharm, 303, 2005, 37–53; [2] A. W. Newman et al., J. Pharm. Sci., 97(3), 2008, 1047–1059.

Question 1b.
b. Related Regulation: Article 7(2)(b)
Reason for Supplement: 3.2.S.2.2. Manufacturing Process and Process Controls, 
specific reprocessing criteria, occurrence frequency of reprocessing, and results 
of reprocessing has not been submitted.

manufacturing process and process control of the drug substance considering the

Bayer Response to Question 1b. ( S.2.2):
ICH Q7 states the following: “Introducing an intermediate or API, including one that does not 
conform to standards or specifications, back into the process and reprocessing by repeating a 
crystallization step or other appropriate chemical or physical manipulation steps (e.g., 
distillation, filtration, chromatography, milling) that are part of the established manufacturing 
process is generally considered acceptable. However, if such reprocessing is used for a 
majority of batches, such reprocessing should be included as part of the standard 
manufacturing process”.
Therefore, we have introduced the possibility of reprocessing in our manufacturing 
description. It is not a routine operation. Although the reprocessing procedures for 
intermediates and APIs do not need to be documented in the quality assessment application, 
we mention it in the manufacturing description for clarity reasons. In line with the local 
guidelines, the reprocessing records for production batches will be maintained by the 
manufacturer and will be available for submission upon request by the MFDS.
In all steps of the manufacturing process of BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug 
substance, the criterion for reprocessing of a manufactured batch is a lack of compliance with 
any specified test item. As of 2025, no batch of any step manufactured according to the 
manufacturing process described in 3.2.S.2.2. failed to comply with any specified test item.
Therefore, no reprocessing has been conducted for the above-mentioned reason up until this 
point.

Question 1e.
e. Related Regulation: Article 7(2)(b)
Reason for Supplement: 3.2.S.3.2. Impurities

not been submitted.
2) Basis for the calculation of the purge factor for mutagenic impurities has not

Supplement Requirement: Please submit additional materials regarding impurities considering

Bayer Response to Question 1e. ( S.2; S.3; S.4):
e.1)
The control strategy for genotoxic impurities is in line with the ICH M7 guideline, which 
states that the Threshold of Toxicological Concern (TTC) concept is not directly applicable in 
the case of a drug substance and drug product intended for advanced cancer indications as 
defined in the scope of ICH S9, which is relevant for BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug 
substance. In this case, impurities are controlled at acceptable levels for non-mutagenic 
impurities. During development, the risk calculations of BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized 
drug substance were based on an acceptable limit of max. 0.10%, as this is the identification 
threshold for organic impurities in the ICH Q3A impurity guideline.
Mutagenic organic impurity 3-Chloro-2-methoxyaniline is analyzed in BAY 2927088 hydrate 
micronized drug substance (active substance) and in BAY 2927088 purified intermediate 
(step 2a) using HPLC method described in S.4.2.01 Test procedure.
The Batch data (S.2.4.05 Batch Analyses for Intermediates and S.4.4.01 Batch Analyses) show 
that “Any unspecified impurity” and therefore 3-Chloro-2-methoxyaniline was < 0.05 % in 
BAY 2927088 purified intermediate and BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance.

e.2)
A spiking experiment demonstrated that a quantity of 5.0% of 3-chloro-2-methoxyaniline 
added to step BAY 2927088 crude (2a) leads to a content of 3-chloro-2-methoxyaniline of 
0.06% in isolated BAY 2927088 crude. Adding 5.0% of 3-chloro-2-methoxyaniline to step 
BAY 2927088 purified (2b) leads to a content of 3-chloro-2-methoxyaniline of <0.05% in 
isolated BAY 2927088 purified. Thus, steps BAY 2927088 crude and purified combined 
render an overall purge factor of at least 8100 (cf. S.2.4.01 Discussion and Control of Critical 
Steps). This would result in 3-chloro-2-methoxyaniline values significantly below 50 ppm in 
the final drug substance, assuming a worst case of 5.0% starting value in step BAY 2927088 crude.
Below, detailed purge factor calculations of relevant potential mutagenic impurities (PMIs) in 
the starting materials of the manufacturing process of BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug 
substance are described.

For the calculation of purge factors, reactivity, solubility and volatility of the impurities are 
identified as physicochemical parameters that influence the removal of the specific impurity 
in the manufacturing process. Under the given process conditions these parameters are 
assessed to define the purge factors for each individual operation.

The total purge factor is obtained by multiplication of the purge factors of each operation and 
step. The concentration of the respective impurity before purging (concentration at start) is 
estimated in a conservative way.
Purge ratios are calculated by division of the obtained total purge factors by the total purge 
factor required to ensure an acceptable level of the respective impurity in BAY 2927088 hydrate 
micronized drug substance, i.e. 1000 ppm = 0.10%, in line with ICH guideline S9. A purge ratio of at least 1000 is considered to provide “sufficient 
confidence that the level of the impurity in the drug substance will be below the acceptable 
limit such that no analytical testing is recommended for this impurity. [4]

Source: S.2.4.01; S.2.4.05; S.2.6.11; S.4.2.01; S.4.4.01; S.4.5.11; [3] A. Teasdale et al.; [4] ICH M7(R2).

Bayer Response to Question 2a. ( P.2.3):
a.1)
Table 4-2 in P.2.3.01 is a summary of all the batches in the commercial scale. The sieve mesh size of 1.0 mm for pre-blend sieving was used in commercial scale only in technical batches not for clinical batches. All clinical batches were produced with a sieve mesh size ≤ 0.8 mm. All commercial batches were and will be produced with a sieve mesh size ≤ 0.8 mm.

a.2)
The process uses a hybrid approach with some batch-mode and some integrated continuous-mode unit operations. The integrated process consists of feeding of the pre-blend, roller compaction/dry granulation, post-blending, tableting and coating. The control strategy is based on a sublot principle; sublots must meet criteria or are diverted. There are no continuous blending operations; back-mixing during roller compaction or tableting is excluded. Extensive testing during process development and process validation showed all sublots are homogeneous and non-conforming material could be identified/discarded without using RTD models; therefore no RTD model was validated for commercial manufacturing.

a.3)
Holding time of pre-blend evaluated by testing pre-blend during storage and coated tablets produced using this pre-blend. Criteria: blend uniformity below 5%; sum of degradation products max. 3%; compliance of microbiological quality; no change of solid state form of the drug substance. Coated tablets met release specification.

(Max-Dohrn-Straße 8, 10589 Berlin, Germany) is, that the INN was not yet available at the

To provide an official and unequivocal bridge between this certificate and the substance’s 
INN, we are requesting an official statement from the competent German authority, the 
Landesamt für Gesundheit und Soziales Berlin (LAGeSo), State Office for Health and Social 
Affairs Berlin, to officially confirm that "HER2 / mutEGFR Inhibitor" and Sevabertinib

of Sevabertinib (BAY 2927088) hydrate micronized drug substance (DS). At present, 
Bayer is the sole DS manufacturer at its sites in Wuppertal, Bergkamen and Berlin,

Bayer AG Wuppertal executes the testing and the storage of the stability studies of the drug 
substance. Bayer AG Wuppertal and Bayer AG Bergkamen use qualified service provider(s) 
for transportation of analytical / stability samples and drug substance.

transportation. Data loggers are used to monitor the temperature during transportation of the 
drug substance. There are no deteriorations expected for transportation between the 
manufacturing sites incl. stability and storage sites which goes beyond the storage situation.

Question:
Question 12
According to the technical data, multiple polymorphic forms of the drug substance were 
discovered during the manufacturing process development. Please provide the manufacturing 
process conditions under which each polymorphic form might be generated and clarify 
whether the current process conditions could lead to the formation of other polymorphic 
forms.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 12 (S.2.4):
Only Hydrate 1 Mod. A and the THF forms are relevant for the DS manufacturing process.
The crystallization process was optimized through an extensive series of experiments to 
produce only Hydrate 1 Mod. A. The only risk is the presence of THF in this step. However, 
the formation of the THF forms is prevented by precise temperature control.
The proven acceptable range (PAR) for step 3 of the manufacturing process has been 
established as 37-47 °C (S.2.4.01 Discussion and Control of Critical Steps).
The unintentional formation of other solvate forms is ruled out due to the absence of the 
necessary solvents in the crystallization step, whereas the solvent-free forms would undergo 
transformations to Hydrate 1 Mod. A under these conditions.
Source:  S.2.4.01_01 _1.0 Discussion and Control of Critical Steps / BAY 2927088
hydrate micronized drug substance (S.2.4.01_022990980_01; unchanged)

Question:
Question 14
Based on the drug substance manufacturing process, it is possible that alkyl sulfonate ester 
impurities could be formed. Please provide a relevant evaluation.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 14 (S.2.4):
Relevant alkyl sulfonate ester impurities that may possibly be formed in the drug substance 
manufacturing process are ethyl and methyl p-toluenesulfonate (tosylate). They are class 2 
compounds according to the classifications in ICH guideline M7. They are potential by-
products from the condensation reaction between p-toluenesulfonic acid and the respective
alcohol, ethanol and methanol. P-toluenesulfonic acid and ethanol are employed in synthesis 
step 2b of the manufacturing process of BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance 
and methanol may be present as a residual solvent in the transiently isolated and dried product 
of step 2a, BAY 2927088 crude.
Yet, the risk of the formation of both ethyl and methyl p-toluenesulfonate in step 2b is 
considered negligible, as the following factors in that step impose substantial barriers for any 
such unwanted sulfonic acid esterification, which are well documented in a review from 
2015.1
• Equimolar amounts of p-toluenesulfonic acid monohydrate and BAY 2927088 crude are
combined to form a salt solution of the drug substance, thus hampering the acid’s ability 
to protonate alcohols, as is a prerequisite for alkyl tosylate formation. Moreover, a 
superstoichiometric amount of sodium hydroxide, employed to generate and crystallize 
the drug substance in its free base form in the later part of the process diminishes the 
chances for such side reactions even further.
• A large fraction of 24% (w/w) of the solvent mixture comprises water, sufficient even in
unbuffered systems to reportedly put sulfonic acid esterification almost entirely to a halt.
• Due to its nature as a (pH-shift) recrystallization, step 2b lacks any prolonged holding or
reaction times and operates at mildly elevated temperatures, thus further reducing the 
likelihood of any notable alkyl tosylate formation.
Despite the above considerations, in order to further safeguard the absence of ethyl and 
methyl tosylate in the final drug substance, the fate and purge of ethyl tosylate was 
investigated by a spiking experiment. Of 10% of ethyl tosylate (with respect to the mass of 
BAY 2927088 crude) which were added at the beginning of step 2b, none was detected in 
isolated BAY 2927088 purified intermediate (at a limit of quantification of 0.02%). With that 
purge alone, even 41% of ethyl tosylate, which would be the amount resulting from the 
esterification of the entire amount of subjected p-toluenesulfonic acid monohydrate, would be 
purged to no more than 0.08% of ethyl tosylate in BAY 2927088 purified, which is already 
below the acceptable limit of max. 0.10%, in line with ICH guideline S9.
As for methyl tosylate, the fact that its precursor methanol may solely be introduced in small 
amounts into step 2b as a residual solvent in BAY 2927088 crude, as opposed to ethanol 
employed as solvent, renders its formation even less likely than that of ethyl tosylate.
In conclusion, the absence of alkyl tosylates in BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug 
substance is secured within step 2b, as neither the formation, nor retention of alkyl tosylates 
are expectable, based on applicable literature precedence and experimentation.


1 D. Snodin, A. Teasdale, Org. Process Res. Dev. 2015, 19, 1465−1485.

Source:  S.2.4.10 Control of Critical Steps and Intermediates - Additional
Information / BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance (IQMS-
400119_1.0; new)

Question:
Question 1
According to the technical data description, the semi-finished products after post-blending are 
tableted in batches (sublot). This tableting step does not involve continuous material in-feed 
and out-feed and should not meet the definition of a continuous process. Please clarify.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1:
The manufacturing process for Sevabertinib tablets combines both batch and continuous 
operations. Key steps such as feeding the pre-blend, roller compaction granulation, post-
blending, tableting, and coating are integrated, with granulation and tableting performed 
continuously. Granules are divided into sublots after roller compaction, which are then 
pneumatically transferred for post-blending with magnesium stearate to create ready-to-press 
sublots. These sublots are moved by gravity from the blender to the tablet press hopper, where 
the sublots are merged. When sufficiently ready to press blend is present in the tablet press 
hopper the tableting process starts and runs continuously for the whole batch. The addition of 
new sublots to the hopper during the tableting means that there is continuous flow of material 
to and from the tablet press.

Question:
Question 2
Please provide an evaluation of the impact on product quality when there are deviations in the 
excipient composition ratio.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2 (P.2.3; P.3.2):
The manufacturing process starts by preparing the pre-blend in batch mode where the drug 
substance, microcrystalline cellulose, lactose monohydrate and crospovidone are weighed for 
the whole batch in the amounts described by the P.3.2.01 Batch Formula. Thus, the 
composition of the granules is the same for the whole batch and no deviations in excipient 
composition ratio is possible during dry granulation. Furthermore, only one excipient 
(magnesium stearate) is added in the post-blending step. The amount of dosed magnesium 
stearate is monitored by the control system (see Chapter 4.1.1.1 of P.2.3.01 Pharmaceutical 
Development - Manufacturing Process for details). In the case of deviations in the specified 
amount of magnesium stearate, the corresponding granulate / post-blending sublot is flagged 
as non-conforming product, diverted from the process and discarded. Finally, one single lot of 
coating suspension is prepared per tablet batch and used for the entire tablet batch. Also here,
the total amount of applied coating suspension is monitored and controlled by the control 
system. If any deviations in the amount of applied coating occur, the corresponding coating 
sublot is flagged as non-conforming product, diverted from the process and discarded. 
In conclusion, the composition of all conforming coated tablets within one batch is 
quantitatively the same. This approach assures that only product is declared as conforming 
product, if the composition complies with the indented specification.
Source:  P.2.3.01_2.0 Pharmaceutical Development - Manufacturing Process / BAY
2927088 coated tablet 10 mg (IQMS-264746_2.0; amended
P.3.2.01_01 Batch Formula/ BAY 2927088 coated tablet 10 mg 
(P.3.2.01_022989200_01; unchanged)

Question:
Question 3
Upon reviewing the manufacturing process development data, it was noted that the impact of 
tableting pressure on product quality was not discussed. Please provide a relevant evaluation 
and specify the operating range. Additionally, the manufacturing process description in 
3.2.P.3.3 does not include tableting pressure parameters. Please clarify and update the 
technical data.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 3 (P.2.3; P.3.1):
The effect of tableting pressure was investigated in the commercial scale DoE (P.2.3.01 
Pharmaceutical Development – Manufacturing Process, chapter 4.5). One of the investigated 
factors of the DoE was the tablet resistance to crushing and the tableting force was considered 
as a response. The main factor influencing the required tableting force is the desired tablet 
resistance to crushing, followed by the ribbon density. Since no other correlations between the 
tablet resistance to crushing and the tablet quality attributes were observed it can be 
concluded that the control of the tablet resistance to crushing is sufficient to achieve quality 
product.
Nonetheless to guide the start of tableting process the operating range for the tableting force 
of 5 – 18 kN is specified and reported in the process parameter recipe summary (R.3.1.02 
Batch Record - Master (Recipe)). The lower limit is required to achieve sufficient tablet 
resistance to crushing and the upper limit is the tableting tool material limit.
Source:  R.3.1.02_1.0 Batch Record – Master (Recipe) / BAY 2927088 coated tablet 10
mg (Recipe) (IQMS-390477_1.0; new)

2927088 coated tablet 10 mg (IQMS-264746_2.0; amended)

Question:
Question 4
Upon reviewing the dissolution method development data for this case, although it can 
distinguish finished product batches with oversized drug substance particles that lead to non-
compliant quality, most tests show dissolution results close to 100% at the setting dissolution 
time point. It is recommended to evaluate and revise the current dissolution specification for 
the finished product to better control product quality.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 4 (P.5): 
Alongside feedback from Rapporteurs on the dissolution method's discriminatory power, the 
Applicant received comments from the FDA, which requested a change to using phosphate 
buffer pH 6.8 with 0.3% SDS at 50 rpm instead of 0.5% SDS.
To address the FDA’s request, the Applicant adapted the dissolution method by reducing the 
SDS concentration in the phosphate buffer pH 6.8 from 0.5% to 0.3% SDS, maintaining a 
paddle speed of 50 rpm. Comparative dissolution testing of the 10 mg tablet formulation 
demonstrated comparable dissolution profiles when using 0.3%, 0.4%, or 0.5% SDS 
(Figure 18), confirming that the reduction in SDS did not compromise dissolution 
performance or product release characteristics while offering better discriminatory power 
between formulations. Please refer to updated P.5.3.21 Method Development - Dissolution.
This new method is detailed in the updated P.5.2.02 Test Procedure – Dissolution. For 
updated validation results, please refer to P.5.3.02 Validation of Test for Dissolution.
Additionally, representative clinical and process validation batches from both batch 
manufacturing process and continuous manufacturing process demonstrated consistent and 
comparable dissolution profiles applying the adapted more discriminative dissolution method, 
which is in line with the comparative dissolution data acquired in ICH M9 media, see 
P.2.2.02 Pharmaceutical Development - Dissolution Profiles. Updated batch analyses data are 
provided in P.5.4.01 Batch Analyses.

To evaluate the discriminatory capabilities of the revised dissolution method, the Applicant 
conducted dissolution studies examining the influence of several variables: drug substance 
particle size distribution (DS PSD), disintegrant (crospovidone) level, compression force, and 
sieve mesh size employed for pre-blend sieving.
For DS PSD, the discriminatory capability of the new method was similar to the prior 
approach, reliably distinguishing between batches with different particle size distributions 
(Figure 19).
Regarding compression force, the new method showed slightly enhanced sensitivity: it could 
more distinctly resolve dissolution differences between tablets compressed at varying forces 
(Figure 20).
Most notably, for crospovidone (disintegrant) level, the new method afforded significantly 
improved discrimination. This was evidenced not only by improved detection of dissolution 
variations with less disintegrant levels (50% of target amount), but also by the clear separation 
observed in batches prepared with no disintegrant at all, which exhibited markedly different 
dissolution profiles compared to those containing the standard level of crospovidone 
(Figure 21).
The results demonstrated that, with respect to sieve mesh size, the new method provided 
superior discriminatory power, clearly differentiating batches prepared with varying mesh 
sizes—a distinction that was less apparent with the previous method. Notably, mesh sizes of 
0.3 mm and 0.8 mm were found to be favorable, supporting optimal dissolution performance, 
whereas employing a 1.0 mm mesh or omitting sieving altogether led to dissolution results 
below 80% at the 30 minutes time point (Figure 22).

Source:  P.2.2.02_3.0 Pharmaceutical Development – Dissolution Profiles / BAY
2927088 coated tablet 10 mg (IQMS-383196_3.0; amended)

(IQMS-397552_1.0; amended)

Question:
Question 6
According to the description of the impurity analytical method, the storage temperature for 
the sample solution is 15-25°C, but the solution stability validation for this method was 
performed at 2-8°C. Please clarify and update the technical data.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 6 (P.5):
The test procedure (P.5.2.01 Test Procedure) gives the default parameters for the 
chromatographic conditions. These include an auto sampler setting of room temperature 
(15 – 25 °C). Effectively speaking, this setting corresponds to no active temperature control of 
the autosampler.
The validation of the test method for degradation products (P.5.3.01 Validation of Test for 
Assay and Impurities) showed that the level of DS-Pyridone increases if the test solution is 
stored at room temperature for several days. Such an increase is not observed when the 
solution is stored at 2 – 8 °C.
This effect is only relevant for test solutions that are not measured on the day of preparation, 
meaning that they are prepared first and then tested several days later. This procedure is 
however not the routine (or default) procedure in any given QC laboratory. Preparation and 
testing of the solution on the same day does not require the autosampler to be set at 2 – 8 °C; 
not controlling the temperature has no effect on the level of DS-Pyridone. Therefore, the test 
procedure refers to room temperature as the default option.
The test procedure may be changed to include 2 – 8 °C at the default for the autosampler. 
However, any interruption of the temperature control and/or excursions > 8 °C would 
correspond to a deviation from the test procedure, although a quality impact is not expected.
Furthermore, standard autosampler units may not be able to maintain temperature robustly 
between 2 and 8 °C, depending on local conditions.
The definition of default parameters in the test procedure instead of specified parameters 
means that the given conditions are applicable for routine use, which is correct regarding the 
temperature of the autosampler. It is however possible to apply more stringent conditions (e.g. 
an autosampler setting of 10 °C) without deviating from the test procedure.
The information given in the P.5.3.01 document is considered sufficient to interpret the 
default parameters stated in the test procedure (P.5.2.01 Test Procedure). In case the test 
solution is not tested on the day of use, it must be stored at 2 – 8 °C. On the day of testing, the 
autosampler can be used without temperature control but may be set to lower temperature if 
there is any concern regarding the level of DS-Pyridone or any unspecified degradant.
A change in the current test procedure is not considered meaningful for the test purpose.
Source:  P.5.2.01_2.0 Test Procedure / BAY 2927088 coated tablet 10 mg (IQMS-
264697_2.0; unchanged) 
P.5.3.01_1.0 Validation of Test for Assay and Impurities / BAY 2927088 coated 
tablet 10 mg (IQMS-263677_1.0; unchanged)

Question:
Question 1
It is noted that you did not provide the mixing process parameters (e.g., percentage of 
equipment occupancy, mixing speed, and mixing time) for the compounding process. Since 
your proposed commercial scale batches range from 30 L to 2500 L, we recommend that you 
provide the established mixing process parameters in a tabulated format for each commercial 
scale, including the equipment capacity. Provide the process parameters used in the exhibit 
batches and the batches that have already been manufactured to support the process 
parameters. Update Sections 3.2.P.3.3 and 3.2.P.3.4 accordingly.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (3.2.P.2, 3.2.P.3):

We acknowledge your request for detailed mixing process parameters and would like to 
provide the following clarifications.
The manufacturing process for Gadoquatrane solution was developed and validated with an 
automated process control system (PCS). The mixing parameters are dynamically controlled 
throughout the manufacturing process by the qualified PCS program, which adjusts 
parameters in real time based on the actual batch size. This ensures a consistent and 
reproducible mixing process without the need for fixed parameter values.
The adequacy of the mixing process, including the mixing speed and energy input, is verified 
during manufacturing through the in-process control (IPC) parameter "clarity of the solution". 
A theoretically longer stirring time does not have a negative impact on the quality of the 
solution. This IPC ensures that the mixing process achieves the intended outcome and meets 
predefined quality standards.
The mixing process and its parameters were evaluated during process development and 
classified as non-critical (see P.2.3.01 section 6.5). The completeness of dissolution of the 
drug substance was found to be independent of these parameters.
Furthermore, the evaluation of the minimum stirring speed has been determined to be non-
critical based on the high solubility of Gadoquatrane in aqueous media, including both water 
and buffer solutions (see S.1.3.01).

In the following more details are provided regarding mixing time, mixing speed, mixing 
equipment, process validation, in-process control and process parameters used in the exhibit 
batches:
• Mixing time:
The mixing time is not limited by process parameters, it is only limited by Holding time 1. 
This was tested and confirmed in a mechanical stress study.

Gadoquatrane solution was subjected to continuous shaking at room temperature for seven 
days using a shaker in horizontal orientation (c). The analytical samples (duplicate 
measurements) were taken at the start (Start), after 4 days (T4 days) and 7 days (T7 days).

• Mixing speed and used equipment
The mixing speeds are predefined within the technical PCS and are dynamically adjusted 
in real time based on the actual mass present in the mixing vessel during preparation of 
the bulk solution. This automated adjustment ensures that the mixing process is optimized 
and tailored to the specific batch size, thereby maintaining process consistency and 
product quality.
The mixing equipment utilized in our manufacturing process includes both mobile and 
stationary mixers, which differ in size, geometry, and material composition. These 
differences are fully accounted during process design, ensuring that consistent and robust 
mixing performance is achieved across all equipment types. The technical settings 
programmed into the PCS ensure that a consistent energy input is applied across the entire 
batch size range. This guarantees uniform mixing performance, regardless of the batch 
size, and ensures process reproducibility. The mixing speeds are limited to a maximum of 
500 rpm. During bulk manufacturing, it is also necessary to temporarily reduce the stirring 
speed to 0 rpm, for example, to check the clarity of the solution. The actual stirring speed
is based on the linear relationship for each piece of equipment according to the following

combination product. However, as reflected in the final rule on CGMPs for combination 
products (21 CFR part 4), manufacturers have the option to demonstrate compliance both with 
the drug CGMP regulations (21 CFR parts 210, 211) and with the device quality system (QS) 
regulation (i.e., 21 CFR part 820) through a streamlined approach.
If utilizing a streamlined approach, you must demonstrate compliance (i) with either the drug 
CGMP regulations or the QS regulation in their entirety and also (ii) with those provisions 
specified in part 4 from the other of these two sets of requirements. Alternatively, you may 
demonstrate compliance with both the drug CGMPs and QS regulation in their entirety (non-
streamlined approach). For further information on 21 CFR part 4, see guidance for industry 
and FDA staff Current Good Manufacturing Practice Requirements for Combination Products 
(January 2017), available at 
http://www.fda.gov/RegulatoryInformation/Guidances/ucm126198.htm.
Based on an assessment of the risk profile of your proposed combination product, FDA has

inspection to demonstrate your compliance with 21 CFR part 4. Please ensure that the
