Question:
Question 2a. a)
Among the data on the starting material manufacturers (Kingchem Life Science LLC and SAI 
Life Science Limited), submit the rationale for not establishing control specifications for 
solvents and catalysts used in starting material synthesis.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2a. a) (S.2.3):
Kingchem Life Science LLC utilizes dichloroethane, tetrahydrofuran, dichloromethane, and 
isopropanol during the manufacturing of the starting material methoxy nitrile aldehyde 
(SM1).
Regarding tetrahydrofuran and isopropanol: Since these solvents are intentionally introduced 
and utilized as processing solvents in subsequent steps of the API synthesis (isopropanol in 
step 2 (ethyl-pyridinone intermediate), tetrahydrofuran in step 5 (rac-Amido-TH-
naphthyridine intermediate), establishing separate control specifications for them in the 
starting material (SM1) is considered redundant. Comprehensive controls for these solvents 
are appropriately implemented and monitored at these later stages of the manufacturing 
process to ensure compliance in the final API.
Regarding dichloromethane and dichloroethane: As part of supplier qualification risk 
assessments, residual dichloromethane and dichloroethane have been detected in the starting 
material methoxy nitrile aldehyde (SM1) at levels already below the established ICH Q3C 
limits for residual solvents. Considering the subsequent 8-step synthesis process, which 
includes purification steps, a significant further depletion of these residual solvents is 
expected. Consequently, any potential impact from these solvents on the quality of the final 
API can be reliably precluded, and therefore, no additional specific control specifications for 
dichloromethane and dichloroethane are deemed necessary within the SM1 specification.
As dichloromethane is classified by ICH Q3C as a class II solvent, a risk assessment was 
performed to evaluate the necessity of setting a specification for dichloromethane in the 
starting material methoxy nitrile aldehyde supplied by Kingchem Life Science LLC.
The starting condition for the worst-case risk assessment was the hypothesis that 
dichloromethane is present in the starting material methoxy nitrile aldehyde at a concentration 
level of 3%, which would exceed the ICH Q3C limit by a factor of 50. In this case, the 
required depletion factor with regard to Finerenone micronized drug substance would be 50 in 
order to reach a concentration level of 600 mg/kg in Finerenone micronized drug substance. 
The depletion capacity of the manufacturing process of Finerenone micronized drug substance 
was evaluated to be greater than 9*1013. Thus, the ratio of the required depletion factor 
compared to the assessed depletion factor of the manufacturing process is at least 1012. In 
other words, even if dichloromethane would be present in the starting material methoxy nitrile 
aldehyde at 3%, it would be depleted to a concentration level of far below 0.00000003 mg/kg 
(3*10-8 mg/kg) by means of the design of the manufacturing process.
In chapter 8.1 of the ICH M7 guideline, the following is stated: “Option 4: Understand 
process parameters and impact on residual impurity levels (including fate and purge 
knowledge) with sufficient confidence that the level of the impurity in the drug substance will 
be below the acceptable limit such that no analytical testing is recommended for this 
impurity. (i.e., the impurity does not need to be listed on any specification).”
Based on the worst-case assessment described above, the residual solvent dichloromethane 
would be reduced to a concentration level far below the allowed concentration threshold of 
600 mg/kg in Finerenone micronized drug substance even if an unrealistically high amount of 
dichloromethane (of 3 %) in the starting material methoxy nitrile aldehyde would be assumed. 
Thus, it is in line with ICH guideline M7 to control this impurity by means of the design of 
the manufacturing process in which methoxy nitrile aldehyde supplied by Kingchem Life 
Science LLC is used as a starting material
As dichloroethane is classified by ICH Q3C as a class I solvent, a risk assessment was 
performed to evaluate the necessity of setting a specification for dichloroethane in the starting 
material methoxy nitrile aldehyde supplied by Kingchem Life Science LLC.
The starting condition for the worst-case risk assessment was the hypothesis that 
dichloroethane is present in the starting material methoxy nitrile aldehyde at a concentration 
level of 3%, which would exceed the ICH Q3C limit by a factor of 6000. In this case, the 
required depletion factor with regard to Finerenone micronized drug substance would be 6000 
in order to reach a concentration level of 5 mg/kg in Finerenone micronized drug substance. 
Therefore, the depletion capacity of the manufacturing process of Finerenone micronized drug 
substance was evaluated to be greater than 1*1013. Thus, the ratio of the required depletion 
factor compared to the assessed depletion factor of the manufacturing process is at least 109. 
In other words, even if dichloroethane were present in the starting material methoxy nitrile
aldehyde at 3%, it would be depleted to a concentration level of far below 0.00003 mg/kg by 
means of the design of the manufacturing process.
In chapter 8.1 of the ICH M7 guideline, the following is stated: “Option 4: Understand 
process parameters and impact on residual impurity levels (including fate and purge 
knowledge) with sufficient confidence that the level of the impurity in the drug substance will 
be below the acceptable limit such that no analytical testing is recommended for this 
impurity. (i.e., the impurity does not need to be listed on any specification).”
Based on the worst-case assessment described above, the residual solvent dichloroethane 
would be reduced to a concentration level far below the allowed concentration threshold of 
5  mg/kg in Finerenone micronized drug substance even if an unrealistically high amount of 
dichloroethane (of 3 %) in the starting material methoxy nitrile aldehyde would be assumed. 
Thus, it is in line with ICH guideline M7 to control this impurity by means of the design of 
the manufacturing process in which methoxy nitrile aldehyde supplied by Kingchem Life 
Science LLC is used as a starting material.
Regarding catalysts: Kingchem Life Science LLC uses copper bromide during the synthesis 
of methoxy nitrile aldehyde. As part of the supplier's qualification risk assessment, elemental 
screening was performed, and copper was detected far below 30% of the ICH limit in the 
starting material.
Data on dichloromethane and dichloroethane and Cu are presented in document S.2.3.12.

SAI Life Science Limited does not use any catalysts or metal reagents during the synthesis of 
methoxy nitrile aldehyde (SM1).
Regarding solvents: They utilize chlorobenzene, dimethylformamide, methyl isobutyl ketone, 
and n-heptane for manufacturing the starting material methoxy nitrile aldehyde (SM1).
Chlorobenzene and n-heptane are routinely controlled within the specification of methoxy 
nitrile aldehyde (SM1).
Regarding dimethylformamide and methyl isobutyl ketone: As part of supplier qualification 
risk assessments, residual dimethylformamide and methyl isobutyl ketone have been detected 
in the starting material methoxy nitrile aldehyde (SM1) at levels already below the established 
ICH Q3C limits for residual solvents. Due to further depletion of theses solvents during the 
subsequent synthesis steps, any potential impact on the Finerenone quality can be reliably 
precluded, and consequently, no specific control limits for dimethylformamide and methyl 
isobutyl ketone are considered necessary within the SM1 specification.
Data on dimethylformamide and methyl isobutyl ketone are presented in document S.2.3.12.
As dimethylformamide is classified by ICH Q3C as a class II solvent, a risk assessment was 
performed to evaluate the necessity of setting a specification for dimethylformamide in the 
starting material methoxy nitrile aldehyde supplied by SAI.
The starting condition for the worst-case risk assessment was the hypothesis that 
dimethylformamide is present in the starting material methoxy nitrile aldehyde at a 
concentration level of 3%, which would exceed the ICH Q3C limit by a factor of 34. In this 
case, the required depletion factor with regard to Finerenone micronized drug substance 
would be 34 in order to reach a concentration level of 880 mg/kg in Finerenone micronized 
drug substance. The depletion capacity of the manufacturing process of Finerenone 
micronized drug substance was evaluated to be greater than 1*107. Thus, the ratio of the 
required depletion factor compared to the assessed depletion factor of the manufacturing 
process is at least 105. In other words, even if dimethylformamide would be present in the 
starting material methoxy nitrile aldehyde at 3%, it would be depleted to a concentration level 
of far below 0.3 mg/kg by means of the design of the manufacturing process.
In chapter 8.1 of the ICH M7 guideline, the following is stated: “Option 4: Understand 
process parameters and impact on residual impurity levels (including fate and purge 
knowledge) with sufficient confidence that the level of the impurity in the drug substance will 
be below the acceptable limit such that no analytical testing is recommended for this 
impurity. (i.e., the impurity does not need to be listed on any specification).”
Based on the worst-case assessment described above, the residual solvent dimethylformamide 
would be reduced to a concentration level far below the allowed concentration threshold of 
880 mg/kg in Finerenone micronized drug substance even if an unrealistically high amount of 
dimethylformamide (of 3 %) in the starting material methoxy nitrile aldehyde would be 
assumed. Thus, it is in line with ICH guideline M7 to control this impurity by means of the 
design of the manufacturing process in which methoxy nitrile aldehyde supplied by SAI is 
used as a starting material.

As methyl isobutyl ketone is classified by ICH Q3C as a class II solvent, a risk assessment was 
performed to evaluate the necessity of setting a specification for methyl isobutyl ketone 
in the starting material methoxy nitrile aldehyde supplied by SAI.
The starting condition for the worst-case risk assessment was the hypothesis that methyl 
isobutyl ketone is present in the starting material methoxy nitrile aldehyde at a concentration 
level of 3%, which would exceed the ICH Q3C limit by a factor of 6.7. In this case, the 
required depletion factor with regard to Finerenone micronized drug substance would be 6.7 
in order to reach a concentration level of 4500 mg/kg in Finerenone micronized drug 
substance. The depletion capacity of the manufacturing process of Finerenone micronized 
drug substance was evaluated to be greater than 3*107. Thus, the ratio of the required 
depletion factor compared to the assessed depletion factor of the manufacturing process is at 
least 106. In other words, even if methyl isobutyl ketone would be present in the starting 
material methoxy nitrile aldehyde at 3%, it would be depleted to a concentration level of far 
below 0.03 mg/kg by means of the design of the manufacturing process.
In chapter 8.1 of the ICH M7 guideline, the following is stated: “Option 4: Understand 
process parameters and impact on residual impurity levels (including fate and purge 
knowledge) with sufficient confidence that the level of the impurity in the drug substance will 
be below the acceptable limit such that no analytical testing is recommended for this 
impurity. (i.e., the impurity does not need to be listed on any specification).”
Based on the worst-case assessment described above, the residual solvent methyl isobutyl 
ketone would be reduced to a concentration level far below the allowed concentration 
threshold of 4500 mg/kg in Finerenone micronized drug substance even if an unrealistically 
high amount of methyl isobutyl ketone (of 3 %) in the starting material methoxy nitrile 
aldehyde would be assumed. Thus, it is in line with ICH guideline M7 to control this impurity 
by means of the design of the manufacturing process in which methoxy nitrile aldehyde 
supplied by SAI is used as a starting material.

Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 3b a) (P.3.3):
The manufacturing process description has been amended, including step-by-step operating 
conditions and information on the respective equipment (please see P.3.3.01). The process 
control items are listed in the section 3.2.P.3.3.02 (please refer to P.3.3.02).
The 3.2.P.3.3. section includes the documents P.3.3.01 as well as P.3.3.02. In‑process control 
(IPC) information for the compression (tableting) step is integrated in the manufacturing flow 
chart of the document P.3.3.01 and in the document P.3.3.02, Table 2. The table in P.3.3.02 
describes the in‑process controls applied during the compression step (e.g. uniformity of 
mass, breaking load, disintegration and friability), including the respective acceptance criteria 
and test procedures according to Ph. Eur./USP/JP.
The operating conditions of the tableting step are selected to ensure compliance with the IPC 
ranges given in P.3.3.02. This means that the compression force is among other things 
adjusted based on the resulting/achieved breaking load of the tablets. Granule properties, such 
as the particle size distribution, can lead to varying compression forces, which is the reason 
why no specific compression force is defined. The operational setting parameters of the 
tableting step are therefore a consequence of adhering to the given IPCs. The max. applicable 
compression force is 16 kN. This information was amended to document P.3.3.01.

Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2:
1. Ames report Fluorodihydropurinone: PH-41351 (Module 4.2.3.7.6)
2. Ames report of compound BAY 576290: PH-35791 (Module 4.2.3.7.6)
o For structural comparison with Fluoroazopyrimidine, Fluoroazopropenenitrile
and 2-Phenylfluoroazopyrimidine: please note that the alert for mutagenicity 
raised by DEREK and Leadscope was based on the alerting aromatic azo 
moiety. This alert is also present in the structurally similar compound BAY 
576290 that was demonstrated to be Ames negative – see also attached EMA 
Day 120 Non Clinical response (Module 1.7.1, Question 64(F), page 8)
o In addition, in the course of the EU approval process (Please, refer to EMA
Day 180 Non Clinical response (Module 1.7.1, Question 18, page 2) 
Fluoroazopropenenitrile was investigated for mutagenic effects using the 
Salmonella/microsome preincubation test (Ames test) to further support the 
refutation of the in silico alert based upon a shared alert with the known 
AMES-negative BAY 576290. In this assay, Fluoroazopropenenitrile was 
shown to be non-mutagenic both without and with S9 mix in the preincubation 
Salmonella/microsome test (Ames test), hereby confirming the previous in 
silico expert assessment (PH-42013 (Module 4.2.3.7.6)).
3. Ames report Pyrimidinyliminoacetonitrile: PH-41400 (Module 4.2.3.7.6)
o For info regarding structural comparison with Fluorobisiminopropionitrile: this
is how it was discussed in the original Tox Written Summary 2.6.6 (Module 
2.6.6, p55) “Accordingly, also the chemically unstable 
fluorbisiminopropionitrile can be regarded as nonmutagenic since 
pyrimidinyliminoacetonitrile and fluorbisiminopropionitrile are structurally 
related and exhibit the same structural element causing the in silico alert 
(aromatic imine).”
4. Ames report BAY 3463663: PH-41857 (Module 4.2.3.7.6)
o With respect to structural comparison with Pteridinetriamine see also attached
EMA Day 120 Non Clinical response (Module 1.7.1, Question 64(E), page 6)
5. Ames report o-Semidine: PH-41211 (Module 4.2.3.7.6)
6. Ames report CAS 2922-28-3 (Module 4.2.3.7.6)

2922-28-3: The impurity Bispyrazolopurinamine was predicted to be negative 
by DEREK (Module 4.2.3.7.6) but “indeterminate” by Leadscope (Module 
4.2.3.7.6). Such inconclusive predictions are generated if there is not enough 
evidence to derive either a mutagenic or a non-mutagenic prediction with 
adequate conﬁdence. Leadscope identified the polycycle aromatic amine 
moiety as alerting structure. This structural moiety is also present in CAS 
2922-28-3 (adenine monohydrochloride), which is not only predicted to be 
negative in Leadscope but for which a negative Ames test is available. Thus, 
the “indeterminate” prediction for Bispyrazolopurinamine was refuted and 
compound assigned to class 4.
o In addition, in the course of the EU approval process (Please, refer to EMA
Day 180 Non Clinical response (Module 1.7.1, Question 18, page 2) attached) 
Bispyrazolopurinamine was investigated for mutagenic effects using the 
Salmonella/microsome preincubation test (Ames test) to further support the 
refutation of the “indeterminate” in silico prediction by Leadscope (negative 
prediction by DEREK) for Bispyrazolopurinamine based upon a shared alert 
with the known AMES-negative CAS 2922-28-3. In this assay, 
Bispyrazolopurinamine was shown to be non-mutagenic both without and with 
S9 mix in the preincubation Salmonella/microsome test (Ames test), hereby 
confirming the previous in silico expert assessment (PH-42014 (Module 
4.2.3.7.6))

(1) The submitted Master Batch Record* states that the quantity of the material added may
differ from that described in the approval application form for marketing authorization in

from what is stated in the approval application form (J-AAF), justify the difference. If the 
applicant considers that the approval application form (J-AAF) should be revised, respond

deadline.

*: Step 4b MBR 2022 Gadoquatrane crude.pdf (Step 4b MBR 2022 Gadoquatrane crude.pdf)
Answer:
Regarding the neopentyltetramine hydrochloride input in step 4b of batch size 1 you pointed out,
explanation is provided below about the description that the charge quantity may differ from that described 
in the AAF depending on the content of GD-GLYDONIP.
During the manufacturing development research phase, studies to optimize stoichiometry were performed
based on the stoichiometry of neopentyltetramine hydrochloride (NPTA HCl) and GD-GLYDONIP. As a 
result, it was confirmed that if the content of GD-GLYDONIP is not less than 60%, a constant equivalent 
ratio with the amount of NPTA HCl does not affect the quality.
Under GMP operations, if the content of GD-GLYDONIP is below 78% in batch size 1, the amount of
NPTA HCl can be adjusted during the manufacturing, and MBR specifies the NPTA HCl input corresponding 
to the content of GD-GLYDONIP indicated by IPC as follows:
1st Limit test: Content of GD-GLYDONIP: not less than 78%
NPTA HCl input 27.5 kg
If the content of GD-GLYDONIP is below 78%, a second limit test is performed on the batch:
2nd Limit test: Content of GD-GLYDONIP (HPLC): not less than 72%
NPTA HCl input 25.3 kg
If the content of GD-GLYDONIP is below 72%, a third, final limit test is performed on the batch:
3rd Limit test: Content of GD-GLYDONIP (HPLC): not less than 60%
NPTA HCl input 21.0 kg
GD-GLYDONIP is not less than 60%, a constant equivalent ratio with the amount of NPTA HCl is 
maintained. Thus, the NPTA HCl input can be adjusted depending on the content of GD-GLYDONIP as 
shown below. A supporting document describing the following adjustment is submitted as Attachment 1:
1st Limit test: Content of GD-GLYDONIP (HPLC): not less than 81%
NPTA HCl input 48.9 kg
If the content of GD-GLYDONIP is below 81%, a second limit test is performed on the batch:
2nd Limit test: Content of GD-GLYDONIP (HPLC): not less than 78%
NPTA HCl input 47.1 kg
If the content of GD-GLYDONIP is below 78%, a third limit test is performed on the batch:
3rd Limit test: Content of GD-GLYDONIP (HPLC): not less than 72%
NPTA HCl input 43.4 kg
If the content of GD-GLYDONIP is below 72%, a fourth, final limit test is performed on the batch:
4th Limit test: Content of GD-GLYDONIP (HPLC): not less than 60%
NPTA HCl input 36.1 kg

Based on the above, we consider it is appropriate to modify the AAF.

Question:
Question 6.2
Section 1.5.7: For the test “Microbiological purity,” a brief description of the method has not 
been provided.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 6.2 (ND, P.5.2):
In accordance with section 3.2.P.5.2, the manufacturer’s QC testing site is conducting the 
microbial enumeration test and test for specified microorganisms according to 
Ph.Eur./USP/JP (current version at the time of testing).
A brief description of the current method is provided here below and will be included in the 
Normative Document in a future submission.
Microbial purity:
The method for the microbiological purity is sufficiently described in the Ph. Eur. 2.6.12, 
USP <61> or JP 4.05 (harmonized method). The test for specified microorganisms are 
described in detail in Ph. Eur. 2.6.13, USP <62> or JP 4.05 (harmonized method).
Procedure:
Weigh 10 g of the product into a tared container and document the weight. Add Buffered 
sodium chloride-peptone solution pH 7,0 to make 100 g and to get 1:10 dilution.
For TAMC-test add to parallel dishes 1 ml of the sample dilution 1:10. Add 15-20 ml of 
liquefied TSA agar (Casein soya bean digest agar) that has been cooled to +45°C. Incubate 
the plates at + 30°C - +35°C for 3-5 days (Pour-Plate Method of the Plate-Count method).
For TYMC-test add to parallel dishes 1 ml of the sample dilution 1:10. Add 15-20 ml of 
liquefied SAB agar (Sabouraud-dextose agar) that has been cooled to +45°C. Incubate the 
plates at + 20°C - +25°C for 5-7 days. (Pour-Plate Method of the Plate-Count method).
For the test for absence of Escherichia coli, shake and transfer 10 ml of 1:10 sample solution 
to 100 ml of Casein soya bean digest broth. Incubate at +30 - +35°C for 18-24 h. Shake and 
transfer 1 ml to 100 ml of MacConkey broth. Incubate at +42 - +44°C for 24-48 h. Subculture 
on a plate of MacConkey agar.  Incubate at +30 - +35°C for 18-72 h. Possible colonies are 
Gram-stained and if needed identified further.

Source:  P.5.2.01-02 Test Procedure / Darolutamide film-coated tablet 0.3 g
(#017747629; unchanged)

products and/or the formation of additional degradation products.

at the time of release and to accomplish it for stability testing, exclusively.

Question:
[Stability Report]:
(i).
Please explain the rationale for counting the initial real-time stability time point (i.e. t=0M) 
from bulk PFS instead of sterilized PFS.
(ii).
For stability data of lot (e.g. KT0KK7S), the stability starts from t=6M. Please clarify why 
there is no testing of product for Sterility (liquid DP) and Sterility (Syringe in Blister Tray).
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (3.2.P.8.1, 3.2.P.8.3):
(i).
Bayer defines the date of manufacturing of prefilled syringes as the time at which the bulk 
solution is filled into its final dosage form and container. Resultantly, the manufacturing date 
of Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in prefilled syringe finished drug product is the filling 
date of the bulk solution into syringes (bulk PFS). The same approach is also registered and 
approved by EMA and in all other Bayer territories globally.
The filling date also marks the beginning of the shelf life of the drug product, meaning that 
the shelf life is already starting before the labeling, assembly, blistering and outer surface 
sterilization process (sterilized PFS). 
To cover the shelf life claim of the finished drug product, the stability studies are starting with 
the bulk PFS instead of the sterilized PFS and thus avoid having an offset of multiple months 
between shelf life start and stability study start.
This concept was established for the already approved Aflibercept solution 40 mg/mL in 
prefilled syringe and is now also applied to the new Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL 
strength.
(ii).
KT0KK7S is a sterilized PFS batch originating from the bulk PFS batch 31226. As explained 
in response to (i) the shelf life of the syringes already started with the manufacturing date of 
the bulk batch 31226. The earliest time point after batch 31226 was manufactured into the 
sterilized PFS batch KT0KK7S was the 6 month time point, meaning the syringes were 6 
months old at that time with only a part of that in sterilized PFS form. The same applies to the 
other sterilized PFS batches.
The stability testing of sterilized PFS batches (e.g., KT0KK7S) is conducted in accordance 
with the protocol given in P.8.1.01-06, requiring sterility testing only at T=0M (not available 
for sterilized PFS) and after 24 months and 36 months of storage. This is in accordance with 
ICH Q5C Quality of Biotechnological Products: Stability Testing of 
Biotechnological/Biological Products which states: “Sterility testing or alternatives (e.g., 
container/closure integrity testing) should be performed at a minimum initially and at the end 
of the proposed shelf-life.”
Results of sterility testing after 24 months are available for all sterilized PFS batches and are 
presented in P.8.3.01-07.
The same stability schedule and data is submitted and approved in all other Bayer territories 
where the Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL PFS is registered, including EU.

114.3 mg/mL in prefilled syringe for intravitreous injection 
(#022984599; unchanged)

prefilled syringe for intravitreous injection (#022980339; unchanged)

The antibody intermediate, BAY 3547905, used in the manufacture of GPC3-TAC, 
BAY 3547926 injection, is based on a germlined and sequence optimized codrituzumab, an 
antibody that has shown signs of clinical efficacy in phase 1/ 2 studies.

variable light and heavy chain were humanized and germlined. Sequence Optimization included 
removal of four Lys residues in the Complementarity Determining Regions (CDR), being 
sensitive to unwanted chelator conjugation, as well as reduction of immunogenicity.

Question:
Question 1:
In R.2.02_022984027_01-comparability exercise, the residual DNA content in clinical batch is 
much higher than non-clinical batch, about 10 times higher. Please analyze the reasons and 
conduct a safety assessment.
Answer:
The difference in residual DNA contents is based on the analytical method used for the testing of 
the non-clinical and clinical batch. The method was validated before measuring the clinical batch. 
This included the determination of the Limit of Quantitation (LOQ) for the method. The non-
clinical batch was analyzed using a non-validated method with a lower quantitation limit. There is 
no safety risk because the clinical batch is well below the specification limit of max. 50.0 ppb with 
a result of <5.9 ppb.

Question:

In Section P.8.3.30 Stability data (IQMS-261194), 3 batches with Batch No. GPC3TAC 240112-
D1, GPC3TAC 240119-D1, GPC3TAC 240119-D2 listed in Table 2-1 cannot be found in other 
submission dossiers. Please provide the specific purposes/uses for these three batches. Please 
confirm if they are used for clinical trials. Please also confirm the specific purposes/uses for 
process verification batches listed in Section P.3.5.01(IQMS-404834).
Answer:
The manufacturing process for BAY 3547926 injection has been documented and verified as 
described and reported in document P.3.5.01 (IQMS-404834). The process verification batches 
are representative of clinical batches and show that the process is reliable and consistently 
produces BAY 3547926 injection doses of high quality.
The batches 240112-D1, GPC3TAC 240119-D1, GPC3TAC 240119-D2 mentioned in P.8.3.30 
(IQMS-261194) were manufactured for technical purposes to study the stability of actinium-225 
labeled antibody-chelator conjugate, BAY 3547926 injection, for up to 120 hours as part of the 
process and product development to support the shelf-life claim for the radiolabeled drug 
product.
The batches reported in document P.3.5.01 and P.8.3.30 are representative but have not been 
used in clinical trials.

Question:
Please clarify the following details:
1. It is noted from the Table of Summary of changes that the proposed change has been approved by EMA. However, based on the submitted EMA’s assessment report, the approved manufacturing sites for parametric release by EMA were Cardinal Health, US and Bayer AS, Norway instead of Agilera Pharma AS, Norway. Hence, please clarify if approval has been obtained from EMA or any HSA's reference agencies for the proposed change. If yes, please submit a copy of the approval letter(s) which should include details on the variations approved by the respective agencies.
Answer:
We, Bayer AG, herewith confirm that the parametric release variation has been approved by EMA for the manufacturing site Agilera Pharma AS, Norway. Our local Bayer subsidiary Bayer AS, Norway, is the final releasing site for Xofigo. Both sites are located in Norway.
During the variation procedure at EMA we were requested to provide the necessary GMP-related proof for the employed contract manufacturer Agilera Pharma AS, Norway, from a competent GMP-inspection authority that no objection against the establishment of parametric release for this manufacturing site exists.
Back at that time, GMP compliance has been confirmed by Norwegian Medical Products Agency (NOMA) indirectly via a new issued manufacturing/import authorisation (MIA) for Agilera Pharma AS, Norway, listing parametric release explicitly as GMP compliant if regulatory bodies approved this procedure (see attachment). While this means that GMP compliance for Agilera Pharma AS, Norway, will legally only achieved after approval of this variation by EMA, we do comply with the requirement that parametric release activities have been properly audited and no objections have been found (see page 5, footnote to section 1.1.2.3 in MIA Agilera Pharma AS). NOMA also clarified that updated GMP certificates were not issued but only in the future, despite positive audit of parametric release activities.
Together with the new MIA for Agilera Pharma AS (dated 22 January 2024) we provided the FDA approval letter (dated 26 September 2024) which states in general terms the approval for this US prior approval supplement for parametric release to EMA and received EMA approval (CHMP Opinion dated 12 December 2024). The US FDA approval comprises the approval of parametric release for both manufacturing sites, Cardinal Health, US and Agilera Pharma AS, Norway.
In the meantime, Agilera Pharma AS, Norway, was inspected by NOMA on 28 March 2025 and issued a new GMP certificate (dated 17 June 2025) which includes parametric release for Xofigo (see footnote to section 1.1.2.3 in GMP Certificate Agilera Pharma AS).

Question:
Question 12 
Please attach validation documentation for the identification test(s) when non‑pharmacopoeial 
test methods are referenced.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 12 (CTD section)  
We acknowledge the Agency’s comment. 
The identification Testosterone Enantate by TLC are tested in with the pharmacopeial method- 
(Ph. Eur. 2.2.27, USP <621>). 
The identification of Testosterone enanthate by HPLC is performed during the assay method. 
As mentioned in TRD 3.2.P.5.2, Identification of testosterone enanthate is made during the 
assay of testosterone enanthate. The identification is based on matching the retention time of 
the testosterone enanthate peak in the chromatogram of the sample solution with that of the 
corresponding peak in the reference solution, with a maximum deviation of ±5%. 
The assay method is performed by HPLC in accordance with Ph. Eur. 2.2.29 and USP <621>,

Question:
Question 2
The COA for the Gadoquatrane RS indicates that, prior to use for quantitative determination, 
it must be equilibrated for at least 7 days at 40%–50% relative humidity.
Please confirm whether the water content and assay as is (Gadoquatrane) in the COA for 
were obtained after 7 days of equilibration.
In addition, please provide the solvent used when determining the water content of the 
Gadoquatrane RS by Karl Fischer coulometric titration..
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2:
The water content and the assay as is for the Gadoquatrane reference standard were 
determined after 7 days of equilibration.

The determination of water content in the Gadoquatrane reference standard is conducted using 
coulometric Karl-Fischer titration, as outlined in S.4.2.01. The measurement system includes 
an oven where the solid sample is heated to 220°C. Water is transferred into the measurement 
cell via an inert gas flow, eliminating the need for a sample solvent. In the measurement cell, 
Hydranal Coulomat AG OVEN is utilized for coulometric titration.

Question:
Question 3
Apart from the requirement for certain reference standards to be equilibrated for 7 days before 
use, are there any other special precautions during the QC testing? Such as whether the 
autosampler tray needs to be temperature-controlled?  Whether reference standard solutions 
must be freshly prepared before use? If so, please provide instructions.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 3:
With respect to the drug product methods (Assay gadoquatrane / degradation products):
We recommend to use Waters, Screw Top Vials, 2 mL, e.g. 12x32 (P/N 186000307C) for 
determination of degradation products.
We recommend to use an Agilent 1290, Infinity II HPLC system.
Bayer uses a “Maximum Flow Gradient” setting of “5 mL/min2” for flow ramp up and flow 
ramp down (i.e. when the flow is switched between 0.4 mL/min and 0.8 mL/min and vice 
versa).
Autosampler / injector temperature is held at 23 +/-2 °C.
The gadoquatrane reference standard solution may be used for 4 days if stored at ambient 
conditions.
The sensitivity solution should be freshly diluted from the gadoquatrane reference standard 
solution on a working daily base.
Comparison solutions of the degradation products (i.e. Gd-GlyMe-DOTA, Glycine-Tris-Gd-
GlyMe-DOTA amide Isomer 2, Mono-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane) are not routinely used. If 
required, they should be prepared and used freshly or prepared, aliquoted, stored at < -15°C 
and each aliquot should preferentially only be used once.
For calculation of the assay gadoquatrane based upon the weight of the solution, the density at 
20°C is required. Determine the density of Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for 
injection at 20°C of the respective batch according to oscillating transducer method 
(Ph. Eur. 2.2.5) with at least four decimals.

Calcobutrol content:
The calcobutrol reference standard solution may be used for a maximum of six days, if stored 
at ambient conditions.
The sensitivity solution should be freshly prepared from the calcobutrol reference standard 
solution.
Determine the density of Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection at 20°C 
according to oscillating transducer method (Ph. Eur. 2.2.5) with at least four decimals.

Please revise the acceptance criteria in the CoAs for Hydrochloric acid, Ethanol 96%, Sodium

For Hydrochloric acid 1N, we have provided the quality specification along with the 
corresponding test methods. Therefore, where the CoA states “according to specification,” this
is fully aligned with the approved in-house specification. All tests required by the in-house

submission already includes the applicable pharmacopoeial monographs that define the detailed

specification,” this indicates conformity to the applicable pharmacopoeial monograph 
referenced in the dossier.
The CoA therefore reflects compliance with the detailed, legally-recognized acceptance limits 
found in those monographs. Referencing a separate, clearly identified specification (inhouse or 
compendial monograph) rather than repeating full acceptance tables on every CoA is an 
accepted and routine practice in global pharmaceutical supply chains. No deficiencies have 
been raised regarding this aspect.
The CoA phrase “according to specification” is not ambiguous in this case because the 
referenced specifications (in-house for HCl 1N; pharmacopeial monographs for the compendial 
excipients) are included in the submission and contain the explicit acceptance limits and test 
methods.
Requiring revision of globally used, multi-market CoAs to list every individual acceptance limit 
is not necessary where the definitive specification is already part of the regulatory dossier and 
the batch test results demonstrate compliance.

Question:
Question 1

Please provide a comprehensive introduction to the continuous manufacturing process based
on the actual production of this product, and further explain the rationale for considering the
collection of dry granules, final blending, and coating of existing sub-lot/lot as part of a
continuous manufacturing process (noting the certain differences compared with continuous
manufacturing processes developed using the conventional RTD model). If necessary, provide
images and videos to facilitate understanding. Please explain how, in commercial production,
effective quality control of the entire sub-lots can be ensured and consistency among sub-lots
maintained, based on the overall batch release requirements.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 ( P.2, P.3):
1) Overall Introduction to the Continuous Manufacturing Process
As shown in the process flow diagram submitted in the application dossier, the complete
manufacturing process for sevabertinib Tablets consists of  two major parts. The first part is
performed in batch mode, involving thorough mixing and sieving of all raw materials and
excipients (except magnesium stearate) to obtain a homogeneous pre-blend. The second part
employs continuous manufacturing on the integrated ConsiGma® 25 production line,
including processes such as powder feeding, roller compaction granulation, post-blending,
tableting, and coating.
A schematic diagram of the continuous manufacturing process is shown below Figure 1. The
specific description for the CM process is as follows:
1. The pre-blended material is filled into loss in weight feeder (the top-left in Figure 1) of
the ConsiGma® 25 for continuous feeding. The throughput rate of the process is
approximately 12kg/h.
2. After feeding, the material is directly conveyed to the roller compactor. With set
parameters for specific compaction force and  gap width, dry granulation is performed.
3. The granules produced are automatically conveyed via tubes to a weighing hopper for
weighing. If the granule weight is within the target range(approximately 1.3 kg), it
enters the blending hopper. A predetermined mass of magnesium stearate is
automatically added from its dedicated hopper for final blending. Each 1.3 kg of final
blended material is defined as a post-blended sublot.
4. After the final blending process, sub-lot is conveyed to a buffer hopper. Any non-
conforming sub-lot is diverted at this point. All confirming material is conveyed to the
tablet press.
5. During tableting, conforming core tablets are conveyed via tubes to  buffer hoppers,
located directly above the pan coaters. Approximately 3 kg sublots of core tablets are
then conveyed via gravity to two parallel, series-connected pan coaters. During film
coating  a predetermined mass of coating suspension is sprayed on the tablets, forming
each coating sublot.

For this continuous manufacturing process, the residence time distribution (RTD)
characterization is not necessary since there are no feeding and/or continuous blending
operations of individual components that would require detailed understanding of mixing
dynamics. The process utilizes a pre-blended material with established uniformity from batch
blending steps, rather than continuous feeding of individual components, eliminating the risk
of compositional variations. Both initial and post-blending are performed in controlled batch
mode, where blend uniformity is verified using traditional methods for the pre-blend and the
final blend quality by content uniformity of tablets.
Uniformity of the material has been consistently demonstrated through content uniformity
testing of all sub-lots across all manufactured batches, confirming that products meeting quality
requirements can be manufactured continuously, and RTD-based process characterization is
not required.

2) A justification about the quality consistency among sub-lots in PPQ batches
The continuous manufacturing process on the ConsiGma® line ensures effective quality control
of all sub‑lots through high‑frequency automated sampling (≥1 IPC test set per sub‑lot) during
tableting, continuous monitoring of process parameters, and full sub‑lot traceability. Deviating
sub‑lots can be uniquely identified and diverted, ensuring that only conforming material
contributes to the final batch. During clinical manufacturing campaigns and throughout
validation, each coating sub‑lot was fully tested (e.g. see P.2.3. Chapter 4.3. for primary stability
batches), confirming that all sub‑lots consistently met the specification. PPQ data further
demonstrated sub-lot quality and inter-batch consistency （see P.3.5.1）. Final batch release
requires both full sub‑lot‑level IPC compliance and batch‑level specification QC testing
compliance. Thus, full consistency among sub‑lots as well overall batch quality are ensured for
each batch.

Question:
Question 2
Please describe the material diversion and traceability strategies for each continuous
manufacturing step, and comprehensively demonstrate how non-conforming samples are
effectively segregated. Please confirm whether PAT tools are used, if yes, please provide the
development and application of PAT tools along with relevant validation information. For the
tablet compression step, the production process description indicates the installation of an
automatic tablet inspection device to measure tablet mass uniformity and hardness online,
enabling automatic adjustment and diversion. Please specify the detection frequency and its
rationale for the online measurements, detailed standards for automatic adjustment and
diversion, as well as supporting study/validation data.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2 ( P.3):
The control strategy of the ConsiGma 25 manufacturing line is designed to ensure final product
quality by monitoring the process parameters and automatically diverting any material that does
not meet pre-defined criteria. Traceability is maintained throughout the process using a “sublot”
principle.

Traceability via sublot principle:
Unit operations, that are intrinsically continuous processes, specifically the roller compaction
and tablet compression, are managed by creating discrete portions of material, hereinafter
referred to as "sublots." Sublots are generated based on a defined time or mass. Each sublot is
assigned a unique identification number by the ConsiGma 25 control system, allowing for
complete traceability as it moves to the next integrated unit operation. This system ensures that
a sublot cannot proceed unless all in-process controls and quality criteria for the current step
have been met. These criteria are defined in the product-specific recipe that governs the entire
manufacturing process.

Segregation of non-conforming material:
If a deviation from a defined criterion occurs, the entire affected sublot is diverted at a
designated diversion point. For the tableting process, individual non-conforming tablets are
diverted.
The primary diversion points are (see Figure 1):
• Post-blending sublot (after post-blending step)
The respective post-blending sublot is discarded before entering the tablet
press
• Individual tablets (directly at the tablet press) of uncoated tablets
The respective uncoated tablets are discarded before entering the coating
units
• Coating sublots (after the coating step)
The respective coating sublots are discarded and collected in separate
waste drums.
Examples for diversion triggers:
• Diversion point a):
A granule sublot, generated at the roller compactor, is diverted if its weight is too high
or low, if the lubricant was not added correctly, or if process parameters during roller
compaction (e.g. specific compaction force, gap width) or blending (e.g. blending
speed)) were outside their validated ranges.
• Diversion point b):
Individual tablets are diverted if the main compression force or the pre-compression
force displacement deviates from the target setpoint
• Diversion point c):
A coating sublot is flagged and diverted if upstream tablet testing shows non-
conforming results, or if coating process parameters (e.g., spray rate, inlet air
temperature/flow, drum speed) deviate from their validated ranges.

Application of Process Analytical Technology (PAT):
While no multivariate PAT tools (such as spectroscopic methods, e.g. NIR) are currently
implemented, the process control strategy relies on an online tablet multicheck for the tablet
compression step. It provides real-time data by direct mass and hardness measurement that is
used to monitor and control the process.
• The multicheck system was integrated into the manufacturing line to provide a high
degree of process assurance. It functions by automatically sampling and testing tablets
at a high frequency (20 tablets every 10 minutes). The data on mass uniformity and
hardness is fed back to the tablet press control system, enabling automatic adjustments
to the compression parameters (e.g., die fill depth) to maintain consistent tablet
quality. This immediate feedback loop ensures the process remains in a state of
control.
• The functionality of the multicheck, including its accuracy, precision, and the
qualification of its integration in the manufacturing line, was part of the equipment
qualification activities and were validated during process performance qualification
(P.3.5.01).

Tablet Compression: Online Measurement, Adjustment, and Diversion
Sampling philosophy:
There are two different types of sampling strategies performed for uniformity of mass and
resistance to crushing of uncoated tablets.
An automated process of highly frequent automated sampling and testing is achieved by the
multicheck. The tablet multicheck samples and tests 20 individual tablets every 10 minutes.
To further safeguard the automated measurements, there is a manual process for measuring
the tablet hardness and tablet weights as at-line IPC on standard stand-alone test equipment at
the beginning, middle and end of each batch (and after possible manual adaptation of
parameters).The combination of both independent measurements, one for direct process
control and adjustment and one as traditional at-line IPC to demonstrate accordance with the
specification allows increased process reliability.

Sampling frequency:
The testing frequency of the multicheck was established based on the process dynamics of the
continuous coating system. A new sublot begins the coating process approximately every 15
minutes. By testing every 10 minutes, it is ensured that every single coating sublot is
evaluated at least once, and often twice, by the multicheck system during its transit and
processing. This frequency guarantees that any potential deviation is detected.

Standards for adjustments:
The standards for action are based on the results from the multicheck. If the measured average
tablet mass begins to drift towards the specification limits, the system automatically adjusts
the fill depth of the tablet press die to bring the mass back to the target. This control prevents
the production of out-of-specification tablets. In the case of drifting resistance to crushing
values, the main compression force is adapted accordingly.
If any tested tablet is measured to be out of specification for mass or resistance to crushing,
the system initiates the following sequence:
1. An alarm notifies the operator.
2. The control system flags all tablets produced between the last conforming
measurement and the next conforming measurement as "non-conforming."
3. Due to the process flow, these flagged tablets will be part of specific coating sublots.
After the coating process for each affected sublot is complete, the control system
automatically diverts the entire non-conforming sublot at diversion point (c).

Verification/ Validation:
The described process control was investigated extensively during manufacturing process
development and is presented in section 4.8 of P.2.3.01. In this study, the process dynamics of
continuous process were investigated. The functionality of the multicheck control loop was an
integral part of this study. In addition, the reliability of the control system was proven during
process performance qualification. The results are presented in P.3.5.01.

Question:
Question 3
Please explain the basis for the selection of process validation batches, batch size, and validation
parameters, giving a comprehensive justification for the reasonableness and suitability of the
process validation activities. Also, please describe the special considerations for process
validation in continuous manufacturing processes
Answer:
Bayer's Reply to Question 3 (P. 2 P.3.5):
Based on equipment performance, product physicochemical properties, and prior DoE stage
studies (see dossier P.2.3.01 Process Development), it was determined that within the proposed
parameter ranges  a production throughput rate of approximately 12 kg/h can ensure continuous
production across the  process.
The drug product manufacturing process has been validated using three consecutive batches,
meeting general process validation requirements and aligning with the scientific and regulatory
principles described in ICH Q13.
The process parameters evaluated as critical process parameters during the process and product
development are sieve size (pre-blend sieving), specific compaction force (roller compaction),
gap width (roller compaction), and spray rate (coating).
As described in the  process description above, a pre-blend is manufactured prior to the
continuous production of tablets  in batch mode, where sieve size was validated as a critical
process parameter.
Granulation and tableting are performed in a continuous process. Based on prior process
development studies, the setting of specific compaction force and  gap width affects granulation
quality and are relevant  parameters for  the continuous production throughput rate. During the
three validation batches, validation was conducted using a constant throughput rate and process
parameters to ensure stability and controllability of the continuous process conditions.
The  spray rate during coating  affects tablet appearance and is a critical parameter for the
coating process. This parameter was validated.

As in continuous manufacturing, batch size is primarily defined by run time rather than
equipment capacity different batch sizes (20 ~ 60 kg) were manufactured by adjusting the total
run time while keeping the process settings/parameters unchanged. ICH Q13 clearly states that
batch definition in continuous manufacturing can be based on run time at a defined throughput
rate (mass flow rate), and batch size can also be defined as a range, e.g., by defining minimum
and maximum run times. Therefore, the continuous manufacturing system allows flexible batch
sizes without equipment changes. The selected batch size range (20 ~ 60 kg) aligns with
anticipated market demands.

During validation, extensive testing was performed, covering both the sub-lots and overall batch
level. Results confirmed consistent quality for all tablets produced under the validated
conditions.

Question:
Question 1
Pharmaceutical Development (3.2.P.2): please provide manufacturer's justiﬁcation regarding 
the requested method for dissolution according to Chapter 32P52 (0.6% Polysorbate 20) as 
discriminatory.
According to the tests presented as part of Chapter 32P22 and according to the proposed 
method development report, The method reveals discriminatory (change) only in relation to 
the particle size of the active ingredient and to a small extent for diﬀerent compression force 
in the process.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 ( 3.2.P.5, P.2.2.02):
The EMA states in its Assessment Report that “The development of the dissolution method 
has been well described, and the use of a surfactant has been acceptably justified. It was 
shown that 0.1 % Tween 20 and 0.3 % Tween 20 did not achieve sink conditions. The 
discriminatory ability of the dissolution method has been shown.”
Finerenone is a poorly soluble drug substance in aqueous solution. This is demonstrated in 
S.1.3.01_022285635_01 (Finerenone micronized drug substance – General information) and 
P.5.3.21_IQMS-451745_2.0 (Finerenone coated tablet 40 mg – Method Development – 
Dissolution) documents.
The development of the dissolution test method is described in P.5.3.21_IQMS-451745_2.0.
In accordance with general requirements on dissolution testing, i.e. as described in USP 
<1092>, dissolution conditions should consider the solubility of the drug substance. To 
improve solubility, the addition of surfactant is allowed in order to achieve sink conditions.
In addition, the dissolution method should show discriminatory power concerning the most 
critical product attributes, as e.g. particle size, compression force, etc., that may affect the 
release of the drug substance and therefore the quality of the drug product.
During development of the dissolution test method the discriminatory power of the method 
was investigated for the following critical attributes :
• Influence of Particle Size Distribution of the Drug Substance (refer to Figure 1) 
• Influence of Disintegrant (refer to Figure 2) 
• Influence of Compression Force (refer to Figure 3) 
• Influence of Accelerated Stability Testing (refer to Figure 4)
Overlays of all investigated critical product attributes examined in the context of determining 
the discriminatory properties of the dissolution method are shown below in Figure 1 to Figure 
4.
Stress stability conditions do not show significant influence of the dissolution behavior that is 
in line with the results of stability testing for Finerenone coated tablet 40 mg.
Differences of compression force shows only a small influence on the dissolution behavior.
Moreover, it was demonstrated that the selected dissolution method shows good 
discriminatory power for the most critical attributes as particle size and the availability of 
disintegrant.

information ( S.1.3.01_IQMS-231278, unchanged)

Question:
Validation of analytical methods (3.2.P.5.3) –
I. In the validation report for the Assay & Impurities method, no reference was found for 
forced degradation tests and within them, results for peak purity and mass balance to 
demonstrate the method as stability indicating. Reference was found to peak purity as part of 
the speciﬁcity on unstressed sol. Also, as part of the stability chapter, the results of Stress 
studies were presented under two conditions, hydrolysis and heating, in which no signiﬁcant
degradation of the active substance/increase in degradation substances was found. Why didn’t 
you considered oxidation and direct light tested on the DP solution?
II. No comparative dissolution proﬁle was found between a 20 mg and 40 mg dose in a 
medium containing a concentration of 0.1% Tween 80.
In addition, are the characteristics for which the method was found to be discriminatory for a 
20 mg dose (0.1% Tween 80) similar to the characteristics for which the method was found to 
be discriminatory for a 40mg dose (0.6% Tween 80), please explained and summarized.
Was the dissolution of a 40mg dose tested using a method containing only 0.1% Tween 80? If 
yes, please provide a dissolution proﬁle and a reference that shows compliance with the 
requested speciﬁcations, and reference to discriminatory characteristics.
If not available, please provide a justiﬁcation as to why it was not tested.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2 (P.5):
I. Although forced degradation studies are not explicitly required with regard to ICH 
guidelines, ICH Q1A (R2) recommends stress testing to help identifying likely 
degradation products which can in turn help establish the intrinsic stability of the molecule 
and validate the stability indicating power of the analytical procedures used. As thermal and 
hydrolytic stress conditions, as well as photolytic stability revealed a high stability 
of Finerenone (P.8.3.04_022987142_01 and P.8.3.05_022987143_01), i.e. only minor 
degradation was observed, additional chemical stress conditions were applied.  
Samples of Finerenone micronized drug substance and Finerenone coated tablet 40 mg were 
subjected to extended stress tests (e.g. thermal, hydrolytic, photolytic and oxidative) as 
summarized in Table 1 in order to investigate the formation of potential degradation products 
and to demonstrate the assay and degradation products method is selective and accurate 
regarding potential degradation products.

The mass balance has been calculated as well (see Table 2 and Table 3) applying the 
following equation:   
(Assay (post-stress) + Impurities (post stress))/ (Assay (pre-stress) + Impurities (pre-stress)) x 
100 = Mass balance (%)  
The additional chemical stress test conditions are well suited to obtain assay drop in the range 
from 5 to 15% and no lack of mass balance (< 95%) was observed, neither for the Finerenone 
micronized drug substance nor for Finerenone coated tablets 40 mg.  
Thus, the methods were shown to be stability indicating and are suitable for determination 
of assay and degradation products.  
Under all stress conditions, the peak purity of the finerenone in drug product was given 
(purity angel < purity threshold) (see purity plots Figure 5 - Figure 12).
The photostability of the drug substance in solution was investigated in the drug substance 
part 3.2.S (please refer to S.7.3.05_022475896_01).
The drug product solution for determination of degradation products is slightly sensitive to 
light. Therefore the sample solution has to be prepared freshly (see test procedure 
P.8.3.05_022987143_01).
Generally, the sensitivity to light of the drug product-solution (acetonitrile/water; 70:30) is 
not relevant in the context of the light stability of the drug product.

II. In accordance with USP <1092>, the dissolution methods for finerenone-coated tablets at 
20 mg and 40 mg were developed with the aim to ensure sink conditions for the drug 
substance and show sufficient discriminatory power regarding important critical attributes 
such as particle size, compression force, etc., to distinguish between acceptable and 
unacceptable batches.
Sink conditions are defined as the volume of dissolution medium which is at least greater than 
three times that is required to form a saturated solution of the drug substance. Sink conditions 
are required to ensure that dissolution testing is not significantly influenced by solubility 
characteristics of the drug substance.
When sink conditions are met, the dissolution process is primarily controlled by the 
dissolution rate of the solid dosage form rather than by the solubility characteristics of the 
drug substance. This allows for a more reliable assessment of the drug product's release 
profile. Maintaining sink conditions is essential to achieve the level of consistency and 
reliability needed for robust methods, particularly for BCS Class II compounds such as 
Finerenone.
During development of the dissolution methods, solubility data (refer to Table 1) of the drug 
substance has shown that sink conditions for 20 mg Finerenone are only achieved, if 0.1% 
Tween 20 has been added to the dissolution medium acetate buffer pH 4.5. Whereas 0.6 % 
Tween 20 has to be added to the selected dissolution medium for Finerenone coated tablet 
40 mg to achieve sink conditions.
In addition, the dissolution method of Finerenone 20 mg that uses a dissolution medium with 
0.1% Tween 20 shows good discriminatory power to the most important critical process 
parameters: particle size of the drug substance and the amount of disintegrant (please refer to 
P.5.3.21_022302454_01 Finerenone coated tablet – Method Development – Dissolution)
The selected dissolution method of Finerenone 40 mg that uses a medium with 0.6% Tween 
20 shows good discriminatory power for the particle size and the disintegrant as well (see 
P.5.3.21_IQMS-451745_2.0). 
Therefore, the dissolution method of Finerenone 20 mg and the method of Finerenone 40 mg 
have comparable discriminatory properties.
Initially, a concentration of 0.1% Tween 20 appears to adequately dissolve 40 mg of 
Finerenone drug substance during the dissolution test. This observation aligns with the 
solubility data presented in Table 4.  
However, sink conditions are not achieved under these parameters. 
Moreover, the dissolution profile of Finerenone coated tablet 40 mg in acetate buffer pH 4.5 + 
0.1% Tween 20 (please refer to Figure 14 and Figure 15) shows a higher scattering of single 
results at the specified timepoint at 15 min. This indicates that sink conditions are not present 
in this media.
Therefore further experiments were performed to investigate sink conditions during the 
dissolution test of the drug product Finerenone coated tablet 40 mg by testing dissolution of 
three tablets per vessel (900 mL in acetate buffer pH 4.5) with the addition of different 
concentrations of Tween 20 (see Figure 16). Three tablets were added per vessel because the 
dissolution medium should be able to dissolve at least 3 times the amount of Finerenone drug 
substance.
The results shown in Figure 16 indicate that Tween 20 concentrations below 0.6% are not 
sufficient to achieve the recommended 3-fold sink conditions.
Based on the results presented above, the chosen surfactant concentration of 0.6% Tween 20 
is selected to avoid artificial and over-discriminatory effects.
Bayer performed dissolution testing in acetate buffer pH 4.5 + 0.1% Tween 20 with 6 items of 
Finerenone coated tablet 40 mg from the primary stability batch KM60385.
Although the dissolution profile of the investigated primary stability batch KM60385 
obtained in acetate buffer pH 4.5 + 0.1% Tween 20 would possibly meet the specification 
limit in stage 2, the dissolution medium acetate buffer pH 4.5 + 0.6% Tween 20 has been 
chosen for release - and stability testing, as this method is found to show good discriminatory 
power in relation to critical formulation attributes and 3 fold sink conditions as required in 
USP<1092>. 
This ensures that the dissolution method is able to reveal physical differences of the 
formulations and solubility of the drug substance does not become the limiting factor during 
dissolution testing.
In conclusion, Bayer shows that the selected dissolution medium acetate buffer pH 4.5 with 
addition of 0.6% Tween 20, provides acceptable sink conditions and has shown 
discriminatory power (see P.5.3.21, section 2.6) and robustness (see P.5.3.21, section 2).
This also corresponds to the dissolution method of Finerenone coated tablet 20 mg.

Question:
Question 2
Please provide the details of the Time Out of Refrigeration (TOR) and Temperature Excursion 
studies to confirm that the excursion condition does not impact batch quality over 36 months. 
Please refer to the guideline for Stability testing for prescription medicines (Sections 14.4.3 
and 14.4.4).
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2:
The current available data of TOR and temperature excursion (cycling) studies for Aflibercept 
solution 114.3 mg/mL in vial and PFS are provided in CTD sections P.8.3.11-2.0, P.8.3.11-
6.0, P.8.3.04-02 and P.8.3.04-1.0. Those include respective results for up to 24 months of 
long-term storage, which are well within the shelf-life specification acceptance criteria. Only 
minor differences in relation to the shelf-life specification acceptance criteria were observed 
between studies subjected to additional cycling/ TOR and studies without additional stress for 
those quality attributes that are linked to the major degradation pathways of Aflibercept, i.e. 
aggregation as determined by SE-UPLC and isoaspartate content formation. The results are 
compiled in the tables below. Note that an additional decimal is provided for aggregation 
results to demonstrate that there is no significant difference between cycled/TOR product and 
non-cycled product. The impact of the additional stress through cycling conditions and 
additional TOR is also negligible compared to the range left up to the shelf-life specification 
acceptance criteria. It is therefore expected that the allowed temperature excursions and 
respective TOR times are also associated with no impact on product quality for a shelf-life of 
36 months.
The TOR and cycling studies for the PFS are still ongoing and will be continued up to 36 
months. The respective data is expected to be available in Q3 2026. Like for the vial 
presentation, it is expected that the allowed temperature excursions and respective TOR times 
are associated with no impact on product quality for a shelf-life of 36 months based on 
available data in the referenced CTD sections and as compiled below in Table 2. and Table 3.
The cycling study of the vial presentation ended after 24 months as the original study protocol 
did not foresee a test point after 36 months storage and the time point had already passed in 
October 2024. The applicant is conducting an additional study where three vial batches that 
are currently on long-term storage will be temperature cycled and tested after 36 months.  
The data obtained in the vial cycling study indicate that an initial temperature cycling at the 
start of the shelf life does not accelerate the drug product degradation when compared to non-
cycled drug product.  
For isoaspartate, the offset between cycled and non-cycled drug product at T=0 was basically 
maintained until the 24 months timepoint, being up to 0.03 mol/mol higher for cycled product 
at T=0 and up to 0.02 mol/mol higher for cycled product at T=24. For SE-UPLC main peak 
purity, the gap between cycled and non-cycled drug product decreases along the shelf-life. 
While at T=0 the maximum observed gap is 1.2 %, at T=24 the gap is 0 %. Similar results are 
obtained for aggregates.

Therefore, the applicant is convinced that a cycling study with the temperature cycling taking 
place at the end of the shelf life is representative for any temperature excursions during the 
shelf life and the study design of the proposed 36M cycling study justified.
Respective data is expected to be available in Q3 2026.
The applicant commits to conduct the stability studies as indicated above and to provide the 
data of the studies to the health authority after their finalization.

The XRPD patterns of the XRPD moisture measurement sorption in the ranges of 1 to 20%

Question 8
In order to assure future batches are representative of submission batches, the assay 
specification limit for drug substance Sevabertinib should be tightened to 98.5-101.5%.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 8 (S.4):
According to internationally valid guidelines for analyses of active pharmaceutical 
ingredients, it is well established to take into account the analytical variability for setting 
specification limits. The Technical Guide for the Elaboration of Monographs (8th Edition, 
2022, page 8) states the following:
“For a specific assay using a separation technique (for example, liquid or gas 
chromatography), the upper assay limit is normally 102.0%; the lower assay limit will take 
account of the impurities present based on the available batch/stability data and approved 
specifications. It may therefore be lower than 98.0%.”
Considering the specification limit of 1.0 % for the organic impurity DS-Pyridone, the lower 
limit for assay i.d.s. has been set to 97.0 %.
The proposed specification limit for assay i.d.s. also reflects data from release and stability 
testing of representative development batches, since only limited data from commercial 
batches are available to date.
Please note that reported values for assay i.d.s. are average values (double determination), and 
all underlying individual results also must comply with the specification limits.

Question:
Question 11
Section 3.2.P.4.1 should include controls on functionality-related characteristics of 
relevant excipients in line with their specific grade. Whether this is reassured by the 
drug product manufacturer by routine testing or solely relying on CoAs from the 
relevant excipient suppliers, it need not be specified in the regulatory dossier as it falls 
under GMP.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 11 (P.2; P.4):
The P.2.2.01 Pharmaceutical Development – Drug Product document (section 2.6) shows a 
comparison of two or more grades of four excipients (microcrystalline cellulose, lactose 
monohydrate, crospovidone, magnesium stearate). The purpose of this comparison was to 
determine whether one or more grades are not suitable for further process development. If a 
grade is not suitable, it follows that the physical-chemical parameter (e.g. particle size 
distribution) that sets it apart from the other grades must be critical. Any such parameter 
would require a control strategy, either via GMP procedures or as a regulatory requirement.
It was found that all grades tested are, in principle, suitable. Therefore, none of the parameters 
are critical and no controls are required. In other words, none of the grades tested had a 
characteristic that was relevant for its function in this product. For each excipient, one grade 
was then selected for further development.
Only one excipient (microcrystalline cellulose) was, however, found to have a potential effect, 
depending on the grade, on a critical quality attribute of the product (dissolution). Although 
all results were within specification, the rate of dissolution may be affected by the grade 
selected. The primary distinguishing feature of each grade is the particle size distribution 
(PSD). Therefore, even though the PSD of the excipient grade is not a critical parameter per 
se, it is indicated in the P.4.1.01 document (T.03.91_5.0 Quality Reference / Cellulose 
microcrystalline excipient) that PSD requires control, if applicable.
The specified ranges and test method for PSD are defined and justified by the qualified 
manufacturer and/or supplier. Bayer therefore controls, if applicable, the PSD of the 
microcrystalline cellulose for use in drug formulation. This case applies to Sevabertinib 10 
mg coated tablet.
The current PSD ranges for Avicel PH 101, set by the supplier are as follows:
d10 
14 – 30 µm
d50 
40 – 75 µm
d90 
77 – 156 µm
The PSD results (by laser diffraction) for the Avicel PH 101 batch that is referenced in the 
P.2.2.01 Pharmaceutical Development – Drug Product (no. BX07559) are within the above-
mentioned specification:
d10 
22 µm
d50 
63 µm
d90 
138 µm
Any change that is proposed by the supplier is evaluated via the established GMP change 
management procedure for any impact on a marketed product, including Sevabertinib 10 mg 
coated tablet.
The other three excipients did not yield a significant difference in dissolution behavior. As a 
result, no additional requirements or controls, beyond the compendial ones, are considered 
meaningful.

Question:
Question 12
An increased frequency of in-process control testing should be adopted to effectively 
monitor the continuous manufacturing process, i.e. every 15 minutes. It should 
additionally be confirmed that testing will be completed following any period of 
downtime.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 12 (P.3; R.3):
Please be aware that the control strategy for the process is based on two independent systems. 
An automated process of highly frequent automated sampling and testing is achieved by a 
tablet multicheck (testing of 20 individual tablets every 10 minutes). The multicheck is 
directly connected to the tablet press, and the measured values allow automatic re-adjustments 
of the tablet press. This part of the control strategy therefore ensures a high degree of process 
reliability due to its immediate process monitoring and short reaction times associated with 
stable production parameters, so that tablets can be reliably produced in accordance with 
specifications. The limits of this automated testing are described in the summary of the 
production recipe (R.3.1.02 Batch Record Master).
To further safeguard the automated measurements, there is a manual process for measuring 
the tablets as at-line IPC on standard stand-alone test equipment at the beginning, middle and 
end of each batch (and after possible adaptation of parameters or downtimes). The 
combination of both independent measurements, one for direct process control (R.3.1.02 
Batch Record Master) and adjustment and one as traditional at-line IPC to demonstrate 
accordance with the specification (P.3.3.01 Manufacturing Process and Process Controls) 
allows increased process reliability.

Question:
Question 14
An in-process control limit for friability of core tablets should be adopted.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 14 (P.3):
With respect to the production of tablets, Ph.Eur. states the following: „In the manufacture of 
tablets, measures are taken to ensure that they possess a suitable mechanical strength to avoid 
crumbling or breaking on handling or subsequent processing. This may be demonstrated using 
the tests described in general chapters 2.9.7. Friability of uncoated tablets and 2.9.8. 
Resistance to crushing of tablets.“
Ph. Eur. 2.9.7 states that “the measurement of tablet friability supplements other physical 
strength tests, such as tablet breaking force.”
Bayer maintains that the originally proposed control strategy, without a supplementary in-
process control for friability, remains scientifically justified. The originally proposed control 
strategy ensures that tablets complying with the established specifications, including release 
testing, are consistently safe and effective for patients. The scientific rationale was reviewed 
and accepted by both the FDA and Health Canada. It is also noted that while the harmonized 
USP/Ph.Eur. chapter describes friability testing as an additional method for assessing physical 
strength, it does not mandate its use as an in-process control.
In line with the argumentation provided above, batches manufactured subsequent to process 
validation, did not include an in-process control for friability.
Bayer acknowledges MHRA’s position and therefore commits to adopting the in-process 
control for the friability of core tablets for all future manufacturing batches intended for the 
UK market. At the same time Bayer respectfully requests that the MHRA accept the batches 
already produced post-process validation for release to the UK as these batches were 
produced under scientifically justified control strategy and are intended to supply the UK as 
well.

Source:  P.3.3.01 Manufacturing Process and Process Controls / BAY 2927088 coated
tablet 10 mg (IQMS-441006_3.0; amended)

Question:
Question 15
Given that the average weight of film-coated tablet is not controlled in the finished drug 
product specification, an in-process control for film-coating uptake should be adopted.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 15 (P.2; P.3; R.3):
We acknowledge the recommendation from MHRA to adopt an in-process control (IPC) for 
film-coating uptake, given that the average weight of the film-coated tablet is not included in 
the finished drug product specification. However, based on extensive process development 
within the Quality by Design (QbD) framework, we have established a comprehensive control 
strategy that ensures process consistency and product quality. We would like to provide 
scientific justification for why our existing control strategy provides robust control and why 
the addition of a formal IPC for coating weight gain would not add value.
The primary purpose of the film coating for BAY 2927088 (Sevabertinib) 10 mg coated tablet 
is cosmetic/ non-functional, i.e. to enable easier identification of tablets for the patients due to 
its red brown color. The effect of the materials and the process parameters on the appearance 
of coated tablets was evaluated within the QbD framework (ICH Q8), and an extensive risk
analysis using FMEA was carried out and its summary is reported in the P.2.3.01 
Manufacturing Process Development section 2.3.
The coating of the BAY 2927088 (Sevabertinib) 10 mg coated tablet has high opacity and 
achieves full color saturation at approx. 50 % of the target coating amount (i.e. at 1.4 mg of 
the final 2.8 mg target). This means that beyond this point, variations in the final coating 
amount have no notable effect on the tablet’s appearance, which is the coating’s primary 
function. Furthermore, the effect of coating amount on drug release was investigated. Even 
with a significant over-coating resulting in a tablet weight gain of 5.6 mg (double the target of 
2.8 mg), no impact on the dissolution profile was observed. Details are provided in the dossier 
(P.2.2.01 Pharmaceutical Development Drug Product, Section 2.5). Thus, within a range of 
50 - 200 % of the intended coating uptake, both appearance and dissolution requirements are 
met.
In addition, thorough process understanding and a multifaceted control strategy have been 
established to ensure effective process control and direct verification of product output.
Control of Tablet Cores:
In-process controls are in place for the uncoated tablet cores including tablet core weight and 
resistance to crushing. This ensures consistency of the tablets entering the coating process.
Control of Process Parameters:
The coating process is managed by a validated recipe (R.3.2.01 Batch Record Master 
(Recipe)) with tightly controlled and monitored process parameters, including:
• Coater load (1.5 – 3.0 kg)
• Spray rate (40 – 50 g/min) (CPP)
• Inlet air temperature (76 – 90°C)
• Inlet air volume (195 – 255 m³/h)
• Drum rotation speed (92 – 98 rpm)
These process parameters were all part of the DoE studies on a commercial scale. A violation 
of any of these ranges leads to a diversion of the respective sublot (as described in P.2.3.01 
Manufacturing Process Development, Section 4.1.3.1 and P.3.3.01 Manufacturing Process 
and Process Controls).
The process parameters that could affect the amount of the deposited sprayed material on the 
tablets such as spray rate, air flow rate, inlet air temperature, drum speed and coater load are 
all controlled.
Direct In-Process and Release Testing of the Appearance:
The most relevant indicator of coating quality is the final appearance. This is controlled via:
• In-Process Control: Appearance testing is performed for each batch.
• Release Testing: Appearance testing is a formal test on the release sample.
During the process development, it has been investigated whether weight gain is an indicator 
of coated tablet appearance, but it turned out that weight gain is not a reliable or relevant 
indicator of quality for this specific process.

BAY 2927088 (Sevabertinib) 10 mg coated tablet.
In conclusion, the control strategy for BAY 2927088 (Sevabertinib) 10 mg coated tablet was 
developed based on a scientific understanding of the product and process.
