Question:
Question 17
In order to assure future batches are representative of submission batches, the total impurities 
specification limit in the drug product should be tightened to 1.0%.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 17 (P.5):
Bayer agrees to tighten the release and shelf-life specification (P.5.1.01, P.5.1.02) for sum of 
degradants in the drug product from max. 1.5% to max. 1.2%.
As explained in the P.5.6.01 Justification of Specification document, this limit combines the 
established specification for DS-Pyridone (max. 1.0%) with a single unspecified degradant 
(max. 0.2%).
It is acknowledged that the submission batches (primary stability and process validation) 
show results for sum of degradants that are consistently below 1.0% and typically show < 
0.1% for any unspecified degradant. Nevertheless, a further restriction to max. 1.0% is not 
warranted. It would contradict the toxicologically confirmed limit for DS-Pyridone, which is 
the main metabolite in vivo. The sum of degradation products must take into account the 
occurrence of at least one degradant, other than DS-Pyridone, at 0.1 – 0.2%. Applying a limit 
of max. 1.0% for the sum would effectively mean lowering the limit for DS-Pyridone to max. 
0.8%, meaning below that of the Drug Substance. Such a change is not considered meaningful 
for control over the quality of the Drug Product.
Based on this rationale, a limit of max. 1.2% for the sum of degradation products is 
considered the most stringent specification that can be appropriately justified.

Question:
Question 1a.
a. Related Regulation: Article 7(2)(b)
Reason for Supplement: 3.2.S.1.3. General Characteristics and 3.2.S.3.1 
Structure and Other Characteristics
1) Submission of detailed results of structural analysis on the non-quantified
hydrate form of the drug substance is required.
2) Molecular formula and molecular weight should be presented based on the
hydrated form of the drug substance.
3) Solubility data for non-polar solvents have not been submitted.
4) XRPD detailed numerical data (2Θ) for verification of the drug substance has
not been submitted and insufficient explanation of results based on the 
hydrated state.
Supplement Requirement: Please submit additional materials regarding the general 
characteristics of the drug substance considering the above matters.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1a. ( S.3.1):
a.1)
The dose strength of the DP, which is critical for correct dosing of the drug, is based on the 
anhydrate form, specifying that each tablet contains 10 mg of sevabertinib. As the dose 
strength is independent of the number of water molecules (x) in the hydrate, and does not 
affect the labeled strength, a specification of (x) is not required from a safety and efficacy 
point of view. From scientific point of view, it is correct to keep the number of water 
molecules (x) unspecified in the molecular formula of the drug substance.
Although the number of water molecules (x) cannot be specified, the amount of water in the 
DS is ensured by the manufacturing process and is controlled by the DS specification (refer to 
Specification S.4.1.01). DS batches that do not comply with the specification will not be used 
to manufacture the drug product (DP).
The drug substance in its crystalline form, Hydrate 1 Mod. A, has been fully characterized by 
thermoanalytical, spectroscopic, and X-ray diffractometric data (see S 3.1.01 Structure 
Elucidation and other Characteristics). In addition, the special non-stoichiometric character 
of this hydrate was clearly demonstrated by an X-ray single-crystal structure based on one
single crystal. In the X-ray single-crystal analysis, it can be seen that the water molecules are 
randomly arranged between the layers of the active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) 
molecules. The crystal packing including the water molecules is shown in the following 
figures.

Figure 1: Crystal packing of Hydrate 1 Mod. A

In addition to the interactions between the API molecule and the water molecules, 
intermolecular hydrogen bonds also occur between the water molecules, which supports the 
nonstoichiometric, variable character of Hydrate 1 Mod. A.

Figure 2: Crystall packing of Hydrate 1 Mod. A – hydrogen bonds

These different types of intermolecular interactions explain why this crystal lattice can 
implement varying numbers of water molecules without the actual lattice structure changing. 
The correlation of XRPD data to the X-ray single-crystal structure was achieved by 
comparing the calculated X-ray powder diffraction pattern with the measured X-ray powder 
diffraction pattern of the various batches of Hydrate 1 Mod. A.

Based on the nonstoichiometric, variable character of Hydrate 1 Mod. A with an undefined 
ratio of sevabertinib to water, a value for (x) cannot be specified.
However, it may seem that based on the water content 1-4% specified for the drug substance, 
it is theoretically possible to calculate a number of water molecules (x) in the crystalline 
lattice. The theoretical value based on measured water content 1-4% is provided for 
information purposes only and corresponds approximately to x = 0.28 – 1.12. This calculated 
number of water molecules does not describe the actual water amount in the lattice structure 
of the drug substance and would not be a correct representation of the DS physical structure. 
The reasons are as follows.
Water content (%) and the hydration number x represent fundamentally different concepts and 
physical dimensions. Water content determined by Karl Fischer titration is a mass‑based 
parameter (w/w%) that reflects the total amount of water present, including surface‑adsorbed 
water, channel/pore water, and lattice‑associated water. In contrast, the hydration number x is
a crystallographic concept describing the molar ratio (mol/mol) of structurally defined water 
molecules within the crystal lattice per mole of the drug substance.
As the lattice occupancy of water can vary with the environmental equilibrium state rather 
than remaining within a specification‑worthy interval, it is not only inappropriate to define a 
fixed hydration number x, but also scientifically unsound to provide a “range” for x. 
Converting a mass‑based water content to a structural x value—fixed or ranged—does not 
accurately represent the crystal structure and may lead to conceptual misunderstanding.

Figure 3: Overlay of calculated and measured XRPD of Hydrate 1 Mod. A

To clarify once again, due to the nonstoichiometric, variable character of Hydrate 1 Mod. A 
varying amounts of water molecules can be included in the lattice structure of the drug 
substance, which go beyond the theoretically calculated range. Therefore, it is scientifically 
not correct to specify a number or a range for the amount of (x) water molecules in the 
molecular formula of the drug substance. Bayer kindly asks the Agency to accept an
undefined amount of water (x = variable, non-stoichiometric hydrate) in the Korean 
application form.

a.2)
It is well-known that two kinds of hydrate formation exist[1]:
Stoichiometric hydrates have a crystal lattice based on an exact water content with a well-
defined mole ratio of water molecules and given API molecule.
Non-stoichiometric hydrates have a continuously variable composition (due to the water 
content) within a certain range without any significant changes in crystalline structure.
Hydrate 1 Mod. A belongs to the second class described above and thus exhibits variability in 
water content. This must be described by the following structural formula:
C24H25ClN4O5 · x H2O

The variable molar fraction of water in the crystal lattice of hydrate 1 Mod. A makes it 
impossible to name a molar mass based on the hydrated form. The molecular weight can only 
be provided for the anhydrous form.
In 2008 Newman, Reutzel-Edens and Zografi[2] described in their minireview the way to 
evaluate sorption data of a given pharmaceutical active ingredient by using the following 
flowchart (figure 4):

Figure 4: Decision tree for hydrate characterization

By using these criteria and based on the given definitions, Sevabertinib Hydrate (BAY 
2927088 hydrate) can be described as a non-stoichiometric hydrate, because its crystalline 
lattice is able to include variable numbers of water molecules without changes in the observed 
XRPD pattern and consequentially the crystalline structure. Water content in the drug 
substance will be controlled with the specification of 1.0 to 4.0 %.

a.3)
We have determined the requested solubility data of the solvents Tetrahydrofuran and 
Isopropyl acetate.
Solubility for Tetrahydrofuran was found to be 41.579 g/l (after 3 hours at 25°C).
Solubility for Isopropyl acetate was found to be 2.695 g/l (after 3 hours at 25°C).
This information is included in S.1.3.01 General Information - General Properties.

a.4)
Detailed numerical data (2Θ) of all technically relevant XRPD patterns of the different 
crystalline forms is provided in S.3.1.01 Structure Elucidation and other Characteristics / 
Additional Information on Polymorphism.
In RH XRPD experiments, the behavior of the crystalline lattice of Hydrate 1 Mod. A was 
examined under different humidity conditions (0 – 90% RH sorption and desorption in 10% 
steps) at a constant temperature of 25°C. In the sorption experiment, the substance (Hydrate 1 
Mod. A, Batch BXR9J78) was initially dried at 0% humidity and was present as Mod. IV at 
1% RH. This modification was retained up to 20% RH and converted in the next step to 
Hydrate 1 Mod. A. This crystal lattice then remained unchanged up to 90% RH. This effect 
was also observed in the desorption experiment: at 20% RH, Hydrate 1 Mod. A was 
converted to the anhydrous form Mod. IV. These experiments clearly demonstrate the 
behavior of Hydrate 1 Mod. A in a kinetic experimental design. It cannot be directly 
correlated with the results of the storage studies, as these are based on a thermodynamic 
approach.

Figure 5: Overlay of XRPD patterns, RH XRPD Sorption

Figure 6: Overlay of XRPD patterns, RH XRPD Desorption

The RH XRPD results perfectly match the data from the DVS measurements, which gives us 
information on the change of water amount in and on the sample BXR9J78 (Hydrate 1 Mod. 
A). Dynamic uptake (sorption) of water was observed between 0 and 10% RH, followed by a 
flatter curve up to 95% RH and a total water uptake of 4%. The desorption curve follows this 
curve in the opposite direction, not without exhibiting a slight hysteresis. This is due to the 
fact that even in a variable non-stoichiometric hydrate, intermolecular interactions must first 
be overcome to remove the water from the lattice. This process, as well as the formation of 
the crystal lattice of the metastable Mod. IV, slightly delays the kinetics of desorption 
compared to sorption.

Figure 7: DVS Isotherm Plot

Another technique for investigating the behavior of Hydrate 1 Mod. A upon loss of water are 
thermoanalytical methods. In this case, Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) and 
Thermogravimetry (TGA) techniques were used. The thermogram of the DSC measurement 
of sample BXR9J78 (Hydrate 1 Mod. A) initially shows a broad endothermic signal, which 
indicates the release of water. This is confirmed by the TGA measurement, which describes a
mass loss. Unlike stoichiometric hydrates, this stage is somewhat soft and continuous, clearly 
highlighting the non-stoichiometric character of the hydrate.
After the water release, the sample fundamentally has the possibility to become amorphous or 
to convert into any of the crystal lattices of the anhydrous modifications, thereby slightly 
stabilizing the lattice. In this case, a further small endothermic process is observed at higher 
temperatures, followed by a similarly small exothermic process. This involves the melting and 
recrystallization of one of the formed anhydrous forms, followed by the melting process of 
Mod. I.
Compared to the previously described techniques, the DSC measurement is energetically non-
neutral for the applied sample and can thus significantly favor transformation processes, 
especially at higher temperatures. This leads to the observation of the melting point of Mod. I, 
while the kinetic experiments (RH XRPD and DVS) did not result in a transformation of 
Hydrate 1 Mod. A to Mod. I.

Figure 8: DSC and TGA thermogram of Hydrate 1 Mod. A

In summary, all available data support the assignment of sevabertinib hydrate as a non-
stoichiometric hydrate.

Question:
Question 1g.
g. Related Regulation: Article 7(2)(b)
Reason for Supplement: 3.2.S.4.5. Justification of Specification
1) Insufficient basis for setting specifications for ‘appearance(color)’.
2) Safety verification results presented as the basis for setting specifications for
‘Enantiomeric Purity’ has not been submitted.
3) Need to demonstrate the validity of the specification of ‘Particle Size’ based on
actually measured values in the particle size test.
Supplement Requirement: Please submit additional materials regarding the basis for setting 
standards considering the above matters.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1g. ( S.4):
g.1)
Appearance is specified as general GMP requirement according to ICH Q6A. Reflecting the 
development history, BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance is specified to be a 
white to off-white to yellow to pinkish powder. All batches manufactured for late phase 
clinical trials comply with these criteria.
The color of BAY 2927088 is not in connection to the purity profile. Light pink or yellow 
crystals were mainly observed on the drug substance prior to micronization. Due to the crystal 
habit (triangular prisms), the light is refracted differently. Prisms can widen light beams and, 
as reflection prisms, can also correspond to a combination of several mirrors. Smaller crystals 
(e.g. after micronization) scatter the light so strongly that they appear white. If the proportion 
of diffuse light decreases as the crystals get larger and larger, the color becomes more intense 
and depends on the side length of the respective prism surfaces.
Whilst the specification for color is set on visual inspection without a microscope, batches can 
appear off-white, whereas the nuance of off-white can appear yellow or pinkish (S.4.5.01 
Justification of Specification and Skip Testing).
Batch overviews in S.4.4.01 for development and commercial batches show that several 
batches have been reported as off-white. Whilst sometimes yellowish is reported, batches may 
also appear pinkish.
Figure 9: Picture of BAY 2927088 hydrate taken under the microscope

g.2)
No dedicated qualification studies were conducted using only the incorrect enantiomer. In the 
course of the 4-week repeat dose toxicology studies in rats and monkeys, two different 
batches of BAY 2927088 were used, which contained slight impurities with the incorrect
enantiomer. The 4-week study in rats was conducted with batch BXR9A7L, which had a 
residual content of 1% of the incorrect enantiomer. The batch BXR9CJK, which was used in 
the monkey study, contained a residual content of 0.71% of the incorrect enantiomer. 
Therefore, based on the conducted in vivo studies, the incorrect enantiomer is considered 
qualified for the aforementioned concentrations.

g.3)
Particle size data obtained for x(10), x(50) and x(90) are provided for micronized drug 
substance batches produced at lab scale during development in section S.4.4.01 Batch 
Analyses (Development).
In step 4, BAY 2927088 hydrate non-micronized is micronized using a fluid energy mill. The 
particles are reduced in size by high-speed particle-to-particle impact.
The substance is ground to the particle-size stipulated in the product specification by adjusting 
the compressed gas pressure and the feeding rate.
As shown in a PAR (proven acceptable ranges) study, both process parameters can be varied 
over a wide range to meet the desired particle size distribution and are therefore considered 
not critical (refer to S.2.6.11 Manufacturing Process Development - Additional Information).
...
In conclusion, based on the data presented, a particle size specification x50) =1-8 μm is 
adequate to control the particle size range of the drug substance.

Question:
Question 2a.
a. Related Regulation: Article 7(2)(d)
Reason for Supplement: 3.2.P.2.3. Manufacturing Process Development
1) The process variable for sieving size at commercial scale in Table 4-2 of
P.2.3.01 is set to 1 mm, which differs from the CPP setting value of 0.8 
mm specified in 3.2.P.3.3, and no justification is provided.
2) Validation results for residence time distribution (RTD) during the post-
mixing process in continuous processing has not been submitted.
3) No suitable criteria provided for holding time settings.
Supplement Requirement: Please submit additional materials regarding manufacturing 
process development considering the above matters.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2a. ( P.2.3):
a.1)
Table 4-2 in P.2.3.01 Pharmaceutical Development - Manufacturing Process is a summary of 
all the batches in the commercial scale. The sieve mesh size of 1.0 mm for pre-blend sieving 
was used in commercial scale only in technical batches not for clinical batches. All clinical 
batches were produced with a sieve mesh size ≤ 0.8 mm. All commercial batches were and 
will be produced with a sieve mesh size ≤ 0.8 mm.
a.2)
The manufacturing process of Sevabertinib/ BAY 2927088 coated tablets 10 mg uses a 
manufacturing approach in which some unit operations are working in a batch mode whereas 
others are fully integrated and operate in a continuous mode. The integrated process consists 
of feeding of the pre-blend, roller compaction/ dry granulation, post-blending, tableting and 
coating (see P.2.3.01 Pharmaceutical Development - Manufacturing Process). The unit 
operations roller compaction/ dry granulation and tableting are intrinsically continuous 
processes, while all other integrated process steps are produced using a sublot principle.
A sublot principle is the basis of the control strategy of the Consigma manufacturing line. 
Process dynamics and material movement are controlled by the creation of post-blending or 
coating sublots respectively. All sublots must meet the criteria before further processing; if 
not, they are automatically diverted from the process. Furthermore, there are no continuous 
blending operations included in the manufacturing process. Due to the sublot principle, back-
mixing during roller compaction or tableting is excluded. Potential disturbances are managed 
at the sublot level where the disturbance has occurred.
...
Therefore, it is not required to identify other portions to be discarded using a residence time 
distribution. As a consequence, no residence time distribution model was validated for 
commercial manufacturing.

a.3)
The evaluation of the holding time of the pre-blend was based on the testing of the pre-blend 
during the storage period and the testing of coated tablets produced using this pre-blend (see 
P.2.3.01 Pharmaceutical Development - Manufacturing Process).
The criteria for the pre-blend were:
• Blend uniformity below 5%
• Sum of degradation products max. 3%
• Compliance of microbiological quality
• No change of solid state form of the drug substance
Other powder bulk properties such as density and particle size were done informatively. No 
relevant change of those properties was observed.
The coated tablets were tested according to the release specification and met all the 
requirements.

Bayer Response to Question 8 (P.8.3):
Bayer uses the following default transport conditions (GSOP 1592):
• (-196 °C) – (-130 °C) (“cryogenic chain”)
• (-80 °C) – (-20 °C) (“ultra low chain”)
• 2-8 °C (“cold chain”)
• 2-25 °C (“ambient chain”)
• no restriction
In principle, BAY 2927088 (Sevabertinib) 10 mg coated tablet falls under “no restriction” 
regarding transport and storage (P.8.3.01 Stability Data). If a defined storage condition is 
however required, 2-25°C (“ambient chain”) may apply. However, since the long-term 
storage conditions tested for primary and post-approval stability include 30 °C, it is 
appropriate to define 2 – 30 °C as the storage condition.

Question:
1. Status of process validation
(1) Explain the manufacturing scale and container (e.g., name of production line) used for the
commercial manufacturing and process validation (PV) for each manufacturing step for 
the drug product of each formulation*.
Answer:
First, we will explain the design of PV performed for this drug and the plan for future commercial
production. Many of gadoquatrane drug products are marketed overseas only, and the combinations of batch 
size of bulk formulation and filled drug product are determined based on the predicted demand and supply 
in each country. A batch of bulk formulation is not usually assumed to be filled into only a single product 
item (e.g., 2-mL vials) or a single product category (e.g., syringes), but rather into drug products which vary 
in type of container and volume.
Therefore, in the PV for the production of bulk formulation, the minimum (33.822 kg) and the maximum
(2818.5 kg) manufacturing scales were determined by considering and examining various potential scenarios 
of the commercial production, and a total of 9 batches of different sizes were manufactured within the range 
(Table 1 and Table 2). As shown inTable 2, since two types of formulation container are used depending on 
the batch size, PV was performed at the batch sizes assumed to be the minimum and maximum scales for 
each container. For all batches, free gadolinium content, calcobutrol content, bioburden, and endotoxin were 
tested as validation items in addition to the usual process control and quality control test items, and all met 
the acceptance criteria.

Mobile formulation container：移動式混合容器 
Stationary formulation container：固定式混合容器
PV of the filling step was performed using the filling line currently planned to be used for commercial
production, and produced three batches of 2 mL vial each filled with a different bulk formulation batch (Table 
3), and a total of nine batches of syringe consisting of three batches each of different fill volumes, each of 
which were filled with a different bulk formulation batch (Table 4). Taking risks into consideration, the 
validation confirmed that stable filling operation can be performed continuously for more than one hour for 
each batch, demonstrating reproducibility and robustness of the step.
Table 3 Batches of vials manufactured in PV of the filling step

Note that the process is controlled with a safety factor determined based on the characteristics and control
methods of microorganisms, and with the maximum processing time of 6 days from the start of filtration step 
(Step 4) to the completion of sterilization step (Step 6).
The minimum batch size for bulk formulation of 33.8 kg is quite small as it assumes the manufacturing of
2 mL vials only, while the minimum batch size for bulk formulation for the manufacturing of other 
presentations is 281.85 kg. For the manufacturing of syringe presentations, the bulk formulation is produced 
within the range of 281.85 - 2818.5 kg and filled according to the type and required amount of the drug 
product required. When a group of products with relatively large volume is manufactured, the batch size of 
bulk formulation is larger, and assumed to be split into multiple batches to separately filling individual 
product items.

In the manufacturing process of bulk formulation of this drug, the drug substance gadoquatrane hydrate
and the excipients are mixed and dissolved in water for injection, and complete dissolution is visually 
confirmed in Step 1, before proceeding to Step 2 (pH adjustment). In Step 2, in-process control is performed 
to confirm that the pH meets the predetermined acceptance criterion, before proceeding to Step 3. In Step 3, 
the density is adjusted, and another in-process control is performed to confirm that the density meets the 
acceptance criterion, before proceeding to Step 4 (filtration). In the filtration step, filter integrity is tested 
after the completion of filtration as an in-process control to confirm that the solution has been properly filtered. 
Thus, the manufacturing process of this drug is not considered to be influenced by the manufacturing scale 
or the manufacturing site, and the manufacturing scale varies among campaigns. Therefore, the process 
validation that repeats the process three times at the same manufacturing scale was not performed. However, 
based on the results of the process validation with nine batches performed, we consider that the established 
manufacturing process ensures manufacturing of products with consistent quality regardless of differences 
in bulk formulation manufacturing scale or manufacturing equipment.

Question:
(2) Explain that consistent manufacturing can be performed with the manufacturing equipment
and scales used for the commercial process. If the explanation uses data such as 
manufacturing historical data of the same drug product for outside of Japan, clarify the type 
of data (explaining any differences from the commercial production or PV, and reason why 
such differences do not affect the quality).
Answer:
As stated in the response to the current Inquiry (1), the manufacturing process of the bulk solution for
Ambelvist drug product has been validated at various assumed manufacturing scales for commercial 
manufacturing. For the filling step, a risk-based filling process is adopted to ensure a reproducible and stable 
process. Additionally, since this is a known process used also for other approved drug products, bulk batch 
size has no impact on the filling step. Furthermore, as stated in the response to the current Inquiry (3), the 
sterilization step after filling was also validated with sufficient load taking into account the variation in the 
number of vials sterilized in the commercial manufacturing. Thus, we consider that the manufacturing 
process for Ambelvist drug product ensures consistent production with the commercial manufacturing 
equipment and scales.

Question:
Question 1
Regarding the submitted labels please address the following:
a) Please clarify the type of primary packaging for the bottle presentation. Where the
medicine is packaged in a primary pack that is a carton, the name of the medicine must 
be included on at least three non-opposing sides of the carton.
b) The name and quantity of each excipient in the medicine must be expressed as the
nominal mass of that excipient in the stated volume of fill of the injection in the 
container.
c) For the multidose use presentations, the quantity of each excipient in the medicine
must be expressed as the quantity of that excipient in one millilitre of the injection.
d) Where a range of medicines contains the same active ingredient(s) in the same dosage
form in a series of strengths then the label must state the quantity of each active 
ingredient in terms of either the highest or lowest metric unit of measurement in the 
series of strengths. Therefore, the 515.8 mg / 2 mL product should be expressed as 
0.5158 g / 2 mL.
e) It is usually recommended to use colour to help distinguish one strength of the
medicine from another. Please provide a clinical justification, which addresses the risk 
of medication errors, for keeping all strengths the same colour.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1: 

a) The 65mL bottle presentation is one 65mL bottle packed into a shipper box of 10 bottles.
For the purposes of review, the TGA can consider that the 65mL bottle is the primary 
package and that the bottle label contains all mandatory information. The shipper box only 
has one label and cannot be labelled on more than one side.
b) As outlined by TGA, the hydrochloric acid excipient is only added for pH adjustment.
Therefore to address this request, we have added “q.s.” at the end of the hydrochloric 
excipient where it is shown on the labels. All other excipients have reported quantities. 
Revised mock ups are provided in 1.3.3.1 and 1.3.3.2.

c) As requested, for the multidose use presentations (30mL and 65mL), the quantity of
each excipient in the medicine is now expressed as the quantity of that excipient in one 
millilitre of the injection. Revised mock ups are provided in 1.3.3.1 and 1.3.3.2.
d) As requested, we have updated the quantity of the active to 0.5158 g / 2 mL on the vial
and outer carton label for the 2mL presentation. Revised mock ups are provided in 
1.3.3.1 and 1.3.3.2.
e) The product maintains a consistent concentration across all formats, differing only in
fill volume and container type (vial vs. pre-filled syringe).

Since dosing is weight-based, healthcare professionals (HCPs) should select the fill 
volume closest to the required dose based on the patient's weight. When using multi-
patient injector systems, the HCP calculates and delivers the precise volume based on

To assist with selection of the presentation, different colours are used to distinguish

Question:
Question 1 (Question 33 in common LoQ)
Please confirm that the pre-sterilisation bioburden sample taken before the vials/bottles/PFS 
are sterilised is collected immediately prior to terminal sterilisation, after any applicable hold 
time. If a hold time is applied after bioburden sampling prior to terminal sterilisation, then this 
period must be microbiologically validated.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (3.2.P.3.5):
We confirm that the pre-sterilisation bioburden sample is taken immediately prior to terminal 
sterilisation. Further, a hold time between sampling and testing is defined: Bioburden testing 
in microbiological QC laboratory occurs within 4 hours (room temperature) or after storage at 
2-8 °C on next working day. This is justified by the isoosmolaric properties of Gadoquatrane  
solution and reflected in the results of the microbiological challenge test (see P.2.5.01), where 
bacteriostasis or growth was shown for all tested microorganisms over the tested holding time 
(max. 48 h) at room temperature. Storage at 2-8 °C is generally considered as stabilizing 
bioburden conditions. Therefore, the defined hold time ensures reliable detection of potential 
contaminants.
For the sake of completeness, we can confirm that the same bioburden testing hold time is 
defined for supplementary bioburden for parametric release: bioburden “first filled container” 
and bioburden (“storage tank last filling day (holding time)”. Sampling occurs immediately 
after filling and at the end of the storage holding time from the storage tank, respectively, see 
P.5.6.01.

Question:
Question 2 (part of Question 34 in LoQ)
It is noted that in the information provided for parametric release, that the bioburden alert and 
action limits were reduced to ≤10 CFU/10 mL in 2025 in response to the EMA. This limit is 
still considered high from a GMP perspective, particularly as the solution has passed through 
a sterilisation grade filter. Please give consideration to lowering it (an appropriate bioburden 
limit would be ≤ 10 CFU/100 mL).
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2 (3.2.P.3.5):
Please refer to response provided regarding Question 3 below.

Question:
Question 3 (Question 34 in common LoQ)
The bioburden sample size of 10 mL is below what is generally expected. The guidance 
provided in EMA/CHMP/CVMP/QWP/850374/2015 Guideline on the sterilisation of the 
medicinal product, active substance, excipient and primary container, adopted by the TGA 8 
June 2023 states that “in most situations, a limit of NMT 10 CFU/100 mL (TAMC) would be 
acceptable for bioburden testing”. Additionally, the guidance states that “bioburden should be 
tested in a bulk sample of 100 mL in order to ensure the sensitivity of the method. Other 
testing regimes to control bioburden at the defined level should be justified”. In this regard, 
please consider increasing the bioburden sample size to 100 mL, specifying an acceptance 
criterion of ≤10 CFU/100 mL, or provide justification as to why this should not occur.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 3 (3.2.P.3.5):
We acknowledge your question and provide further clarification for the bioburden limit and 
sample size below.
At Bayer AG, Berlin bioburden limits are defined according to last microbiological 
reduction step. To our understanding, this is independent of previous germ-reducing steps. 
Fill finish process of Gadoquatrane solution is a process of terminal steam sterilization (“Ph. 
Eur. 5.1.1 Reference Cycle ≥121 °C for 15 min”, see Table 1, 
EMA/CHMP/CVMP/QWP/850374/2015). Upstream filtration step(s) are “bioburden 
reduction filtration” as part of the contamination control strategy and not terminal “sterile 
filtration”. The process is not considered aseptic processing and therefore bioburden limits are 
justified to be higher than 10 CFU/100 mL (which at Bayer AG, Berlin is the standard limit 
for aseptic processed parenteral drug products according to chapter 4.1.5 “sterile filtration" 
EMA/CHMP/CVMP/QWP/850374/2015 Guideline on the sterilisation of the medicinal 
product, active substance, excipient and primary container).
For definition of Gadoquatrane solution bioburden limits chapter 4.1.1. “Steam sterilisation” 
of EMA/CHMP/CVMP/QWP/850374/2015 was used as a regulatory basis, by taking into 
consideration that "For aqueous solutions, the limits stated in Table 1 [100 CFU /100 mL]
are acceptable for […] drug product formulations without further justification. Other testing 
regimes and limits to control bioburden at the defined level should be justified.” A testing 
regime with sample size of (2x) 10 mL but equivalent limit (10 CFU/10 mL corresponds to 
100 CFU/ 100 mL) will be provided herewith:
• 
A microbiological monitoring program of the bulk solution prior to sterilization using 
the abovementioned sampling size for a similar product portfolio of terminally 
sterilized drug products is established at Supply Center Berlin since 2004. Bioburden 
limit was lowered for the product portfolio in 2008. For Gadoquatrane bioburden limit 
was lowered to 10 CFU / 10 mL which corresponds to EMA requirement of 100 CFU 
/ 100 mL. Further, an alert level of 5 CFU / 10 mL is installed.
• 
A long history of good microbial quality of drug solutions prior terminal sterilization 
with sample volume of (2x) 10 mL and action limit of 100 CFU / 10 mL can be 
reported at the affected (and all other) filling lines at SCB. Generally, no 
microorganisms are detected. The rarely detected microorganisms are always 
identified and trended. A very low rate of OOS results (no confirmed OOS) exists (see 
P.5.6.01 chapter 8.1.2 “Bioburden Trend Data”)
• 
A Sample volume of 10 mL homologous to the existing testing regime is proposed for 
Gadoquatrane solution, because
o A firm contamination control strategy (including microbiological incoming
goods control for API, excipients, and packaging material, controlled WFI, 
microbial reduction filters, cleanroom class C surrounding) is installed and 
also valid for the new product Gadoquatrane solution.
o A firm Endotoxin Control and testing strategy is installed (see P.5.6.01 chapter
8.1.3 “Bacterial Endotoxin Test (BET) Trend Data)
o Based on the manufacturing process and the product properties the aqueous
solution tested can be considered as homogenous. Based on these conditions it 
is not to be expected that increasing the sample volume to 100 mL would result 
in higher germ counts or more reliable results. The proposed detection limit 
(<10 CFU/ 100 mL) of a 10 mL testing regime is 1/10th or 1/5th of the 
respective action and alert level and therefore high enough to allow 
extrapolation of quantitative result to target level and identify trends. There is 
no risk of "missing" bioburden out of trend results, every CFU is identified, 
half-yearly bioburden trend reports and investigation both for alert and action 
limit excursion are installed. Sensitivity is considered sufficient.
o Especially for small volume formats (e.g. 2 mL vials) the sample size for a 100
mL testing volume would exceed sample size for end product release testing (> 
50 pc. for bioburden vs. 20 pc. for sterility test and 3 pc. for bacterial
endotoxin test). The effort would be disproportionately high compared to 
release test sample size and given the low risk of contamination.
o Sample volume of 100 mL would require the pooling of > 50 vials instead of 5
vials for testing 10 mL. With every additional manual process step the risk of 
secondary contamination is higher. We believe the risk of a potential 
secondary contamination during the laboratory testing is higher than the 
knowledge gained.
o A harmonization with other drug products (produced and tested) in a very
similar way minimizes sampling errors.
o Good microbiological status of Gadoquatrane solution prior to terminal
sterilisation and after sterilisation was shown and reported in process 
validation (see P.3.5.01) and Justification of Parametric release (see P.5.6.01 
chapter 8.2 and 8.2.2 “Bioburden Data”). It is shown that experience of the 
testing regime with other products can be transferred to the new product.
In conclusion, we herewith show that a testing regime of (2x) 10 mL bioburden sampling 
volume and equivalent EMA limit for terminally steam sterilized drug products (10 CFU / 10 
mL) can be justified through sufficiently high detection limit/sensitivity, firm contamination 
control strategy and both historical as well as process validation-based good experience. 
Under the currently submitted bioburden limits of 10 CFU / 10 mL (Action Limit) a SAL of 
10-6 for terminally sterilized drug solutions will be ensured.

bottle for injection (amended due to further question)

Question:
Question 4 (Question 35 in common LoQ)
With regard to microbiological validation of terminal sterilisation for the 2 mL product vials 
by autoclave, please provide:
a. A description of the solution used for validation studies. If actual product wasn’t used, a
justification should be provided.
b. Details of the BI configuration within the load, including confirmation that the BIs are
placed in the locations determined to be hardest to sterilise.
c. The number of BIs included in each load, and confirmation the BIs are placed in contact
with the product.
d. Calculations to show how an SAL of 10-6 is achieved. 
e. Frequency of revalidation.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 4 (3.2.P.3.5):
a. In general during sterilization validation studies, water for injection (WFI)
is utilized as the liquid content for all containers (vials, bottles and syringes).
For (re-)validations conducted up to 2015, product solutions from various products 
were partly used as the liquid content. This practice was replaced by WFI, as it 
demonstrated comparable effectiveness in microbial eradication. A study was 
conducted to analyze killing efficiency of Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores 
inoculated in Gadoquatrane solution compared to WFI by performing D121°C value 
determination under saturated steam conditions using survival curve method according 
to DIN EN ISO 11138-1 and 11138-3 and viable spore count according to USP 
(see P.3.5.01 BAY 1747846 solution 0.4 mol/L). The results show that microbes are 
eradicated with comparable effectiveness in both WFI and Gadoquatrane solution, 
independent of potential viscosity- or heat penetration differences. This finding 
supports the justification for using WFI as the liquid content during validation.
b. Temperature mapping of the empty autoclave chamber (Operation qualification (OQ))
did not reveal any critical cold spots and showed a uniform heat distribution 
throughout the autoclave chamber. 
During validation of the minimum load biological indicators were distributed evenly 
throughout the load.
c. During validation of the minimum load 12 biological indicators were distributed
evenly throughout the load.  
All BIs were placed within the liquid content of the objects (vials).
d. Terminal sterilization is performed using a Ph.Eur. 5.1.1 Reference cycle (≥ 121 °C
for ≥ 15 min). The goal of sterilization process validation is to show that the routine
overkill process always delivers an effectivity (F0) of at least 12 minutes at 121 °C 
(SAL 10-06, 12 log reduction of spores with D121=1 min). In dependence of the F0 
value of the used biological indicators (BIs) this is facilitated in an additional worst-
case approach by:
I. 
using a partial cycle approach (BIs with F0 value <12 min),
II. 
using a shortened sterilization time (BIs with F0 value 12 – 15 min) or
III. 
using routine cycle time (20 min) but BIs with high resistance  
(BIs with F0 value >15 min)
If the partial cycle approach is used for revalidation, partial cycle 
parameters are calculated (considering overkill requirements, F0 of routine, F0 and D 
value of BI), and the sterilization run is stopped significantly earlier. Subsequently, 
the lethality of the routine sterilization process can be extrapolated to show that a 
biological indicator with an F0 value of 12 minutes or greater would be inactivated in 
the routine process. During evaluation of the validation runs of the partial 
cycle approach the biological effectivity of routine sterilization is calculated 
(considering physical effectiveness of routine sterilization, physical effectiveness of 
used partial cycle and biological effectiveness of the BI) and shown to be higher than 
12 min.   
The BIs used during validation had a F0 value of 13.91 min (see table 2-6 in P.3.5.01_ 
Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection (sterilization)). The BIs showed 
no growth and therefore the requirements of the microbial effectiveness study to 
demonstrate a 12-log reduction during routine conditions were met.
e. The revalidation of the sterilization process for autoclave of 2mL vials is conducted
annually. A run with the minimum load of vials is performed annually based on the 
qualification validation master plan and justified on the worst-case approach.

Source:  P.3.5.01_022969750_01 (IQMS-243486) Process Validation and/or
Evaluation / BAY 1747846 solution 0.4 mol/L (new)
P.3.5.01_022992945_01 (IQMS-266428) Process Validation and/or 
Evaluation / Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection 
(sterilization) (unchanged)

parameters are calculated (considering overkill requirements, F0 of routine, F0 and D 
value of BI), and the sterilization run is stopped significantly earlier. Subsequently, 
the lethality of the routine sterilization process can be extrapolated to show that a 
biological indicator with an F0 value of 12 minutes or greater would be inactivated in 
the routine process. During evaluation of the validation runs of the partial 
cycle approach the biological effectivity of routine sterilization is calculated 
(considering physical effectiveness of routine sterilization, physical effectiveness of 
used partial cycle and biological effectiveness of the BI) and shown to be higher than 
12 min.   
The BIs used during validation had a F0 value of 13.03 min (see table 3-5 in P.3.5.01 
Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection (sterilization)). The BIs showed 
no growth and therefore the requirements of the microbial effectiveness study to 
demonstrate a 12-log reduction during routine conditions were met.
e. The revalidation of the sterilization process for autoclave of 10, 15 and 30 mL vials
and 100 mL bottles is conducted annually. A run with the minimum load of vials is 
performed annually based on the qualification validation master plan and justified on 
the worst-case approach.

Question:
Question 14 (Question 29 in common LoQ)
Ideally, the repeat testing provided in Table 6-2 should have been performed using the same 
batch i.e. KT0F6PS. As such, it is concerning that the two separate batches tested showed 
contradicting results at the 6 hr time point for E. coli and P. aeruginosa. The study results 
provided therefore do not support an in-use period of 6 hours. To demonstrate a 6 hr in-use 
period at 20 – 25°C, please provide a study which should ideally include information to show 
that when the product is presented with a microbial challenge (similar to a preservative 
efficacy test), the results obtained show continued evidence of microbial death. However, the 
minimum requirement is demonstration of stasis (i.e., not more than 0.5 log10 higher than the 
initial value of the inoculum) over the proposed storage period. The results should be supplied 
as either raw data or log reductions. Please note that if acceptable data cannot be provided in 
relation to the 6 hour in-use period, the labelling and PI will need to be revised.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 14 (P.2.5.):

Please find an updated P.2.5.01 enclosed for your review, it includes Tables 6-2 and 6-3 
which show the results of the microbial challenge test on two additional batches, carried out 
on two different days with increased resolution in the time window from 0 to 24 hours, using 
all germs that had produced unexpected or even implausible results.
We would like to clarify the results of the two batches once again by adding the log10 
representation of the results and showing the log10 difference over time, see Table 1 and 
Table 2.

[Table 1 and Table 2 with microbial challenge test results]

We conclude that the results are not contradictory among the two batches but rather fluctuate 
within the usual microbiological range by a factor of 2. This results in borderline data 
between 6 and 12 hours, which may therefore be just below or above the acceptance limit.
We interpret the results from these two measurement series for the most critical two micro-
organisms as follows:
E. coli: The requirement of <= 0.5log compared to the value at 0 hours is met up to 10 hours.
P. aeruginosa: The requirement of <= 0.5log compared to the value at 0 hours is met up to 6 
hours.
Also, the results obtained previously with #KT0F6PS should have been not included in 
determining the maximum permissible hold time, as the suspicion of implausibility was 
confirmed. However, we did not consider it meaningful to repeat the test with #KT0F6PS, as 
no batch-specific variation in product properties or effect on microbiological growth is to be 
expected due to the narrow physical and chemical specification limits.
We conclude that the product is protected against microbiological growth within the stasis 
requirement of less than or equal to 0.5 log10 for up to 6 hours after opening. A reduction in 
the bacterial count by the product itself could only be achieved by using a preservative.

However, we consider this to be an additional burden on the patient and deliberately decided 
against it during the development phase. The addition of a preservative is more commonly 
associated with formulations for prolonged use with repeated withdrawals over days to weeks 
and the associated risk of repeated contamination, usually under home use conditions. The 
multi-patient use planned for our product only requires initial piercing of the rubber stopper 
and therefore only presents a low risk of contamination when pierced under clinical 
conditions. To ensure correct handling, the following statement is included in the label for 
vials and bottles: Do not pierce the rubber stopper more than once.

Question:
Question 1
The submitted risk assessments concerning the possible formation and presence of nitrosamines in 
the drug substance and finished product are not detailed enough and should therefore be revised.
Regarding the drug substance, the following points should be clarified:
a) It has not been mentioned that 4-Nitrophenol will be released in stoichiometric amounts during 
step 4b formation of intermediate Gadoquatrane crude where also nucleophilic hydroxide anions 
will be present (basification using aqueous sodium hydroxide). The applicant should therefore 
appropriately address potential de-nitration during this step of the synthesis. If de-nitration cannot 
unambiguously be ruled out, confirmatory testing should be performed, e.g. concerning potential 
nitrosamine derivatives of relevant impurities like heptamine, secondary amines stemming from 
diisopropylethylamine or synthesis intermediates, etc.
b) Regarding the potential nitrosamine contamination of starting material NPTA HCl, the applicant 
focusses on the reduction of nitrite impurities in sodium azide and potential NDMA during the 
hydrogenation step. Nevertheless, this is solely a theoretical claim, and relevant data, e.g. 
concerning actual nitrite content in sodium azide, should be provided for further justification. If 
necessary, confirmatory testing should be performed to rule out the presence of NDMA as well as 
nitrosamine derivatives of heptamine.
c) If confirmatory testing is necessary, suitably validated analytical methods should be used as 
described in Q&A paper EMA/409815/2020.
Regarding the finished product, the following points should be clarified:
d) In the risk assessment on the presence of nitrosamine impurities in the drug product under 
review it is indicated that supportive documentation on the excipients and container closure system 
of the drug product is available. These documents should be provided.
e) The applicant has indicated that the presence of nitrosating agents, nitrosamines or vulnerable 
amines in the API is excluded. However, some points for clarification have been identified (see 
above). Based on the outcome of these concerns, there might be a risk of presence of nitrosamine 
impurities in the drug product as well, which may require further scientific discussion and, if 
necessary, confirmatory testing. (S.3.2. + P.5.5)
Answer:
Applicant’s response:

Abstract drug substance nitrosamine risk assessment:
In the following, the risk of the potential denitration of 4-Nitrophenol (released in step 4b) as well
as the potential nitrite content in sodium azide are addressed in more detail.
Furthermore, data is presented to support the theoretical risk assessment. Batch data for nitrite in
three commercial batches of sodium azide and starting material NPTA HCl are shown, both
revealing that there is no risk for the contamination of NPTA HCl with significant amounts of
residual nitrite.

nitrosamines were tested in commercial batches using suitably validated analytical methods as
described in Questions and answers for marketing authorisation holders/applicants on the CHMP
Opinion for the Article 5(3) of Regulation (EC) No 726/2004 referral on nitrosamine impurities in
human medicinal products (EMA/409815/2020). NDMA was tested in starting material NPTA HCl
and Gadoquatrane drug substance. Furthermore, DIPEA, NEIPA, NDMA and NO-Heptamine-
Gadoquatrane were tested in Gadoquatrane drug substance. All tested potential nitrosamines were
determined to be at least below 10% of their respective acceptable intake (AI).
A detailed discussion of the data can be found in the answers below and in the updated version of
S.3.2.07 and P.5.5.07.
In summary, the presented data supports the risk assessment that there is no risk for nitrosamine
contamination of Gadoquatrane drug substance.

a) We acknowledge the Rapporteur’s comment that a risk assessment concerning the possibility of
4-Nitrophenol denitration under the aqueous basic conditions in Step 4b is missing. In the
following, we will address this concern:
As stated in S.3.2.07, 4-Nitrophenol does not represent a particularly electron-poor nitro arene. 
Therefore, it is not - even in the presence of strong nucleophiles - susceptible to a denitration 
reaction. In theory, such a reaction would proceed via a nucleophilic aromatic substitution reaction 
(SNAr) in the case of 4-Nitrophenol.
Scheme 1: A Hypothetical mechanistic pathway of denitration via hydroxide-mediated
SNAr

As illustrated in Scheme 1, the key reaction intermediate – in the literature commonly referred to 
as Meisenheimer complex – is a negatively charged arene. Stabilization of the negative charge in 
the Meisenheimer complex, typically via multiple electron-withdrawing substituents, would be 
required for the denitration reaction to proceed at a reasonable rate. In the case of the 4-
Nitrophenol substitution pattern, said strongly electron-withdrawing substitution pattern is not 
given. Thus, a productive denitration pathway is not favored. 
To further substantiate our assessment that there is no risk of denitration of 4-Nitrophenol in an 
aqueous, sodium hydroxide containing medium, the acidity of 4-Nitrophenol shall be taken into 
account. It is well-established in the literature that 4-Nitrophenol is a fairly acidic compound, with a 
pKa value of ~ 7.15 owing to the acidity of the phenolic proton. Thus, the species prevalent in the 
basic aqueous reaction mixture is the negatively charged 4-Nitrophenolate anion (see Scheme 2)
Owing to the strongly electron donating properties of the phenoxide group (which already includes 
a negative charge), the formation of a Meisenheimer complex after nucleophilic attack of hydroxide 
is not possible. Consequently, denitration is not possible. 
To conclude, there is no risk of nitrite formation from 4-Nitrophenol during step 4b. 
 
This theoretical assessment is supported by analytical data demonstrating the absence of potential 
nitrosamines NEIPA and NDIPA, which may arise from secondary amine impurities in DIPEA during 
step 4b, as well as of the potential nitrosamine NO-Heptamine-Gadoquatrane in Gadoquatrane 
drug substance. All theoretically possible nitrosamines have been tested using dedicated analytical 
methods and found to be at least below 10% of the respective AI in three commercial batches of 
Gadoquatrane drug substance. Supportive data and information about the analytical methods 
including tested validation parameters as well as the setting of appropriate AI limits and AI-based 
maximum allowed concentrations in Gadoquatrane drug substance are included in section S.3.2.07.

b) We acknowledge the Rapporteur’s comment regarding the need for a more comprehensive risk
assessment concerning the potential nitrosamine risk in the synthesis of NPTA HCl via the azide
route. In the first step of the azide route towards starting material NPTA HCl, the reagent sodium
azide is used. Sodium azide to a certain extent contains sodium nitrite. Nitrite in the raw material
sodium azide was measured during release testing of sodium azide. The determined nitrite levels
are comparably low (≤ 0.01%) as shown in Table 1.

Secondly, the impurity Heptamine in NPTA HCl has been evaluated regarding its theoretical risk for
the formation of a related nitrosamine. Due to the presence of six primary amine functions in
addition to one secondary amine in the molecule, the risk for the formation of a Heptamine-related
nitrosamine is considered to be negligible. Primary amines are generally not considered vulnerable
nitrosamine precursors, as nitrosamines derived from primary amines are not stable; moreover,
due to the higher reactivity toward nitrosylation when compared to secondary amines, primary
amines can act as nitrite scavengers and may inhibit nitrosamine formation under relevant
primary amines, any risk for the formation of a Heptamine-related nitrosamine can be excluded.
However, it has been considered that Heptamine can form the downstream impurity Heptamine-
Gadoquatrane, a secondary amine, which could theoretically form a related nitrosamine (Figure

Conclusion of supporting analyses
The outcome of the theoretical risk evaluation that no risk for nitrosamine contamination was
identified for Gadoquatrane drug substance is fully supported by analytical results demonstrating
the absence of any potential nitrosamines in commercial-scale batches (i.e. all tested nitrosamines
in Gadoquatrane drug substance and starting material NPTA HCl are at least below 10% of their
acceptable limit).

Abstract drug product nitrosamine risk assessment:
We acknowledge the Rapporteur’s comment regarding the drug product nitrosamine risk
assessment. In the following, these concerns are addressed in more detail. In conclusion, the
updated nitrosamine risk assessment for Gadoquatrane drug product demonstrates that there is no
risk for the presence of nitrosamine impurities.

d) Supportive documentation on the excipients and container closure system of the drug product is

e) Given the explanations in the responses to a) and b) the presence of nitrosating agents and
nitrosamines in the drug substance is excluded. Consequently, no risk has been identified for the
presence of nitrosamine impurities in the drug product resulting from drug substance. Based on
this assessment, confirmatory testing is not required.
As mentioned above, the nitrosamine risk assessments in S.3.2.07 and P.5.5.07 have been
thoroughly updated and now contain a comprehensive discussion of the potential nitrosamine risks
raised by EMA. For each identified risk, it is concluded that no relevant amounts of nitrosamines
can be formed in either the drug substance or the drug product. This is demonstrated by
supportive data regarding all theoretical nitrosamines in the drug substance and drug product.
For Gadoquatrane drug substance the updated section S.3.2.07 provides data for the theoretical
nitrosamine NEIPA, NDIPA, NDMA and NO-Heptamine-Gadoquatrane. For Gadoquatrane drug
product, the potential nitrosamines NEIPA, NDIPA, NDMA and NO-Heptamine-Gadoquatrane have
also been tested in representative batches. None of the nitrosamines was detectable in the drug
substance or the drug product. The applied methods have been demonstrated to be capable of
detecting the respective nitrosamines below 10% of the maximum acceptable concentration
(calculated based on the AI).
Moreover, Heptamine-Gadoquatrane has been identified as the only potential secondary amine,
which could, in principle, be present in the drug substance in trace amounts. This impurity can
solely be formed during the synthesis (i.e. it is not a degradation product) and has been shown to
be consistently absent in commercial API batches (below LOD, LOD = 100 ppb, refer to S.3.2.07).
Therefore, also the formation of relevant amounts of nitrosamines in the drug product based on
potential secondary amines in the drug substance can be ruled out.

General notes
It should be noted that in S.3.2.07, section 3.3, the discussion on potential nitrite in potable and
purified water, which is used in the synthesis of the drug substance, has also been updated. Based
on data from nitrite measurements in water, the discussion has been revised to reflect these
results, and the previously applied justifications based on conductivity have been
removed. Importantly, this update has no impact on the nitrosamine risk in the drug substance.
Any risk for the potential formation of nitrosamines based on potential trace levels of nitrite in
potable or purified water can be safely excluded. The same applies to the discussion and conclusion
concerning water for injection in P.5.5.07, section 2.2.
Moreover, S.3.2.07, section 3.5 has been updated based on EMA request to reevaluate the use of
recovered solvents during the drug substance synthesis process (refer to Question 2e) for drug
substance). Toluene, used in early synthesis steps (1a/1b, 2a), has been identified to be reused
upon process-related solvent recovery. Solvent recovery is done by distillation and after the
recovery, Toluene is released according to the same specification as the fresh solvents and only for
re-use in the same synthesis step. The presence of secondary amines, as well as nitrite during
solvent recovery can be excluded for the recovery process. Therefore, this update has no impact on
the overall risk assessment for nitrosamines in Gadoquatrane drug substance.

Question:
Question 8
Please revise the acceptance criteria in the CoAs for Hydrochloric acid, Ethanol 96%, Sodium 
chloride, Trometamol, and Water for injection to be explicit; replace “According to 
specification” with clear, detailed acceptance limits.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 8 ( CTD section):
We acknowledge the Agency’s comment and we would like to clarify the following:
For Hydrochloric acid 1N, we have provided the quality specification along with the 
corresponding test methods. Therefore, where the CoA states “according to specification,” this 
is fully aligned with the approved in-house specification. All tests required by the in-house 
specification have been performed and meet the defined acceptance limits. The CoA language 
is therefore fully aligned with the approved specification.
For the remaining excipients, namely ethanol 96%, sodium chloride, trometamol, and water for 
injection, these are compendial excipients with established pharmacopoeial monographs. The 
submission already includes the applicable pharmacopoeial monographs that define the detailed 
test methods and acceptance criteria. Where the CoAs use the phrase “according to 
specification,” this indicates conformity to the applicable pharmacopoeial monograph 
referenced in the dossier.
The CoA therefore reflects compliance with the detailed, legally-recognized acceptance limits 
found in those monographs. Referencing a separate, clearly identified specification (inhouse or 
compendial monograph) rather than repeating full acceptance tables on every CoA is an
accepted and routine practice in global pharmaceutical supply chains. No deficiencies have 
been raised regarding this aspect.
The CoA phrase “according to specification” is not ambiguous in this case because the 
referenced specifications (in-house for HCl 1N; pharmacopeial monographs for the compendial 
excipients) are included in the submission and contain the explicit acceptance limits and test 
methods.
Requiring revision of globally used, multi-market CoAs to list every individual acceptance limit 
is not necessary where the definitive specification is already part of the regulatory dossier and 
the batch test results demonstrate compliance.
Please find attached a declaration confirming the preceding statements as Attachment 3.

Question:
Question 1
Commitment to the USP monograph 724/Ph Eur 2.9.3 limits accredited from your side for the 
release rate test.
Answer:
The general chapters <724> in the USP and 2.9.3. in the European Pharmacopoeia do not 
contain limits for release rate testing applicable for a drug product like Mirena intrauterine 
delivery system, which is a reservoir type product with the purpose of releasing it’s drug 
substance, levonorgestrel, during a very long time period, during up to at least 5 years. The 
mentioned general chapters are applicable for drug products which will release fully their 
contents during 15 to 30 minutes, or during some hours at maximum. Therefore the limits 
mentioned in these Pharmacopeial chapters do not apply to Mirena.
Mirena intrauterine delivery system releases levonorgestrel slowly even for 5 years with a 
slightly decreasing rate. The concentration of LNG in the core has very little effect on the 
initial release rate and affects mainly on the effective using time of the system. As a reservoir 
type product, the amount of drug substance released even after the 5 years’ time does not 
reach 100 % release of drug substance.
Therefore, the limits applied for the release rate (dissolution) test of Mirena can’t be drawn 
from any Pharmacopoeia or guideline. The limits applied by Bayer Oy are specific for Mirena 
drug product. The purpose of the release rate limits applied for Mirena at the beginning of use 
time of 5 years is to verify that the release is at a level to guarantee that the amount of drug 
substance remains high enough for providing appropriate drug release and contraception 
efficacy up to end of the use period.

Source:  P.2.2.01_IQMS-171047_1.0_Levonorgestrel intrauterine delivery system 52
mg with inserter (MIRENA)

Question:
Question 2
Providing the ISO 7439 document which was accredited from your side as a reference for the 
tests: (Breaking force, detachment force and recovery of horizontal arms).
Answer:
For the two tests, Breaking force and recovery of horizontal arms, ISO 7439 standard was 
mentioned as reference. ISO 7439 standard describes these tests for Copper-bearing 
contraceptive intrauterine devices (ISO 7439 Copper-bearing contraceptive intrauterine 
devices — Requirements and tests). This ISO standard describes principles for Breaking force 
test in chapter “Determination of tensile force” and the principles of test Recovery of 
horizontal arms in chapter “Test of elastic recovery (memory test)”.
The tests described in Test Procedure and Justification of Specification documents are based 
on those mentioned tests in ISO 7439. Corresponding pages (8 and 9) of ISO 7439 are 
provided for review. The whole standard can’t be provided.
Recovery of horizontal arms test is used to test the visco-elastic properties of the T-body in 
stability studies. Test confirms that the shape of the T-body is recovered when inserted into 
uterus.
Breaking force test is a feasible method to determine that the system withstands the 
mechanical stress when the system is pulled into the insertion tube prior to insertion and when 
it is removed after use by pulling the threads. The test is applies to Mirena at release and 
during the shelf-life in stability studies also.
The third test mentioned, Detachment force test, is not described in ISO 7439 standard. 
Detachment force test is specific for Mirena and it has been developed at Bayer Oy. The 
purpose of this test is to confirm the functionality of the product during insertion. The IUS 
must slide out of the inserter without significant peak forces. The intention of the test is to 
demonstrate that there are no forces acting upon the T-body that have the potential to alter the 
T-body positioning, and that the IUS remains in the uterine cavity when the inserter is 
retracted after insertion.

Source:  P.5.6.01_IQMS-187354_2.0_ Levonorgestrel intrauterine delivery system 52
mg with inserter (MIRENA)
Copy of pages 8 and 9 of the ISO standard 7439 containing tests
“Determination of tensile force” and “Test of elastic recovery (memory test)”.

Question:
Question 5
Providing DS degradation products classification to process and degradants from the DS 
manufacturer, to ensure that there is no degradant impurities required to be included to the DP 
specification
Answer:
In document S.3.2.01, Potential impurities, the drug substance manufacturer lists the potential 
degradation products of Levonorgestrel drug substance manufactured by Bayer AG. Only 3 
potential degradation products are mentioned. They are Ph. Eur. impurity M, Ph. Eur. 
impurity H and Ph. Eur. impurity J.
In the validation document of Mirena for the impurity test these 3 potential degradation 
products are included as substances to be analyzed and calculated in the impurity test of 
Mirena. In addition to the previously mentioned 3 substances, the validation report mentions 
four other substances as possible degradants in Mirena. These are Ph. Eur. impurity I, Ph. Eur. 
impurity L, Δ1(10)-4,5-dihydro-levonorgestrel and epi-levonorgestrel. The latter two 
substances are not listed in the European Pharmacopoeia. Epi-levonorgestrel was not 
available as isolated material for the validation. It should be noted also, that the test method 
applied on the drug product is adapted from the impurity test of levonorgestrel described in 
the levonorgestrel monograph of European Pharmacopoeia.
The validation document for impurity test presents basis for the analysis, separation and 
quantification of the potential degradation products. The document verifies that all mentioned 
7 substances can be separated and analyzed with the proposed test method.
In example chromatograms on pages 16 and 17 presenting analysis of samples exposed to 
high thermal stress (150°C for 10 days) and to high photolytic stress (UV light for 21 days) 
also the separation of epi-levonorgestrel is shown and verified.
The documentation provided confirms that all degradation products relevant for Mirena can 
be separated and quantified with the proposed analytical method. Degradation of 
levonorgestrel in normal conditions do not even occur significantly. In the examples presented 
here the product has been exposed to extreme conditions which do not normally exist during 
the product lifecycle. Based on the studies performed it can be stated that the all relevant 
degradation products of levonorgestrel are considered in the impurity determination, and there 
is no risk of non-inclusion of degradation product(s) into the calculation and quantification of 
impurities in the Mirena degradation products testing. Furthermore, all unidentified impurities 
observed in routine analysis are calculated into the sum of degradation products.
The validation report P.5.3.10 concludes that the data provided show that the method is 
suitable for determination of the potential levonorgestrel degradation products / related 
substances in Levonorgestrel intrauterine delivery system 52 mg. The method is considered 
valid for batch release and stability analyses since it covers both potential synthesis and 
degradation impurities.

intrauterine delivery system 52 mg with inserter (MIRENA) (amended)

Question:
Question 8
Providing an updated stability studies covering the shelf life on 30C/65% RH conditions once 
available
Answer:
Applicant acknowledges the agency’s question and wanted to confirm Stability studies at 
30 °C/65% RH are not required for this product because the long-term stability condition 
selected in our approved protocol is 30 °C ± 2 °C / 75% RH ± 5% RH, fully complies with the 
requirements of ICH Q1A(R2) for products intended for Climatic Zone IVb.
According to ICH Q1A(R2), the recommended long-term storage condition for Zone IVb is 
30 °C/75% RH, which replaces the 30 °C/65% RH condition used for Zone IVa. The 
guideline requires only one appropriate long-term condition, selected based on the climatic 
zone relevant to the product’s intended markets. Therefore, conducting studies at both 
30 °C/65% RH and 30 °C/75% RH is not expected and does not provide additional regulatory 
value.
Data generated at 30 °C/75% RH represent a more stringent humidity challenge than 
30 °C/65% RH. As a result, product performance under 30 °C/75% RH inherently covers the 
lower humidity condition of 30 °C/65% RH.
Based on this regulatory framework, the existing stability studies at 30 °C/75% RH and 
40 °C/75% RH are scientifically justified and sufficient to support the product’s shelf life. No 
additional studies at 30 °C/65% RH are planned.

Source:  P.8.3.01_IQMS-263018_2.0_Levonorgestrel intrauterine delivery system 52
mg with inserter (MIRENA)

Question:
Question 2
Finished Product and Excipient:
More clarification on the proposed variations in the specification sheet (Section 3.2.P.5.1) and 
Manufacturing process (removing of manual assembly)
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2 ( P.5.1):
Applicant acknowledges the agency’s question and confirm that the release and Shelf-life 
specifications and the associated analytical procedures for the drug product Mirena, 
Intrauterine delivery system, 52 mg have been updated. These updates are deleting certain test 
parameters and limits. We affirm that these changes have been made in alignment with 
regulatory guideline and will not impact the quality, safety, or efficacy of the drug product 

Change of the specification of drug product (Deletion of test criteria and limits).

Sum of all impurities: Deletion of specification parameter from release specification

• The synthesis impurities that are not potential degradation products are controlled in LNG
release testing and are therefore omitted from the drug product specifications. The 
potential known and unidentified LNG degradation products above ≥ 0.1% reporting
threshold are included in the proposed Shelf-life test and in the corresponding stability 
study test results.
• Levonorgestrel is inherently stable. The long history of Mirena IUS has verified that LNG
remains virtually unchanged in the product manufacture, and during the shelf-life. This is 
demonstrated by comparing results of five MIRENA IUS drug product stability batches 
with the results for corresponding drug substance batches in document “Justification of 
Specification”. The results for drug substance batches in accordance with the Ph. Eur. 
method indicate for Mirena IUS actual low amount of the potential degradation products, 
from which the synthesis related impurities are omitted. Even at the end of Shelf-life the 
level of degradation products is negligible. This outstanding stability of LNG justifies the 
non-inclusion of the impurity test into the release specification.

Deletion of specification parameter Ethylene oxide and Ethylene chlorohydrin from shelf life 
specification

• Only parameters which have relevance with regard to product quality during the Shelf-
life, and therefore tested in stability studies, are included in the shelf life specification.
• According to ICH Topic Q 1 A (R2) Stability Testing of new Drug Substances and
Products parameters of the drug product that are susceptible to change during storage and 
are likely to influence quality, safety, and/or efficacy should be included in stability 
studies.
• Ethylene oxide (EO) which is used as a sterilization agent for sterilization of the product is
removed from Mirena IUS during the process, and therefore it does not exist anymore in 
the finished IUS product. It will suffice to determine the EO residues at release only, as 
they can’t increase during storage, and therefore are not tested during the Shelf-
life. Ethylene chlorohydrin (ECH) is also originated from the EO sterilization process, and 
it is removed during the aeration step from the product similarly as EO.

Deletion of specification parameter Sterility from Shelf-life specification
“Sterility” test parameter will be deleted from Shelf-Life Specification as redundant because 
sterility test was replaced already in 2014 with container closure integrity test in stability 
studies.
The maintenance of the sterile barrier integrity, and hence the sterility throughout the shelf 
life is demonstrated during stability testing by testing the integrity of the primary package. 
The integrity of the package is tested with bubble test and the seal strength of the package 
with strip test.

Change of release and shelf-life specifications and associated analytical procedure of the 
drug product (Tightening of specification limits and Addition of new acceptance criteria 
and quality levels).

Identity:
Current "Identity (TLC)" test which is performed in connection with current TLC purity test 
will be replaced with two new identification test methods to comply with ICH Topic Q6A 
guideline. First new test method will be "Identity (LC)" test which is performed in connection 
with revised assay test and uses liquid chromatography technology. Second new test method 
will be "Identity (IR)" test which uses Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy - attenuated 
total reflectance (FTIR-ATR) technology).
New acceptance criteria will be implemented in Release Specification, accordingly.
Identification test parameter will be deleted from Shelf-Life Specification as redundant.

Assay of system and Uniformity of dosage units:
Current "Assay of system" test method has been optimized and revalidated. Extraction phase 
has been revised and two alternative liquid chromatography instruments (HPLC and UPLC) 
can be used. Acceptance criterion for "Assay of system" will be tightened from 47 – 58 mg to 
47 – 57 mg in Release and Shelf-Life Specifications.  Current "Uniformity of content" 
procedure will be replaced with USP <905> and Ph. Eur. 2.9.40 harmonized "Uniformity of 
dosage units" procedure.
Current "Uniformity of content" test parameter will be deleted and replaced with new 
"Uniformity of dosage units" test parameter with new acceptance criteria in Release 
Specification. Uniformity of content test parameter will be deleted from Shelf-Life 
Specification because it is adequate to report only "Assay of system" test result in stability 
studies.

Release rate:
Current 1-point in vitro release rate test method (test point: Day 15) in 1.0 % 2-
hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin (2-HPBCD) dissolution medium will be replaced with new 3-
point in vitro release rate test method (test points: Day 2, 5 and 8) to comply with 
requirements of relevant guidelines ICH Topic Q6A, USP <724> and Ph. Eur. 2.9.3. New 3-
point release rate test method has been modified from the current 1-point 1.0 % 2- HPBCD 
release rate test method used for several years. Dissolution medium remains unchanged, two 
alternative liquid chromatography instruments (HPLC and UPLC) and two alternative water 
bath shakers (rotating and reciprocal) can be used. Current "Release rate during 24h" test 
parameter will be deleted and replaced with new "Release rate, day 2, day 5 and day 8" test 
parameters with new acceptance criteria in Release and Shelf-Life Specifications.

Breaking force:
Current breaking force test method has been slightly optimized by increasing the length of the 
removal thread from approx. 2.5 cm to approx. 5 cm. Acceptance criteria will be re-worded to
clarify that acceptance criteria are for individual results and not for average. Acceptance 
criterion for one individual result will be tightened from min. 9 N to min. 9.5 N in Release 
and Shelf-Life Specifications to comply with EN ISO 7439 standard.

Loading of IUS:
New specification parameter "Loading of IUS" with its corresponding test method will be 
added to confirm the functionality of the product prior to insertion. New "Loading of IUS" 
test parameter will be added to Release Specification.

Detachment force:
New specification parameter "Detachment force" with its corresponding test method will be 
added to confirm the functionality of the product during the insertion. New "Detachment 
force" test parameter will be added to Release Specification.

Recovery of horizontal arms:
New specification parameter "Recovery of horizontal arms" and its corresponding test method 
will be added to confirm the elastic recovery of the T-body after acute bending as described in 
EN ISO 7439 standard. New "Recovery of horizontal arms" test parameter will be added to  
Shelf-Life Specification.

Container closure integrity (Strip 180 deg):
New specification parameter "Container closure integrity (Strip 180 deg)" and its 
corresponding test method will be added to confirm the strength of the seal as described in EN 
868-5 standard. New "Container closure integrity (Strip 180 deg)" test parameter will be 
added to Shelf-Life Specification.

Container closure integrity (Bubble):
New specification parameter "Container closure integrity (Bubble)" and its corresponding test 
method will be added to confirm the integrity of the complete package as described in ASTM 
F2096 standard. New "Container closure integrity (Bubble)" test parameter will be added to 
Shelf-Life Specification.

Clarification for deletion of manual assembly:
The manual assembly method has not been used in the manufacture of any batches of the 
Mirena, Intrauterine delivery system, 52 mg,  within the past 10 years. The current 
manufacturing process employs only mechanical assembly.
Furthermore, we intend to formally delete the obsolete manual assembly method and the 
associated procedures from the registration dossier through a variation submission (Deletion 
of manual assembly including in-process control (IPC) parameters for manual assembly.
