required to submit the MiV-PA20 documents and pay the applicable fee of PHP 510.00 for 
the additional variation code.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 ( CTD section):
Applicant acknowledges agencies comment and would like to confirm that, As an editorial 
change the current naming of the mixer, "helical mixer", will be changed to "convection 
mixer". In the change the mixer naming is adapted to reflect the mixing principle of the mixer 
in accordance with the US FDA SUPAC -guidance document (Scale-up and Post approval 
changes) concerning terms for manufacturing equipment. The proposed naming defines better 
the mixing process describing the actual mode of action of the mixer. It should be noted that 
the mixer is not changed in this context, only the naming of the mixer is changed in the 
regulatory manufacturing process description of drug product Levonorgestrel implant 75 mg 
without inserter (JADELLE).  
  
The mixer naming is adapted to be in line with the actual mixing principle of the mixer, as 
convection mixing, in accordance with FDA’s SUPAC guidance document, December 2014. 
In convection mixer particles are reoriented in relation to one another as a result of 
mechanical movement, these mixers are therefore also known as paddle or plow mixers. The 
operating principle of the mixer used in manufacture of Jadelle is exactly in accordance with 
this definition.  
 
No changes to the manufacturing process of Jadelle are done in this context. Therefore, 
validation of the manufacturing process has not been performed, and validation data is not 
relevant for this editorial adaptation on the naming of the mixer used in manufacture of drug 
product Levonorgestrel implant 75 mg without inserter (JADELLE).

Serious Cases
1. Case Number: 2025A006746 This spontaneous, serious and non-medically
confirmed case was reported in Russia. The case refers to a female patient of unknown 
age who experienced a cerebrovascular accident (stroke, serious, listed) along with 
intermenstrual bleeding, breast pain, abdominal pain, and abnormal hormone levels 
after taking Qlaira for an unknown indication. Information about the start time of 
therapy and occurrence of the event is unknown. The case was classified as serious 
due to the cerebrovascular accident, which is a listed and expected adverse event of 
COC therapy. Dechallenge information was not provided. The woman also reported, 
“The product quality is completely different,” without any further details, which led to 
the classification of the case as a “Product Issue.” No further assessment of the 
product quality could be made as no information about the package or sample was 
provided. According to WHO-UMC criteria, the relationship between the drug and the 
event is likely, given the listed nature and seriousness of the adverse effects.
2. Case Number: 2025A021409
This spontaneous, serious and medically confirmed case was reported in Russia. The 
case involves a female patient of unknown age who experienced intermenstrual 
bleeding (serious, listed) requiring daytime hospitalization after taking Qlaira for 
contraception. The case was classified as serious due to the hospitalization. Dechallenge information was not provided. The reporter was concerned about the 
quality of the product because she did not have such side effects on the previous 
Qlaira packs. It was not possible to assess the quality of the product she took as no 
sample was provided. As per Bayer's Product Technical Complaint (PTC) assessment, 
no product quality defect was identified. Therefore, the reported medical events are 
not indicative of a quality deficit per se. According to WHO-UMC criteria, the 
relationship between the drug and the event is likely given listedness of the adverse 
event.
3. Case Number: 2025A023968
This spontaneous, serious and non-medically confirmed case was reported in Russia. 
The case refers to a female patient of unknown age, who experienced intermenstrual 
bleeding (serious, listed) and severe lower abdominal pain (non-serious, listed) after 
starting Qlaira for an unknown indication. The patient was treated with Tranexam 
(Tranexamic acid) as well as surgery. No further details about the nature and location 
of surgery were provided. The case was classified as serious due to the medical 
importance of the events, bleeding and surgery. Dechallenge information was not 
provided. The consumer was concerned if “there were any changes to the drug’s 
composition or any changes in our raw materials supply” has caused the event. As per 
Bayer's Product Technical Complaint (PTC) assessment, no product quality defect was 
identified. Therefore, the reported medical events are not indicative of a quality deficit 
per se. According to WHO-UMC criteria, the relationship between the drug and the 
event is likely given the listedness of the adverse event.
4. Case Number: 2025A039164
This spontaneous, serious and non-medically confirmed case was reported in Russia. 
The case involves a 41-year-old female patient who experienced hypertension 
(serious, listed), bilateral deafness (serious, unlisted), and hypersensitivity (non-
serious, listed) after taking Qlaira. Dechallenge information was not provided. While 
hypertension and hypersensitivity are known potential side effects, bilateral deafness 
is not listed as an adverse effect of Qlaira. The reporter suspected a product issue as 
she had been taking Qlaira for a long time and never had hypersensitivity reaction 
before. No further assessment of the product quality could be made as no information 
about the package or sample was provided. According to WHO-UMC criteria, the 
relationship between the drug and the events hypertension and hypersensitivity is 
likely given the listedness of the adverse events. However, the relationship between 
deafness and Qlaira is uncertain due to lack of adequate information.
5. Case Number: 2025A109110
This spontaneous, serious, and non-medically confirmed case was reported in Russia. 
The case refers to a female patient of unknown age who experienced hallucinations 
(serious, unlisted) along with intermenstrual bleeding (non-serious, listed), lower 
abdominal pain (non-serious, listed), herpes virus infection (non-serious, unlisted), 
urinary calculus (non-serious, unlisted), and crying (non-serious, unlisted) after taking 
Qlaira for endometriosis (off-label use). The case was classified as serious due to the 
medically important nature of the hallucinations. The reporter noted improvement 
upon discontinuation of the drug. The events of hallucinations, herpes virus infection, 
urinary calculus, and crying are not listed adverse effects in the Qlaira label. Since the case is not medically confirmed, the occurrence of the reported events 
remains uncertain. Combined oral contraceptives (COCs) are not known to reduce 
immunity; however, ongoing living conditions can affect human immunity, making 
individuals susceptible to opportunistic infections such as herpes virus infections. 
There is evidence that COCs can contribute to the formation of urinary calculus. 
Urinary stones typically develop over a longer period, and the duration of Qlaira 
exposure remains unknown in this case, preventing a clear association from being 
established. 
Although depression and mood changes are listed events in the Qlaira label, the crying 
and hallucinations in this patient appear to be sequelae of the severe abdominal pain 
due to endometriosis. The reporter speculated that there might be a product quality 
issue or simple intolerance. No product quality defect was identified by Bayer's 
Product Technical Complaint (PTC) assessment; therefore, the reported medical 
events are not indicative of a quality deficit per se. According to WHO-UMC criteria, 
the relationship between the drug and the listed events is likely; however, due to the 
course of the disease, the availability of limited information, and the presence of 
alternative explanations, the relationship between the drug and the unlisted events 
remains uncertain.

Overall assessment of serious cases:
In summary, above five spontaneous cases were reported by consumers in Russia. Four of these 
five cases are not medically confirmed. The PTC review of the cases where batch numbers were 
provided found no quality issues in Qlaira badges. All cases were categorized as serious, either 
due to the nature of the events, such as intermenstrual bleeding, CVA, surgery, hypertension, 
hallucinations, deafness or due to hospitalization. Most reported events are listed and expected 
with combined oral contraceptive (COC) use. However, most of the cases provided limited 
information necessary to assess causal associations, such as temporal association, dechallenge, 
and rechallenge data. The relationship between unlisted events, such as bilateral deafness in a 
patient with hypertension or hallucinations in a woman with endometriosis, is considered 
uncertain. Overall, the events do not raise significant product quality concerns in any of these 
reports, and individual analyses do not identify a new safety concern regarding the use of Qlaira 
for the licensed indication of use.

Non-Serious cases
In the SOC Product Issue cases (155), the total number of non-serious cases amounts to 150 
(97%), which includes 66 categorized as listed and 84 as unlisted. The majority of the non-
serious cases were reported by consumers in Russia, totaling 146 out of 150. Among the 66 
non-serious listed cases, 14 are medically confirmed (MC) and 52 are non-medically 
confirmed (NMC). These reports are categorized as listed cases because the reported adverse 
events (AEs) are included in the labeling of Qlaira.
Additionally, there are 84 non-serious cases categorized as unlisted. Within this group, 6 
cases are medically confirmed (MC), while 78 are non-medically confirmed (NMC). This 
breakdown indicates that the majority of the SOC "Product Issue" cases are non-serious, with 
a significant number of them being non-medically confirmed.
The six non-serious unlisted MC cases primarily report occurrences of irregular bleeding (n = 
4), abdominal pain (n = 2), breast pain (n = 1), blood pressure increased (n = 1), and chest 
pain (n = 1), all of which are considered listed events. These cases are categorized as unlisted 
due to women feeling unwell corresponding to PTs: Feeling abnormal, Malaise, Asthenia, etc, 
which are not listed events in the Qlaira label.
The 78 non-serious unlisted NMC consumer reports predominantly detail irregular bleeding 
(n = 47), abdominal pain (n = 25), breast pain (n = 14), blood pressure increased/fluctuation 
(n = 10), swelling/edema (n = 9), depressed mood/depression (n = 5), and chest 
pain/discomfort (n = 4), all of which are listed events. These cases were categorized as 
unlisted because they reported at least one unlisted event such as headache (n = 10), hot flush 
(n = 4), endometriosis (n = 4), or various other events (≤2) including feeling unwell, fatigue, 
malaise, asthenia, somnolence, irritability, vaginal discharge, bloating, allergic reaction, 
ovarian cyst, acne, arthralgia, rash, anxiety, aggression, dizziness, palpitations, tearfulness, 
etc. The four consumer reports mentioning occurrences of endometriosis (unlisted) alongside 
other listed events provided very limited information for causality assessment.

Overall assessment of non-serious cases:
In summary, the majority of the non-serious cases were reported by consumers in Russia, 
totaling 146 out of 150. Among these, only 20 cases were medically confirmed. The unlisted 
cases were categorized as unlisted because they reported at least one unlisted event. Most of 
the reported events in these unlisted cases are listed and might occur during the use of 
combined oral contraceptives (COCs). The reported unlisted events were primarily non-
specific symptoms, provided limited information for causality assessment, or had an 
alternative explanation of the event such as in the case of endometriosis.
The PTC review of the cases where the product was traceable found no quality issues with the 
Qlaira. Overall, the reported cases do not raise significant product quality concerns, and 
individual analyses do not identify any new safety concerns regarding the use of Qlaira for the 
licensed indication.

Question:
FDA Question 2:
Increased Reporting of Product Quality Issues
The summary tabulation report indicates a significant increase in the number of
post-marketing reports (“non-serious”) for several Preferred Terms (PTs) within
the SOC "Product issues" during this reporting interval. Specifically:
• "Suspected product quality issue" accounted for 89 of 110 (81%)
cumulative reports.
• "Product quality issue" accounted for 36 of 55 (65%) cumulative reports.
• "Suspected counterfeit product" accounted for 40 of 80 (50%) cumulative
reports.
Provide a detailed analysis and any narratives for these non-serious cases.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2:
During the current reporting period, 155 new reports in the SOC: “Product Issue” were 
recorded, representing a significant increase of 13 times compared to the last reporting period, 
which had only 12 cases. The majority of these cases originated from Russia (151), 
highlighting a concentrated burden of cases from this region. Notably, 40 of these reports 
expressed suspicions of counterfeit products specifically, while the remaining 111 cases 
documented adverse events and requested confirmation of product quality. 
Among the 151 Russian cases, batch numbers were obtained for 104 reports, with samples 
collected for three cases, and photographs provided for two. In 20 instances, when consumers 
were contacted for additional information, they indicated no ongoing concerns regarding the 
quality or authenticity of the product. A detailed analysis of the scenarios surrounding these 
product issue cases is presented here, with all cases and their respective abstracts submitted as 
CIOMS I output.

Based on a thorough PTC investigation involving batch documentation, historical data, and 
any applicable samples or photographs, the following conclusions were drawn:

• The reports primarily pertained to products with shared packaging layouts for
Kazakhstan and Russia, featuring bilingual packaging. This situation contributed to a 
higher volume of requests for confirmation of product quality and authenticity from 
Russian consumers. Notably, the delivery of Qlaira registered within the Eurasian 
Economic Union (EAEU), which included Kazakh language packaging, commenced 
on August 27, 2024.
• On 03-Dec-2024 Bayer published a statement on the local company website to inform
stakeholders about the shared labeling available in the market. The statement was 
additionally submitted to the Health Authority (HA) and published on the HA website 
on 13-Feb-2025. On May 21, 2025, new package mock-ups were approved that 
excluded the Kazakh language (Russian only). Following these measures, there was a 
significant decline in cases requesting confirmation of product quality and 
authenticity.
• All cases for which batch numbers, samples, or photographs were available were
confirmed as genuine Bayer products. No quality defects were identified in Bayer 
product in any of the investigations conducted.

The remaining four cases originated from Brazil, Colombia, Germany, and the United 
Kingdom, with no commonalities in terms of batches or reported events. No quality defects 
were identified in any of these cases.

Germany: One case reported a bee found alongside a tablet in a blister pack. 
Photographic evidence showed an intact bee next to the blister, indicating that the 
insect was undamaged and too large to fit within the blister cavity. An investigation of 
batch documentation and historical data found no quality defects attributable to Bayer.

Brazil: A consumer reported intermenstrual bleeding and requested confirmation of 
product quality, claiming that some tablets appeared to contain hormones while others 
did not. It is important to note that Qlaira is a combined oral contraceptive that utilizes 
a sequential dosing schedule. Each blister consists of 26 hormone-containing tablets 
and 2 hormone-free tablets with five different colors. This might have caused
confusion for the patent. No sample was provided for analysis. Investigations into 
batch documentation and historical data did not confirm any quality defects. 
Intermenstrual bleeding is a recognized adverse event associated with Qlaira/Natazia 
use, as listed in the Company Core Data Sheet (CCDS), and is not indicative of a 
consequence of a quality defect.

United Kingdom: A report indicated difficulties in accessing the product; however, 
no quality or technical issues were identified, and no further investigation was 
warranted.

Colombia: A report of an incomplete blister indicated that a tablet was missing. The 
sample was received by the responsible quality unit, revealing that the upper row was 
empty, but all other tablets were present and correctly configured within the blister. A 
review of batch records, historical data, and retain samples did not confirm any quality 
defects.

Overall Conclusion:
The high number (97%) of product issue cases reported from Russia can be attributed to 
consumer confusion stemming from the presence of the Kazakh language on the product 
label, alongside Russian. This bilingual labeling led users to associate any adverse events 
(AEs) with potential product quality issues, despite the fact that most reported AEs were 
listed events for Qlaira use, even in the absence of any actual product quality issues.
Bayer actively addressed these concerns, conducting thorough investigations into the 
traceable products. No genuine product quality issues were identified in these traceable 
products, and it is assumed that similar conclusions apply to the non-traceable products. 
Following the removal of the Kazakh language from the Russian label, there has been a 
dramatic decrease in the number of product issue cases from Russia. This further supports the 
notion that the spike in reports was primarily driven by confusion related to bilingual labeling.
A detailed analysis of the product issue cases and the aforementioned scenario indicates that 
no new safety concerns have emerged and the benefit-risk ratio of Qlaira in its approved 
indications remains positive.

Question:
Question 3.
Regarding the hydrate issue in the basic properties of the drug substance, it is recommended 
to provide detailed research data and diffractograms to prove that XH2O in the molecular 
formula of the drug substance is a non-stoichiometric variable hydrate (channel hydrate?), for 
example, can variable humidity XRPD diffractograms at different humidity levels be provided 
to demonstrate that change in moisture does not affect the crystal structure? Alternatively, as 
mentioned in the submission documentation: “single crystal X-ray structure analysis 
performed on a crystal from recrystallization batch OLB 270722-10a indicated a 
stoichiometry of 4/5 and demonstrated these weak interactions.” Please provide representative 
diffractograms and data. 
It is recommended to specify the upper and lower limits of X in the molecular formula in 
the instructions for use.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 3 ( S.3):
It is well-known that two kinds of hydrate formation exist: [1]
Stoichiometric hydrates have a crystal lattice based on an exact water content with a well-
defined mole ratio of water molecules and given API molecule.
Non-stoichiometric hydrates have a continuously variable composition (due to the water 
content) within a certain range without any significant changes in crystalline structure.
Hydrate 1 Mod. A belongs to the second class described above and thus exhibits variability in 
water content. This must be described by the following structural formula:
C24H25ClN4O5 · x H2O

In 2008 Newman, Reutzel-Edens and Zografi [2] described in their minireview the way to 
evaluate sorption data of a given pharmaceutical active ingredient by using the following 
flowchart (Figure 1):
References：
[1] J.-R. Authelin, Int. J. Pharm, 303, 2005, 37 – 53
[2] A. W. Newman, S. M. Reutzel-Edens, G. Zografi, J. Pharm. Sci., 97, 3, 2008, 1047 -
1059

By using these criteria and based on the given definitions, Sevabertinib Hydrate 
(BAY 2927088 hydrate) can be described as a non-stoichiometric hydrate, because its 
crystalline lattice is able to include variable numbers of water molecules without changes in 
the observed XRPD pattern and consequentially the crystalline structure. Water content in the 
drug substance will be controlled with the specification of 1.0 to 4.0 %.
The drug substance in its crystalline form, Hydrate 1 Mod. A, has been fully characterized by 
thermoanalytical, spectroscopic, and X-ray diffractometric data (see S 3.1.01 Structure 
Elucidation and other Characteristics).

In addition, the special non-stoichiometric character of this hydrate was clearly demonstrated by an X-ray single-crystal structure based on one single crystal. In the X-ray single-crystal analysis, it can be seen that the water molecules are randomly arranged between the layers of the active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) molecules.

These different types of intermolecular interactions explain why this crystal lattice can implement varying numbers of water molecules without the actual lattice structure changing. The correlation of XRPD data to the X-ray single-crystal structure was achieved by comparing the calculated X-ray powder diffraction pattern with the measured X-ray powder diffraction pattern of the various batches of Hydrate 1 Mod. A.

In RH XRPD experiments, the behavior of the crystalline lattice of Hydrate 1 Mod. A was examined under different humidity conditions (0 – 90% RH sorption and desorption in 10% steps) at a constant temperature of 25°C. In the sorption experiment, the substance (Hydrate 1 Mod. A, Batch BXR9J78) was initially dried at 0% humidity and was present as Mod. IV at 1% RH. This modification was retained up to 20% RH and converted in the next step to Hydrate 1 Mod. A. This crystal lattice then remained unchanged up to 90% RH. This effect was also observed in the desorption experiment: at 20% RH, Hydrate 1 Mod. A was converted to the anhydrous form Mod. IV. These experiments clearly demonstrate the behavior of Hydrate 1 Mod. A in a kinetic experimental design.

The RH XRPD results perfectly match the data from the DVS measurements, which gives us information on the change of water amount in and on the sample BXR9J78 (Hydrate 1 Mod. A). Dynamic uptake (sorption) of water was observed between 0 and 10% RH, followed by a flatter curve up to 95% RH and a total water uptake of 4%. The desorption curve follows this curve in the opposite direction, not without exhibiting a slight hysteresis.

Another technique for investigating the behavior of Hydrate 1 Mod. A upon loss of water is thermoanalytical methods. In this case, Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) and Thermogravimetry (TGA) techniques were used. The thermogram of the DSC measurement of sample BXR9J78 (Hydrate 1 Mod. A) initially shows a broad endothermic signal, which indicates the release of water. This is confirmed by the TGA measurement, which describes a mass loss. Unlike stoichiometric hydrates, this stage is somewhat soft and continuous, clearly highlighting the non-stoichiometric character of the hydrate.

Batch data for sevabertinib hydrate with different water content and the corresponding XRPDs are shown in Table 1 and Figure 9 through to Figure 16. These data demonstrate that the water content can vary widely without a change in the crystalline lattice, supporting the assignment of sevabertinib hydrate as a non-stoichiometric hydrate.

In summary, all available data support the assignment of sevabertinib hydrate as a non-stoichiometric hydrate.

Based on the nonstoichiometric, variable character of Hydrate 1 Mod. A with an undefined ratio of sevabertinib to water, a value for (x) cannot be specified.
Water content (%) and the hydration number x represent fundamentally different concepts and physical dimensions.
As the lattice occupancy of water can vary with the environmental equilibrium state rather than remaining within a specification‑worthy interval, it is not only inappropriate to define a fixed hydration number x, but also scientifically unsound to provide a “range” for x.
Converting a mass‑based water content to a structural x value—fixed or ranged—does not accurately represent the crystal structure and may lead to conceptual misunderstanding.

Source:  
S.3.1.01 Structure Elucidation and other Characteristics/ BAY 2927088 
hydrate micronized drug substance (#S.3.1.01_022988327_02; 
unchanged)

Question:
Question 4
Given the significant crystal transformation in the drug product, please further clarify:
(1) Why was Hydrate 1 Mod A selected as the form for commercial development, and why
were other forms such as the anhydrous form or more stable forms not chosen? Please 
provide specific solubility data of Modification I (Mod I) and Hydrate I Mod A under 
different pH conditions.
(2) Please provide the crystal form testing diffractogram at the end of shelf life for all
registration batches (DP), and attempt to analyze the overall trend of drug product 
polymorphic transformation from the perspective of CMC control.
(3) Please provide the formulation information of the liquid service formulation (LSF) used
in the study 21607 subject's pharmacokinetics data, specify the type and amount of 
excipients, whether the drug substance is completely dissolved, and specify the batch 
number and crystal form determination of the tablets used in the study (whether it is pure 
hydrate 1 crystal form A), which are used to demonstrate the bridgebility between crystal 
form 1 and target crystal form A.
Based on this, please further elaborate in detail why it can be concluded that the absorption 
rate of Mod I in vivo is necessarily higher, given its greater solubility and faster dissolution 
rate. The applicant’s in vivo bridging relies on the rationale that differences in the absorption 
rate affect safety and efficacy. In other words, is there a possibility that Mod I has a lower in 
vivo absorption rate? If so, how should this risk be assessed?
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 4 ( S.1, P.2, P.5):
(1)
The selection of Hydrate 1 Mod. A as the solid state form to be developed was based on a holistic assessment of all data available at the time of decision. The solid state information came from an extensive externally conducted polymorphism screening. In this screening data evaluation did not identify any anhydrous forms. A large number of solvates with organic solvents was found in addition to four forms identified as non-stoichiometric hydrates. Solvates including organic solvents were excluded from further considerations. Because no anhydrous forms had been identified the selection of a suitable form was narrowed down to the hydrates. As all hydrates were identified to be non-stoichiometric, manufacturing considerations were also included. We had already shown that we could manufacture Hydrate 1 reproducibly. Thus, Hydrate 1, which is now called Hydrate 1 Mod. A, was selected as the solid state form for development.

Since it had been shown that BAY 2927088 shows a complicated solid state landscape, an in-depth polymorphism study was initiated in-house. This led to the realization that four anhydrous forms of BAY 2927088 exist, three of which Mod. II, Mod. III and Mod. IV, are metastable. The fourth anhydrous form, Mod. I, was found to be identical with the form called Hydrate II in the external polymorphism screening. It had not been recognized in the initial investigation that it was an anhydrous form. Based on the in-house polymorphism study Mod. I is the thermodynamically stable anhydrous form. The in-house study also showed that Hydrate 1 exists in three different polymorphs: Hydrate 1 Mod. A, Hydrate 1 Mod. B and Hydrate 1 Mod. C. Of these Hydrate 1 Mod. A was shown to be the most suitable form. Hydrate 1 Mod. A is identical with the form called Hydrate 1 in the initial screening.

At the time when the results from the in-house polymorphism study became available, a process to manufacture Drug Substance in the form of Hydrate 1 Mod. A in commercial scale had been established. It had also been demonstrated that the solid state form did not change during DS stability. Also, Drug Product batches manufactured from this DS consistently contained Hydrate 1 Mod. A at time of release. The partial transition of this solid state form in the Drug Product to Mod. I became only apparent with the primary stability batches. The change in solid state form was assessed not to impact safety and efficacy of the Drug Product and has therefore no impact on the commercial product.

Solubility data for Hydrate 1 Mod. A and Mod. I are provided below.
The solubility of BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance was determined by stirring batch no. UNGG220 (hydrate 1 mod. A) in aqueous buffer solutions, to be tested in a thermostatically controlled water bath at 25 °C and 37 °C for 24 hours. The suspension was passed through a 0.45 µm membrane filter. The concentration was monitored by HPLC (method see S.4.2.01 “Test Procedure”).
The solubility of BAY 2927088 Modification I was determined by stirring batch no. OLB 090724-7e (Modification I) in aqueous buffer solutions, to be tested in a thermostatically controlled water bath at 25 °C and 37 °C for 24 hours. The suspension was passed through a 0.45 µm membrane filter. The concentration was monitored by HPLC (method see S.4.2.01 “Test Procedure”).
The solubility in aqueous buffer solutions at different pH values of BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized are shown in Table 2 and Table 3 and for BAY 2927088 Modification I in Table 4 and Table 5.

(2)
The crystal form testing diffractogram at the end of shelf life (batches MSAT230906 and KM60497) or the latest available pull point for all registration batches (DP) are summarized and provided (Table 6; Figures 17–36 listed).
The observed transition from Hydrate 1 Mod. A to Mod. I in the tablets is a solid-solid phase transition that can be triggered by a wide range of events, e.g. temperature cycling, mechanical stress, humidity. While the overall direction of the transition is governed by thermodynamics, predicting the kinetics of the transformation is not possible. Deducing a trend of drug product polymorphic transformation would therefore be scientifically unsound. From the perspective of CMC control it is also not necessary as it has been demonstrated that even for a complete change from Hydrate 1 Mod. A to Mod. I, safety and efficacy of the drug product would not be impacted.

(3)
LSF: Composition of BAY 2927088 solution 0.5 % (also referred to as “LSF”) is provided in Table 7 (drug substance; macrogol 400; butylhydroxyanisole; polysorbate 20; levomenthol; quantities).
For all clinical batches of the LSF the drug substance was completely dissolved, i.e. a clear solution was obtained (please see P.5.4.01_IQMS-435663_1.0_BAY 2927088 solution 0.5 % for oral use 201 (Clinical Batches). No change of this test item was observed in the stability studies.
Tablets: Only tablets containing Hydrate 1 Mod A, as determined at release of the DP by informative XRPD testing, were provided for distribution to use in study 21607. Release test results including polymorphic form are provided (Tables 8 and 9 for 20 mg; and for 10 mg tablets in documents P.5.4.01_IQMS-261279_1.0 and P.5.4.01_IQMS-263273_2.0).

(4)
In vitro permeability studies revealed sevabertinib to be highly permeable (Module 4.2.2.6, Report B002815). Taking into account solubility and high permeability in Caco-2-cells, the compound can be classified as BCS class 2 [3]. For this class, oral absorption is predominantly controlled by dissolution under physiological conditions [4]. Faster dissolution leads to earlier and higher intestinal concentrations, resulting in a faster onset of absorption and an increased absorption rate [4].
Based on these considerations, the higher solubility of Mod. I compared to Hydrate 1 Mod. A (see response to Question 4 (1)) and the comparable or faster dissolution kinetics of tablets containing only Mod. I (see P.2.2.10_IQMS-265402_1.0_BAY 2927088 coated tablet 10 mg), the possibility that Mod I has a lower in vivo absorption rate is considered very unlikely.
A higher absorption rate may lead to higher and earlier maximum concentrations. Therefore, the potential impact of absorption rate on safety and efficacy was analyzed. The analyses demonstrated that absorption rate had no impact on safety or efficacy (Module 5.3.3.5, Report B003834).

References:
[3] ICH Guideline M9: Biopharmaceutics Classification System-Based Biowaivers and Q&A Document thereof
[4] Amidon, G.L., Lennernäs, H., Shah, V.P. et al. A Theoretical Basis for a Biopharmaceutic Drug Classification: The Correlation of in Vitro Drug Product Dissolution and in Vivo Bioavailability. Pharm Res 12, 413–420 (1995). https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1016212804288

Question:
Question 5
Regarding commercial manufacturing batch size: It is recommended that the 
manufacturing batch size be fixed at 20 kg in the current manufacturing process 
information table. The batch size may be scaled up to 60 kg after accumulating more batch 
production data at post-approval stage.
The reasons are as follows:
(1) Step 1: Mixing, sieving, and mixing follow a batch production model. Therefore, the
batch size cannot typically be defined by production time as required for process 
validation of a continuous manufacturing model. Please clarify whether the same 
production equipment (whether a 200 L mixing equipment or mixing equipment of 
different volumes is used?) and the same process parameters (whether mixing speed and 
mixing time are the same?) are adopted for production at batch sizes of 20 kg, 30 kg, and 
60 kg?
(2) In accordance with the Process Validation Guidelines issued by CFDI in 2025,
prospective process validation shall be adopted for the first marketing application, and at 
least three consecutive successful batches of process validation should generally be 
performed under commercial-scale production conditions. If other validation batch 
numbers are to be used (e.g., if approval for 60 kg is sought, currently only one batch of 
validation data exists for 60 kg (based on the fact that Premix Step 1 is not a continuous 
manufacturing process and the process validation requirements for batch production are 
applied)), the rationality needs to be justified (e.g., in cases where advanced 
manufacturing technologies such as PAT are adopted, but such technologies were not 
actually used in Premix Step).
Given the currently limited overall development and production batches, it is recommended 
that the manufacturing process information table first fix the batch size at 20 kg, and 
supportive data be submitted to increase it to 60 kg at the post-marketing stage.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 5 ( P.2, P.3):
(1) Bayer acknowledges that the CFDI Guideline for Process Validation Inspection (April 2025), states that prospective process validation is the preferred method for initial process validation and that this validation should generally be carried out on a minimum of three consecutive batches. However, the validation strategy employed for the pre-blend and subsequent continuous manufacturing process was not designed to validate a single fixed batch size, but rather to validate a commercial batch size range of 20 to 60 kg (as amount of pre-blend) using a risk-based bracketing approach, consistent with the risk management principles of the CFDI Guideline and requirements of ICH Q13 Guideline.

The scientific basis for the bracketing approach was to produce representative batches for the intended batch size extremes, more specifically 20 to 60 kg. This approach is compliant to the “Process Validation for Multi-strength Products” procedure described in section 7.1 of CFDI Guideline. In our specific case, the variable process element is the batch size of the input material. All other process parameters were kept constant. The batch size is not solely defined by the manufacturing line run time at a defined mass flow rate; our batch size definition also considers the amount of input material as described in section 2.2 of ICH Q13. Therefore, it is Bayer’s understanding that the process validation of BAY 2927088 (Sevabertinib) 10 mg coated tablets was successfully conducted on three consecutive commercial-scale batches.

The validation batch configuration (refer to P.3.5.01) was as follows:
• Two consecutive batches at 20 kg
• One consecutive batch at 60 kg

The blending process uses a 200 L or 400 L vessel for the first blending step and a 300 L vessel for the second blending step. The process parameters (blending speed and blending time) of both blending steps are kept constant for all clinical and validation batches produced on the continuous manufacturing line.

In our approach, the quality attribute that is affected by the blending process is the blend uniformity. Thus, the validation was set-up to demonstrate process robustness over the whole range of batch sizes. The uniformity of the pre-blend was validated by using the two extremes of the batch size range (20 kg and 60 kg).

A potential impact of both, vessel size and batch size is most suitably investigated by calculating the filling load (batch size divided by vessel size). The investigated ranges during process development and validation of the filling load range were:
• 0.10 kg/L - 0.15 kg/L for the first blending step
• 0.07 kg/L - 0.20 kg/L for the second blending step.

As described in P.3.5.01, the homogeneity of all three pre-blends was analyzed during process validation, and the results for the three validation batches and one clinical batch are provided for reference (Table 11).

In addition to blend uniformity measurement during validation, further evidence on batch homogeneity has been generated via content uniformity testing (CU) of coated tablets. CU of all coating sublots produced in the subsequent continuous manufacturing process during process validation was tested and met the specification.

The results of the process validation study, the obtained process knowledge during process development and the overall control strategy of the manufacturing line show reliable evidence, that the established process conditions and controls during blending of the pre-blend are capable of producing BAY 2927088 (Sevabertinib) 10 mg coated tablets in the specified quality within the investigated pre-blend batch size range of 20 – 60 kg.

(2) As described in Point (1), our validation approach used three consecutive batches with the batch size range 20 - 60 kg defined by the pre-blend as input material for the continuous manufacturing line. This approach is considered compliant with the referenced Guideline for Process Validation from CFDI (Status April 2025), specifically section “4.1 Initial process validation”, “5.1 Traditional process validation” and “7.1 Process Validation for Multi-strength Products”. The evidence collected with extensive blend homogeneity testing of the blend and content uniformity testing after continuous manufacturing is sufficient to justify our proposal to register a batch size range of 20 – 60 kg. Therefore, Bayer respectfully ask to maintain the proposed batch size range in the MPIT.

Question:
Question 1
The presence of polymorphic form II in the drug substance might have an impact on 
safety/efficacy of the drug product. Parameter polymorphism is therefore considered a critical 
attribute and should be kept in the specifications of the drug substance unless otherwise 
justified. The MAH is therefore asked to retain the parameter polymorphism in the 
specifications of the drug substance with the mention “must comply if tested” and to leave the 
information regarding laboratory responsible for XRPD testing as well as the description and 
validation of the analytical method.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (3.2.S.4):
We agree to the agency’s comment and therefore agree to keep polymorphism as a critical 
attribute of the drug substance. However, polymorphic form I is the thermodynamically stable 
form at ambient temperature and producing metastable polymorphic form II under the 
established process conditions is highly unlikely.  Based on the data provided with this 
variation in section 3.2.S.4.5, it was shown that in approximately 300 batches, manufactured 
in two years, the result for polymorphism was constantly polymorphic form I. Throughout the 
manufacturing history of darolutamide only polymorphic form I has been produced.
The test for polymorphism by X-ray analysis is kept in the specification as a periodic skip test 
of every twentieth batch. Please see below the documentation that has been amended in order 
to keep the dossier aligned.
We consider the proposed period of testing (every twentieth batch) sufficient considering the 
large number of batches already manufactured and the large number of batches which are 
manufactured annually.
For additional assurance of the polymorphic form, the identity test by IR will remain in the 
specification as a routine test for all manufactured batches. The spectra of Polymorphic form I 
and polymorphic form II are compared in Figure 1, and the match of the IR spectra is only 
64%. Polymorphic form II would not comply with the criteria that the spectrum of the sample 
must comply with that of the reference standard.

The following dossier sections have been amended for this response:
• 3.2.S.2.1 Manufacturer(s): testing site for polymorphism was included again (same
site as previously)
• 3.2.S.2.4 Control of Critical Steps and Intermediates: Polymorphism is again classified
as a critical quality attribute. A justification for the skip testing has been included.
• 3.2.S.2.6 Manufacturing Process Development: Polymorphic form has been added
again in the list of critical quality attributes
• 3.2.S.4.1 Specification: Polymorphism has been included again in the specification
with the following footnote: “Must comply if tested. Analysis is performed 
as periodic skip testing of every twentieth batch.”
• 3.2.S.4.2 Test Procedure: the test procedure for polymorphism has been re-introduced
to the document (same wording as before). We have taken the opportunity to include 
an exemplary diffractogram of a more current batch.
• 3.2.S.4.4 Batch Analyses: inclusion of test for Polymorphism (with footnote regarding
skip testing on every twentieth batch).
• 3.2.S.4.5 Justification of Specification and Skip Testing: Discussion of specification
for Polymorphism has been moved from chapter 3 “Non-specified Test Items” to
chapter 2 “Discussion of Individual Tests and Limits”, and justification of skip testing 
has been introduced.

Source:  S.2.1.01-09 Manufacturer(s) / Darolutamide milled drug substance (#IQMS-

drug substance (#IQMS-223899; amended)

Question:

It is known that capitalisation reduces readability of names for patients. As advised in 
the MHRA Guideline for the Naming of Medicinal Products and Braille Requirements 
for Name on Label, ‘the invented name should not comprise wholly of initial letters or 
code numbers’. It remains our recommendation for the proposed invented name 
‘HYRNUO’ to be amended to ‘Hyrnuo (i.e., use of capitalised 'H' and lower case 
'yrnuo') in order to improve readability. The labelling should be updated accordingly.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2
In order to conclude the procedure positively, Bayer has implemented MHRA’s request, and 
changed the appearance of the brand name from HYRNUO to Hyrnuo.
Bayer wish to respectfully note, however, that we do not agree that capital letters adversely 
affect readability for Hyrnuo. We acknowledge MHRA’s guidance on Naming of Medicinal 
Products and Braille Requirements for Name on Label, which states to avoid widespread use 
of words in all capitals particularly in blocks of text. Our understanding is that in this 
guidance, reference to ‘initial letters’ is understood to mean acronyms or abbreviations 
formed from the first (initial) letters of multiple words (e.g. HRT, SSRI), and does not 
preclude the use of capitals for a short, distinctive brand name.
However, we respect MHRA’s position that all capitals should not be used, and look forward 
to seeing the updated naming guidance that will clearly state this.

Question:
Question 10
Since Levomefolate calcium is known to be unstable, please provide discussion on why the step 
where levomefolate calcium is introduced into the granulator is not considered critical since 
loss of the active substance occurs at this stage.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 10 ( CTD section):
We have identified three critical process steps: granulation, tableting, and film-coating. The 
addition of Levomefolate calcium is an integral part of the granulation process and is therefore 
considered critical.
The loss of LMCA can be attributed to several factors, including adhesion of LMCA to the 
surfaces of production equipment, adsorption at the exhaust filters of the granulator, and the 
chemical instability of LMCA, which is exacerbated by temperature and humidity.
To mitigate these risks and prevent LMCA from being exposed to high temperatures and 
humidity, we ensure that it is mixed under the fluidized bed with a cold volumetric flow 
immediately after the granulation process is completed. Furthermore, to minimize sticking to 
the surfaces of the feeding system, LMCA is mixed with croscarmellose sodium. Additionally, 
magnesium stearate is added and mixed subsequently to effectively "flush" the feeding system, 
reducing the potential for loss of the active substance.
Additionally, all process steps are monitored through the IPC mentioned in P.3.3.02_IQMS-
145041_1.0 via the MBR, ensuring that any deviation from the validated process is immediately 
detected.
Source:  P.3.3.021-1.0 Process Controls/ Drospirenone + Ethinylestradiol +
Levomefolate calcium coated tablet 3.0 mg + 0.03 mg + 0.451 mg 
(#P.3.3.02_IQMS-145041_1.0; unchanged)

Question:
Question 12
Regarding the finished product finished product specification, please address as follows:
i. 
Revise the upper limit for assay at release for levomefolate calcium to 105% i.e., 
assay limit at release should be 95.0 – 105%.
ii. 
Revise the limits for all the specified impurities to not more than their qualification 
threshold based on ICHQ3B or provide qualification data for the higher limits being 
proposed. These impurities include Δ9,11-Ethinylestradiol impurity of estradiol, 
MeFox, ABGA, and Mefguan impurities of Levomefolate calcium.
iii. 
Your response should include a copy of the revised, signed, dated and version-
controlled FPP specifications at release and shelf-life along with the updated change 
history. Sections 2.3.P.5.1 and 2.3.P.8.2 of the QIS should be updated accordingly.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 12 ( CTD section):
Please find the response mentioned below:
i) The specification limits for release and shelf life are based on the experience gained during 
product development and are approved and well-established in many countries worldwide since 
decades  .
Levomefolate calcium is a folate vitamin. Within the USP a monograph for “Folic acid tablets” 
specifies the content with 90-115% of the labelled claim. Since the vitamin is no hormone, a 
broader specification limit than for the drug substances Drospirenone and Ethinylestradiol are 
proposed and generally accepted. Therefore, and considering the long lasting experience with 
the drug product, the proposed specification limit for assay of levomefolate calcium of 95.0 -
110.0% is considered justified.

ii)  The current limit in the release specification for Δ9,11-ethinylestradiol as the degradation 
product of Ethinylestradiol is below the identification threshold of 1.0% according to the ICH 
guideline Q3B (R2) <Impurities in new drug products>. The shelf life limit of 1.2% was set up 
with regard to the limit in the drug substance of 0.5%, the release specification of the drug 
product of 0.8% and observed increase during storage as well as under consideration of the 
variability of the analytical test method. This limit is toxicologically qualified (please refer to 
the toxicological assessment of degradation products derived from Ethinylestradiol in oral 
contraceptive preparations).

For Levomefolate calcium, an increase of degradation products within the stability studies was 
observed. Please note, that the limits for release and shelf life testing of the degradation products 
MeFox (3.0% and 7.0%), ABGA (1.0% and 2.0%) and Mefguan (1.0% and 2.0%) are within 
or below the toxicological qualified level of 10% for MeFox, 5% for AGBA and 2% for 
Mefguan (Seibert, 2010; Seibert, 2011).

iii) The signed copies for both Ethinylestradiol and Levomefolate degradation products are 
attached with this response. However, QIS update will be taken care locally.

Question:
Question 13
The use of 7% overage quantity of Levomefolate calcium justification is noted but not 
satisfactory. Levomefolate calcium is known to be unstable. Furthermore, levomefolate calcium 
partly remains in the feeding tubes to fluid bed granulator and on the fluidized bed granulator 
surface, please specify if the analytical method is suitable to ensure full potency of the finished 
drug and does not result in a super potent drug product.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 13 ( CTD section):
The vitamin Levomefolate calcium (LMCA) is used for the prevention of neuronal tube defects 
of newborn children. According to literature, a dose of 0.451 mg LMCA equivalent to 0.4 mg 
folic acid are the target amounts for the prevention of these defects. LMCA is known for its 
instability towards increased temperatures and adhesion to surfaces. In order to guarantee for 
correct dosage and statistically cover the worst case scenarios for physical and chemical losses, 
the overage was calculated as a sum of mean overall production loss (and standard deviation) 
during the manufacturing. A mean overall production loss during the manufacturing of LMCA 
tablets of 4.3% with a standard deviation of ± 2.5% was observed (see P.2.2.01_IQMS-
145030_3.0). Therefore, a 7% overage for manufacturing of LMCA containing coated tablets 
is justified.
Prior to setup of the overage, an extensive evaluation on the production loss of LMCA was 
performed (P.2.2.10_IQMS-176943_1.0). Physical loss (e.g., due to adhesion of material) as 
well as chemical loss (caused by degradation) were investigated at every process step. Based 
on this in-depth investigation, the overage of 7% for the production of LMCA-containing film-
coated products was determined and confirmed. The whole manufacturing process was 
inspected and the chemical loss (increase of by-products) for all manufacturing steps was 
determined. Furthermore the physical loss of LMCA due to adhesion of the material on 
equipment surfaces was determined for the first two steps (addition of LMCA and compression 
to tablets) and for the film coating process, respectively.
A chemical loss of 1.0% standard deviation of ± 0.3% was observed over the whole production 
process (P.2.2.10_IQMS-176943_1.0, Table 7). For a detailed discussion of the extent of 
degradation in the different production steps (P.2.2.10_IQMS-176943_1.0, chapter 5). The 
physical loss over the whole process was 3.3% with a standard deviation of ± 2.7%. The loss 
of LMCA is related to the following factors: adhesion of LMCA at surfaces of production 
equipment, adsorption at exhaust filters of granulator and chemical instability of LMCA 
(promoted by temperature and humidity).
Regarding the analytical method, the range determined within the linearity test covers 
concentrations from 0.1 to 130%. The investigations of the accuracy covers a range of up to
130% of levomefolate calcium. This means, the method is capable to quantify the exact amounts 
of levomefolate calcium within the drug product.
Source:  P.5.3.01-1.0 Validation of Test for Assay and Impurities/ Drospirenone +
Ethinylestradiol + Levomefolate calcium coated tablet 3.0 mg + 0.03 mg + 
0.451 mg (#P.5.3.01_IQMS-145213_1.0; unchanged)

Question:
Question 14
Since Levomefolate calcium coated tablet acts as a placebo in this product, please include test 
for absence of the actives (Drospirenone and Ethinylestradiol) in the specifications for 
Levomefolate calcium coated tablet.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 14 ( CTD section):
The levomefolate calcium coated tablet is not registered as placebo because it is used for the 
prevention of neuronal tube defects of newborn children , it is generally considered as drug 
substance.
In the Supply Center Weimar (Weimar, Germany), GMP-processes and measurements are in 
place to minimize the risk of a possible cross-contamination. These take into account the 
following factors:
• 
Room and equipment design and usage,
• 
Personnel and material flow,
• 
Physical-chemical, pharmacological, and toxicological properties of the active
substance(s),
• 
Manufacturing processes and product characteristics,
• 
Campaign concepts,
• 
Cleaning and cleaning verification processes,
• 
Sensitivity of analytical methods in relation to the established "Maximum Allowable
Carry Over" (MACO).

This comprehensive evaluation highlights the importance of each factor in maintaining a safe 
and compliant manufacturing environment. The careful design and utilization of rooms and 
equipment ensure that the workflow minimizes the potential for contamination. Additionally, 
understanding the properties of the substances involved allows for tailored approaches to 
handling and processing, further mitigating risks.
Rigorous cleaning protocols and verification processes are in place to ensure that all equipment 
is thoroughly cleaned between uses, effectively reducing any possible residual contaminants.
The evaluation of the presence (and eventually the amount) of previous drug substances in the 
subsequent formulations (drug products or placebo) which may be relevant for patient safety is 
considered by cleaning validation. In adherence to current regulations, the manufacturing 
equipment used at our site undergoes defined cleaning procedures. These cleaning processes 
are validated, among others, regarding the residual amount of drug substance after cleaning 
which may be transferred in the following manufactured batch via the product contact surfaces. 
From an analytical perspective, the effectiveness of the cleaning procedures is evaluated by 
sampling predefined points of the manufacturing equipment (e.g., with adequate sampling 
procedures) and analyzing the samples regarding the residual amount of drug substance(s). The 
implemented procedure at the site for cleaning validation ensures that any possible carryover 
from precious drug substances in the subsequent formulation is below the defined maximal 
acceptable carryover (MACO) and therefore poses no risk for product quality or patient safety.

Question:
Question 1
(3.2.P.2.4) The information that you have provided to support the absence of leachables, in your 
proposed drug product, is not considered adequate.  You have provided a brief discussion 
regarding a simulated leachables study, however, you have not provided a justification for the 
simulated study as required by USP <1664> Assessment of Drug Product Leachables 
Associated with Pharmaceutical Packaging/Delivery Systems.  The following is therefore 
requested:
a) Confirm that the simulated leachables study was conducted using actual drug product
manufactured as per current manufacturing process.  Batch number(s) should be provided 
and should be consistent with the batch number(s) used in the extractables study.
b) Provide the results of a leachables study over the proposed storage conditions and proposed
shelf-life using the actual drug product solution, manufactured as per current process, placed 
on inverted orientation.
c) In the absence of real-time leachable study data, provide a scientific justification as to why
a simulated leachables study was conducted instead of a real-time assessment over the 
proposed storage conditions and shelf-life of the product.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1:
a) 
Bayer confirms that the simulated leachables study was conducted using PRIMOVIST, 
sodium gadoxetate solution 0.25 mol/L for parenteral use, batch number KT0K9TJ 
manufactured according to the current manufacturing process.
The sample was collected at the end of filling line into a separate glass container to avoid 
contact with the new bromobutyl rubber stopper material.
The stoppers used in the extractables and simulated leachables studies had all the same 
pretreatments as used in the current PRIMOVIST, sodium gadoxetate solution 0.25 mol/L 
for parenteral use filling process.
Stoppers from the same lots were used in both the extractables and simulated leachables 
studies.

b) Real-time leachable shelf-life data is currently not available, please refer to the response
provided under Question 1c that discusses the justification for using a simulated leachables 
study.

c) Based on Health Canada’s feedback from the GADOVIST 1.0 (Ctrl no. 294352) and
ULTRAVIST (Ctrl. No. 294064) reviews, Bayer had provided the additional information 
pre-emptively in the note to reviewer, which we have now also discussed below.
With the introduction of the bromobutyl stopper, extractables data was prepared in 
exaggerated conditions of 50°C / 72 h and 85°C / 1 h (see Module 3.2.P.2.4.06_IQMS- 
254544_1.0 Extractions Studies). The stability study for sodium gadoxetate solution 
0.25 mol/L in vials using the alternative bromobutyl closure system, had not yet been 
initiated. Therefore, a simulated leachables study using sodium gadoxetate solution 
0.25 mol/L as extractant, in exaggerated conditions of 50 °C / 72 h and 85 °C / 1 h was 
conducted to confirm the safety of the new stopper material.
In the simulated leachables study no simulated leachables exceeding the study analytical 
evaluation threshold (AETs) was observed.
For the new bromobutyl stoppers an extensive extractables study was initially performed 
using several different extraction media, at elevated temperatures as stated above, with 
relatively long extraction time. These conditions were chosen to reflect recommendations 
in USP <1663> monograph, and ISO 10993-18 and 10993-12. For the AETs, when feasible, 
higher Uncertainty Factors (UF) of 4 and 10, than the usual UF 2 were used to confirm that 
all extractables are measured. The analyses were performed using state-of-art mass 
spectroscopic instruments.
Extractions with 2-propanol as extractant, 50% EtOH/water were performed, and also with 
water. In pH 4 and pH 9.5 buffer solutions only a few extractables in low amounts were 
detected. These were mainly fatty acids like palmitoleic, palmitic and oleic acids that are 
relatively non-toxic and common in elastomers and plastics. In addition to the extractables 
study, Bayer decided to conduct a simulated leachables study. In the simulated leachables 
study, using similar exaggerated extraction conditions to the extractables study, no 
reportable compounds were found. It was therefore considered adequate proof of stopper 
material suitability and safety for its intended use as container closure system and therefore 
no formal leachables stability study was planned.
A real-time stability study is on-going and a leachables study after 36 months testing and 
also at the end of 60 months shelf-life will be performed as per the USP <1664> Assessment 
of Drug Product Leachables Associated with Pharmaceutical Packaging/Delivery Systems, 
to further confirm the safety of the material
Source:  P.2.4.06-01 Extraction Studies / Sodium gadoxetate solution 0.25 mol/L for
parenteral use (PRIMOVIST) (#022985400/IQMS-254544_1.0; unchanged)

Question 2
It is recommended to set an upper limit for specific activity to reflect consistency between 
batches.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2:
Bayer acknowledges the recommendation to implement an upper limit for specific activity, to 
address this concern a upper specification limit for ‘Total Protein’ has been implemented in 
Drug Product. The drug substance and drug product total protein specifications ensure 
production process continuity and batch-to-batch consistency. Since specific activity is 
calculated by dividing the potency result by the total protein result and both potency and total 
protein have two-sided specification limits (upper and lower), the upper limit of specific activity 
is indirectly controlled by the potency and total protein specifications.
The specification for total protein at the drug product level sufficiently addresses control of 
Specific Activity.

Question:
Bayer Question 2

2. Section 3.2.P.3.5: Subsequent to the OOS in stability studies, Revise the release
specification to include a test and acceptance criteria for water content at NMT 5%.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2) ( CTD section):
Applicant acknowledges the agency’s question and would like to clarify that the water content
is not a mandatory specification parameter for solid oral dosage forms (drug products)  in
accordance to ICH Q6A, “Test procedures and acceptance criteria for new drug substances
and new drug products: chemical substances”. As per ICH Q6A, water content test is
“important for drug substances in cases where the new drug substance is known to be
hygroscopic or degraded by moisture or when the drug substance is known to be a
stoichiometric hydrate”.
For the drug product, water content has only an indirect impact on quality. Water content or
loss on drying, respectively is determined for all drug substances (refer to the drug substance
specifications S.4.1.01).
Relative humidity is the target parameter at the end of the granulation step. It is included as an
in-process control test for the final mixture, with an acceptance criterion of 45% ±10% (refer
to section  P.3.3.901). This ensure uniform humidity levels in the granulate for subsequent
processing steps.
Additionally, during the film-coating process, a minimum exhaust air temperature of >40°C is
maintained. This measure prevents any increase in the moisture content of the tablets. The
corresponding exhaust air temperature limit is defined and controlled within the TRD section
P.3.3.901 as part of the in-process controls.

Finally, the consistent quality of the finished drug product, which may be affected by humidity,
is assured through direct evaluation of key quality attributes, including, assay, impurities,
appearance, dissolution and  microbial purity. These quality parameters are relevant for release
and shelf-life testing.

4. Section 3.2.P.8.3: Please note that we have concerns on your proposed shelf life (of 36
months) for the product when packaged in PVC/aluminium blisters and ‘Stored at or below 30
°C’. The concern arises from the observed out of specification (OOS) results for dissolution
tests for drospirenone and estradiol for batches no. 01603A, 01604B & 01605A at T24. Your
OOS investigation attributed the OOS to the high relative humidity level (75% RH) that were
used at that stability investigation. Please take note of the unique climatic conditions of our
region: a greater part of the East African region has a ‘hot and humid climate’ (ICH Climatic
zone IVB). In addition, the patients are often unable to store the product in controlled conditions
of humidity. Please consider a combination of some or all the following, so as to address the
above concern:-
a) Change of the container closure system from PVC-blister foil to a more moisture
resistant container system, such as a high barrier blister foil (HBF) in a hermetic
pouch, or ALU-ALU blisters.
b) Inclusion of desiccants to offer additional protection against the high moisture levels
that are typical the Zone IVB climatic zone.
c) Revise of the storage statement in the SmPC and Secondary Pack to “Store at or below
30 °C, Protect from moisture”
d) Revision of the release specification and the shelf-life specifications for Zone IVB (30
°C/75% RH) to include a test and limit for water determination. The limit should be
justified, with data on the effects of hydration or water absorption on the drug product
(ICH Q6A).
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 4 ( CTD section):
Applicant acknowledges the agency’s question and would like to inform that, at the time of
initial submission, the correct documents were not submitted.

Based on the observations during the initial ICH study section P.8.3.01 (IQMS-178805_4.0),
the shelf life specification of Angeliq 1/2 was subsequently  re-evaluated (refer to section
P.5.1.02; IQMS-185390) and a new report for CZ IVb was compiled - P.8.3.01 (IQMS-
178806_5.0). This report provides a detailed assessment of the dissolution behavior (refer to
the dissolution-section in chapter 3.1 of IQMS-178806_5.0). The rationale for the updated
specification can be found in the document ‘Justification of Specification’ P.5.6.01 (IQMS-
178095).

Angeliq 1/2 is an established and globally marketed drug product with demonstrated  quality
throughout its shelf life. To ensure continued product quality, an on-going stability program is
implemented in accordance with international guidelines such as EU-GMP and ICH Q1A(R2).
The current on-going stability report for CZ IVb P.8.3.02 (IQMS-224104) contains data from
batches manufactured within the last seven years. All evaluated batches comply with the shelf
life specifications and support the approved shelf life of 36 months. Based on these data, the
current packaging (PVC/aluminum blisters) is considered adequate to maintain product quality,
and no changes to the packaging are deemed necessary.

In light of the above justification, we kindly request the heath authority to accept the proposed
approach.

Question:
Based on our review of the microbial challenge test data submitted for Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection, we note that while microbial growth inhibition is observed up to 6 hours after opening, the stasis criterion of ≤ 0.5 log10 change relative to initial values is consistently met across all test organisms and both batches with an adequate margin only up to 4 hours. In particular, at the 6-hour timepoint, Pseudomonas aeruginosa demonstrates increases at the upper limit of the stasis criterion, indicating borderline performance.
In view of the above, the proposed in-use microbiological protection claim of 6 hours is not sufficiently supported. The available data support a 4-hour in-use period for 20°C to 25°C.
Please revise the in-use claim accordingly and update the proposed product labels and package insert, to reflect a 4-hour in-use period after opening, where applicable.
Answer:
We acknowledge the evaluation regarding microbiological attributes. The recommended holding time after first opening in P.2.5.01 has been revised to 4 hours and the proposed product label mock-ups and Product Information for Australia and Singapore have been revised accordingly.
However, we would like to refer to study data supporting a specific in-use claim with regards to Gadoquatrane administration in conjunction with an automatic injector which has been approved for multi-patient use, see P.8.3.06 Stability Data - In-use Stability. Based on the study data, Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection can be considered safe from a microbiological, physical and chemical perspective for multi-patient use for up to 24 hours.
Furthermore, a study with added microbial stress has been finalized recently (microbial ingress challenge study). The MEDRAD® MRXperion Multi Patient Kit was intentionally and independently inoculated with Pseudomonas aeruginosa (ATCC 9027) and Escherichia coli (ATCC 8739). In conclusion, it was demonstrated that the automated multi-patient injection system, when used in accordance with its intended use and instructions for use, effectively prevents microbial ingress from gross contamination when administering gadoquatrane solution (0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection) and normal saline over a 24-hour use period across up to 24 patient procedures. An executive summary is provided, see“Summary Microbial Ingress Evaluation”, please note that the actual data is currently undergoing a formatting workflow. As such, the finalized data can be shared on request as soon as the formatting process is complete. Additionally, to reflect this information, the Product Information for Australia and Singapore has been updated.

Question:
The response indicates that the helium leak test was not validated and that no positive controls or method detection limits were established. While equipment calibration is described, this does not demonstrate method suitability at the container closure system level. Accordingly, the data are considered developmental only and are insufficient to confirm container closure integrity for the proposed product. Please note that validated analytical methods are expected in line with ICH Q2 and USP <1207>.

Please provide:
a. Validation data for the helium leak test, including precision, accuracy, and detection limits.
b. The positive control strategy employed and corresponding results.
c. A justification explaining how equipment calibration alone ensures method reliability at the container level.

If validation has not been performed, please commit to completing method validation or provide alternative container closure integrity data generated using a validated method.
Answer:
We acknowledge the request and would like to provide the subsequent explanations:
Holistic container closure integrity (CCI) concept:
A holistic CCI concept has been established to provide a robust data basis to demonstrate package integrity across all drug product–packaging combinations throughout the product lifecycle. This concept is consistent with the principles outlined in USP <1207> and EU-GMP Annex 1, which require a lifecycle-based approach integrating development, product manufacturing, and commercial product stability for the assurance of CCI and maintenance of critical quality attributes. The concept comprises complementary components addressing CCI at different lifecycle stages, thereby ensuring a scientifically justified and risk-based control strategy.
During the development phase, based on prior knowledge and established control strategies for the materials, a one-time verification of inherent package integrity is performed to confirm conformance to the defined maximum allowable leakage limit (MALL) of 6 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s (Kirsch et al., 1997; USP <1207>). This verification is conducted on empty container-closure systems using the highly sensitive and quantitative helium leak test method. A detailed method description is provided below.
During product manufacturing and commercial product stability, the holistic concept applies a risk-based approach in line with EU-GMP Annex 1 expectations. Dedicated risk assessments are performed to evaluate the potential impact of fill-and-finish operations, packaging processes, storage, and distribution on container closure integrity. Identified residual risks are mitigated, where feasible, through process optimization or addressed through appropriate CCI testing. For Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL, two mitigation actions were defined on GMP level:
• Regular packaging seal testing (for vials and bottles)
• Implementation of a product-specific CCI test method
As packaging seal testing, in alignment with USP <1207.3>, crimping quality is checked during the filling process. The test forms part of the parametric release strategy and is mentioned in P.5.6.01.
The product-specific CCI test methods are in implementation as validated test method for routine manufacturing. In combination with routine visual inspection, these tests are considered an appropriate measure for confirming CCI. Test method selection was based on compatibility with the specific drug product–packaging combination. A dye ingress test was selected for this purpose and is intended to monitor and confirm CCI during routine manufacturing. To generate a statistically meaningful data basis for CCI after development, 10 consecutive batches per drug product packaging combination will be tested according to AQL (Special inspection level S-4, critical defect classification, normal sampling). If no failures occur, sampling is reduced, upon continued compliance, to a skip-lot approach.
The dye ingress test method has been successfully validated for several vial presentations, see P.5.3.08. Validation activities demonstrated the suitability of the method for the intended use as a GMP control to CCI. During the validation activities, negative samples showed integrity, further supporting the presented data from P.2.4.02.
We commit to complete the validation of the dye ingress CCIT method for the remaining presentations included in a bracketing concept, representative for the entire contrast media portfolio at manufacturing site Bayer AG Berlin, specifically:
• 
Vial formats 10/10 mL, 30 mL
• 
Bottle 65/100 mL
• 
Prefilled syringes 5/10 mL, 7.5/10 mL, 10 mL, 15/20 mL.

Detailed method description helium leak test:
Helium leak testing is performed as a format-specific qualification activity for container–closure systems (CCS) used for parenteral drug products. The study is conducted in the absence of drug product.
The method is based on the quantitative determination of helium flow across the interface of the respective CCS. Depending on the container format, the container closure system includes vial or bottle closures (incl. rubber stopper and crimp cap) or, for prefilled syringes, the tip cap and plunger stopper interface. Helium leak testing is performed in open mode, whereby helium is introduced into the closure-side compartment of the format specific format part while vacuum is applied to the opposing container-side compartment of the format specific format part to drive helium flow across the container closure interface. For vials and bottles, sample preparation includes the introduction of a defined opening (approximately 6 mm) at the container bottom to enable helium flow through the CCS. For prefilled syringes, preparation involves removal of the tip cap or plunger stopper respectively.
The helium leak detection system is subject to routine maintenance and calibration. Annual maintenance is performed by the equipment supplier following proprietary procedures. During maintenance, the system is calibrated using certified standards covering a leak rate range of 1.81 × 10⁻⁸ to 4.76 × 10⁻⁵ mbar·L/s, traceable to external certification in accordance with DIN EN ISO 20486:2018.
Instrument conditioning and system suitability testing are performed on each day of measurement. Conditioning is achieved by directly coupling the helium source to the mass spectrometer to verify the absence of background helium signals originating from the test setup e.g. tubing and seals. System suitability is subsequently confirmed using an internal standard with a defined leak rate of 1.00 × 10⁻⁷ mbar·L/s and two certified external standards. One of the external standards represents a negative sample and the other external standard a positive sample, so that helium flow rates of either less than or greater than 6.00 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s are confirmed respectively. The applicant wants to emphasize, that with this system suitability testing, a certified negative and positive control was included in all measurements.
System performance and method reliability are additionally verified on format level using metallic master samples representing the respective container format. These samples serve as negative controls and are measured prior to a sample sequence. Acceptance is achieved if all values remain below 1.00 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s.
Following system suitability confirmation, prepared empty CCS samples are analysed. Signal detection is independent from the tested format. Format-specific format parts are used to fit the containers into the equipment. Tight fit is verified as system suitability test prior each measurement series, guaranteeing the absence of leaks between container and format parts.
CCS qualification includes, for vials and bottles, the evaluation of at least three sample populations, representing low, nominal, and high crimping forces to cover expected process variability during routine manufacturing. All samples are subjected to terminal sterilization prior to testing. For each condition, 30 units are tested in accordance with USP <382>. This approach is designed to challenge closure integrity under worst-case processing and thermal stress conditions, particularly regarding elastomeric components. Reported results from P.2.4.02 are representing the worst-case scenario.

Question:
Given that calcobutrol is added at a nominal concentration of 0.196 mg/mL in the drug product formulation and long-term stability data consistently show levels around ~0.12 mg/mL, please provide a data-driven justification for retaining the current upper specification limit of 0.235 mg/mL for release and shelf-life. In particular, clarify whether:
- 
Any batches (including development, validation, or worst-case drug substance scenarios) have demonstrated calcobutrol levels approaching the proposed upper limit, and
- 
A tighter upper limit could be established based on observed stability trends and manufacturing experience without compromising the intended complexing function.
Answer:
We acknowledge that the assessor requested a data-driven justification and based upon available data concluded that the upper specification limit of 0.235 mg/mL cannot be derived based on batch data only.
The theoretical concentration of calcobutrol based upon the batch formula is 0.196 mg/mL. As discussed in P.5.6.01, during the manufacturing process, a decrease in calcobutrol occurs. Therefore, typically calcobutrol concentration will be lower than 0.196 mg/mL at time of release and during shelf-life. To derive an upper limit for the calcobutrol release and shelf-life specification based upon available data, batch results from the clinical phase and from process validation (altogether 13 batches of Gadoquatrane solution in vial, bottle or prefilled syringe each filled from one of 13 distinct bulk solution batches, see Table 1) were considered. The data set was assessed for normality using the Anderson-Darling test (p = 0.386). No significant deviation from normality was observed (α = 0.05). The upper tolerance bound with 99% coverage at the 99% confidence level was calculated assuming normality. Calculations and statistical analysis were performed using Minitab® 21.4.1. The calculated upper tolerance bound of 0.185 mg/mL is proposed as upper specification limit for calcobutrol content. The specifications have been updated accordingly, see updated P.5.1.01, P.5.1.02, P.5.4.01 and P.5.6.01.
However, we would like to confirm that calcobutrol is safe and effective when occurring in the formulation within the originally proposed specification range and mention that ICH Q6A explicitly recognizes that “The basis for the acceptance criteria at the time of filing should necessarily focus on safety and efficacy” due to a “limited amount of data”.
