Question 2
Please provide the Certificate of Analysis (CoA) for the active pharmaceutical ingredient
from the raw material manufacturer (supplier).
Answer:
We would like to inform the agency that Bayer AG is the Marketing Authorization Holder and
the legal manufacturer for both the Drug Substance (DS) and the Drug Product (DP) of
Gadobutrol.
The DS is manufactured and tested at Bayer Bergkamen, while the DP is manufactured at
Bayer Berlin. Both sites operate under the same global Bayer Quality System and are part of
the same corporate entity.
As the DS is produced and fully tested at Bayer Bergkamen in accordance with the approved
specifications, GMP requirements, and validated analytical procedures, the Certificate of
Analysis (COA) issued by the DS site is considered fully sufficient and representative for
regulatory and quality control purposes.

Since Bayer Bergkamen and Bayer Berlin belong to the same company and the DS undergoes
complete release testing at the manufacturing site (Bergkamen), no additional or repeated DS
testing is performed at the DP site (Berlin). This approach is fully in line with ICH Q7 and
global GMP principles, which do not require duplicate analytical testing when the DS is
manufactured and released within the same integrated quality system.
Accordingly, the COA issued by Bayer Bergkamen is the valid and applicable DS release
documentation for the product.

Question: Provide justification for the storage conditions after opening at 2°C–8°C.
Answer:
Please note that the information included in the SmPC and in the leaflet:
“6.3        Shelf life
3 years.
Chemical and physical in-use stability has been demonstrated for 72 hours at room 
temperature. From a microbiological point of view, the product should be used immediately. If 
not used immediately, in-use storage times and conditions prior to use are the responsibility of 
the user and would normally not be longer than 24 hours at 2 to 8 °C, unless opening has taken 
place in controlled and validated aseptic conditions.”
Is justified by the corresponding in-use stability studies included in section P.8.1 “Stability 
Summary and Conclusion” as well as in section P.2.5 “Microbial Attributes”.

Please refer to 3.2.P.8.1.3 In-use stability (page 14) enclosed in the responses (also please see 
below the main information extracted for your reference). Note that revision 06 of the technical 
document [TRD - M3.2.P.8.1-06 (#010689023)] is included as data has been updated and 
additional information included.
“3.2.P.8.1.3 In-use stability
In-use testing was done according to the Note for Guidance CPMP/QWP/2934/99. Vials with 
a filling volume of 100 mL of batch PL1267 stored under controlled conditions were used for 
in-use stability testing over 72 hours. As 12 mL is the minimum dose recommended for single 
application (0.2 mL/kg body weight x 60 kg = 12 mL), 12 mL were taken from each vial with 
a sterile syringe at the time of opening and after 6, 12, 24, 30, 48 and 72 hours, respectively.
…
Conclusion
Gadoteric acid, 0.5 mM solution for injection is stable for 72 hours after first opening.”

Also kindly refer to 3.2.P.2.5 Microbial Attributes enclosed in the responses (also please see 
below the main information extracted for your reference)
“3.2.P.2.5 Microbial Attributes
(Gadoteric acid, 0.5 mM Solution for Injection)
…
Sterility of the drug product is confirmed by the results of the stability tests (refer to Module 
3.2.P.8.3). Although Gadoteric acid, 0.5 mM solution for injection is a drug product intended 
for single use, an in-use stability test was performed to prove the stability including 
sterility and bacterial endotoxins up to 72 hours after first opening. The results are provided 
in Module 3.2.P.8.1 and show no unfavourable results. Therefore an in-use stability of at 
least 24 hours after first opening can be claimed in the SPC (which is in line with the 
approved SPC of the reference medicinal drug product).”

In addition to the above mentioned justifications, the exact wording “24 hours at 2 to 8°C” is 
following CPMP/QWP/159/96 corr Note for Guidance on Maximum Shelf-Life for Sterile 
Products for Human Use After First Opening or Following Reconstitution.
Considering that Dotagraf is a sterile product that does not contain preservatives in its formula 
and it is intended for injection. 24h at the mentioned range of temperature at 2ºC to 8ºC  
(refrigeration conditions) will minimize the risk of microbial growth.

Please find the mentioned note for guidance enclosed in the responses and also see below the 
extract for your reference.
“…
UNPRESERVED STERILE PRODUCTS
…
Specific text for Preparations for Infusion or Injection
Chemical and physical in-use stability has been demonstrated for x hours/days at y oC.
From a microbiological point of view, the product should be used immediately. If not used 
immediately, in-use storage times and conditions prior to use are the responsibility of the user 
and would normally not be longer than 24 hours at 2 to 8 oC, unless reconstitution / dilution 
(etc) has taken place in controlled and validated aseptic conditions”

Question:
Question 1
Regarding the identified N-nitroso-meglumine, as of March 11, 2026, a revised Acceptable 
Intake (AI) limit for N-Nitroso-Meglumine is 100 ng/day has been published for this 
nitrosamine (Appendix 1 of Health Canada's Guidance on nitrosamine impurities in 
medications). You are reminded that the revision of the analytical procedure, and repeat 
confirmatory testing are expected (to meet this new limit) and if warranted, the update of the 
drug product specification by August 1 2028 is required as the change falls under the phase 3 
of the call for review. Please confirm and provide a commitment.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1
In response to the inquiry regarding N-Nitroso-Meglumine, Bayer Inc. (Bayer) acknowledges 
the revised Acceptable Intake (AI) limit of 100 ng/day as published on 11-Mar-2026.
As per Section 15 of the Guidance on nitrosamine impurities in medications effective 2025-
Aug-01, on 12-Mar-2026, Bayer shared with Health Canada the results of the confirmatory 
testing of the nitrosamine drug-substance related impurity N-Nitroso- Meglumine (referred to 
as NO-Meglumine) in the drug product Gadopentetate dimeglumine solution 0.5 mol/L for 
injection (MAGNEVIST), as well as the findings from an in-vivo mutagenicity mouse study 
of NO-Meglumine (see Module 1.0.4, MAGNEVIST Confirmatory Testing Results email 
dated 12-March-2026).
As subsequently requested by Health Canada on 26-March-2026, Bayer will be submitting the 
full transgenic rodent mutation assay study report at the end of May 2026 (see Module 1.0.3, 
Health Canada Email dated 26-March-2026).
Based on the outcome of Health Canada’s ongoing assessment, Bayer commits to revise the 
analytical procedure and update the drug product specification by 01-Aug-2028, as applicable.
For convenience, the information shared with Health Canada on 12-Mar-2026 is copied 
below.
1. Acceptable Intake Limit (AIL)
NO-meglumine is recognized by EMA and FDA as a Nitrosamine Drug Substance-Related 
Impurity (NDSRI) having a recommended Acceptable Intake limit of 100 ng/d based on the 
predicted Carcinogenic Potency Categorization Approach (CPCA) which is described as a 
conservative approach.
According to EMA “Appendix 1: Acceptable intakes (AI) established for N-nitrosamines” the 
limit was increased to 1500 ng/d for NO-meglumine based on the negative results of an 
Enhanced Ames Test in 2024. Bayer continued evaluation of NO-Meglumine by an in-vivo
mutagenicity study (MutaMouse study). The experimental results of this study became
available in January 2026.
Based on the statistically significant and dose-dependent increase of mutation frequency in
the liver of MutaMice N-Nitroso-meglumine was found to be genotoxic and potentially
carcinogenic in mice at the levels tested. Consequently, and in accordance with the EMA
Nitrosamine Q&A guidance (Question 10, updated in October 2025), the AI limit for NO-
Meglumine is established at 100 ng/day, derived using the Carcinogenic Potency
Categorization Approach (CPCA).
The EMA Q&A guidance allows for the adaption of the Acceptance Intake Limit (AIL)
according to the Less-than-Lifetime (LTL) approach (as outlined in ICH M7(R2)) for medicinal
products with a treatment duration of up to 12 months by a factor of 13.3. This factor can be
applied to the AI for an interim period of 3 years to enable CAPA implementation.
For contrast agents, administrations during lifetime are on an infrequent and occasional basis.
The LTL approach with a (daily) treatment duration of up to 12 months implies n=365
treatments during lifetime with a contrast agent as a conservative scenario. As this number is
extremely high given actual usage, the derived LTL AI of 1330 ng/day can be regarded as safe
for patients during lifetime.
Bayer submits that the LTL adjusted AI of 1330 ng/day represents a scientifically appropriate
and general safety limit for NO-Meglumine in contrast agents, rather than limiting its
application to an interim period of three years.

3. Toxicological evaluation
Administering the maximum daily dose of 30 ml for MAGNEVIST, the maximum amount of
150 ng/d NO-Meglumine would be applied to a patient in one treatment with MAGNEVIST.
This amount is well below the LTL AIL of 1330 ng/day for NO-Meglumine.
4. Clinical Benefit-Risk Assessment
Based on the review of the literature data, no publications suggesting mutagenic or carcinogenic
potential of MAGNEVIST were retrieved. As a general precautionary measure, healthcare
professionals should weigh diagnostic benefits against potential risks and employ the minimum
effective dose when contrast media are indicated.
5. Mitigation measures / Root cause evaluation
NO-Meglumine can be formed during the bulk manufacturing and/or sterilization process
and/or storage.
The following activities are planned to evaluate the formation of NO-meglumine in
Gadopentetate dimeglumine solution 0.5 mol/L for injection (MAGNEVIST):
• The nitrite level in relevant excipients will be determined to identify the main sources
for nitrite. Following that, possibilities to reduce the introduction of nitrite will be
evaluated.
• Further MAGNEVIST batches will be tested to evaluate a potential increase of NO-
Meglumine during shelf life.
6. Conclusion
Based on the currently available data, Bayer believes it is justified to establish an LTL
acceptable limit at 1330 ng/day as a general safety limit for NO-Meglumine in Gadopentetate
dimeglumine solution 0.5 mol/L for injection (MAGNEVIST) in compliance with EMA
precautionary guideline, rather than limiting its application to an interim period of three years.
All available data indicate that tested MAGNEVIST batches comply with the updated limits

Question:
Question 2
(3.2.P.2.4) The information that you have provided to support the absence of leachables, in your 
proposed drug product, is not considered adequate.  You have provided a brief discussion 
regarding a simulated leachables study, however, you have not provided a justification for the 
simulated study as required by USP <1664> Assessment of Drug Product Leachables 
Associated with Pharmaceutical Packaging/Delivery Systems.  The following is therefore 
requested:
a) Confirm that the simulated leachables study was conducted using actual drug product
manufactured as per current manufacturing process.  Batch number(s) should be 
provided and should be consistent with the batch number(s) used in the extractables 
study.
b) Provide the results of a leachables study over the proposed storage conditions and
proposed shelf-life using the actual drug product solution, manufactured as per current 
process, placed on inverted orientation.
c) In the absence of real-time leachable study data, provide a scientific justification as to
why a simulated leachables study was conducted instead of a real-time assessment over 
the proposed storage conditions and shelf-life of the product.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2
a) Bayer confirms that the simulated leachables study was conducted using MAGNEVIST,
gadopentetate dimeglumine solution 0.5 mol/L for parenteral use, batch number KT0J7VP
manufactured according to the current manufacturing process.
The sample was collected at the end of filling line into a separate glass container to avoid
contact with the new bromobutyl rubber stopper material.
The stoppers used in the extractables and simulated leachables studies had all the same
pre-treatments as used in the current MAGNEVIST, gadopentetate dimeglumine solution
0.5 mol/L for parenteral use filling process.
Stoppers from the same lots were used in both the extractables and simulated leachables
studies.

b) Real-time leachable shelf-life data is currently not available, please refer to the response
provided under Question 2c that discusses the justification for using a simulated leachables
study.

c) With the introduction of the bromobutyl stopper, extractables data was prepared in
exaggerated conditions of 50°C / 72 h and 85°C / 1 h (see Module 3.2.P.2.4.06_IQMS-
254392_1.0 Extraction Studies). The stability study for gadopentetate dimeglumine solution
0.5 mol/L in vials using the alternative bromobutyl closure system, had not yet been
initiated. Therefore, a simulated leachables study using gadopentetate dimeglumine solution
0.5 mol/L as extractant, in exaggerated conditions of 50 °C / 72 h and 85 °C / 1 h was
conducted to confirm the safety of the new stopper material.
In the simulated leachables study no simulated leachables exceeding the study analytical
evaluation threshold (AETs) was observed.
For the new bromobutyl stoppers an extensive extractables study was initially performed
using several different extraction media, at elevated temperatures as stated above, with
relatively long extraction time. These conditions were chosen to reflect recommendations
in USP <1663> monograph, and ISO 10993-18 and 10993-12. For the AETs, when feasible,
higher Uncertainty Factors (UF) of 4 and 10, than the usual UF 2 were used to confirm that
all extractables are measured. The analyses were performed using state-of-art mass
spectroscopic instruments.
Extractions with 2-propanol as extractant, 50% EtOH/water were performed, and also with
water. In pH 4 and pH 9.5 buffer solutions only a few extractables in low amounts were
detected. These were mainly fatty acids like palmitoleic, palmitic and oleic acids that are
relatively non-toxic and common in elastomers and plastics. In addition to the extractables
study, Bayer decided to conduct a simulated leachables study.
In the simulated leachables study, using similar exaggerated extraction conditions to the
extractables study, no reportable compounds were found. It was therefore considered
adequate proof of stopper material suitability and safety for its intended use as container
closure system and therefore no formal leachables stability study was planned.
A real-time stability study is on-going and a leachables study after 36 months testing and
also at the end of 60 months shelf-life will be performed as per the USP <1664> Assessment
of Drug Product Leachables Associated with Pharmaceutical Packaging/Delivery Systems,
to further confirm the safety of the material.

Based on our review of the microbial challenge test data submitted for Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection, we note that while microbial growth inhibition is observed up to 6 hours after opening, the stasis criterion of ≤ 0.5 log10 change relative to initial values is consistently met across all test organisms and both batches with an adequate margin only up to 4 hours. In particular, at the 6-hour timepoint, Pseudomonas aeruginosa demonstrates increases at the upper limit of the stasis criterion, indicating borderline performance.
In view of the above, the proposed in-use microbiological protection claim of 6 hours is not sufficiently supported. The available data support a 4-hour in-use period for 20°C to 25°C.
Please revise the in-use claim accordingly and update the proposed product labels and package insert, to reflect a 4-hour in-use period after opening, where applicable.

Based on the study data, Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection can be considered safe from a microbiological, physical and chemical perspective for multi-patient use for up to 24 hours.

The MEDRAD® MRXperion Multi Patient Kit was intentionally and independently inoculated with Pseudomonas aeruginosa (ATCC 9027) and Escherichia coli (ATCC 8739). In conclusion, it was demonstrated that the automated multi-patient injection system, when used in accordance with its intended use and instructions for use, effectively prevents microbial ingress from gross contamination when administering gadoquatrane solution (0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection) and normal saline over a 24-hour use period across up to 24 patient procedures. An executive summary is provided, see“Summary Microbial Ingress Evaluation”, please note that the actual data is currently undergoing a formatting workflow. Additionally, to reflect this information, the Product Information for Australia and Singapore has been updated.

Question:
The response indicates that the helium leak test was not validated and that no positive controls or method detection limits were established. While equipment calibration is described, this does not demonstrate method suitability at the container closure system level. Accordingly, the data are considered developmental only and are insufficient to confirm container closure integrity for the proposed product. Please note that validated analytical methods are expected in line with ICH Q2 and USP <1207>.

Please provide:
a. Validation data for the helium leak test, including precision, accuracy, and detection limits.
b. The positive control strategy employed and corresponding results.

c. A justification explaining how equipment calibration alone ensures method reliability at the container level.

If validation has not been performed, please commit to completing method validation or provide alternative container closure integrity data generated using a validated method.
Answer:
We acknowledge the request and would like to provide the subsequent explanations:
Holistic container closure integrity (CCI) concept:
A holistic CCI concept has been established to provide a robust data basis to demonstrate package integrity across all drug product–packaging combinations throughout the product lifecycle. This concept is consistent with the principles outlined in USP <1207> and EU-GMP Annex 1, which require a lifecycle-based approach integrating development, product manufacturing, and commercial product stability for the assurance of CCI and maintenance of critical quality attributes. The concept comprises complementary components addressing CCI at different lifecycle stages, thereby ensuring a scientifically justified and risk-based control strategy.
During the development phase, based on prior knowledge and established control strategies for the materials, a one-time verification of inherent package integrity is performed to confirm conformance to the defined maximum allowable leakage limit (MALL) of 6 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s (Kirsch et al., 1997; USP <1207>). This verification is conducted on empty container-closure systems using the highly sensitive and quantitative helium leak test method. A detailed method description is provided below.
During product manufacturing and commercial product stability, the holistic concept applies a risk-based approach in line with EU-GMP Annex 1 expectations. Dedicated risk assessments are performed to evaluate the potential impact of fill-and-finish operations, packaging processes, storage, and distribution on container closure integrity. Identified residual risks are mitigated, where feasible, through process optimization or addressed through appropriate CCI testing. For Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL, two mitigation actions were defined on GMP level:
• Regular packaging seal testing (for vials and bottles)
• Implementation of a product-specific CCI test method
As packaging seal testing, in alignment with USP <1207.3>, crimping quality is checked during the filling process. The test forms part of the parametric release strategy and is mentioned in P.5.6.01.
The product-specific CCI test methods are in implementation as validated test method for routine manufacturing. In combination with routine visual inspection, these tests are considered an appropriate measure for confirming CCI. Test method selection was based on compatibility with the specific drug product–packaging combination. A dye ingress test was selected for this purpose and is intended to monitor and confirm CCI during routine manufacturing. To generate a statistically meaningful data basis for CCI after development, 10 consecutive batches per drug product packaging combination will be tested according to AQL (Special inspection level S-4, critical defect classification, normal sampling). If no failures occur, sampling is reduced, upon continued compliance, to a skip-lot approach.
The dye ingress test method has been successfully validated for several vial presentations, see P.5.3.08. Validation activities demonstrated the suitability of the method for the intended use as a GMP control to CCI. During the validation activities, negative samples showed integrity, further supporting the presented data from P.2.4.02.
We commit to complete the validation of the dye ingress CCIT method for the remaining presentations included in a bracketing concept, representative for the entire contrast media portfolio at manufacturing site Bayer AG Berlin, specifically:
• Vial formats 10/10 mL, 30 mL
• Bottle 65/100 mL
• Prefilled syringes 5/10 mL, 7.5/10 mL, 10 mL, 15/20 mL.

Detailed method description helium leak test:
Helium leak testing is performed as a format-specific qualification activity for container–closure systems (CCS) used for parenteral drug products. The study is conducted in the absence of drug product.
The method is based on the quantitative determination of helium flow across the interface of the respective CCS. Depending on the container format, the container closure system includes vial or bottle closures (incl. rubber stopper and crimp cap) or, for prefilled syringes, the tip cap and plunger stopper interface. Helium leak testing is performed in open mode, whereby helium is introduced into the closure-side compartment of the format specific format part while vacuum is applied to the opposing container-side compartment of the format specific format part to drive helium flow across the container closure interface. For vials and bottles, sample preparation includes the introduction of a defined opening (approximately 6 mm) at the container bottom to enable helium flow through the CCS. For prefilled syringes, preparation involves removal of the tip cap or plunger stopper respectively.
The helium leak detection system is subject to routine maintenance and calibration. Annual maintenance is performed by the equipment supplier following proprietary procedures. During maintenance, the system is calibrated using certified standards covering a leak rate range of 1.81 × 10⁻⁸ to 4.76 × 10⁻⁵ mbar·L/s, traceable to external certification in accordance with DIN EN ISO 20486:2018.
Instrument conditioning and system suitability testing are performed on each day of measurement. Conditioning is achieved by directly coupling the helium source to the mass spectrometer to verify the absence of background helium signals originating from the test setup e.g. tubing and seals. System suitability is subsequently confirmed using an internal standard with a defined leak rate of 1.00 × 10⁻⁷ mbar·L/s and two certified external standards. One of the external standards represents a negative sample and the other external standard a positive sample, so that helium flow rates of either less than or greater than 6.00 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s are confirmed respectively. The applicant wants to emphasize, that with this system suitability testing, a certified negative and positive control was included in all measurements.
System performance and method reliability are additionally verified on format level using metallic master samples representing the respective container format. These samples serve as negative controls and are measured prior to a sample sequence. Acceptance is achieved if all values remain below 1.00 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s.
Following system suitability confirmation, prepared empty CCS samples are analysed. Signal detection is independent from the tested format. Format-specific format parts are used to fit the containers into the equipment. Tight fit is verified as system suitability test prior each measurement series, guaranteeing the absence of leaks between container and format parts.
CCS qualification includes, for vials and bottles, the evaluation of at least three sample populations, representing low, nominal, and high crimping forces to cover expected process variability during routine manufacturing. All samples are subjected to terminal sterilization prior to testing. For each condition, 30 units are tested in accordance with USP <382>. This approach is designed to challenge closure integrity under worst-case processing and thermal stress conditions, particularly regarding elastomeric components. Reported results from P.2.4.02 are representing the worst-case scenario.

Question:
Given that calcobutrol is added at a nominal concentration of 0.196 mg/mL in the drug product formulation and long-term stability data consistently show levels around ~0.12 mg/mL, please provide a data-driven justification for retaining the current upper specification limit of 0.235 mg/mL for release and shelf-life. In particular, clarify whether:
- 
Any batches (including development, validation, or worst-case drug substance scenarios) have demonstrated calcobutrol levels approaching the proposed upper limit, and
- 
A tighter upper limit could be established based on observed stability trends and manufacturing experience without compromising the intended complexing function.
Answer:
We acknowledge that the assessor requested a data-driven justification and based upon available data concluded that the upper specification limit of 0.235 mg/mL cannot be derived based on batch data only.
The theoretical concentration of calcobutrol based upon the batch formula is 0.196 mg/mL. As discussed in P.5.6.01, during the manufacturing process, a decrease in calcobutrol occurs. Therefore, typically calcobutrol concentration will be lower than 0.196 mg/mL at time of release and during shelf-life. To derive an upper limit for the calcobutrol release and shelf-life specification based upon available data, batch results from the clinical phase and from process validation (altogether 13 batches of Gadoquatrane solution in vial, bottle or prefilled syringe each filled from one of 13 distinct bulk solution batches, see Table 1) were considered. The data set was assessed for normality using the Anderson-Darling test (p = 0.386). No significant deviation from normality was observed (α = 0.05). The upper tolerance bound with 99% coverage at the 99% confidence level was calculated assuming normality. Calculations and statistical analysis were performed using Minitab® 21.4.1. The calculated upper tolerance bound of 0.185 mg/mL is proposed as upper specification limit for calcobutrol content. The specifications have been updated accordingly, see updated P.5.1.01, P.5.1.02, P.5.4.01 and P.5.6.01.
However, we would like to confirm that calcobutrol is safe and effective when occurring in the formulation within the originally proposed specification range and mention that ICH Q6A explicitly recognizes that “The basis for the acceptance criteria at the time of filing should necessarily focus on safety and efficacy” due to a “limited amount of data”.

Question:
The response indicates that the helium leak test was not validated and that no positive controls or method detection limits were established. While equipment calibration is described, this does not demonstrate method suitability at the container closure system level. Accordingly, the data are considered developmental only and are insufficient to confirm container closure integrity for the proposed product. Please note that validated analytical methods are expected in line with ICH Q2 and USP <1207>.

Please provide:
a. Validation data for the helium leak test, including precision, accuracy, and detection limits.
b. The positive control strategy employed and corresponding results.

c. A justification explaining how equipment calibration alone ensures method reliability at the container level.

If validation has not been performed, please commit to completing method validation or provide alternative container closure integrity data generated using a validated method.
Answer:
We acknowledge the request and would like to provide the subsequent explanations:
Holistic container closure integrity (CCI) concept:
A holistic CCI concept has been established to provide a robust data basis to demonstrate package integrity across all drug product–packaging combinations throughout the product lifecycle. This concept is consistent with the principles outlined in USP <1207> and EU-GMP Annex 1, which require a lifecycle-based approach integrating development, product manufacturing, and commercial product stability for the assurance of CCI and maintenance of critical quality attributes. The concept comprises complementary components addressing CCI at different lifecycle stages, thereby ensuring a scientifically justified and risk-based control strategy.
During the development phase, based on prior knowledge and established control strategies for the materials, a one-time verification of inherent package integrity is performed to confirm conformance to the defined maximum allowable leakage limit (MALL) of 6 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s (Kirsch et al., 1997; USP <1207>). This verification is conducted on empty container-closure systems using the highly sensitive and quantitative helium leak test method. A detailed method description is provided below.
During product manufacturing and commercial product stability, the holistic concept applies a risk-based approach in line with EU-GMP Annex 1 expectations. Dedicated risk assessments are performed to evaluate the potential impact of fill-and-finish operations, packaging processes, storage, and distribution on container closure integrity. Identified residual risks are mitigated, where feasible, through process optimization or addressed through appropriate CCI testing. For Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL, two mitigation actions were defined on GMP level:
• Regular packaging seal testing (for vials and bottles)
• Implementation of a product-specific CCI test method
As packaging seal testing, in alignment with USP <1207.3>, crimping quality is checked during the filling process. The test forms part of the parametric release strategy and is mentioned in P.5.6.01.
The product-specific CCI test methods are in implementation as validated test method for routine manufacturing. In combination with routine visual inspection, these tests are considered an appropriate measure for confirming CCI. Test method selection was based on compatibility with the specific drug product–packaging combination. A dye ingress test was selected for this purpose and is intended to monitor and confirm CCI during routine manufacturing. To generate a statistically meaningful data basis for CCI after development, 10 consecutive batches per drug product packaging combination will be tested according to AQL (Special inspection level S-4, critical defect classification, normal sampling). If no failures occur, sampling is reduced, upon continued compliance, to a skip-lot approach.
The dye ingress test method has been successfully validated for several vial presentations, see P.5.3.08. Validation activities demonstrated the suitability of the method for the intended use as a GMP control to CCI. During the validation activities, negative samples showed integrity, further supporting the presented data from P.2.4.02.
We commit to complete the validation of the dye ingress CCIT method for the remaining presentations included in a bracketing concept, representative for the entire contrast media portfolio at manufacturing site Bayer AG Berlin, specifically:
• Vial formats 10/10 mL, 30 mL
• Bottle 65/100 mL
• Prefilled syringes 5/10 mL, 7.5/10 mL, 10 mL, 15/20 mL.

Detailed method description helium leak test:
Helium leak testing is performed as a format-specific qualification activity for container–closure systems (CCS) used for parenteral drug products. The study is conducted in the absence of drug product.
The method is based on the quantitative determination of helium flow across the interface of the respective CCS. Depending on the container format, the container closure system includes vial or bottle closures (incl. rubber stopper and crimp cap) or, for prefilled syringes, the tip cap and plunger stopper interface. Helium leak testing is performed in open mode, whereby helium is introduced into the closure-side compartment of the format specific format part while vacuum is applied to the opposing container-side compartment of the format specific format part to drive helium flow across the container closure interface. For vials and bottles, sample preparation includes the introduction of a defined opening (approximately 6 mm) at the container bottom to enable helium flow through the CCS. For prefilled syringes, preparation involves removal of the tip cap or plunger stopper respectively.
The helium leak detection system is subject to routine maintenance and calibration. Annual maintenance is performed by the equipment supplier following proprietary procedures. During maintenance, the system is calibrated using certified standards covering a leak rate range of 1.81 × 10⁻⁸ to 4.76 × 10⁻⁵ mbar·L/s, traceable to external certification in accordance with DIN EN ISO 20486:2018.
Instrument conditioning and system suitability testing are performed on each day of measurement. Conditioning is achieved by directly coupling the helium source to the mass spectrometer to verify the absence of background helium signals originating from the test setup e.g. tubing and seals. System suitability is subsequently confirmed using an internal standard with a defined leak rate of 1.00 × 10⁻⁷ mbar·L/s and two certified external standards. One of the external standards represents a negative sample and the other external standard a positive sample, so that helium flow rates of either less than or greater than 6.00 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s are confirmed respectively. The applicant wants to emphasize, that with this system suitability testing, a certified negative and positive control was included in all measurements.
System performance and method reliability are additionally verified on format level using metallic master samples representing the respective container format. These samples serve as negative controls and are measured prior to a sample sequence. Acceptance is achieved if all values remain below 1.00 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s.
Following system suitability confirmation, prepared empty CCS samples are analysed. Signal detection is independent from the tested format. Format-specific format parts are used to fit the containers into the equipment. Tight fit is verified as system suitability test prior each measurement series, guaranteeing the absence of leaks between container and format parts.
CCS qualification includes, for vials and bottles, the evaluation of at least three sample populations, representing low, nominal, and high crimping forces to cover expected process variability during routine manufacturing. All samples are subjected to terminal sterilization prior to testing. For each condition, 30 units are tested in accordance with USP <382>. This approach is designed to challenge closure integrity under worst-case processing and thermal stress conditions, particularly regarding elastomeric components. Reported results from P.2.4.02 are representing the worst-case scenario.

Question:
Given that calcobutrol is added at a nominal concentration of 0.196 mg/mL in the drug product formulation and long-term stability data consistently show levels around ~0.12 mg/mL, please provide a data-driven justification for retaining the current upper specification limit of 0.235 mg/mL for release and shelf-life. In particular, clarify whether:
- 
Any batches (including development, validation, or worst-case drug substance scenarios) have demonstrated calcobutrol levels approaching the proposed upper limit, and
- 
A tighter upper limit could be established based on observed stability trends and manufacturing experience without compromising the intended complexing function.
Answer:
We acknowledge that the assessor requested a data-driven justification and based upon available data concluded that the upper specification limit of 0.235 mg/mL cannot be derived based on batch data only.
The theoretical concentration of calcobutrol based upon the batch formula is 0.196 mg/mL. As discussed in P.5.6.01, during the manufacturing process, a decrease in calcobutrol occurs. Therefore, typically calcobutrol concentration will be lower than 0.196 mg/mL at time of release and during shelf-life. To derive an upper limit for the calcobutrol release and shelf-life specification based upon available data, batch results from the clinical phase and from process validation (altogether 13 batches of Gadoquatrane solution in vial, bottle or prefilled syringe each filled from one of 13 distinct bulk solution batches, see Table 1) were considered. The data set was assessed for normality using the Anderson-Darling test (p = 0.386). No significant deviation from normality was observed (α = 0.05). The upper tolerance bound with 99% coverage at the 99% confidence level was calculated assuming normality. Calculations and statistical analysis were performed using Minitab® 21.4.1. The calculated upper tolerance bound of 0.185 mg/mL is proposed as upper specification limit for calcobutrol content. The specifications have been updated accordingly, see updated P.5.1.01, P.5.1.02, P.5.4.01 and P.5.6.01.
However, we would like to confirm that calcobutrol is safe and effective when occurring in the formulation within the originally proposed specification range and mention that ICH Q6A explicitly recognizes that “The basis for the acceptance criteria at the time of filing should necessarily focus on safety and efficacy” due to a “limited amount of data”.

Question:
Based on our review of the microbial challenge test data submitted for Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection, we note that while microbial growth inhibition is observed up to 6 hours after opening, the stasis criterion of ≤ 0.5 log10 change relative to initial values is consistently met across all test organisms and both batches with an adequate margin only up to 4 hours. In particular, at the 6-hour timepoint, Pseudomonas aeruginosa demonstrates increases at the upper limit of the stasis criterion, indicating borderline performance.
In view of the above, the proposed in-use microbiological protection claim of 6 hours is not sufficiently supported. The available data support a 4-hour in-use period for 20°C to 25°C.
Please revise the in-use claim accordingly and update the proposed product labels and package insert, to reflect a 4-hour in-use period after opening, where applicable.
Answer:
We acknowledge the evaluation regarding microbiological attributes. The recommended holding time after first opening in P.2.5.01 has been revised to 4 hours and the proposed product label mock-ups and Product Information for Australia and Singapore have been revised accordingly.
However, we would like to refer to study data supporting a specific in-use claim with regards to Gadoquatrane administration in conjunction with an automatic injector which has been approved for multi-patient use, see P.8.3.06 Stability Data - In-use Stability. Based on the study data, Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection can be considered safe from a microbiological, physical and chemical perspective for multi-patient use for up to 24 hours.
Furthermore, a study with added microbial stress has been finalized recently (microbial ingress challenge study). The MEDRAD® MRXperion Multi Patient Kit was intentionally and independently inoculated with Pseudomonas aeruginosa (ATCC 9027) and Escherichia coli (ATCC 8739). In conclusion, it was demonstrated that the automated multi-patient injection system, when used in accordance with its intended use and instructions for use, effectively prevents microbial ingress from gross contamination when administering gadoquatrane solution (0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection) and normal saline over a 24-hour use period across up to 24 patient procedures. An executive summary is provided, see“Summary Microbial Ingress Evaluation”, please note that the actual data is currently undergoing a formatting workflow. As such, the finalized data can be shared on request as soon as the formatting process is complete. Additionally, to reflect this information, the Product Information for Australia and Singapore has been updated.

Question:
The response indicates that the helium leak test was not validated and that no positive controls or method detection limits were established. While equipment calibration is described, this does not demonstrate method suitability at the container closure system level. Accordingly, the data are considered developmental only and are insufficient to confirm container closure integrity for the proposed product. Please note that validated analytical methods are expected in line with ICH Q2 and USP <1207>.

Please provide:
a. Validation data for the helium leak test, including precision, accuracy, and detection limits.
b. The positive control strategy employed and corresponding results.
c. A justification explaining how equipment calibration alone ensures method reliability at the container level.

If validation has not been performed, please commit to completing method validation or provide alternative container closure integrity data generated using a validated method.
Answer:
We acknowledge the request and would like to provide the subsequent explanations:
Holistic container closure integrity (CCI) concept:
A holistic CCI concept has been established to provide a robust data basis to demonstrate package integrity across all drug product–packaging combinations throughout the product lifecycle. This concept is consistent with the principles outlined in USP <1207> and EU-GMP Annex 1, which require a lifecycle-based approach integrating development, product manufacturing, and commercial product stability for the assurance of CCI and maintenance of critical quality attributes. The concept comprises complementary components addressing CCI at different lifecycle stages, thereby ensuring a scientifically justified and risk-based control strategy.
During the development phase, based on prior knowledge and established control strategies for the materials, a one-time verification of inherent package integrity is performed to confirm conformance to the defined maximum allowable leakage limit (MALL) of 6 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s (Kirsch et al., 1997; USP <1207>). This verification is conducted on empty container-closure systems using the highly sensitive and quantitative helium leak test method. A detailed method description is provided below.
During product manufacturing and commercial product stability, the holistic concept applies a risk-based approach in line with EU-GMP Annex 1 expectations. Dedicated risk assessments are performed to evaluate the potential impact of fill-and-finish operations, packaging processes, storage, and distribution on container closure integrity. Identified residual risks are mitigated, where feasible, through process optimization or addressed through appropriate CCI testing. For Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL, two mitigation actions were defined on GMP level:
• Regular packaging seal testing (for vials and bottles)
• Implementation of a product-specific CCI test method
As packaging seal testing, in alignment with USP <1207.3>, crimping quality is checked during the filling process. The test forms part of the parametric release strategy and is mentioned in P.5.6.01.
The product-specific CCI test methods are in implementation as validated test method for routine manufacturing. In combination with routine visual inspection, these tests are considered an appropriate measure for confirming CCI. Test method selection was based on compatibility with the specific drug product–packaging combination. A dye ingress test was selected for this purpose and is intended to monitor and confirm CCI during routine manufacturing. To generate a statistically meaningful data basis for CCI after development, 10 consecutive batches per drug product packaging combination will be tested according to AQL (Special inspection level S-4, critical defect classification, normal sampling). If no failures occur, sampling is reduced, upon continued compliance, to a skip-lot approach.
The dye ingress test method has been successfully validated for several vial presentations, see P.5.3.08. Validation activities demonstrated the suitability of the method for the intended use as a GMP control to CCI. During the validation activities, negative samples showed integrity, further supporting the presented data from P.2.4.02.
We commit to complete the validation of the dye ingress CCIT method for the remaining presentations included in a bracketing concept, representative for the entire contrast media portfolio at manufacturing site Bayer AG Berlin, specifically:
• Vial formats 10/10 mL, 30 mL
• Bottle 65/100 mL
• Prefilled syringes 5/10 mL, 7.5/10 mL, 10 mL, 15/20 mL.

Detailed method description helium leak test:
Helium leak testing is performed as a format-specific qualification activity for container–closure systems (CCS) used for parenteral drug products. The study is conducted in the absence of drug product.
The method is based on the quantitative determination of helium flow across the interface of the respective CCS. Depending on the container format, the container closure system includes vial or bottle closures (incl. rubber stopper and crimp cap) or, for prefilled syringes, the tip cap and plunger stopper interface. Helium leak testing is performed in open mode, whereby helium is introduced into the closure-side compartment of the format specific format part while vacuum is applied to the opposing container-side compartment of the format specific format part to drive helium flow across the container closure interface. For vials and bottles, sample preparation includes the introduction of a defined opening (approximately 6 mm) at the container bottom to enable helium flow through the CCS. For prefilled syringes, preparation involves removal of the tip cap or plunger stopper respectively.
The helium leak detection system is subject to routine maintenance and calibration. Annual maintenance is performed by the equipment supplier following proprietary procedures. During maintenance, the system is calibrated using certified standards covering a leak rate range of 1.81 × 10⁻⁸ to 4.76 × 10⁻⁵ mbar·L/s, traceable to external certification in accordance with DIN EN ISO 20486:2018.
Instrument conditioning and system suitability testing are performed on each day of measurement. Conditioning is achieved by directly coupling the helium source to the mass spectrometer to verify the absence of background helium signals originating from the test setup e.g. tubing and seals. System suitability is subsequently confirmed using an internal standard with a defined leak rate of 1.00 × 10⁻⁷ mbar·L/s and two certified external standards. One of the external standards represents a negative sample and the other external standard a positive sample, so that helium flow rates of either less than or greater than 6.00 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s are confirmed respectively. The applicant wants to emphasize, that with this system suitability testing, a certified negative and positive control was included in all measurements.
System performance and method reliability are additionally verified on format level using metallic master samples representing the respective container format. These samples serve as negative controls and are measured prior to a sample sequence. Acceptance is achieved if all values remain below 1.00 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s.
Following system suitability confirmation, prepared empty CCS samples are analysed. Signal detection is independent from the tested format. Format-specific format parts are used to fit the containers into the equipment. Tight fit is verified as system suitability test prior each measurement series, guaranteeing the absence of leaks between container and format parts.
CCS qualification includes, for vials and bottles, the evaluation of at least three sample populations, representing low, nominal, and high crimping forces to cover expected process variability during routine manufacturing. All samples are subjected to terminal sterilization prior to testing. For each condition, 30 units are tested in accordance with USP <382>. This approach is designed to challenge closure integrity under worst-case processing and thermal stress conditions, particularly regarding elastomeric components. Reported results from P.2.4.02 are representing the worst-case scenario.

Question:
The response indicates that the helium leak test was not validated and that no positive controls 
or method detection limits were established. While equipment calibration is described, this 
does not demonstrate method suitability at the container closure system level. Accordingly, 
the data are considered developmental only and are insufficient to confirm container closure 
integrity for the proposed product. Please note that validated analytical methods are expected 
in line with ICH Q2 and USP <1207>.
Please provide:
a. Validation data for the helium leak test, including precision, accuracy, and
detection limits.
b. The positive control strategy employed and corresponding results.
c. A justification explaining how equipment calibration alone ensures method
reliability at the container level.

If validation has not been performed, please commit to completing method validation or 
provide alternative container closure integrity data generated using a validated method.
Answer:
We acknowledge the request and would like to provide the subsequent explanations:
Holistic container closure integrity (CCI) concept:
A holistic CCI concept has been established to provide a robust data basis to demonstrate 
package integrity across all drug product–packaging combinations throughout the product 
lifecycle. This concept is consistent with the principles outlined in USP <1207> and EU-GMP 
Annex 1, which require a lifecycle-based approach integrating development, product 
manufacturing, and commercial product stability for the assurance of CCI and maintenance of 
critical quality attributes. The concept comprises complementary components addressing CCI 
at different lifecycle stages, thereby ensuring a scientifically justified and risk-based control 
strategy.
During the development phase, based on prior knowledge and established control strategies for 
the materials, a one-time verification of inherent package integrity is performed to confirm 
conformance to the defined maximum allowable leakage limit (MALL) of 6 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s 
(Kirsch et al., 1997; USP <1207>). This verification is conducted on empty container-closure 
systems using the highly sensitive and quantitative helium leak test method. A detailed method 
description is provided below.
During product manufacturing and commercial product stability, the holistic concept applies a 
risk-based approach in line with EU-GMP Annex 1 expectations. Dedicated risk assessments 
are performed to evaluate the potential impact of fill-and-finish operations, packaging 
processes, storage, and distribution on container closure integrity. Identified residual risks are 
mitigated, where feasible, through process optimization or addressed through appropriate CCI 
testing. For Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL, two mitigation actions were defined on 
GMP level:
• Regular packaging seal testing (for vials and bottles)
• Implementation of a product-specific CCI test method
As packaging seal testing, in alignment with USP <1207.3>, crimping quality is checked during 
the filling process. The test forms part of the parametric release strategy and is mentioned in 
3.2.P.5.6.01.
The product-specific CCI test methods are in implementation as validated test method for 
routine manufacturing. In combination with routine visual inspection, these tests are considered
an appropriate measure for confirming CCI. Test method selection was based on compatibility 
with the specific drug product–packaging combination. A dye ingress test was selected for this 
purpose and is intended to monitor and confirm CCI during routine manufacturing. To generate 
a statistically meaningful data basis for CCI after development, 10 consecutive batches per drug 
product packaging combination will be tested according to AQL (Special inspection level S-4, 
critical defect classification, normal sampling). If no failures occur, sampling is reduced, upon 
continued compliance, to a skip-lot approach.
The dye ingress test method has been successfully validated for several vial presentations, see 
3.2.P.5.3.08. Validation activities demonstrated the suitability of the method for the intended 
use as a GMP control to CCI. During the validation activities, negative samples showed 
integrity, further supporting the presented data from 3.2.P.2.4.02.
We commit to complete the validation of the dye ingress CCIT method for the remaining 
presentations included in a bracketing concept, representative for the entire contrast media 
portfolio at manufacturing site Bayer AG Berlin, specifically:
• 
Vial formats 10/10 mL, 30 mL
• 
Bottle 65/100 mL
• 
Prefilled syringes 5/10 mL, 7.5/10 mL, 10 mL, 15/20 mL.

Detailed method description helium leak test:
Helium leak testing is performed as a format-specific qualification activity for container–
closure systems (CCS) used for parenteral drug products. The study is conducted in the absence 
of drug product.
The method is based on the quantitative determination of helium flow across the interface of 
the respective CCS. Depending on the container format, the container closure system includes 
vial or bottle closures (incl. rubber stopper and crimp cap) or, for prefilled syringes, the tip cap 
and plunger stopper interface. Helium leak testing is performed in open mode, whereby helium 
is introduced into the closure-side compartment of the format specific format part while vacuum 
is applied to the opposing container-side compartment of the format specific format part to drive 
helium flow across the container closure interface. For vials and bottles, sample preparation 
includes the introduction of a defined opening (approximately 6 mm) at the container bottom to 
enable helium flow through the CCS. For prefilled syringes, preparation involves removal of 
the tip cap or plunger stopper respectively.
The helium leak detection system is subject to routine maintenance and calibration. Annual 
maintenance is performed by the equipment supplier following proprietary procedures. During 
maintenance, the system is calibrated using certified standards covering a leak rate range of
1.81 × 10⁻⁸ to 4.76 × 10⁻⁵ mbar·L/s, traceable to external certification in accordance with 
DIN EN ISO 20486:2018.
Instrument conditioning and system suitability testing are performed on each day of 
measurement. Conditioning is achieved by directly coupling the helium source to the mass 
spectrometer to verify the absence of background helium signals originating from the test setup 
e.g. tubing and seals. System suitability is subsequently confirmed using an internal standard 
with a defined leak rate of 1.00 × 10⁻⁷ mbar·L/s and two certified external standards. One of the 
external standards represents a negative sample and the other external standard a positive 
sample, so that helium flow rates of either less than or greater than 6.00 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s are 
confirmed respectively. The applicant wants to emphasize, that with this system suitability 
testing, a certified negative and positive control was included in all measurements.
System performance and method reliability are additionally verified on format level using 
metallic master samples representing the respective container format. These samples serve as 
negative controls and are measured prior to a sample sequence. Acceptance is achieved if all 
values remain below 1.00 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s.
Following system suitability confirmation, prepared empty CCS samples are analysed. Signal 
detection is independent from the tested format. Format-specific format parts are used to fit the 
containers into the equipment. Tight fit is verified as system suitability test prior each 
measurement series, guaranteeing the absence of leaks between container and format parts.
CCS qualification includes, for vials and bottles, the evaluation of at least three sample 
populations, representing low, nominal, and high crimping forces to cover expected process 
variability during routine manufacturing. All samples are subjected to terminal sterilization 
prior to testing. For each condition, 30 units are tested in accordance with USP <382>. This 
approach is designed to challenge closure integrity under worst-case processing and thermal 
stress conditions, particularly regarding elastomeric components. Reported results from 
3.2.P.2.4.02 are representing the worst-case scenario.

Question:
Given that calcobutrol is added at a nominal concentration of 0.196 mg/mL in the drug 
product formulation and long-term stability data consistently show levels around ~0.12 
mg/mL, please provide a data-driven justification for retaining the current upper specification 
limit of 0.235 mg/mL for release and shelf-life. In particular, clarify whether:
- 
Any batches (including development, validation, or worst-case drug substance 
scenarios) have demonstrated calcobutrol levels approaching the proposed upper 
limit, and
- 
A tighter upper limit could be established based on observed stability trends and 
manufacturing experience without compromising the intended complexing 
function.
Answer:
We acknowledge that the assessor requested a data-driven justification and based upon 
available data concluded that the upper specification limit of 0.235 mg/mL cannot be derived 
based on batch data only.
The theoretical concentration of calcobutrol based upon the batch formula is 0.196 mg/mL. As 
discussed in 3.2.P.5.6.01, during the manufacturing process, a decrease in calcobutrol occurs. 
Therefore, typically calcobutrol concentration will be lower than 0.196 mg/mL at time of 
release and during shelf-life. To derive an upper limit for the calcobutrol release and shelf-life 
specification based upon available data, batch results from the clinical phase and from process 
validation (altogether 13 batches of Gadoquatrane solution in vial, bottle or prefilled syringe 
each filled from one of 13 distinct bulk solution batches, see Table 1) were considered. The 
data set was assessed for normality using the Anderson-Darling test (p = 0.386). No 
significant deviation from normality was observed (α = 0.05). The upper tolerance bound with 
99% coverage at the 99% confidence level was calculated assuming normality. Calculations 
and statistical analysis were performed using Minitab® 21.4.1. The calculated upper tolerance 
bound of 0.185 mg/mL is proposed as upper specification limit for calcobutrol content. The
specifications have been updated accordingly, see updated 3.2.P.5.1.01, 3.2.P.5.1.02, 
3.2.P.5.4.01 and 3.2.P.5.6.01.
However, we would like to confirm that calcobutrol is safe and effective when occurring in 
the formulation within the originally proposed specification range and mention that ICH Q6A 
explicitly recognizes that “The basis for the acceptance criteria at the time of filing should 
necessarily focus on safety and efficacy” due to a “limited amount of data”.

(1) Regarding the pretreatment time for the determination of substances and their
content, the preparation of the test solution mentions that “Transfer 5 tablets to a 500 mL

In all likelihood, the practical performance is “overnight”, which is generally at least 12  h but

spectrophotometry (European Pharmacopoeia 2.2.25) to measure the absorbance of the test solution and 
the reference solution separately at the wavelength of 263 nm and with a cuvette path length of 5 mm, and

Question:
Question 1
Please explain why when calculating Assay (on water-free and solvent-free basis) of 
Vericiguat, the benzene content is not deducted.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (S.4.2.01):
The reason for benzene of not being deducted in the calculation of vericiguat assay is that 
benzene is present at trace (ppm) level and foreign contaminant, and it does not contribute to 
the bulk mass.
Residual solvents present at quantifiable levels (e.g. ethanol, dimethyl acetate) are corrected 
in the assay calculation to account for their contribution to the bulk mass. Class 1 solvents 
such as benzene are present, if at all, at trace (ppm) levels and are controlled as impurities in 
accordance with ICH Q3C; therefore, they are not included in assay normalization.
Residual solvents are corrected in the assay calculation, as they contribute to the overall mass 
of the material. However, in accordance with ICH Q3C, benzene doesn’t contribute to the 
calculation below.

Source:  ICH Q3C

Question: Regarding the Control of critical steps, please explain why the acceptance criteria for the parameter “inlet air temperature” in “Film-coating” step has been changed to 70-90℃ and provide the justification for this setting.
Answer:
The film-coating equipment implemented at Patheon Bourgoin is different from the film-coating equipment at Bayer Leverkusen. The different equipment scale and technical design require adapted processing parameters to achieve similar product temperature and drying conditions during film-coating. The film-coating equipment at Patheon Bourgoin requires a higher inlet air temperature (70-90°C) compared to Bayer Leverkusen (63-67°C) to achieve the same product temperature (50-60°C) during the film-coating process. By keeping the product temperature and thereby the drying conditions similar, it is ensured to obtain product with the same quality in both film-coating processes, as demonstrated via successful process validation (P.3.5.01).

Question: Regarding the specification “Sum of all degradation products: Max 0.3%” as indicated in 3.2.P.5.1, which is inconsistent with the approved acceptance criteria of “Max 1.0%”. Furthermore, in 3.2.P.5.4 Batch Results, it indicates “Max 1.0%” as the acceptance criteria. Please clarify whether this application is intended to propose a revision to the acceptance criterion for this specification.
Answer:
The approved tighter acceptance criterion is aligned with the current requirements of the European Pharmacopoeia and reflects the applicant’s intention to comply with the pharmacopoeial standard.

The discrepancy noted between sections 3.2.P.5.1 and 3.2.P.5.4 is due to the timing of the underlying data generation. The batch results presented in section 3.2.P.5.4 were obtained prior to the implementation of the adapted acceptance criterion and were therefore evaluated against the previously approved specification of NMT 1.0%.
The applicant would like to mention that all reported batch results for “Sum of all degradation products” are well below the approved tightened limit of NMT 0.3%, thereby demonstrating that the product consistently complies with the revised specification.

No impact on product quality, safety, or efficacy is anticipated as a result of this change. The revision represents a specification of tightening based on alignment with current pharmacopoeial expectations.

Question:
Question 3.2
Specifications – expand justification for:
* Potency: Based on the results submitted, the selected potency specifications are considered 
quite broad.

* Particulate matter: Based on the data submitted for particles ≤ 10 µm, a specification of less 
than 2000 per container is not considered adequate. New specifications must be proposed and 
their selection justified.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 3.2 (3.2.P.5.6):
Potency:
Potency by bioassay acceptance criteria are aligned between product stages based on the 
demonstrated poolability of the respective data sets and the understanding that potency is not 
meaningfully changed by the formulation, filling and finishing steps. Resultantly, the same 
acceptance criteria were defined for the drug product as is proposed for the formulated drug 
substance and as established for the drug substance intermediate (DSI) – refer to S.4.5.01-01 
and P.5.6.01-02. The DSI for Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL is the same as used for the 
approved strength Aflibercept solution 40 mg/mL (EYLEA), where the registered DSI 
potency limit is 60 – 140%.
The proposed DP acceptance criterion of 60 – 140% of reference standard was also covered 
by using a tolerance interval approach (99% coverage, 95% confidence) on the DP data 
available at the time, which supported limits of approximately 66% to 146%, while also 
considering the inherently high variability of the cell-based bioassay.
Particulate Matter:
Particulate matter acceptance criteria are based on the applicable pharmacopeial requirements 
for subvisible particles. Ph. Eur. 2.9.19, Method 1 (light obscuration), states for solutions for 
injection in containers with a nominal content of less than 100 mL that the preparation 
complies if the average number of particles does not exceed 6000 per container for particles 
≥ 10 µm and 600 per container for particles ≥ 25 µm. The currently proposed specification of 
≤ 2000 particles/mL for particles ≥ 10 µm and ≤ 50 particles/mL for particles ≥ 25 µm is 
therefore substantially more stringent than the pharmacopeial acceptance criteria.
For Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in vial, the target fill volume is 0.263 mL per 
container. Accordingly, the proposed limits correspond to approximately 527 particles per 
container for particles ≥ 10 µm and approximately 14 particles per container for particles ≥ 25 
µm. Compared with the pharmacopeial limits per container, this represents an approximate 
tightening by a factor of 11 for particles ≥ 10 µm and 43 for particles ≥ 25 µm.
In addition, the currently available batch data set for Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL 
indicates that subvisible particle results are not normally distributed and therefore do not 
support establishment of a meaningfully tighter and statistically robust specification at this 
stage. On this basis, Bayer considers the proposed limits of ≤ 2000 particles/mL for particles 
≥  10 µm and ≤ 50 particles/mL for particles ≥ 25 µm to be appropriate and adequately 
justified for release and shelf life.
The same specification limits for Potency and Particulate Matter have been accepted by EMA.

Manufacturing step / Commercial Route / Route F / Route E / Route D

- Pyridone-TFM-triazole (step 2): aqueous hydrochloric acid / no difference / lithium chloride, p-toluene sulfonic acid / lithium chloride, p-toluene sulfonic acid

- Asundexian acetone solvate pure (step 5): isolation as asundexian acetone solvate / no difference / no difference / no difference
- Asundexian drug substance (step 6): isolation as crystalline asundexian (modification I) / no difference / no difference / isolation as amorphous asundexian

DP:
The differences between these manufacturing processes and the commercial manufacturing process are discussed in P.2.3.01. A gap analysis and an overview of process parameters can be found in the following tables.

Aspects identified as not equivalent in gap analysis (external manufacturer + Bayer clinical supply operation, pilot scale and Bayer commercial site, commercial scale):
- Incorporation of disintegrant: Pilot 77% in pre-blend, 23% in post-blend vs Commercial 100% in pre-blend; tested in pilot scale experiments - no influence
- Residual solvents: Pilot acetone/ethanol absolute = 1/1 vs Commercial acetone/ethanol 96 per cent = 1/1
- Rinsing solvent: Pilot acetone/ethanol absolute = 1/1 vs Commercial ethanol 96 per cent; tested on a commercial scale - no influence
- Batch size: Pilot granulation 120 kg; tablet compression and film-coating 40-55 kg vs Commercial overall 220 kg; larger batch size due to commercial site
- Preparation of spraying solution: Pilot vessel 400 L vs Commercial vessel with rotor-stator disperser and additional propeller type stirrer, 700 L; different geometries due to other mixing/homogenization principle
- Filtration of spraying solution (optional): Pilot two batching tanks connected via silicon tube with interconnected screen vs Commercial filtration unit (pilot: 32 µm, ⌀ 34.8 mm; commercial: 500 µm)
- Mixing (fluidized bed granulator): Pilot 525 L vs Commercial 800 L; operationally equivalent equipment from different vendors

- Inlet air dehumidification (granulation): Pilot inlet air de-humidified – 5 g/kg water content applicable vs Commercial 53 g/kg (sprayingdrying, cooling); inlet air humidity altered during processing to reduce granules water content

All batches used within the CDTs have comparable content of the drug substances, with values 
between 98.4% and 99.7% for dienogest (difference not more than 1.3%) and values between 
99.7% and 101.3% for ethinylestradiol (difference not more than 1.6%). Therefore, the 
requirement of not more than 5% differences in assayed content is fulfilled for all batches.

Furthermore, the applicant confirms that all Valette G batches used were manufactured 
according to the validated manufacturing process described in P.3.5.01_IQMS-398670_1.0.
In accordance with ICH M9 comparative dissolution testing (CDT) was performed using 
biowaiver-conditions 
(P.2.2.02_IQMS-255078_2.0) 
and 
the

(P.2.2.02_IQMS-397168_1.0). 
Within the CDT using biowaiver conditions, at pH 6.8 four out of six batches show dissolution 
rates > 85% for both drug substances within 15 minutes. For the two batches with lower 
dissolution rates than 85% WEW9M8 (Valette) and WEX2B1 (Valette G) – f2-values were 
calculated. The obtained results of 65 for dienogest and 62 for Ethinylestradiol confirm the 
similarity of these two batches. Additionally the f2-calculations are backed-up by calculating 
the more robust version of f2-bootstrapped, which accounts also at some extent for the 
variability of observed data at the different time points (here the same timepoints as before were 
considered). The bootstrap-f2 values are 59.97 for dienogest and 58.16 for Ethinylestradiol. 
Therefore, also via bootstrapping, the equivalence of the two batches was confirmed.
Furthermore, the following pharmacokinetic aspects of Ethinylestradiol and dienogest 
containing oral tablets should be considered. Dissolution performance of tablets is of primary 
relevance for the absorption processes of orally administered drugs but has no impact on other 
pharmacokinetic processes such as distribution, metabolism and excretion. Therefore, the 
pharmacokinetic characteristics of Ethinylestradiol and dienogest containing oral tablets are 
described with respect to absorption in the following.
Ethinylestradiol is completely absorbed after oral administration. The steroid ester 
Ethinylestradiol is cleaved into estradiol, the pharmacologically active moiety during 
absorption and the first liver passage. Following single oral administration of 0.03 mg 
Ethinylestradiol, maximum concentrations are generally reached with a median Tmax of 1.5 hr, 
range 1.0 to 3.0 hours after tablet intake (Shimizu et al. 2026 and Shilpa Madari et al. 2025). 
Dienogest has a high oral bioavailability of greater than 90% (M. Oettel at al.1995), following 
oral administration of 2 mg dienogest maximum concentrations are generally reached 0.66 to 
2.0 hours after intake (H. Zimmerman et al.2000).
Dissolution processes in the stomach after oral administration in humans are best simulated 
with an in vitro dissolution system at pH 1.2. More than an average of 87% of the 
Ethinylestradiol and dienogest was dissolved after 15 minutes (Table 5-1 of P.2.2.02_IQMS-
255078_2.0), which reflects a typical minimal time tablets reside in the stomach. Based on 
these data it can be assumed that the vast majority of Ethinylestradiol and dienogest leaves the 
stomach dissolved and is immediately available for absorption.
The in vitro dissolution results obtained at pH 4.5 and pH 6.8, reflecting the dissolution 
conditions in the small intestine, are less relevant for the Ethinylestradiol and dienogest in vivo 
situation in humans, because major parts of the drug substance reach the small intestine already 
dissolved as discussed above. Nonetheless after 15 minutes more than 87% of Ethinylestradiol 
and dienogest are dissolved (Table 5-2) at pH 4.5. At least an average of 78% of Ethinylestradiol 
and 83% of dienogest (Table 5-3) is dissolved at pH 6.8 within 15 minutes during the in vitro
dissolution procedure with no relevant differences in the final amount dissolved between the 
two different tablet formulations.
Considering the in vivo pharmacokinetics of Ethinylestradiol and dienogest after administration 
of Valette in humans, the slight differences of the obtained in vitro dissolution profiles of tablets 
at pH 6.8 are unlikely to be visible in vivo, as the vast majority of the drug substance amount 
(more than 87%) leaves the stomach dissolved (Table 5-1) and is immediately available for 
absorption. Not later than after 30 minutes, dissolution reached a similar extend for tablets from 
both formulations under all test conditions. In vivo maximum concentrations were reached 1 to 
2 hours after oral administration of the tablets, further supporting that dissolution at pH 1.2 is a 
very important parameter and given the consistency between the two formulations, no in vivo 
impact in humans on the absorption of Ethinylestradiol and dienogest is expected.
In summary, in vitro dissolution tests at pH 1.2, pH 4.5 and pH 6.8 were conducted for the two 
different formulations of Valette. Considering the in vivo pharmacokinetics of Ethinylestradiol 
and dienogest after administration of Valette in humans, the slight differences of the obtained 
in vitro dissolution profiles of the two formulations at pH 6.8 is considered to be 
overdiscriminating and unlikely to be relevant in vivo.
The results demonstrate similar drug product quality, and no in vivo impact in humans is 
expected. Therefore, the new formulation can be considered similar without conducting 
bioequivalence studies.
