Question:
Question 2
The applicant should add the IPC Test for Blend Uniformity of the final mixture before 
compression. This is required because the manufacturing process is considered a non-standard 
process due to the very small amount of active substance ethinylestradiol, which is less than 2 
% of the composition. The homogeneity of the active ingredient in the final mixture is therefore 
highly critical and should therefore be routinely controlled from batch to batch per IPC Blend 
Uniformity of mixture, regardless of whether this has been checked during process validation.
Answer:
The applicant acknowledges the agency’s request.
We understand that according to Annex 2 of the EMA guideline on process validation 
(EMA/CHMP/CVMP/QWP/749073/2016) the designation of a process as non-standard is 
determined by a combination of factors, including the nature of the active substance, the 
finished product, the actual process, and the production experience of the manufacturer. 
Furthermore, products containing low-dose active ingredients (≤ 2% of composition) may be 
considered as “specialized pharmaceutical dose forms” and therefore, the manufacturing 
process could be considered as non-standard.
Within the EMA guideline it is stated, that “It is possible for the applicant to justify that the 
product process can be considered standard for a particular manufacturer / site taking into 
account the risk to the patient of failure of the product or process.“  
In these cases, information on the following aspects should be discussed:
• experience with the same or essentially similar product or process
• amount of knowledge gained during the development of the product
• history of GMP compliance of manufacturing sites for that type of process
Below, the applicant would like to demonstrate that the manufacturing process of Valette G , 
despite the Ethinylestradiol-content which is less than 2% of the composition can be considered 
standard.
The manufacturing process of Valette G has been established at the Supply Center Weimar 
(SCW) for over 15 years. During this time, nearly 2000 batches of Valette G were successfully 
produced. For the lower dosed Ethinylestradiol the results of the content uniformity testing 
(CUT) of these batches are displayed in Figure 1., its acceptance values (AV) are displayed in 
Figure 2.

The CUTs of the 2000 batches were determined to be mostly between 90 and 110% whereas 
the mean is 101%. In every case, the acceptance value (AV value) was below 13% 
(specification limit: 15%) whereas 90% of the AV are below 6.2%. Based on the charts 
presented,  low variability is observed. Within the nearly 2000 batches produced, only 6 batches 
needed to be tested in stage 2 (according to Ph. Eur. 2.9.40). There were no OOS events in the 
last decade that involved the assay or the CUT for either of the two active ingredients. This 
extensive experience demonstrates the robustness and reliability of the manufacturing process.
Additionally, the Weimar manufacturing site has conducted a new validation study on three 
production scale batches (please refer to P.3.5.01_IQMS-398670_1.0). In section 4.5 
“Statistical evaluation of the blend uniformity test (BUT) and content uniformity test (CUT 
data)” of the validation report, a scientifically proven statistical analysis is given that supports 
our assertion that blend uniformity can be adequately assessed through content uniformity 
testing. This approach is aligned with the recommendations outlined in the paper titled 
"Recommendations for the Assessment of Blend and Content Uniformity: Modifications to 
Withdrawn FDA Draft Stratified Sampling Guidance," authored by Garcia et al. (2014). This 
publication discusses the importance of using statistically sound methods for evaluating blend 
and content uniformity and emphasizes that alternative statistical approaches can be justified. 
The implementation of a variance component analysis according to the ASTM E2810 
standard, yielded the results demonstrating a positive outcome for the Uniformity of Dosage 
Units (UDU) test. Further, the variance component analysis also reveals that the variance 
between the sampling points is lower than the variance within a sampling point, indicating a 
very stable process with minimal fluctuations throughout the entire duration of the process . 
These results are shown in TRD P.3.5.01.
As mentioned in TRD P.3.4.01_IQMS-236581_2.0 (Controls of critical steps) several critical 
steps (granulation, tableting and sugar-coating) were identified during the production of
Valette G. All three process steps are well controlled by various in-process-controls to 
guarantee the high quality of the product. The acceptance criteria of the in-process controls as 
listed in P.3.3.01 and P.3.4.01, as well as in the master batch record, are based on the 
knowledge gained during the development of the manufacturing process at laboratory scale 
and during scale-up to final scale. It was clearly demonstrated during development that the 
transferred and validated process, as described in the above mentioned TRD leads to products 
which meet the requirements of the in-process controls and the release specification.
In accordance with the guideline (EMA/CHMP/CVMP/QWP/749073/2016) we would like to 
underline the experience of GMP compliance in the manufacturing of low-dose drug products 
containing Ethinylestradiol. Therefore we would like to highlight/emphasize that Valette G is 
one of 10 products that SCW is producing for more than 30 years. Furthermore, SCW is 
successfully producing 43 different bulk products with API concentrations (hormones) below 
2%. Therefore, and backed by 30 years of experience, we refer to the production of products 
with very low active ingredient concentrations as a standard process as allowed according to 
the EMA guideline on process validation.
When implementing a standard blend uniformity control, it should also be considered that it 
further increases the risks for the bulk product associated with disrupting the implemented 
closed container principle through extensive sampling, which necessitates interrupting the 
ongoing process.
In summary, we consider the validation data and content uniformity assessments, combined 
with our extensive experience in the production process of Valette G and other established 
low-dose products, the classification of the production process as standard process. The 
homogeneity of the active ingredients, Ethinylestradiol and Dienogest, in our final mixture is 
also ensured by our implemented control strategies (critical steps, CUT). We kindly request 
that due consideration be given to the arguments presented above.

Question:
Question 3
No data on permeability were provided in section 3.2.P.2. As BCS class III drug substances are 
more susceptible to the effects of excipients on the in vivo absorption, permeability data for
both drug substances should be provided and an assessment of the different excipients for their 
potential to affect in vivo absorption as outlined in ICH M9.
Answer:
Permeability data were not presented separately in section 3.2.P.2 because the available human 
pharmacokinetic data already demonstrate rapid and extensive absorption of both active 
substances as mentioned answer 1. Ethinylestradiol is completely absorbed after oral 
administration, and dienogest shows an absolute oral bioavailability of approximately 90%, 
with both substances reaching maximum plasma concentrations within about 1 to 2 hours. In 
addition, dissolution of both compounds is rapid, with more than 87% dissolved within 15 
minutes at pH 1.2 (Table 5-1 of P.2.2.02_IQMS-255078_2.0). Taken together, these data do 
not indicate permeability-limited absorption and therefore do not support a relevant risk of 
excipient-driven in vivo absorption effects as described for BCS class III substances in ICH 
M9. The excipients used in the revised formulation are conventional immediate-release tablet 
excipients and are not expected to affect gastrointestinal permeability or the in vivo absorption 
of Ethinylestradiol and dienogest. Therefore, the formulation change is not considered to 
adversely affect bioavailability.

Source:  P.2.2.02-2.0 Pharmaceutical Development – Dissolution Profiles/ Dienogest +
Ethinylestradiol sugar-coated tablet 2 mg + 30 µg (VALETTE without lactose) 
- Biowaiver conditions (#IQMS-255078; unchanged)

Question:

Skip testing in test procedure for immediate packaging PVC foil was included in section 3.2.P.7. 
According to the definitions of skip testing and reduced testing provided in EMA “Quality of 
medicines: questions and answers - Part 2”, the partial testing of starting material (e.g. active 
substance, excipients and packaging materials) is rather reduced testing as skip testing. 
Therefore, the note on reduced testing should be removed form section 3.2.P.7 as this is a GMP 
topic and the relevant registered specifications in the dossier should not include any reference 
to reduced testing on receipt of staring material the finished product manufacturer.
Answer:
The Applicant confirms that no skip testing is performed for the drug product Valette G, despite 
the general note on possible skip testing mentioned in the P.7 document. Each incoming batch 
of PVC/PE.EVOH.PE/PCTFE foil is thoroughly tested and released to ensure quality.
Given that the P.7 document serves as a global reference for all PVC/PE.EVOH.PE/PCTFE 
foils across various drug products and production sites at Bayer, we kindly ask not to revise this 
TRD specifically for Valette G, as this helps to reduce complexity.
Each 
production 
site 
must 
ensure 
that, 
the 
manufacturer 
of 
the 
materials
(PVC/PE/EVOH/PE/PCTFE) is qualified according to the applicable GMP rules. This can be 
achieved through audits, document reviews, and, if necessary, testing. If certification is 
obtained, skip testing can be conducted. This means that not every batch needs to be tested, but 
only every 5th batch or at least one batch per year will be fully tested. This significantly reduces 
the testing effort.  This is not used at the Weimar site, as the manufacturer is qualified but not 
certified.
Through these measures, flexibility within the company can be maintained, and the complexity 
of documentation can be reduced, while ensuring the quality and safety of the products.

Question:
Question 1
Please provide review questions/comments raised by overseas health authorities (at least 
including FDA, EMA, and PMDA) concerning radionuclide-related content.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 ( N.a.):
The available Health Authority questions/comments on radionuclide-related content raised by 
EU national competent authorities and Health Canada were reviewed. Neither FDA, EMA nor 
PMDA raised any questions.
• 
Radionuclide source: Comments addressed the origin, production, purification, and control 
of actinium-225 and its starting materials.
• 
Impurity control: Comments focused on radionuclidic purity controls and source-related 
impurity risks.
• 
Specifications: Acceptance criteria were expected to be justified by impurity profile, process 
knowledge, analytical capability, stability, and safety.
• 
Analytical methods: Method descriptions, qualification or validation status, and suitability 
for proposed limits were commented.
• 
Radiochemical impurities: Comments addressed distinction between free actinium-225, 
labelled product-related species, and other radioactive impurities.
• 
Supplier comparability: New sources were linked to comparability of quality attributes.
• 
Lifecycle control: Stability data, risk-based verification, monitoring, and reassessment after 
changes were identified as relevant control elements.
Overall, the reviewed comments were focused on clarification and justification of the 
actinium-225 control strategy. They were not considered critical, did not result in authority 
non-acceptance of initial clinical trial applications or amendments.

Question:
Question 2
For the two newly introduced actinium sources (SRX and PanTera), the levels of thorium-227 
and bismuth identified during extended characterization are higher than those in the other six 
actinium sources. Please compare and analyze the potential impact on the radiolabeling 
performance.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2 ( R.2.02 Actinium-225):
For the PanTera batches Ac-2025-001 and Ac-2026-001, thorium-227 was below the limit of 
detection (<0.02%), and bismuth levels were comparable to the other actinium-225 sources.
For SpectronRx batches CPA210BH25A-G and CPA224IN25A-G, trace levels of thorium-
227 were reported. These values may be overestimated due to analytical interference of
thorium-227 with actinium-227 sharing the same mass. Thorium-227 cannot be directly 
produced by the SpectronRx irradiation process, and it is reasonable to attribute the detected 
traces to actinium-227.  The reported trace levels (0.53 and 0.34 ng/MBq, respectively) are 
not considered relevant for radiolabeling performance. Bismuth levels in the SpectronRx 
batches were slightly higher than in the other actinium-225 sources, but they were still very 
low. Bayer has evaluated that bismuth levels up to 25 ng/MBq do not adversely affect 
radiolabeling.
Technical and process verification batches produced with actinium-225 from PanTera and 
SpectronRx showed comparable radiolabeling performance, confirmed by iTLC results for 
radiochemical purity.
Therefore, no adverse impact on radiolabeling performance is expected. Actinium-225 from 
both suppliers is considered suitable and qualified for the manufacture of BAY 3547926.
Source:  R.2.02-8.0 Comparability Exercise / BAY 3607112 / BAY 3607119 Actinium-
225 drug substance intermediate (IQMS-249903; amended)

Question:
Question 1
The acceptance criteria of the CCIT by dye ingress test is indicated as “none of the tested 
samples shows a greenish colour” which is not consistent with the pink-red colour typically 
observed for aqueous Eosin 1% solution. Please confirm the dye used for the CCIT and 
rectify the discrepancy for 3.2.P.5.2, 3.2.P.5.3 and 3.2.P.5.6 accordingly, where applicable.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 ( 3.2.P.5.2; 3.2.P.5.3; 3.2.P.5.6 ):
The dye used for the container closure integrity test (CCIT) by dye ingress is confirmed to be 
an aqueous Eosin Y 1% solution. However, the term “greenish colour” refers to the visual 
appearance used for assessment under the specified illumination conditions of the CCIT 
method, and not to the inherent appearance of the bulk dye solution under ordinary 
transmitted or ambient light. Eosin Y 1% is a xanthene dye and is fluorescent. While aqueous 
Eosin Y 1% solution appears pink-red under normal viewing conditions, under the method-
specific inspection conditions used for this test, dye ingress upon excitation by visible light, 
the dye may emit fluorescence in the green region depending on the optical set up.
Therefore, while an aqueous Eosin Y 1% solution appears pink-red under ordinary transmitted 
or ambient light, small amounts of dye that have entered the product container may be 
detected as a greenish fluorescent signal under the halogen-light inspection conditions.
No revisions to 3.2.P.5.2, 3.2.P.5.3 and 3.2.P.5.6 are required.

Question:
Question 1
P.2 Pharmaceutical Development
The MAH should provide more details on the lab scale study for the freeze-drying process; 
how the study was conducted, the equipment used, and further, the number and nature of 
samples included in the study should be described. The lab scale data is presented in Figure 
1-1, 1-2 and 1-3. However, the data used for the figures (raw data points) should also be 
provided, preferable in tables. Further, the MAH should justify the feasibility of the lab scale 
study as model for the manufacturing scale freeze-drying process, including a comparison of 
the set-point process parameters. An overall conclusion on the confirmation of the freeze-
drying cycles and set points and the applicability to the commercial manufacturing process 
should also be provided. The dossier should be updated accordingly.
Answer:
A feasibility lab scale study for using the commercial platform 5 mL lyophilization process to 
manufacture 4000 IU Damoctocog Alfa Pegol Drug Product was performed. The 4000 IU 
Damoctocog Alfa Pegol lyophilizate vials were prepared by filling diluted drug substance into 
Glass type I vial/Stopper bromobutyl gray type I, partially stoppered and then lyophilized 
with the 5 mL commercial lyophilization process in a lab scale freeze drier. The 2000 IU 
Damoctocog Alfa Pegol Drug Product lyophilizate vials were also prepared using the same 
vial/stopper/equipment but using the commercial 2.5 mL lyophilization process as a control, 
since 4000 IU and 2000 IU have the same nominal concentration after reconstitution (IU/mL). 
Freeze drier setpoints, segment durations and ramp rates for the lab scale freeze drier were the 
same as that for both 5 mL and 2.5 mL commercial processes, where Table 1 summarizes the 
5 mL lyophilization parameters at lab and commercial scale.
After lyophilization, the vials were manually capped with flip-off caps and stored in a stability 
chamber at 40°C for a four-month stability study. The duration of 4 months is to perform a 
feasibility assessment of the 5 mL lyophilization process for the manufacturing of 4000 IU 
Damoctocog Alfa Pegol rather than demonstrating formal stability. At each pre-determined 
time point of four months, vials were sampled and verified for headspace vacuum using a 
head space pressure analyzer. Samples were then analyzed for potency and HMW/LMW of 
lyophilized 4000 IU drug product vials and compared with 2000 IU lyophilized drug product 
vials as a control to understand the performance of the 5 mL lyophilization process. The 
number of samples for each analytical test, raw data and timepoint are shown in Table 2 and 
Table 3.
Set point (shelf temperature, pressure), ramp rates and segment durations for both the lab 
scale and commercial scale processes were identical (Table 1), thus the applicability of the lab 
scale study is relevant for the 5 mL commercial manufacturing processes.
Source TRD: P.2.3.60_022985496_02 Pharmaceutical Development - Manufacturing Process - Freeze Drying - amended

Question:
Question 7
For the 5.0 mL diluent PFS a nominal overfill of 0.15 mL and 0.1 mL is proposed for SCB 
and Vetter, respectively. The MAH justifies the 0.15 mL overfill at SCB by stating that the 
overfill ensures that a volume of 5.0 mL of reconstituted product is delivered to the patient. 
Considering the previously performed retention volume study including both PFS from Vetter 
and SCB (SCB section P.2.6) in combination with the delivery systems, the 0.15 mL/0.1 mL 
overfill for the 5.0 mL PFS is not found fully justified. The MAH should reconsider the overfill 
and/or provide further justification that the 0.15 mL/0.1 mL overfill will ensures that a volume 
of 5.0 mL of reconstituted product is delivered to the patient during infusion in the clinical 
setup. The dossier should be updated as appropriate.
Answer:
The diluent prefilled syringe used for the reconstitution of Factor VIII requires an overfill to 
compensate for transfer loss.
Based on retention volume studies in section 3 of P.2.6.01_022985338_01 with a maximum 
retention volume of 0.25 mL for either Vetter or Berlin, combination of overfill contained in 
the Drug Product vials, the sWFI overfill in either Vetter or SCB prefilled syringes, and 
approximately 0.2 g of the lyophilized solids in the Drug Product vials, ensures that adequate 
amount of reconstituted rFVIII product is delivered to the patient.
For the 5.0 mL diluent PFS a nominal overfill of 0.15 mL and 0.1 mL is proposed for SCB 
and Vetter, respectively in P.2.2.01_004384890_02 and P.2.2.01#009151807_02.
For the 5 mL fill size, the target fill weight of final formulation bulk in the vial is 5.25 g 
(equivalent to 5.2 mL) for rFVIII Drug Product. A nominal overfills of 0.1 mL of diluent in 
the Vetter prefilled syringe assures the combined volume of reconstituted product in the 
product vial is greater than 5.2 mL (resulting from 5.1 g of diluent and approximately 0.2 g of 
lyophilized solids) and an extractable volume of 5.0 mL. Similarly, a nominal overfill of 
0.15 mL of diluent in the SCB prefilled syringe assures the combined volume of reconstituted 
product in the product vial is greater than 5.2 mL (resulting from 5.15 g of diluent and 
approximately 0.2 g of lyophilized solids) and an extractable volume of 5.0 mL.
Furthermore, the overfill volumes for Vetter and SCB prefilled syringes used for licensed 
Kovaltry 5 mL products are the same for the 4000 IU Jivi. There are no changes to the 
physical properties of the 4000 IU since the formulation composition is the same as the 
Kovaltry 5 mL licensed product.

Question:
Question 5
Regarding the Following point: 
To widen the initial viable cell density in-process limit, applied during the manufacturer of the 
active substance Aflibercept, from 0.40-0.68 x 106 viable cells /ml to 0.27-0.68 x 106  
The following [points a-d below] is required:
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 5 (3.2.S.2.4):
a) Revised information on the controls performed at critical steps of the manufacturing
process and on intermediates of the proposed drug substance.
and
b) Comparative table or description, where applicable, of pre-change and post-change in-
process tests/limits.
With this change, only the initial viable cell density is impacted, please see below:

Source:
S.2.4.01 - Aflibercept intermediate - Discussion and Control of Critical Steps 
(S.2.4.01_022971475_02; replacing S.2.4.01#006492525_16)

c) Description of the batches and summary of in-process and release testing results as
quantitative data, in a comparative tabular format, for commercial-scale batches of the 
pre-change and post-change drug
and
d) Justification for the new in-process test and limits with risk-based assessment.
• In preparation of the proposed change to the IPC limit, an impact assessment was performed.
The IPC “Initial Viable Cell Density (VCD)” at the step thawing of the cell bank is classified as a 
general quality attribute (GQA) per the aflibercept IPCs program summarized in the approved 
S.2.4.01 – Chapter 2 Critical and General Controls (see response above).
• The purpose of the aflibercept seed expansion unit operations is to expand the aflibercept cell
culture from the 500 mL shake flask to the 3,000 L bioreactor to achieve a sufficient number of 
cells to seed the 10,000 L production bioreactor. This quality attribute is categorized as a general 
(non-critical) attribute since it is used to monitor operational consistency and, historically, has not 
had a direct impact on the product quality when maintained within normal operating ranges. Of
note, transfer of cells for the 20 L cell bag and for the 50 L, 500 L, and 3,000 L bioreactors is VCD-
driven whereas the transfer of cells, to subsequent steps, for shake flask and the 2 L cell bag is time-
driven. Therefore, the expansion of permissible VCD limit for shake flask initial VCD does not 
impact the transfer determinations for the cells. Furthermore, historical review of aflibercept drug 
substance production data showed that any variability seen in the early seed expansion unit 
operations does not persist into the production bioreactor (10,000 L), as the cell density is able to 
recover to levels that are in alignment with historical experience at the production bioreactor step.
• Additionally, there are other IPCs in-place that ensure consistent cell growth and expansion.
These include, but are not limited to, the initial VCD, final VCD and final viability of the 2 L and 
20 L cell bags along with the respective IPCs of the 50 L, 500 L, and 3,000 L expansion 
bioreactors.
• The evaluation confirmed that the process will continue to operate within the established
process time limits which are well within the validated LIVCA Limit (839 hr:57min – 
1068 hr:59min), therefore there is not a risk of experiencing population doublings beyond those 
proven with the LIVCA lot or a risk to the genetic stability of the cell culture as a result of the 
proposed updates to expansion times.
• Therefore, with these controls in place, the Sponsor concluded that it is acceptable to modify
the initial VCD for cell thaw as this change shows no impact to cell culture performance and 
product quality.
• The currently approved limit was established based on guidance, practices, and data available
at the time to be able to detect any variability outside historical experience. The reassessment of the 
shake flask initial VCD GQA is based on the approach defined in S.2.4.01 in section “On-Going 
Process Monitoring and Improvements in IPC Limits: As additional experience and data are gained 
during commercial manufacturing, the proposed IPCs and their action limits will be re-evaluated.”
• Considering the low risk of the proposed change, formal validation runs were not performed.
Data have been collected from multiple commercial lots produced within the expanded viable cell 
density (VCD) range (0.27 – 0.68 x 106). Data for eight commercial lots are provided in this 
response and demonstrate that there is no downstream impact to the process.
Trending charts have been provided in Annex 1 at the end of this document for in-process 
controls (IPCs) and lot release data.

2. Justification for the proposed drug substance Appearance test deletion please clarify the
risk related to this deletion
Visible particulates testing is not required according to guidance for intermediate stages of a 
parenteral or intraocular protein formulation (DSI, DS and FB). Also, in line with ICH Q6B 
“Specifications: Test Procedures and Acceptance Criteria for Biotechnological/Biological 
Products”, only the physical state (e.g., solid, liquid) and color testing is required for drug 
substance. Additionally, tests specified in United States Pharmacopoeia (USP) <790> 
“Visible Particulates in Injections” and European Pharmacopoeia (Ph. Eur.) 2.9.20 
“Particulate contamination - visible particles” are specific for Drug Product (DP) only.
• The Aflibercept manufacturing process at Regeneron is well established and supported
with long-standing historical manufacturing and quality control (QC) experiences to 
control and minimize the presence of particles during processing. Every lot of DSI, 
DS and/or FB, if stored, is filtered through 0.2 µm filter into mixing bag and dispensed 
into sterile biotainers. The dispensing of the material occurs in a classified area which 
is monitored through environmental monitoring program, in accordance with internal 
procedures. All produced lots are sampled and tested for bioburden and turbidity as a 
part of release testing. Turbidity testing is performed to ensure product/process 
consistency, and that the material is clear. This testing provides detection of 
proteinaceous instability and/or potential large quantity particle loads introduced 
beyond the characterized levels.
• Visible particles in the final DP are minimized and their presence is controlled. During
DP manufacture (filling), the FB solution undergoes a double filtration as part of the 
aseptic manufacturing process. The test item “visible particulates” is and will remain a 
release criterion for DP final release and stability specification. In addition, 100% 
Visual Inspection of DP containers for visible particles according to Pharmacopeia is 
performed  at the DP filling site.

Question:
Question 1.1.3.1:  
Exclude the first criterion, as exceeding the specified range of optical densities may indicate 
either improperly prepared solutions, an out-of-specification result, or an unsuitable standard 
sample and does not allow conclusions to be drawn about the suitability of the system.
Answer:
Response 1.1.3.1: 
Exceeding the linear range of the method gives an indication that the validated range of the 
method is not met for a specific measurement (for various reasons) and as such no 
conclusions with regard to the content of the sample measured can be taken, as the signal 
obtained is not linear to the analyte anymore. Therefore, it is important to ensure that the 
linear range of the analysis is met, otherwise no valid results will be obtained as per the 
method validation. It is highly recommended to keep this criterion as a measure to guarantee 
that all measured values are generated within the frame of the validated method and do not 
exceed the validated range of this absorbance method.

Question:
Question 1.1.4:  
Eliminate the use of a standard sample and associated manipulations, since the essence of the 
system suitability test is actually the evaluation of the relative standard deviation of the 
optical densities (which can be performed on the test solution), and the calculation of the 
result does not require the use of a standard.
Answer:
Response 1.1.4:
It is correct that calculation of the result for the sample does not require the use of a standard. 
The use of a qualified reference material (i.e. the reference standard or standard sample) to 
confirm that all equipment used is working properly and all necessary liquid handling steps 
have been executed as per the procedure. An expected result obtained for the standard, which 
is a qualified material stored at conditions preventing change over time, confirms the 
functionality of all used equipment and appropriateness of all standard handling steps under 
the actual conditions of use. If an unexpected result is obtained for the reference standard, it 
can be assumed that there are issues in the analysis and an investigation needs to be carried
out to identify the cause. Therefore, our recommendation is to keep the reference standard in 
the method description and use it as a tool to confirm the suitability of the equipment used on 
a daily basis.

Question:
Question 1.3.6.5:  
In accordance with the requirements of EAEU Ph. 2.1.2.37 "Capillary electrophoresis", State 
Pharmacopoeia of Russia (GPM. 1.2.1.0022.15 "Capillary electrophoresis") to supplement the 
subsection with an assessment of the sensitivity of the system. For this:
Answer:
Response 1.3.6.5.1: 
The Applicant proposes a system sensitivity criterion based on the IgG standard. Monoclonal
IgG is the established system suitability standard for the method and supports the existing
criteria. The same system sensitivity solution and resulting sensitivity criterion was already
established for the approved 40mg/mL strength.
During method validation, the LOQ (0.005 mg/mL) was determined through the analysis of
the signal/ noise (S/N) of the main peak of a monoclonal IgG system suitability standard
under non-reduced conditions.  The monoclonal IgG system suitability standard was chosen
since the main peak of IgG standard has better resolution than aflibercept sample under
electrophoresis, which makes the S/N evaluation more accurate. Also, the migration time of
the main peak of IgG standard is similar to the typical size variants observed for aflibercept.
The LOQ is the lowest amount of analyte in a sample that can be determined with acceptable
precision and accuracy under the stated experimental conditions. As experimental conditions
(i.e., instrument parameters) are not changing in between reduced and non-reduced assay
conditions, and as the purpose of the sensitivity standard is to ensure system performance, it is
only necessary to evaluate under the one condition. Hence, the monoclonal IgG system
suitability standard was analyzed by CE-SDS under non-reduced conditions. The single intact
main peak generated from the dilution of the standard was used to ascertain the LOQ of the
assay method and S/N ratio for main peak of IgG sample was analyzed by Empower 3
software.
It is therefore proposed to add a sensitivity standard and system suitability criterion based on
the validated LOQ for the diluted monoclonal IgG standard under non-reduced CE-SDS
conditions.
This sensitivity standard solution should be prepared from the monoclonal IgG standard at a
concentration of 0.01 mg/ml under non-reducing conditions.

The applicant therefore recommends that the following is added to the protocol:
Stock Monoclonal IgG solution for sensitivity assessment (0.05 mg/mL):
Add 40 µL of an aliquot of prepared monoclonal IgG stock standard solution (2.5
mg/mL) to 1960 µL of water and mix thoroughly.
Use the solution freshly prepared.

Non-reduced monoclonal IgG control for sensitivity assessment (0.01 mg/mL):
In a separate tube, make a single preparation by combining 40 µL of the Stock
Monoclonal IgG solution for sensitivity assessment (0.05 mg/mL) with 160 μL of
Dilution Buffer (Non-Reducing) for a final concentration of 0.01 mg/mL.
Record all dilutions.

Note: Sensitivity assessment, including preparation of non-reduced monoclonal IgG solution
for sensitivity assessment, is included in the ND in accordance with requirements of the EAEU
regulatory authorities; it is not presented in the original documentation of the company, and it
is not performed by the manufacturer during routine analysis.

Question:
Question 1.10.3.3.  
Assessment of asymmetry factor of reference peaks 5(M1), 17(M2), 25(M3/SS), 37(M4), 
47(M5). Establish an appropriate validated requirement to account for pronounced peak 
asymmetry under selected chromatographic separation conditions (e.g., "no more than 3").
Answer:
Response 1.10.3.3: 
In accordance with ICH guidelines, identification tests are specifically designed to verify the
identity of an analyte within a sample. In the context of peptide mapping, this verification is
accomplished through the visual comparison of the test article chromatogram with the
reference standard and example chromatograms. The primary aim is to ensure that all of the
47 peaks are distinct and align accurately with those in the reference standard, which confirms
the identity of the analyte. While assessing the asymmetry factor of reference peaks such as
5(M1), 17(M2), 25(M3/SS), 37(M4), and 47(M5) can be important in quantitative analyses to
ensure precision and accuracy, it is less relevant in qualitative methods like peptide mapping.
As such, even if peak asymmetry is observed, it should not impact the ability to unequivocally
identify the analyte. Therefore, establishing strict requirements for peak asymmetry, such as
the suggested "no more than 3," is not considered necessary in the context of qualitative
identification methods, as the qualitative nature of peptide mapping inherently accommodates
variations in peak shape without compromising the identification. The same method with the
same set of suitability criteria was established and approved for the 40 mg/mL strength in
compliance with the Russian Pharmacopoeia

Question:
Question 1.10.3.4.  
Assessment of the sensitivity of the chromatographic system by calculating the actual value of 
the limit of quantification expressed as a percentage of the total area of all peaks of peptide 
fragments in the chromatogram of the standard solution. It is reasonable to perform such 
calculation for one of the reference peaks (for example, peak 5(M1)) by the formula LOQ = 
(S×10)/(s/n), where s/n is the value of the signal-to-noise ratio calculated for the selected 
reference peak, S is relative peak area (in %) calculated from the total area of all peaks of 
peptide fragments in the chromatogram;
Answer:
Response 1.10.3.4: 
Peptide mapping is used as an identity test and not a quantitation test, therefore signal-to-
noise ratio for the marker peaks is not obtained during method validation. The qualitative
comparison between the test article chromatogram, the reference standard chromatogram, and
the example chromatograms, in addition to the quantitative comparisons between the marker
peaks, is sufficient to determine test article and system suitability, resulting in the correct
validation of identity.
Moreover, the method states that the reference standard chromatograms must be similar to
one another in terms of relative retention time and overall elution pattern, specifically peak
retention time, peak shape and peak height. Furthermore, the comparison between reference
standard chromatograms is not limited to 5 marker peaks, as all of the 47 peaks must be
evaluated. Since this is an identification method, and the comparison is performed by visual
assessment, an estimation of LOQ is not recommended by EAEU Ph. GPM 2.1.2.39 "Peptide
Mapping".

Question:
Question 1.10.3.5.  
Alternatively, the sensitivity of the chromatographic system can be assessed by calculating the 
signal-to-noise ratio for one of the reference peaks with a validated requirement for the 
resulting value corresponding to a typical value of the relative area of the selected peak 
relative to the total peak area of the peptide fragments in the chromatogram. For example, for 
a reference peak with a typical relative area value of about 1% (of the total peak area), set the 
requirement for the calculated signal-to-noise ratio as "at least 20", which would correspond 
to an LOQ of 0.5%.
Answer:
Response 1.10.3.5: 
In response to the question regarding the necessity of assessing sensitivity in a
chromatographic system for peptide mapping, it is important to note that peptide mapping is
primarily used as a qualitative identity assay rather than a quantitative one. This means that
the focus is on identifying the presence of specific peptide fragments rather than measuring
their concentration. Consequently, there is no requirement to calculate the signal-to-noise
ratio for marker peaks during method validation, as would be necessary in a quantitative
assay. The identity of the test article is confirmed through a qualitative comparison of the
chromatogram with reference standards and example chromatograms, ensuring that the
relative retention time, peak shape, and peak height are consistent. This visual assessment of
the chromatograms, which includes evaluating all 47 peaks rather than just a subset, is
sufficient to establish the identity of the sample. Therefore, the Applicant proposes that
estimating the limit of quantitation (LOQ) is not applicable or recommended, as per the
guidelines set by EAEU Ph. GPM 2.1.2.39 "Peptide Mapping". The method relies on the
qualitative similarity in the elution pattern and retention times across chromatograms,
ensuring system suitability and correct identity validation without the need for sensitivity
assessment.

Question:
Question 1.10.4.1:  
Set a validated value for the disregard limit (significance threshold) of the peaks, e.g. "0.5%" 
(a threshold value of the relative peak area (calculated, relative to the total area of all peptide 
peaks in the chromatogram) below which the corresponding peak is not taken into account).
Answer:
Response 1.10.4.1: 
In the context of peptide mapping, which is a qualitative method used for identity
confirmation, setting a disregard limit for peaks based on their relative area, such as "0.5%",
is not typically necessary. The primary goal of peptide mapping is to ensure that the test
article's chromatogram is qualitatively similar to that of the reference standard and example
chromatograms, focusing on the presence and alignment of specific marker peaks rather than
their quantitative measurement. As such, the significance of minor peaks below a certain
threshold does not impact the qualitative assessment of identity. The disregard limit is more
relevant in quantitative analyses where precise quantitation of impurities or minor
components is necessary. In qualitative methods like peptide mapping, the emphasis is on the
overall pattern and alignment of peaks, ensuring that key identity peaks are consistent with the
reference standard, rather than on the detailed quantitation of every peak. Therefore, the
Applicant proposes that applying a disregard limit is not applicable or required for the visual
identity confirmation in peptide mapping.

Question:
Question 1.10.4.2:

with the chromatogram of the standard solution shall contain all peaks whose relative area in 
the chromatogram of the standard solution is greater than or equal to the value of the peaks 
disregard limit.

Response 1.10.4.2: 
The method procedure states that the chromatograms of the test sample that are digested at the

those of the reference standard in terms of retention time and elution profile, including aspects
such as peak retention time, shape, and height. The comparison of chromatograms is not
restricted to the five marker peaks and, and all 47 peaks must be visually assessed. Since this
is an identification method relying on visual assessment, and since emphasis should be placed
on the overall elution pattern between the reference standard and the test article
chromatograms, setting a disregard limit for additional or missing peaks is not recommended.

Question:
Question 1
The submitted risk assessments concerning the possible formation and presence of nitrosamines in 
the drug substance and finished product are not detailed enough and should therefore be revised.
Regarding the drug substance, the following points should be clarified:
a) It has not been mentioned that 4-Nitrophenol will be released in stoichiometric amounts during 
step 4b formation of intermediate Gadoquatrane crude where also nucleophilic hydroxide anions 
will be present (basification using aqueous sodium hydroxide). The applicant should therefore 
appropriately address potential de-nitration during this step of the synthesis. If de-nitration cannot 
unambiguously be ruled out, confirmatory testing should be performed, e.g. concerning potential 
nitrosamine derivatives of relevant impurities like heptamine, secondary amines stemming from 
diisopropylethylamine or synthesis intermediates, etc.
b) Regarding the potential nitrosamine contamination of starting material NPTA HCl, the applicant 
focusses on the reduction of nitrite impurities in sodium azide and potential NDMA during the 
hydrogenation step. Nevertheless, this is solely a theoretical claim, and relevant data, e.g. 
concerning actual nitrite content in sodium azide, should be provided for further justification. If 
necessary, confirmatory testing should be performed to rule out the presence of NDMA as well as 
nitrosamine derivatives of heptamine.
c) If confirmatory testing is necessary, suitably validated analytical methods should be used as 
described in Q&A paper EMA/409815/2020.
Regarding the finished product, the following points should be clarified:
d) In the risk assessment on the presence of nitrosamine impurities in the drug product under 
review it is indicated that supportive documentation on the excipients and container closure system 
of the drug product is available. These documents should be provided.
e) The applicant has indicated that the presence of nitrosating agents, nitrosamines or vulnerable 
amines in the API is excluded. However, some points for clarification have been identified (see 
above). Based on the outcome of these concerns, there might be a risk of presence of nitrosamine 
impurities in the drug product as well, which may require further scientific discussion and, if 
necessary, confirmatory testing. (S.3.2. + P.5.5)
Answer:
Applicant’s response:

Abstract drug substance nitrosamine risk assessment:
In the following, the risk of the potential denitration of 4-Nitrophenol (released in step 4b) as well
as the potential nitrite content in sodium azide are addressed in more detail.
Furthermore, data is presented to support the theoretical risk assessment. Batch data for nitrite in
three commercial batches of sodium azide and starting material NPTA HCl are shown, both
revealing that there is no risk for the contamination of NPTA HCl with significant amounts of
residual nitrite.

nitrosamines were tested in commercial batches using suitably validated analytical methods as
described in Questions and answers for marketing authorisation holders/applicants on the CHMP
Opinion for the Article 5(3) of Regulation (EC) No 726/2004 referral on nitrosamine impurities in
human medicinal products (EMA/409815/2020). NDMA was tested in starting material NPTA HCl
and Gadoquatrane drug substance. Furthermore, DIPEA, NEIPA, NDMA and NO-Heptamine-
Gadoquatrane were tested in Gadoquatrane drug substance. All tested potential nitrosamines were
determined to be at least below 10% of their respective acceptable intake (AI).
A detailed discussion of the data can be found in the answers below and in the updated version of
S.3.2.07 and P.5.5.07.
In summary, the presented data supports the risk assessment that there is no risk for nitrosamine
contamination of Gadoquatrane drug substance.

a) We acknowledge the Rapporteur’s comment that a risk assessment concerning the possibility of
4-Nitrophenol denitration under the aqueous basic conditions in Step 4b is missing. In the
following, we will address this concern:
As stated in S.3.2.07, 4-Nitrophenol does not represent a particularly electron-poor nitro arene. 
Therefore, it is not - even in the presence of strong nucleophiles - susceptible to a denitration 
reaction. In theory, such a reaction would proceed via a nucleophilic aromatic substitution reaction 
(SNAr) in the case of 4-Nitrophenol.
Scheme 1: A Hypothetical mechanistic pathway of denitration via hydroxide-mediated
SNAr
￼

As illustrated in Scheme 1, the key reaction intermediate – in the literature commonly referred to 
as Meisenheimer complex – is a negatively charged arene. Stabilization of the negative charge in 
the Meisenheimer complex, typically via multiple electron-withdrawing substituents, would be 
required for the denitration reaction to proceed at a reasonable rate. In the case of the 4-
Nitrophenol substitution pattern, said strongly electron-withdrawing substitution pattern is not 
given. Thus, a productive denitration pathway is not favored. 
To further substantiate our assessment that there is no risk of denitration of 4-Nitrophenol in an 
aqueous, sodium hydroxide containing medium, the acidity of 4-Nitrophenol shall be taken into 
account. It is well-established in the literature that 4-Nitrophenol is a fairly acidic compound, with a 
pKa value of ~ 7.15 owing to the acidity of the phenolic proton. Thus, the species prevalent in the 
basic aqueous reaction mixture is the negatively charged 4-Nitrophenolate anion (see Scheme 2)

Owing to the strongly electron donating properties of the phenoxide group (which already includes 
a negative charge), the formation of a Meisenheimer complex after nucleophilic attack of hydroxide 
is not possible. Consequently, denitration is not possible. 
To conclude, there is no risk of nitrite formation from 4-Nitrophenol during step 4b. 
 
This theoretical assessment is supported by analytical data demonstrating the absence of potential 
nitrosamines NEIPA and NDIPA, which may arise from secondary amine impurities in DIPEA during 
step 4b, as well as of the potential nitrosamine NO-Heptamine-Gadoquatrane in Gadoquatrane 
drug substance. All theoretically possible nitrosamines have been tested using dedicated analytical 
methods and found to be at least below 10% of the respective AI in three commercial batches of 
Gadoquatrane drug substance. Supportive data and information about the analytical methods 
including tested validation parameters as well as the setting of appropriate AI limits and AI-based 
maximum allowed concentrations in Gadoquatrane drug substance are included in section S.3.2.07.

Secondly, the impurity Heptamine in NPTA HCl has been evaluated regarding its theoretical risk for
the formation of a related nitrosamine. Due to the presence of six primary amine functions in
addition to one secondary amine in the molecule, the risk for the formation of a Heptamine-related
nitrosamine is considered to be negligible. Primary amines are generally not considered vulnerable
nitrosamine precursors, as nitrosamines derived from primary amines are not stable; moreover,
due to the higher reactivity toward nitrosylation when compared to secondary amines, primary
amines can act as nitrite scavengers and may inhibit nitrosamine formation under relevant
primary amines, any risk for the formation of a Heptamine-related nitrosamine can be excluded.

The outcome of the theoretical risk evaluation that no risk for nitrosamine contamination was
identified for Gadoquatrane drug substance is fully supported by analytical results demonstrating

in Gadoquatrane drug substance and starting material NPTA HCl are at least below 10% of their
acceptable limit).

Abstract drug product nitrosamine risk assessment:
We acknowledge the Rapporteur’s comment regarding the drug product nitrosamine risk
assessment. In the following, these concerns are addressed in more detail. In conclusion, the
updated nitrosamine risk assessment for Gadoquatrane drug product demonstrates that there is no
risk for the presence of nitrosamine impurities.

d) Supportive documentation on the excipients and container closure system of the drug product is

e) Given the explanations in the responses to a) and b) the presence of nitrosating agents and
nitrosamines in the drug substance is excluded. Consequently, no risk has been identified for the
presence of nitrosamine impurities in the drug product resulting from drug substance. Based on
this assessment, confirmatory testing is not required.
As mentioned above, the nitrosamine risk assessments in S.3.2.07 and P.5.5.07 have been
thoroughly updated and now contain a comprehensive discussion of the potential nitrosamine risks
raised by EMA. For each identified risk, it is concluded that no relevant amounts of nitrosamines
can be formed in either the drug substance or the drug product. This is demonstrated by
supportive data regarding all theoretical nitrosamines in the drug substance and drug product.
For Gadoquatrane drug substance the updated section S.3.2.07 provides data for the theoretical
nitrosamine NEIPA, NDIPA, NDMA and NO-Heptamine-Gadoquatrane. For Gadoquatrane drug
product, the potential nitrosamines NEIPA, NDIPA, NDMA and NO-Heptamine-Gadoquatrane have
also been tested in representative batches. None of the nitrosamines was detectable in the drug
substance or the drug product. The applied methods have been demonstrated to be capable of
detecting the respective nitrosamines below 10% of the maximum acceptable concentration
(calculated based on the AI).
Moreover, Heptamine-Gadoquatrane has been identified as the only potential secondary amine,
which could, in principle, be present in the drug substance in trace amounts. This impurity can
solely be formed during the synthesis (i.e. it is not a degradation product) and has been shown to
be consistently absent in commercial API batches (below LOD, LOD = 100 ppb, refer to S.3.2.07).
Therefore, also the formation of relevant amounts of nitrosamines in the drug product based on
potential secondary amines in the drug substance can be ruled out.

General notes
It should be noted that in S.3.2.07, section 3.3, the discussion on potential nitrite in potable and
purified water, which is used in the synthesis of the drug substance, has also been updated. Based
on data from nitrite measurements in water, the discussion has been revised to reflect these
results, and the previously applied justifications based on conductivity have been
removed. Importantly, this update has no impact on the nitrosamine risk in the drug substance.
Any risk for the potential formation of nitrosamines based on potential trace levels of nitrite in
potable or purified water can be safely excluded. The same applies to the discussion and conclusion
concerning water for injection in P.5.5.07, section 2.2.
Moreover, S.3.2.07, section 3.5 has been updated based on EMA request to reevaluate the use of
recovered solvents during the drug substance synthesis process (refer to Question 2e) for drug
substance). Toluene, used in early synthesis steps (1a/1b, 2a), has been identified to be reused
upon process-related solvent recovery. Solvent recovery is done by distillation and after the
recovery, Toluene is released according to the same specification as the fresh solvents and only for
re-use in the same synthesis step. The presence of secondary amines, as well as nitrite during
solvent recovery can be excluded for the recovery process. Therefore, this update has no impact on
the overall risk assessment for nitrosamines in Gadoquatrane drug substance.

Question 2
Data regarding the already mentioned experimental determination of complexation constants, DTF
calculations, comparison with Gadobutrol, calculations with various residues, etc. and a discussion
thereof should be provided. (S.1)
Answer:
Applicant’s response:
Due to the complexity of the molecule and very slow dissociation kinetics even at low pH, the 
experimental determination of complexation constants is not feasible by established methods. In 
the following we would like to present the details of the computational experiments performed.
Description and discussion of the computational approach to assess the Gadoquatrane 
thermodynamic complex stability by density functional theory (DFT) calculations on monomeric 
units with different residues:
- 
The gadoquatrane molecule, due to its tetrameric structure (C81H128N24O32Gd4) is too large 
to be described by accurate quantum-chemical methods. Therefore, to computationally 
assess the complex stability of Gadoquatrane, a number of model compounds were
considered. We calculated the complex free energy, ∆GComplex Formation, of a series of 
gadolinium chelates with known stability constants and compared them to two derivatives 
which contain the monomeric unit of gadoquatrane with different residue chain lengths. 
These model compounds are shown as “Gadoquatrane-Unit I” and “Unit II” in Figure 2. 
Both model compounds were constructed as fragments of the entire gadoquatrane 
molecule with varying length of the linker connecting the monomers in a tetramer and were 
selected to investigate the influence of the linker atoms on the overall complex stability.
Figure 2: Chemical structures of the gadoquatrane tetramer (left) and the two
monomeric Gadoquatrane model units (middle and right) used to assess the
thermodynamic complex stability constant log kGdL
= R
Structure Gadoquatrane
Gadoquatrane-Unit I
Gadoquatrane-Unit II

- 
The applied computational methods are suited to calculate thermodynamic stabilities of the 
Gd complex, but not their kinetic stabilities.
- 
Complex free energies were calculated via: ∆GComplex Formation = G(ML+H2O)-G(M)-G(L)-
G(H2O); where G(ML+H2O) is the entropy corrected energy of a gadolinium metal-ligand 
complex including one water molecule, G(M) is the energy of a single gadolinium ion Gd3+, 
G(L) is the free energy of the free ligand, and G(H2O) is the free energy of a single water 
molecule. Energies were calculated via density functional theory (DFT) calculations after a 
semiempirical conformational search, followed by a DFT geometry optimization with implicit 
solvation. Further details of employed computational methods, basis sets, and solvation 
model are summarized in [1].
- 
All calculations were performed using the ORCA software package, version 6.0.1 [2].
- 
As shown in Figure 2, the calculated complex free energies of both model compounds 
(monomeric gadoquatrane units) lie in a similar energy range as for gadobutrol 
(Gadovist®), indicating that the thermodynamic complex stability constant, log kGdL, of 
gadoquatrane is well above 20 with negligible influence from varying the residue.

Figure 3: Comparison of the measured complex stability constant to the calculated free 
energy of complex formation for a series of gadolinium chelates

Comparison of the measured complex stability constant, log kGdL (left panel), to the calculated 
free energy of complex formation, ∆GComplex Formation in kcal/mol (right panel), for a series of 
gadolinium chelates. Lower free energy values correspond to higher complex stability constants 
(see Figure 3). Experimental reference value for the gadolinium chelates with known stability 
values were taken from Port et al. 2008 [3].
In conclusion the complex stability of each single Gadoquatrane unit is highly comparable with the 
complex stability of gadobutrol. The small variation in calculated complex stability between the two 
model units further indicates that the linker atoms, which connect the monomers in a tetramer 
unit, have little influence on the overall stability. Thus, the complex stability of the gadoquatrane 
tetramer is primarily driven by the sub-unit stability which is comparable to gadobutrol.

References:
[1] Calculation workflow: Conformational search with the semiempirical GFN2-xTB method 
(Bannwarth C, Ehlert S, Grimme S. Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation 2019 15 (3), 
1652-1671); geometry optimization with the composite electronic-structure method r2SCAN-3c 
(Grimme S, Hansen A, Ehlert S, Mewes JM. r2SCAN-3c: A “Swiss army knife” composite electronic-

[2] Neese, F. (2012), The ORCA program system. WIREs Comput Mol Sci, 2: 73-78.
[3] Port M, Idée JM, Medina C, Robic C, Sabatou M, Corot C. Efficiency, thermodynamic and kinetic

The description of the manufacturing process should be updated regarding the following points:
a) All reagents and solvents as described in the narrative description of the synthesis should be
indicated in the detailed reaction schemes (e.g. toluene in step 1b (DO3A route), activated
charcoal in step 2a, water in step 2b, Gd-Glydonip seeds in step 4a, etc. are missing) as well as the
overall flow diagram presented in section 3.2.S.2.2 of the dossier.
b) Concerning step 1b, it has been stated that 0-0.75 eq of Sodium bromide can be added.
Therefore, it appears that the addition of Sodium bromide is optional. This should be unmistakenly

criteria for deciding when Sodium bromide will be added should be detailed.

detailed.

e) It should be clarified if recovery (e.g. from mother liquors or filtrates) of solvents, reactants,
intermediates or the active substance will be performed.

applicant should present appropriate justifications and descriptions of each reprocessing procedure
including criteria for deciding when reprocessing can be performed.

manufacturing process.
h) The production of “gaseous water” should be explained. Moreover, flow diagrams should detail
the use of potable or purified water in each relevant step. (S.2.2).
Answer:
Applicant’s response:
a) Reagents and solvents
All reagents and solvents as described in the narrative description of the synthesis are now
indicated in the detailed reaction schemes as well as in the overall flow diagram presented in
section 3.2.S.2.2 of the dossier. A detailed list on changes performed is provided below.

The S.2.2.02 reaction scheme of step 2a was updated to indicate the use of activated charcoal.
Moreover, the reaction scheme of step 2b was updated to reflect the use of potable water.
The S.2.2.02 reaction scheme of step 4a was updated to indicate the optional addition of Gd-
Glydonip seeds. The Flow Diagram shown in S.2.2.01 was amended as well accordingly. Moreover,
it was noticed that “activated charcoal” was described as “charcoal” in the narrative description of
step 4d, which was corrected.

b) Addition of sodium bromide
As was presented in S.2.6.01 in section 5.1.2.2, addition of sodium bromide to the step 1b process
is not relevant for the quality of Glyptac intermediate, but has an impact on the yield of the
isolated product. We acknowledge that by stating a PAR with a lower limit of 0 eq, it is not clear
whether the addition of sodium bromide is optional. The addition of sodium bromide at the setpoint
amount is a fixed part of the manufacturing process and is thus not optional. We therefore
modified the respective section in S.2.2.02 by tightening the PAR space to 0.1 eq – 0.75 eq as
such:
Then, the mixture is cooled, filtered and 17.2 kg (0.25 eq) sodium bromide (PAR: 0.1 – 0.75 eq) is
added to the filtrate.
In addition, data from a PAR experiment performed using 0.1 eq NaBr was added to the respective
chapter in S.2.6.01.

c) Seeding with Gd-Glydonip
As was presented in S.2.6.01 in section 5.1.5, seeding in Step 4a is not relevant for the quality of
gadoquatrane drug substance, but has an impact on the yield and content of Gd-Glydonip as the
isolated product of Step 4a. This was also demonstrated during a commercial scale production
campaign, where out of 19 total batches Gd-Glydonip produced, 2 batches were not seeded during
manufacturing but still met acceptance criteria of in-process control 1. Consequently, the quality of
the resulting drug substance produced from these Gd-Glydonip batches was unaffected. Thus,
there is no criterion which steers if a batch is seeded or not, as the seeding operation itself is non-
critical. Nonetheless, due to the impact on the process step’s yield, the preferred production mode
includes seeding every batch. Due to the potential occurrence of isolated cases in which, strictly for
logistical reasons, seeding material cannot be supplied in time to support a tightly orchestrated
high-volume production campaign, the Applicant prefers to keep the option as it was demonstrated
that the seeding process is not mandatory but can be performed optionally depending on the
operational situation.

d) Stirring/Reaction times
Regarding stirring times of reactions, the manufacturing process descriptions S.2.2.02 follow two
concepts, which offer the same level of control on the conversion of reactants:
For steps 1 and 2, reactions are performed at fixed temperature setpoints and are stirred until the
associated in-process control on conversion indicates sufficient progress of the reaction. Thus, a
fixed stirring time is not specifically given since control is sufficient.

For the final Step 4a, a fixed temperature and stirring time is stated, which, in tandem with the
strict control of the critical process parameter in step 4a, governs the conversion. In-process
control 1 assures an appropriate level of conversion to the active ester Gd-Glydonip which is
subsequently reacted with neopentyltetramine hydrochloride (NPTA HCl). The fixed stirring time
(setpoint 2 h) and reaction temperature (setpoint 50 °C) control conversion to gadoquatrane crude
adequately to obtain the quality necessary for efficient final processing to the drug substance in
steps 4c and 4d.
Thus, the Applicant is of the opinion that adequate control of the chemical reactions is given as
stated in the S.2.2.02 Manufacturing descriptions and no adaption is required.

e) Recovery processes
Toluene is a solvent used in steps 1a/b as well as 2a of the manufacturing process. As part of the
processes, a distillation stream from solvent removal from the reaction mixture is recovered. The
recovered toluene is tested against the valid raw material specifications of toluene and, if the
quality testing indicates full compliance, this recovered stream may be used solely in the respective
process step from which the solvent was recovered. A risk assessment in regard to potential
impurities in the recovered toluene concluded that the release of recovered solvent using the raw
material specification is sufficient to safeguard quality of the drug substance.
To indicate this, the respective manufacturing descriptions S.2.2.02 were amended with footnotes
that describe the process, as well as detailed risk assessments in S.2.6.01 chapters 5.1.2.2 and
5.1.3.2.

f) Reprocessing procedures
The Applicant proposes to amend the reprocessing statements as follows to reflect the required 
criteria for reprocessing as well as the process description:

Step 1 a + b (Glyptac intermediate, DO3A Route):
Glyptac intermediate (DO3A Route) batches which do not comply with the release specification can 
be reprocessed by repeating the final crystallization step (isopropyl alcohol, n-heptane, washing 
with n-heptane and drying) using the failed batch as input material in place of crude glyptac.

Step 1 c + d (Glyptac intermediate, Cyglyp Route):
Glyptac intermediate (Cyglyp Route) batches which do not comply with the release specification 
can be reprocessed by repeating the final crystallization step (isopropyl alcohol, n-heptane, 
washing with n-heptane and drying) using the failed batch as input material in place of crude 
glyptac.

Step 2 (Gd-GlyMe-DOTA crude intermediate):
Gd-GlyMe-DOTA crude batches which do not comply with the release specification can be 
reprocessed by re-suspension of the material in ethanol, filtration, washing with ethanol, and 
subsequent drying.

Gd-GlyMe-DOTA intermediate batches which do not comply with the release specification can be 
reprocessed by repeating the step 3 process using the failed batch as input material.

Step 4 (Gadoquatrane drug substance):
Gd-Glydonip (Step 4a) batches that do not comply to in-process control 1 can be reprocessed by 
repeating the step 4a process using the failed batch as input material in place of Gd-GlyMe-DOTA 
intermediate.
Gadoquatrane drug substance batches which do not comply with the release specification can be 
reprocessed by repeating the steps 4c and 4d using the failed batch as input material in place of

The filter plate employed in the isolation of gadoquatrane drug substance may be, after removal of

diafiltration/ultrafiltration in step 4c.
These reprocessing procedures were added to the respective S.2.2.02 documents under the 
chapter “Reprocessing”.

Question:
Question 4
Some general points applying to all proposed starting materials should be clarified:
a) Regarding class 1, 2 or 3 impurities, if analysis on pilot/industrial scale batches or spiking
studies are necessary or have already been performed, results (including batch numbers if
possible) should be presented in tabulated format and the ability of the respective analytical
method to reliably detect the specific impurity should be demonstrated by method validation.
Moreover, purge factor calculations should be detailed and explained based on chemical reactivity,
solubility, volatility, ionizability, etc.
b) For several mutagenic impurities, spiking/purge studies show depletion of impurity content down
to <0.03% in a starting material or in an intermediate in the manufacturing process of
gadoquatrane. This value (300 ppm) is much higher than the concentration limit for mutagenic
impurities and is then not suitable. Purge to below the concentration limit for mutagenic impurities
should be demonstrated.
c) Brief descriptions of the analytical procedures used in the specification of the starting materials
as well as summarized validation results should be submitted.
d) Chemical names according to IUPAC should be provided for all specified impurities as a footnote
under each starting material specification. (S.2.3.)
Answer:
Applicant’s response:
a) As requested, additional information regarding potential genotoxic impurities in the starting
materials Glypro, Cyclen, and NPTA HCl is provided. The requested information is summarized in an
additional document (refer to S.2.6.11). This document includes:
1. Informative data on mutagenic impurities in commercial batches of each starting material.
2. Additional information on fate and purge experiments.
3. Detailed fate and purge calculations for potential mutagenic impurities.
Furthermore, the document summarizes analytical information on the methods used and their
suitability for monitoring potential mutagenic impurities in commercial batches and in spiking
experiments
b) ICH M7 outlines different potential approaches to control mutagenic impurities in drug substance
synthesis. The mutagenic impurities in the starting materials Glypro, Cyclen, and NPTA HCl are
controlled according to Option 4 of the ICH M7 guideline. This option allows for the control of
potential mutagenic impurities based on predictive purge calculations. If Option 4 is applied as the
control strategy for mutagenic impurities, the predictive purge calculations based on scientific
principles (e.g., impurity reactivity or solubility) should result in impurity levels of < 1% of the
acceptable intake (EMA/CHMP/ICH/321999/2020). This requirement is met for all potential
mutagenic impurities in the synthesis of the Gadoquatrane drug substance, with each purge ratio
exceeding 1000. The calculated purge ratios and the control strategy according to option 4 are
outlined in S.3.2.01 for each potential mutagenic impurity in the synthesis of Gadoquatrane drug
substance. Additionally, detailed calculations of the purge ratios are presented in S.2.6.11, as
requested by the rapporteur.
For certain mutagenic impurities in Glypro, Cyclen, and NPTA, spiking experiments have been
conducted in addition to the purge ratio calculations, as advised by the EMA guideline
EMA/CHMP/ICH/321999/2020. These studies experimentally investigate the fate of each impurity
and the formation of potential downstream products, which may also be non-mutagenic but could
still impact the quality of the downstream intermediates. Depending on the entry point of the
mutagenic impurity, the synthesis was performed towards a suitable intermediate for analysis. For
early starting materials like Cyclen and Glypro, spiking experiments were conducted up to Glyptac
or Gd-GlyMe-DOTA, with subsequent evaluation of their quality. Since both intermediates undergo
several purification steps before the final drug substance, it is not necessary to demonstrate
absence below 10% of the respective acceptable intake for these intermediates.
In the case of NPTA HCl, additional spiking studies for potential mutagenic impurities were
conducted as requested by the rapporteur in Question 8. Given that NPTA HCl is introduced later in
the synthesis process and spiking experiments were conducted up to the Gadoquatrane drug
substance, it has been proven that the absence of these impurities is below 10% of the acceptable
intake. All spiking experiments are described in S.2.3.03 and additional information is provided in
S.2.6.11.
Even though, spiking studies for early introduced potential mutagenic impurities have not been
conducted up to the final drug substance our purge ratio calculations clearly demonstrate that all
mutagenic impurities are sufficiently reduced below the acceptable intake levels. These calculations
fulfil the requirements set forth by ICH M7, showing that in each case, the calculated purge is a
factor of 1000 lower than the required purge. Based on this data, we assert that our current
approach is adequate and compliant with regulatory standards.
c) Descriptions of the chromatographic methods used for the impurity testing of the starting
presented as S.2.3.05 documents. The summary of the respective analytical validation is presented
in S.2.3.06 documents.
d) Chemical names according to IUPAC are provided for all specified impurities as a footnote under
the starting material specifications of Glypro chemical and Neopentyltetramine hydrochloride
chemical. Please refer to updated S.2.3.08 documents. The specification for starting material
Cyclen chemical does not contain specified impurities and the impurities listed in Gadolinium oxide
chemical specification are chemically defined elemental impurities that do not need further
clarification.

Question:
Question 1
The proposed starting material, Phenyl-oxodihydropyridine-carbothioamide is not considered 
to be acceptable. In line with ICH guideline Q11 (EMA/CHMP/ICH/425213/2011) critical 
steps such as major chemical transformations which introduce essential molecular structural 
fragments should be included within scope. The manufacturing process should therefore be 
described from further back in the synthesis. 3-chloro-2-methoxyaniline and tert-butyl 2,4-
dioxopiperidine-1-carboxylate could be suitable starting materials. The appropriate sections of 
the dossier should be comprehensively revised in order to reflect this change. It should also be 
noted that if a new manufacturing site is subsequently required, a revised QP declaration should 
be provided.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (S.2):
During development of the control strategy, the synthesis route of the Starting Material Phenyl-
oxodihydropyridine-carbothioamide as shown in S.2.3.04 Flow Chart of the Starting Material 
was carefully evaluated. In this evaluation, no critical steps, potentially affecting the drug 
substance quality, were identified in the synthesis route leading to the starting material. The 
proposed starting material is synthesized from the two precursor 3-chloro-2-methoxyaniline 
and 
tert-butyl 
2,4-dioxopiperidine-1-carboxylate 
forming 
Phenyl-oxodihydropyridine-
carbothioamide by custom synthesis. Within ICH Q11 it is clearly stated that chemicals made 
from custom synthesis can be proposed as starting material if the selection is justified in 
accordance with all general principles for the selection of the starting materials. In addition, 
“significant structural fragment” is defined within the guideline only to distinguish starting 
materials from reagents, solvents, or other raw materials but major chemical transformations 
are not explicitly mentioned as a limiting factor.
Therefore, Phenyl-oxodihydropyridine-carbothioamide was selected as proposed starting 
material from custom synthesis as the properties and excellent quality of Phenyl-
oxodihydropyridine-carbothioamide are in line with the criteria from the guidelines 
EMA/454576/2016 and ICH Q11 as follows:
The proposed starting material Phenyl-oxodihydropyridine-carbothioamide forms a significant 
structural fragment of BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance. The material is a 
stable solid with defined chemical properties and structure, of excellent quality and fully 
characterized. The limit for any unspecified impurities of 0.10% already represents drug 
substance specification quality. Except for the specified impurities, no further impurities are 
observed above the reporting threshold of 0.05%. The analytical method is fully validated and 
selective to monitor further potential impurities next to the specified impurities (see also S.2.3.05 Control of Materials - Starting Materials - Test Procedure / Phenyl-
oxodihydropyridine-carbothioamide chemical).
The starting material manufacturing process delivered consistent impurity profiles. The 
specified impurities in those batches are well understood and characterized. Fate & Purge 
studies clearly demonstrate that no specified impurities in the starting material or their 
derivatives are present in BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance (see also S.2.3.03 
– Justification of the Starting Materials and S.2.6.11- Manufacturing Process - Additional 
Information).
In addition, the starting material will only be obtained from qualified suppliers who 
manufacture the regulatory starting material according to the documentation cited in S.2.3.04 
Flow Chart of the Starting Material.
To demonstrate the consistent quality, the batch data for Phenyl-oxodihydropyridine-
carbothioamide is presented in S.2.3.10 Control of Materials - Starting Materials - Batch 
Analyses and is also provided below.
Table 1: Batch data for Phenyl-oxodihydropyridine-carbothioamide
[...table content as provided in DOCUMENT...]
In addition to the reproducible, API-like quality for the proposed starting material, Phenyl-
oxodihydropyridine-carbothioamide, two additional synthesis steps are implemented. These 
include isolation after crystallization and two additional crystallization steps to control 
impurities and polymorphism. This approach, starting from the two starting materials to BAY 
2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance ensures an excellent purge of potential impurities 
up to the final drug substance.
All organic impurities and solvents specified for the starting material Phenyl-
oxodihydropyridine-carbothioamide are completely depleted in the subsequent steps and the 
final processing of the drug substance. No impurity of the starting material is carried over to 
the drug substance. All provided details underline the suitability of Phenyl-oxodihydropyridine-
carbothioamide as acceptable proposed regulatory starting material.
