Question:
Question 2
Regarding the characterisation data provided for the selected form of the drug substance, 
Hydrate 1 Mod. A, the following points should be addressed satisfactorily and supported by 
adequate data:
a) XRPD was presented for the different polymorphic, hydrates and solvated forms, however it 
is difficult to compare the diffractograms when these are presented individually. An overlay of 
the XRPD diffractograms for the different forms should be provided. Furthermore, a complete 
list of the respective peaks, including the characteristic peaks for each of the forms, should also 
be presented in a tabulated format.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2a (S.3):
An overlay of the XRPD patterns of reflections for the various solid-state forms are compiled 
below Figure 1. Unfortunately, it is not possible to name characteristic reflections due to the 
large number of crystalline forms that frequently overlap. Nevertheless, the patterns as a whole 
are characteristic of each solid-state form, but individual reflections are not.
The individual data points of the peak maxima of the reflections for each solid-state form are 
presented in S.3.1.01_IQMS_408096_2.0 BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance 
(Additional Information on Polymorphism), see Tables 2-1, 2-2 and 2-3.

Question:
Question 2b
Characterisation of Hydrate 1 Mod. A using variable relative humidity (RH) - XRPD is required 
in order to understand the behaviour of this nonstoichiometric hydrate under different moisture 
conditions.
Answer:
Bayer Response to 2b:
In RH XRPD experiments, the behaviour of the crystalline lattice of Hydrate 1 Mod. A was 
examined under different humidity conditions (0 – 90% RH sorption and desorption in 10% 
steps) at a constant temperature of 25°C. In the sorption experiment, the substance (Hydrate 1 
Mod. A, Batch BXR9J78) was initially dried at 0% humidity and was present as Mod. IV at 1% 
RH. This modification was retained up to 20% RH and converted in the next step to Hydrate 1 
Mod. A. This crystal lattice then remained unchanged up to 90% RH. This effect was also 
observed in the desorption experiment: At 20% RH, Hydrate 1 Mod. A was converted to the 
anhydrous form Mod. IV. These experiments clearly demonstrate the behaviour of Hydrate 1 
Mod. A in a kinetic experimental design. It cannot be directly correlated with the results of the 
storage studies, as these are based on a thermodynamic approach.
The overlays of the XRPD pattern of the sorption and desorption RH XRPD measurements are 
presented in S.3.1.01_IQMS_408096_2.0 BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance 
(Additional Information on Polymorphism), see Figure 3-1 and 3-2.

Question:
Question 2c
The DVS results should be further discussed. It is noted that although the sorption and 
desorption events are to some extent reversible, these curves are not superimposable, suggesting 
that there may be a change in the structure during the process, such as a phase transition or a 
change in the way water is bound. The results should be discussed in conjunction with the X-
ray single crystallography and variable RH-XRPD results.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2c:
The RH XRPD results perfectly match the data from the DVS measurements, which gives us 
information on the change of water amount in and on the sample BXR9J78 (Hydrate 1 Mod. 
A). Dynamic uptake (sorption) of water was observed between 0 and 10% RH, followed by a 
flatter curve up to 95% RH and a total water uptake of 4%. The desorption curve follows this 
curve in the opposite direction, not without exhibiting a slight hysteresis. This is due to the fact 
that even in a variable non-stoichiometric hydrate, intermolecular interactions must first be 
overcome to remove the water from the lattice. This process, as well as the formation of the 
crystal lattice of the metastable Mod. IV, slightly delays the kinetics of desorption compared to 
sorption (see Figure 2 below).

Question:
Question 2d
The transitions observed in the DSC thermogram (Figure 5-2) should be discussed.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2d:
Another technique for investigating the behaviour of Hydrate 1 Mod. A upon loss of water is 
through thermoanalytical methods. In this case, Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) and 
Thermogravimetry (TGA) techniques were used. The thermogram of the DSC measurement 
(see below Figure 3) of sample BXR9J78 (Hydrate 1 Mod. A) initially displays a broad 
endothermic signal, indicating water release. This observation is confirmed by the TGA 
measurement, which describes a corresponding mass loss. Unlike stoichiometric hydrates, this 
stage is somewhat gradual and continuous, clearly highlighting the non-stoichiometric character 
of the hydrate. After the water release, the sample fundamentally has the possibility to become 
amorphous or to convert into any of the crystal lattices of the anhydrous modifications, thereby 
slightly stabilizing the lattice. In this case, a further small endothermic process is observed at 
higher temperatures, followed by a similarly small exothermic process. This involves the 
melting and recrystallization of one of the formed anhydrous forms, followed by the melting 
process of Mod. I. Compared to the previously described techniques, the DSC measurement is 
energetically non-neutral for the applied sample and can thus significantly favour 
transformation processes, especially at higher temperatures. This leads to the observation of the 
melting point of Mod. I, while the kinetic experiments (RH XRPD and DVS) did not result in 
a transformation of Hydrate 1 Mod. A to Mod. I. (see Figure 3).

Question:
Question 1
The submitted risk assessments concerning the possible formation and presence of nitrosamines in 
the drug substance and finished product are not detailed enough and should therefore be revised.
Regarding the drug substance, the following points should be clarified:
a) It has not been mentioned that 4-Nitrophenol will be released in stoichiometric amounts during 
step 4b formation of intermediate Gadoquatrane crude where also nucleophilic hydroxide anions 
will be present (basification using aqueous sodium hydroxide). The applicant should therefore 
appropriately address potential de-nitration during this step of the synthesis. If de-nitration cannot 
unambiguously be ruled out, confirmatory testing should be performed, e.g. concerning potential 
nitrosamine derivatives of relevant impurities like heptamine, secondary amines stemming from 
diisopropylethylamine or synthesis intermediates, etc.
b) Regarding the potential nitrosamine contamination of starting material NPTA HCl, the applicant 
focusses on the reduction of nitrite impurities in sodium azide and potential NDMA during the 
hydrogenation step. Nevertheless, this is solely a theoretical claim, and relevant data, e.g. 
concerning actual nitrite content in sodium azide, should be provided for further justification. If 
necessary, confirmatory testing should be performed to rule out the presence of NDMA as well as 
nitrosamine derivatives of heptamine.
c) If confirmatory testing is necessary, suitably validated analytical methods should be used as 
described in Q&A paper EMA/409815/2020.
Regarding the finished product, the following points should be clarified:
d) In the risk assessment on the presence of nitrosamine impurities in the drug product under 
review it is indicated that supportive documentation on the excipients and container closure system 
of the drug product is available. These documents should be provided.
e) The applicant has indicated that the presence of nitrosating agents, nitrosamines or vulnerable 
amines in the API is excluded. However, some points for clarification have been identified (see

a) We acknowledge the Rapporteur’s comment that a risk assessment concerning the possibility of
4-Nitrophenol denitration under the aqueous basic conditions in Step 4b is missing. In the
following, we will address this concern:
As stated in S.3.2.07, 4-Nitrophenol does not represent a particularly electron-poor nitro arene. 
Therefore, it is not - even in the presence of strong nucleophiles - susceptible to a denitration 
reaction. In theory, such a reaction would proceed via a nucleophilic aromatic substitution reaction 
(SNAr) in the case of 4-Nitrophenol.

As illustrated in Scheme 1, the key reaction intermediate – in the literature commonly referred to 
as Meisenheimer complex – is a negatively charged arene. Stabilization of the negative charge in 
the Meisenheimer complex, typically via multiple electron-withdrawing substituents, would be 
required for the denitration reaction to proceed at a reasonable rate. In the case of the 4-
Nitrophenol substitution pattern, said strongly electron-withdrawing substitution pattern is not 
given. Thus, a productive denitration pathway is not favored. 
To further substantiate our assessment that there is no risk of denitration of 4-Nitrophenol in an 
aqueous, sodium hydroxide containing medium, the acidity of 4-Nitrophenol shall be taken into 
account. It is well-established in the literature that 4-Nitrophenol is a fairly acidic compound, with a 
pKa value of ~ 7.15 owing to the acidity of the phenolic proton. Thus, the species prevalent in the 
basic aqueous reaction mixture is the negatively charged 4-Nitrophenolate anion (see Scheme 2)
Owing to the strongly electron donating properties of the phenoxide group (which already includes 
a negative charge), the formation of a Meisenheimer complex after nucleophilic attack of hydroxide 
is not possible. Consequently, denitration is not possible. 
To conclude, there is no risk of nitrite formation from 4-Nitrophenol during step 4b.

Data regarding the already mentioned experimental determination of complexation constants, DTF
calculations, comparison with Gadobutrol, calculations with various residues, etc. and a discussion
thereof should be provided. (S.1)
Answer:
Applicant’s response:
Due to the complexity of the molecule and very slow dissociation kinetics even at low pH, the 
experimental determination of complexation constants is not feasible by established methods. In 
the following we would like to present the details of the computational experiments performed.
Description and discussion of the computational approach to assess the Gadoquatrane 
thermodynamic complex stability by density functional theory (DFT) calculations on monomeric 
units with different residues:
- 
The gadoquatrane molecule, due to its tetrameric structure (C81H128N24O32Gd4) is too large 
to be described by accurate quantum-chemical methods. Therefore, to computationally 
assess the complex stability of Gadoquatrane, a number of model compounds were
considered. We calculated the complex free energy, ∆GComplex Formation, of a series of 
gadolinium chelates with known stability constants and compared them to two derivatives 
which contain the monomeric unit of gadoquatrane with different residue chain lengths. 
These model compounds are shown as “Gadoquatrane-Unit I” and “Unit II” in Figure 2. 
Both model compounds were constructed as fragments of the entire gadoquatrane 
molecule with varying length of the linker connecting the monomers in a tetramer and were 
selected to investigate the influence of the linker atoms on the overall complex stability.
Figure 2: Chemical structures of the gadoquatrane tetramer (left) and the two
monomeric Gadoquatrane model units (middle and right) used to assess the
thermodynamic complex stability constant log kGdL
= R
Structure Gadoquatrane
Gadoquatrane-Unit I
Gadoquatrane-Unit II

- 
The applied computational methods are suited to calculate thermodynamic stabilities of the 
Gd complex, but not their kinetic stabilities.
- 
Complex free energies were calculated via: ∆GComplex Formation = G(ML+H2O)-G(M)-G(L)-
G(H2O); where G(ML+H2O) is the entropy corrected energy of a gadolinium metal-ligand 
complex including one water molecule, G(M) is the energy of a single gadolinium ion Gd3+, 
G(L) is the free energy of the free ligand, and G(H2O) is the free energy of a single water 
molecule. Energies were calculated via density functional theory (DFT) calculations after a 
semiempirical conformational search, followed by a DFT geometry optimization with implicit 
solvation. Further details of employed computational methods, basis sets, and solvation 
model are summarized in [1].
- 
All calculations were performed using the ORCA software package, version 6.0.1 [2].
- 
As shown in Figure 2, the calculated complex free energies of both model compounds 
(monomeric gadoquatrane units) lie in a similar energy range as for gadobutrol 
(Gadovist®), indicating that the thermodynamic complex stability constant, log kGdL, of 
gadoquatrane is well above 20 with negligible influence from varying the residue.

Figure 3: Comparison of the measured complex stability constant to the calculated free 
energy of complex formation for a series of gadolinium chelates

Comparison of the measured complex stability constant, log kGdL (left panel), to the calculated 
free energy of complex formation, ∆GComplex Formation in kcal/mol (right panel), for a series of 
gadolinium chelates. Lower free energy values correspond to higher complex stability constants 
(see Figure 3). Experimental reference value for the gadolinium chelates with known stability 
values were taken from Port et al. 2008 [3].
In conclusion the complex stability of each single Gadoquatrane unit is highly comparable with the 
complex stability of gadobutrol. The small variation in calculated complex stability between the two 
model units further indicates that the linker atoms, which connect the monomers in a tetramer 
unit, have little influence on the overall stability. Thus, the complex stability of the gadoquatrane 
tetramer is primarily driven by the sub-unit stability which is comparable to gadobutrol.

c) Seeding with Gd-Glydonip
As was presented in S.2.6.01 in section 5.1.5, seeding in Step 4a is not relevant for the quality of

control 1 assures an appropriate level of conversion to the active ester Gd-Glydonip which is
subsequently reacted with neopentyltetramine hydrochloride (NPTA HCl). The fixed stirring time
(setpoint 2 h) and reaction temperature (setpoint 50 °C) control conversion to gadoquatrane crude
adequately to obtain the quality necessary for efficient final processing to the drug substance in
steps 4c and 4d.
Thus, the Applicant is of the opinion that adequate control of the chemical reactions is given as
stated in the S.2.2.02 Manufacturing descriptions and no adaption is required.

e) Recovery processes
Toluene is a solvent used in steps 1a/b as well as 2a of the manufacturing process. As part of the
processes, a distillation stream from solvent removal from the reaction mixture is recovered. The
recovered toluene is tested against the valid raw material specifications of toluene and, if the
quality testing indicates full compliance, this recovered stream may be used solely in the respective
process step from which the solvent was recovered. A risk assessment in regard to potential
impurities in the recovered toluene concluded that the release of recovered solvent using the raw
material specification is sufficient to safeguard quality of the drug substance.
To indicate this, the respective manufacturing descriptions S.2.2.02 were amended with footnotes
that describe the process, as well as detailed risk assessments in S.2.6.01 chapters 5.1.2.2 and
5.1.3.2.

f) Reprocessing procedures
The Applicant proposes to amend the reprocessing statements as follows to reflect the required 
criteria for reprocessing as well as the process description:

Step 1 a + b (Glyptac intermediate, DO3A Route):
Glyptac intermediate (DO3A Route) batches which do not comply with the release specification can 
be reprocessed by repeating the final crystallization step (isopropyl alcohol, n-heptane, washing 
with n-heptane and drying) using the failed batch as input material in place of crude glyptac.

Step 1 c + d (Glyptac intermediate, Cyglyp Route):
Glyptac intermediate (Cyglyp Route) batches which do not comply with the release specification 
can be reprocessed by repeating the final crystallization step (isopropyl alcohol, n-heptane, 
washing with n-heptane and drying) using the failed batch as input material in place of crude 
glyptac.

Step 2 (Gd-GlyMe-DOTA crude intermediate):
Gd-GlyMe-DOTA crude batches which do not comply with the release specification can be 
reprocessed by re-suspension of the material in ethanol, filtration, washing with ethanol, and 
subsequent drying.

Gd-GlyMe-DOTA intermediate batches which do not comply with the release specification can be 
reprocessed by repeating the step 3 process using the failed batch as input material.

Step 4 (Gadoquatrane drug substance):
Gd-Glydonip (Step 4a) batches that do not comply to in-process control 1 can be reprocessed by 
repeating the step 4a process using the failed batch as input material in place of Gd-GlyMe-DOTA 
intermediate.
Gadoquatrane drug substance batches which do not comply with the release specification can be 
reprocessed by repeating the steps 4c and 4d using the failed batch as input material in place of 
Gadoquatrane crude.
The filter plate employed in the isolation of gadoquatrane drug substance may be, after removal of 
the bulk material, rinsed with purified water and the obtained solution of gadoquatrane drug 
substance can be added to the solution of gadoquatrane crude before purification via 
diafiltration/ultrafiltration in step 4c.
These reprocessing procedures were added to the respective S.2.2.02 documents under the 
chapter “Reprocessing”.

g) CPP highlighting
We modified the manufacturing descriptions S.2.2.02 of the steps 2, 3 and 4 accordingly to
highlight critical steps, as well as the individual critical process parameters according to table 3-1 in
S.2.4.01.

h) Gaseous water and potable vs. purified water
Gaseous water as described in S.2.2.02 is produced from purified water. In the manufacturing
setting, purified water is evaporated to gaseous water directly at the point of use in a separate
vessel to be directly transferred to the dryer. We amended the manufacturing description to reflect
the origin of gaseous water from purified water.
Moreover, all Flow Diagrams shown in S.2.2.01 and S.2.2.02 as well as the narrative descriptions
in respective S.2.2.02 were amended to reflect if potable, or purified water is employed.

Question:
Question 4
Some general points applying to all proposed starting materials should be clarified:
a) Regarding class 1, 2 or 3 impurities, if analysis on pilot/industrial scale batches or spiking
studies are necessary or have already been performed, results (including batch numbers if
possible) should be presented in tabulated format and the ability of the respective analytical
method to reliably detect the specific impurity should be demonstrated by method validation.
Moreover, purge factor calculations should be detailed and explained based on chemical reactivity,
solubility, volatility, ionizability, etc.
b) For several mutagenic impurities, spiking/purge studies show depletion of impurity content down
to <0.03% in a starting material or in an intermediate in the manufacturing process of
gadoquatrane. This value (300 ppm) is much higher than the concentration limit for mutagenic
impurities and is then not suitable. Purge to below the concentration limit for mutagenic impurities
should be demonstrated.
c) Brief descriptions of the analytical procedures used in the specification of the starting materials
as well as summarized validation results should be submitted.
d) Chemical names according to IUPAC should be provided for all specified impurities as a footnote
under each starting material specification. (S.2.3.)
Answer:
Applicant’s response:
a) As requested, additional information regarding potential genotoxic impurities in the starting
materials Glypro, Cyclen, and NPTA HCl is provided. The requested information is summarized in an
additional document (refer to S.2.6.11). This document includes:
1. Informative data on mutagenic impurities in commercial batches of each starting material.
2. Additional information on fate and purge experiments.
3. Detailed fate and purge calculations for potential mutagenic impurities.
Furthermore, the document summarizes analytical information on the methods used and their
suitability for monitoring potential mutagenic impurities in commercial batches and in spiking
experiments
b) ICH M7 outlines different potential approaches to control mutagenic impurities in drug substance
synthesis. The mutagenic impurities in the starting materials Glypro, Cyclen, and NPTA HCl are
controlled according to Option 4 of the ICH M7 guideline. This option allows for the control of
potential mutagenic impurities based on predictive purge calculations. If Option 4 is applied as the
control strategy for mutagenic impurities, the predictive purge calculations based on scientific
principles (e.g., impurity reactivity or solubility) should result in impurity levels of < 1% of the
acceptable intake (EMA/CHMP/ICH/321999/2020). This requirement is met for all potential
mutagenic impurities in the synthesis of the Gadoquatrane drug substance, with each purge ratio
exceeding 1000. The calculated purge ratios and the control strategy according to option 4 are
outlined in S.3.2.01 for each potential mutagenic impurity in the synthesis of Gadoquatrane drug
substance. Additionally, detailed calculations of the purge ratios are presented in S.2.6.11, as
requested by the rapporteur.
For certain mutagenic impurities in Glypro, Cyclen, and NPTA, spiking experiments have been
conducted in addition to the purge ratio calculations, as advised by the EMA guideline
EMA/CHMP/ICH/321999/2020. These studies experimentally investigate the fate of each impurity
and the formation of potential downstream products, which may also be non-mutagenic but could
still impact the quality of the downstream intermediates. Depending on the entry point of the
mutagenic impurity, the synthesis was performed towards a suitable intermediate for analysis. For
early starting materials like Cyclen and Glypro, spiking experiments were conducted up to Glyptac
or Gd-GlyMe-DOTA, with subsequent evaluation of their quality. Since both intermediates undergo
several purification steps before the final drug substance, it is not necessary to demonstrate
absence below 10% of the respective acceptable intake for these intermediates.
In the case of NPTA HCl, additional spiking studies for potential mutagenic impurities were
conducted as requested by the rapporteur in Question 8. Given that NPTA HCl is introduced later in
the synthesis process and spiking experiments were conducted up to the Gadoquatrane drug
substance, it has been proven that the absence of these impurities is below 10% of the acceptable
intake. All spiking experiments are described in S.2.3.03 and additional information is provided in
S.2.6.11.
Even though, spiking studies for early introduced potential mutagenic impurities have not been
conducted up to the final drug substance our purge ratio calculations clearly demonstrate that all
mutagenic impurities are sufficiently reduced below the acceptable intake levels. These calculations
fulfil the requirements set forth by ICH M7, showing that in each case, the calculated purge is a
factor of 1000 lower than the required purge. Based on this data, we assert that our current
approach is adequate and compliant with regulatory standards.
c) Descriptions of the chromatographic methods used for the impurity testing of the starting
presented as S.2.3.05 documents. The summary of the respective analytical validation is presented
in S.2.3.06 documents.
d) Chemical names according to IUPAC are provided for all specified impurities as a footnote under
the starting material specifications of Glypro chemical and Neopentyltetramine hydrochloride
chemical. Please refer to updated S.2.3.08 documents. The specification for starting material
Cyclen chemical does not contain specified impurities and the impurities listed in Gadolinium oxide
chemical specification are chemically defined elemental impurities that do not need further
clarification.

Handling of Warning and Action Limit Exceedances in Environmental and Utilities 
Monitoring
1. Warning limit
If a warning limit exceedance occurs, the Head of Manufacturing, Quality Assurance, and the 
responsible Monitoring Officer must be informed immediately.
A repeat test must be performed within 5 working days at the same sampling point unless it 
has already been performed.
The trend of the affected system is reviewed and assessed to determine whether it is an 
isolated event or a negative trend. If applicable, microbial identification is performed and 
evaluated.
If an isolated event is confirmed, no further action is required. 
 If a negative trend is identified, or if the warning limit is exceeded three times consecutively 
at the same sampling point, this is considered an action limit exceedance, and measures 
equivalent to those for action limit exceedances must be initiated.
The assessment results and the repeat test must be documented in the monitoring database.
2. Action Limit
If an action limit exceedance occurs, the Head of Manufacturing, Quality Assurance, 
Engineering, and the Monitoring Officer must be informed immediately.
A repeat test must be performed within 1 working day at the same sampling point unless 
already completed.
A deviation must be created in the deviation management system, and an investigation must 
be initiated. The investigation involves the monitoring officer, the laboratory, production, 
engineering, and Quality Assurance.
The following results must be included in the root cause analysis:
• At least one repeat test (within 1 working day if no subsequent routine test has already
occurred)
• Review of trends at the sampling point and surrounding area 
• Microbial identification 
• Review of logbooks and batch documentation 
• Review of cleaning/disinfection measures 
• Discussions with personnel involved in the production of the affected batch 
• Discussions with the sampler 
• Technical inspection of the affected equipment
The investigation results must be available within 10 calendar days, or 15 days if microbial 
identification is required.
Possible measures following root cause identification include:
• Cleaning, disinfection, sanitization to eliminate contamination sources 
• Changing or adjusting disinfectant concentration 
• Modifying operating procedures 
• Technical modifications 
• Additional staff training 
• Changes to the gowning concept 
• Adjusting cleaning/disinfection frequency

An assessment must always be performed to determine whether product quality may have 
been impacted. The deviation is classified as minor, major, or critical.

Question:
Question 2
We acknowledge that pre-sterilization bioburden testing is performed during 
manufacturing of Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection, and the in-
process bulk bioburden sample is collected after filtration (p.6-7 and p.36/46 of 
manufacturing-process-iqms-412963_30.pdf). Further, it is noted on p.8/17 of document 
‘justification-specification022993012-parametric-release.pdf’, under section 3.2.P.5.6., 
that a second 0.2 μm filtration step is implemented in-line immediately before filling the 
final product containers. Bioburden is indicated to be tested before the second filtration. 
However, the agency requests that bioburden sampling be performed prior to any 
filtration step to control for potentially high bioburden in the un-filtered bulk solution, 
which could produce high levels of endotoxins, microbial metabolites, and/or proteins 
and may not be removed by filtration or terminal sterilization. Additionally, the subject
drug product is growth promotive as observed in the microbial challenge study 
(pharmaceutical-development-holding-time-iqms-412961_10.pdf).
Therefore, address the following:
a. Clarify the number of filtration steps during manufacturing.

b. Propose bioburden sampling prior to any filtration step and indicate the
corresponding alert/ action levels and acceptance criterion for bulk drug solution
bioburden. Provide justification for the bioburden limit prior to any filtration step
based on historical knowledge of the manufacturing process.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2a ( 3.2.P.5.6.):
As indicated in figure 6-1 and figure 6-2 in P.5.6.01_ IQMS- 426579_2.0 Justification of 
Specification / Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection (Parametric Release) 
(stated as P.5.6.01_2.0 (PR) in the remainer of the document) the Gadoquatrane 0.4 mmol 
Gd/mL production process involves two filtration steps, followed by final sterilization of 
filled containers.
The first filtration step takes place during bulk manufacturing during the final bulk solution 
transfer from formulation container into the storage container.
The second filtration step is performed right before filling into the filling line.

Source:  P.5.6.01_ IQMS-426579_2.0 Justification of Specification / Gadoquatrane
solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection (Parametric Release) (amended)

Bayer Response to Question 2b (3.2.P.5.6.):
Bayer acknowledges the Agency’s recommendation to propose bioburden sampling prior to 
any filtration step and indicate the corresponding alert/ action levels and acceptance criterion 
for bulk drug solution bioburden. We would like to emphasize that rigorous monitoring and 
quality control measures are implemented during the production of Gadoquatrane solution to 
ensure its sterility and microbiological quality prior to microbial reduction steps. Key aspects 
include:
• Bioburden reduction: As stated in question 2a, two filtrations of the bulk solutions are
performed. The first one occurs during the transfer of the solution into the storage
containers, and the second one occurs before feeding the bulk solution in the
respective filling lines.
• Bioburden monitoring:
  o Two bioburden analysis prior to terminal sterilization (represented by IPC “last
filled container” and first filled container “Beginning of the batch”) and a
supplementary bioburden analysis for parametric release prior to last filtration
step (“Stored solution (holding time)”, “Before Refiltration”) where defined
and analyzed during development, validation and stability runs for
Gadoquatrane solution at line 1 and 8, see chapter 8.2.2, table 8-4 in
P.5.6.01_2.0 (PR).
  o The quality of similar drug products before sterilization complies with the
product specification. Supplementary monitoring shows the high
microbiological quality of each batch throughout the whole production process
and ensures that any quality-relevant deviation is addressed adequately.
Bioburden trend reports are generated biannually for each filling line in the
Supply Center Berlin (see chapter 8.1.2 and 8.2.2, P.5.6.01_2.0 (PR)).
• Contamination control strategy (CCS): A robust CCS (including good equipment and
facility design, procedures for cleaning, disinfection and sanitization, use of microbial
retentive filters, procedures for personnel hygiene and garment control,
microbiological specifications for raw materials, intermediates and process aids,
Nitrogen overlay of storage tank) and holding time restriction has been established,
supported by historical production data of sterile and endotoxin-free products.

Microbial Growth Control: Gadoquatrane solution was shown to be susceptible to the
growth of compendial microorganisms (esp. Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas
aeruginosa, ATCC). Historical data show that these compendial strains are not part of
the typical in-house flora. Occurrence of those microorganisms can be avoided by
following personal hygiene rules of cleanroom class D. The most likely source of
unlikely contamination would be production staff (skin flora). The estimated actual
microbial intake would be much lower than the inoculum used in the challenge test.
The tested in-house isolates, further exhibited much lower growth rates (5 fold in 48
h) than the compendial microorganisms, therefore reducing likelihood of microbial
growth as result of contamination of bulk solution in preparation vessel
(P.2.5.01_IQMS-426636_2.0).
• Historical Compliance: Historical endotoxin data from all terminally sterilized
products produced with line 1 and 8 meet the required standards, confirming the
effectiveness of the control measures in place (chapter 8.1.3, P.5.6.01_2.0 (PR)).
• Endotoxin and Metabolite Control: endotoxin levels are closely monitored as quality
attributes through:
  o Use of endotoxin-controlled materials (use of endotoxin-controlled WFI,
controlled API and packaging material)
  o A bacterial endotoxin IPC program during batch record reviews (bulk sample
in the preparation tank and an additional WFI sample).
  o Compliance with release and shelf-life specifications after terminal
sterilization
Additionally, an increase in endotoxin levels usually results from the thermal or manual
destruction of gram-negative cell walls. However, this scenario does not pertain to the
preparation of the bulk solution or the initial filtration step. As a result, any potential
endotoxin in the bulk preparation can be identified in subsequent endotoxin IPC or release
testing, making bioburden sampling prior to the first filtration step unnecessary.
The combination of rigorous bioburden testing, a robust contamination control strategy, and
historical compliance ensures the safe production of sterile Gadoquatrane solution. All
endotoxin levels and product specifications have been met during validation and stability
testing, confirming the effectiveness of the measures in place.

Question:
Question 5
Regarding the terminal sterilization of the drug product using the Belimed/ BST 14-8-12 
HS2 autoclave (inventory no. 136488), ... Address the following:
a. Describe the method of controlling the production cycle progression. Indicate the types of 
monitors used and the location of each within the chamber for monitoring the critical 
parameters during commercial production. Indicate how the critical parameters are controlled 
(e.g., by PLC)

b. Describe the proposed routine production loads for the subject drug 
product filled in 2 mL vials ...

c. ... Provide study data to support this 2 mL minimal load as the worst-case load ...

d. Identify the liquid contents of the validation load and explain how the contents
are representative of the drug product solution with respect to viscosity
and heat penetration.

e. ... Clarify whether 
the 12 external temperature sensors used for the studies represent heat 
distribution or heat penetration sensors. ...

f. ... Provide the number of heat penetration 
sensors and biological indicators used and describe the rationale for 
their placement within the load.

g. ... provide the results of a recent requalification study ...

h. Describe the requalification program for autoclave 136488 including the frequency, 
types of runs and load patterns, as applicable.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 5a ( 3.2.P.3.5.):
We acknowledge your request. We have an automated and qualified process control system 
(PCS) that ensures the correct execution of the complete sterilization process. The PCS is 
controlled and regulated by internal temperature sensors within the autoclave. The temperature
sensors are placed in reference containers which are designed to mimic the thermal behavior
and heat penetration of the objects being sterilized.
For the sterilization chamber of the Belimed/ BST 14-8-12 HS2 autoclave (inventory no.
136488), a total of three controlling temperature sensors are used. These sensors are evenly
distributed throughout the load being sterilized and regulate the transition between the
individual process steps (heating, sterilization, cooling phase). This distribution is justified on
the results in the equipment qualification, which showed no cold spots and a uniform heat
distribution.

Bayer Response to Question 5b ( 3.2.P.3.):
We acknowledge your request. The validations performed on the Belimed/BST 14-8-12 HS2
autoclave (inventory no. 136488) cover a load in routine production between the specified
minimum and maximum loads.
Table 4: Belimed/BST 14-8-12 HS2 autoclave 136488 - Minimum and Maximum load
description
Minimum load: 2 sterilization racks, 6 magazines each containing 200 2R vials/2 ml filling volume (1,200 pcs)
Maximum load: 2 sterilization racks, 60 magazines each containing 200 2R vials/2 ml filling volume (12,000 pcs)

Bayer Response to Question 5c ( 3.2.P.3.5.):
A bracketing concept was applied for the validation of sterilization process. For the maximal
load, the format/fill volume with the largest liquid quantity and highest heat exposure was
chosen. For the minimal load, the format/fill volume with the smallest liquid quantity and
lowest heat exposure, thus having the lowest physical F0 value, was selected as overall worst
case (e.g. for requalification). This approach ensures that all intermediate formats/fill volumes
are adequately covered between the specified minimum and maximum loads. The
Belimed/BST 14-8-12 HS2 autoclave (inventory no. 136488) is used for routine sterilization
of 2 mL vials exclusively.

Bayer Response to Question 5d ( 3.2.P.3.5.):
During validation loads, water for injection (WfI) is utilized as the liquid content for all
containers (vials, bottles and syringes). A study was conducted to analyze killing efficiency of
Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores inoculated in Gadoquatrane solution compared to WfI
by performing D121°C value determination under saturated steam conditions using survival
curve method according to DIN EN ISO 11138-1 and -11138-3 and viable spore count
according to USP (see P.3.5.01_022969750_01 (IQMS-243486_1.0) Process Validation
and/or Evaluation / BAY 1747846 solution 0.4 mol/L – note: BAY 1747846 solution 0.4 mol/L
(development code for Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/ mL)). The results show that
microbes are eradicated with comparable effectiveness in both WfI and Gadoquatrane
solution, independent of potential viscosity- or heat penetration differences. This finding
supports the justification for using WfI as the liquid content during validation.
Source:  P.3.5.01_022969750_01 (IQMS-243486_1.0) Process Validation and/or
Evaluation / BAY 1747846 solution 0.4 mol/L (new)

Bayer Response to Question 5e ( 3.2.P.3.5.):
We acknowledge your request. During the thermal temperature mapping and process
validation of the sterilization process for autoclave 136488, the external temperature sensors
used in the studies represent heat distribution. These sensors are “Kaye Thermoelements”,
Type T. We understand that no further summary reports are necessary. Based on the results
from the equipment qualification, no cold spots and a uniform heat distribution were shown.

Bayer Response to Question 5f ( 3.2.P.3.5.):
We acknowledge your request. The execution of the microbial effectiveness studies is
analogous to chapter 2.2, thermal qualification of the cycle in process-validation-022992945-
sterilization.pdf. Similarly, 12 biological indicators and 12 external temperature sensors (heat
distribution sensors) were used and distributed within the chamber to ensure a uniform
assessment according to figure 2-1 in chapter 2.2. This distribution is based on the results
from the equipment qualification, which showed no cold spots and a uniform heat distribution
within the sterilization chamber.
Source:
P.3.5.01_022992945_01 (IQMS IQMS-266428) Process Validation and/or
Evaluation / Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection (Sterilization
process) (amended to P.3.5.01_ IQMS_426644_2.0 due to other questions)

Bayer Response to Question 5g ( 3.2.P.3.5.):
We acknowledge your request. The initial performance of the thermal qualification and
microbial effectiveness studies reported in process-validation-022992945-sterilization.pdf was
conducted on 2023-08-31.
During the annual requalification program, the last requalification was performed on 2024-10-
24. The existing requalification data has been updated in P.3.5.01_ IQMS_426644_2.0. The
annual requalification from 2025 has not yet been finalized.
Source:
P.3.5.01_IQMS_426644_2.0 Process Validation and/or Evaluation /
Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection (Sterilization process) (amended)

We acknowledge your request. The requalification of the sterilization process for autoclave

Question:
Question 4
Please provide the scientific justification for not considering t-butyl bromoacetate as a starting 
material, although part of its structure is retained and contributes to the overall structure of the 
final drug substance.
Answer:
Response to Question 4 ( 3.2.S.2.3):
Selection of Starting Materials for the synthesis of Gadoquatrane drug substance was based 
on the guideline ICH Q11, the “Reflection paper on the requirements for selection and 
justification of starting materials for the manufacture of chemical active substances 
(EMA/448443/2014)” as well as scientific advice of regulatory authorities (EMA and FDA).
Several factors were considered together to ensure a thorough and comprehensive evaluation.

t-Butyl bromoacetate (TBBA) is employed to introduce a t-butyl acetyl group into the 
synthesis of the first intermediate, Glyptac (step 1). In the downstream chemistry, the t-butyl 
ester is cleaved (step 2), while the acetyl moiety remains in the molecule and contributes to 
the overall structure of the final drug substance Gadoquatrane.
According to ICH Q11 and EMA/448443/2014, a starting material is defined as a significant 
structural moiety that is incorporated into the drug substance structure. The term “significant 
structural fragment” is used to differentiate starting materials from reagents, solvents, or other 
raw materials. Commonly available chemicals used to create salts, esters, or other simple 
derivatives should be considered reagents. TBBA is a straightforward molecule that 
introduces a simple acetyl moiety. It is a commodity, widely available from multiple global 
chemical suppliers in the non-pharmaceutical market. Therefore, it is justified to define 
TBBA as raw material and not as starting material.
Figure 1 demonstrates the difference in the structural complexity of the starting materials 
Glypro, Cyclen, and TBBA. In contrast to Cyclen and Glypro, TBBA does not provide a 
complex structural feature like the ring provided by Cyclen or the stereocenter, which is a 
structural feature of Glypro. Thus, both Cyclen and Glypro provide significant structural 
fragments retained in the final Gadoquatrane drug substance, whereas the acetyl group 
provided by TBBA as alkylating reagent can be considered as a simple fragment not affecting 
a critical quality attribute of Gadoquatrane.

In addition, it is important to note that TBBA is used very early in the synthesis followed by 
multiple chemical steps and purification steps prior to the isolation of the final drug 
substance. The high number of downstream process steps provides numerous opportunities
for the depletion of impurities related to TBBA. Moreover, the raw material specification 
ensures that TBBA-related impurities do not affect the quality of the Gadoquatrane drug 
substance, regardless of the supplier or the production process applied to this raw material 
(see S.2.3.02). Typically observed organic impurities in TBBA that could potentially affect 
the quality of downstream intermediates are well understood. They are controlled by the limit 
for unspecified impurities (max 0.5%) in the raw material specification of TBBA, and a 
sufficient purge is ensured by fate and purge studies as well as purge calculations (refer to 
S.2.6.01, chapter 5.2.5. Potential impurities in step 1).
In conclusion, TBBA introduces an acetyl moiety in the drug substance, which is a simple 
fragment and should not be regarded as a significant structural fragment. This fact, combined 
with the understanding of impurities and the stringent control provided by the raw material 
specification, justifies the classification of TBBA as a raw material in accordance with ICH 
Q11.

Source:  S.2.3.02_022991191_01 (IQMS-260627) Raw Material – Specification / t-Butyl
bromoacetate chemical (Malladi) (unchanged)
S.2.6.01_022992795_01 (IQMS-260401) Manufacturing Process 
Development / Gadoquatrane drug substance (unchanged)

Question:
Question 6
With respect to the specification for Glypro,
a. We note that the batch analyses results for impurities presented in Table 1-1 for Batch Nos 
181B00624/724/824 are significantly lower than the proposed specifications and the declared 
maximum levels observed in commercial batches. Please tighten the following limits for the 
specification of Glypro as supported by the consistently low batch analyses results presented:
- Desbenzyl-Glypro
- P-toluenesulfonic acid
- Benzyl alcohol
- Dipropionic acid-Glypro
- Sum of propionic acid Glypro (Isomer 1 and 2)
b. Please tighten the limits for sum of all impurities and assay (calculated on anhydrous basis) 
accordingly.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 6 ( 3.2.S.2.3):
a. The requested tightening of the acceptance criteria for the starting material Glypro is 
comprehensible based on the batch data presented in the initially submitted 
S.2.3.10_022992310_01so far. However, the variability in batch data across all commercial 
Glypro batches produced to date is higher and justifies the specified limits for Glypro. In 
order to show the variation of batch data for Glypro, additional batches have been added to 
the batch overview in an updated S.2.3.10. Additionally, a justification for each parameter is 
provided below.
The impurities Desbenzyl-Glypro and Benzyl alcohol are formed upon hydrolysis of the 
benzyl ester motif in glypro. Desbenzyl-Glypro is controlled by the specification limit of max. 
1.0% in Glypro. As can be seen from the updated batch overview in S.2.3.10, Desbenzyl-
Glypro is typically found in commercial production at varying concentrations between 0.1% 
and 0.4%. Desbenzyl-Glypro has been studied during storage of Glypro. It has been found 
that at ambient temperature for six months, Desbenzyl-Glypro and also Benzyl alcohol level 
increased from not detectable up to 0.3%. Since the fate and purge experiments for 
Desbenzyl-Glypro have proven that even a level of 1.87% Desbenzyl-Glypro can be purged 
below the detection limit in Glyptac, it has been decided to specify the compound with max. 
1.0% in Glypro. At this level, any impact on the quality of Gadoquatrane drug substance is 
excluded, while also a robust production process is ensured.
Benzyl alcohol is a reagent used in the synthesis of Glypro. Moreover, the impurity is formed 
upon hydrolysis of the benzyl ester motif in Glypro. In the downstream synthesis (step 2) the 
impurity is formed by intended cleavage of the benzyl ester. It is controlled by the 
specification limit of max. 1.0% in Glypro. As can be seen from the updated batch overview 
in S.2.3.10, Benzyl alcohol is typically found in commercial Glypro production at a 
concentration of <0.03% up to 0.6%. As already described for Desbenzyl-Glypro, Benzyl 
alcohol has been studied during storage of Glypro. It has been found that at ambient 
temperature for six months, Benzyl alcohol level increased from 0.1% to 0.3%. Since the fate 
and purge experiments for Benzyl alcohol have proven that even a level of 1.2% Benzyl 
alcohol can be purged below the detection limit in Glyptac, it is justified to specify the
compound with max. 1.0% in Glypro. At this level, any impact on the quality of 
Gadoquatrane drug substance is excluded, while also ensuring a robust production process.
p-Toluene sulfonic acid (pTSA) is a process impurity which is formed in the synthesis of 
Glypro. It is controlled by the specification limit of max. 1.2% in Glypro. As can be seen 
from the updated batch overview in S.2.3.10, pTSA is typically found in commercial 
production at a concentration of 0.1% up to 1.1%. pTSA has been studied by fate and purge 
experiments and it has been proven that levels of 1.5% pTSA in Glypro can be purged below 
the detection limit in the downstream intermediates. Moreover, it has been demonstrated that 
the potential formation of mutagenic tosylate is excluded (isopropyl tosylate in Glyptac 
intermediate < 3ppm). Based on the batch data and the fate and purge data it is justified to 
specify pTSA with max. 1.2% in Glypro.
Propionic acid-Glypro Isomer 1 and 2 and Dipropionic acid-Glypro are byproducts formed in 
the synthesis of Glypro. As can be seen from the updated batch overview in S.2.3.10, the 
impurities are typically found in commercial production at a concentration level between 
<0.05% and 0.4%. Therefore, it is justified to set the specification limits to max. 0.6%. The 
specification limits are well covered by fate and purge data, showing that even 1.1% of the 
Propionic acid-Glypro can be purged in the downstream synthesis, without any impact on the 
quality of Gadoquatrane drug substance.

b. The limit for the sum of impurities of max. 3.0% is deduced from the sum of individually 
specified impurities. In total, seven impurities are specified individually, and the respective 
specification levels are in total 4.75%. Thus, the limit for the sum of impurities is already 
significantly lower than the sum of all individually specified impurities and ensures high 
quality, therefore the limit of 3.0% is justified. Additionally, the limit is supported based on 
commercial batch data, see S.2.3.10, typical batch data for the sum of impurities are found 
between 0.4 and 2.2%.. The limit ensures a robust process that delivers the required quality 
for the starting material Glypro.
The assay of Glypro is limited to 95.0-102.0%. The lower limit is justified by the analytical 
variation of +/- 2.0% as well as the limit for sum of all impurities (max. 3.0%).

Source:  S.2.3.10_IQMS-448651_2.0 Control of Materials - Starting Materials - Batch
Analysis / Glypro chemical (amended)

Question:
Question 7
With respect to the specification for neopentyltetramine hydrochloride,
a. Please tighten the specification for sum of all impurities and assay for neopentyltetramine 
hydrochloride (NPTA HCl) as supported by the batch analyses results presented.

b. Since neopentyltetramine hydrochloride (NPTA HCl) is added to the late synthetic process 
(Step 4), you are requested to provide supporting data for the justification of absence of 
controls of the residual solvents in the specification of NPTA HCl.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 7 ( 3.2.S.2.3):
a. As requested and based on the batch analyses results, the limit for the sum of impurities has 
been tightened from max. 1.0% to max. 0.4%, see updated S.2.3.08 and accordingly S.2.3.10. 
The new limit is deduced from the sum of individually specified impurity and the limit for 
any unspecified impurities. Heptamine is individually specified in NPTA HCl with max. 
0.10%. Any unspecified impurities are controlled at a limit of max. 0.05%. Potential 
impurities in NPTA HCl, which are controlled as any unspecified impurities, are discussed in 
S.2.3.03 and include for example Azetidine-diamine and N-acetyl-NPTA.
Accordingly, the limit of the assay (i.d.s) for NPTA HCl has been changed from 97.0% - 
102.0% to 98.0% - 101.5%.  This adjustment to the lower limit is supported by the 
cumulative consideration of organic impurities, which have a maximum allowable 
concentration of 0.4%, and the analytical method's error margin of ±1.5%. This error margin 
is derived from the intermediate precision results obtained during method validation, which 
yielded a relative standard deviation of 0.42%, as well as the guidelines outlined in the 
“Technical guide for the Elaboration of Monographs, 8th edition - 2022” published by EDQM 
(Chapter III.3.7, Volumetric Titrations) which propose content limits of ±1.5% for 
argentometric titrations. The new assay limit of 98.0% - 101.5% ensures the required quality 
for the starting material NPTA HCl and is in line with the new specification limit for the sum 
of impurities.

b. Supportive data for all potential residual solvents in NPTA HCl are provided in 
supplemental document S.2.3.12. For each solvent which is used in the synthesis of NPTA 
HCl via the Azide route or the Benzylamine route, the absence of below the limit of detection 
(LOD) has been shown in commercial batches. Testing has been done using a validated HS-
GC (Headspace Gas Chromatography) method. As can be seen from the tabulated overviews 
below (Table 2, Table 3), the established LOD for all potential solvents is below 10% of the 
respective ICH Q3C limit. Thus, it is justified to not individually specify the residual solvent 
in NPTA HCl. For the solvent isopropyl alcohol (class 3 solvent), which is used in the latest 
synthesis step of NPTA HCl manufacturing, a control is indirectly given by the limit for loss 
on drying (max. 0.5%).

Question:
Question 10
We note that diisopropylethylamine is not classified in ICH Q3C and the proposed limit is 
max 0.57%. Please provide justification for the basis of the use of the PDE of 7.4mg/day for 
diisopropylethylamine. In 3.2.S.3.2, results of diisopropylethylamine in Gadoquatrane drug 
substance are all below LOQ of 0.05% and the limit could be further tightened.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 10  (3.2.S.2.4):
Since diisopropylethylamine is not listed in ICH Q3C, a toxicological evaluation has been 
performed by Bayer. The full assessment and the justification for the derived PDE is outlined 
in the Module 3.3: N-Ethyl-diisopropylamin_CAS 7087-68-5 V2.
As outlined in S.3.2.03, diisopropylethylamine is introduced in step 4b and has been 
monitored for information in all Gadoquatrane drug substance batches. 
Diisopropylethylamine was found to be consistently below the calculated acceptable 
concentration of max. 0.57% in all tested batches. This acceptable concentration has been 
calculated based on the PDE of diisopropylethylamine (7.4 mg/50 kg) and the max. daily dose 
of 1.290 g/day Gadoquatrane drug substance. Diisopropylethylamine was not detectable in 
any of the tested batches (limit of detection 0.05%). Thus, the results for diisopropylamine in 
Gadoquatrane drug substance were consistently below 10% of the acceptable concentration.
Due to absence of diisopropylethylamine in all tested commercial batches, the specification 
for diisopropylethylamine can be omitted.
It should be noted, that the acceptable concentration of 0.57% diisopropylethylamine in 
Gadoquatrane drug substance is not a formal specification limit, but rather an acceptable
concentration level that has been applied to evaluate the absence of relevant amounts of 
diisopropylethylamine in the drug substance.

Question:
Question 1
In the manufacturing method of the drug substance, some are found where the amount of the 
solvent, catalyst, and reagent to be used is not shown. Based on the "Guidelines for Items to 
be Used in Application for Marketing Approval of Drugs, etc. in accordance with the revised 
Pharmaceutical Affairs Law" (Notification No. 0210001 of the Evaluation and Licensing 
Division, PFSB dated February 10, 2005), present all the amounts of raw materials, solvents, 
catalysts, and reagents, and describe them in the application form.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (3.2.S.2):
Bayer acknowledges the request to include further information in Module 3.2.S.2.2 
manufacturing process descriptions.
The process knowledge obtained during development, which is based on process robustness 
studies, including multivariate (DoE) and OVAT-(one-variable-at-a-time-method) 
experiments, allowed for a sound selection of parameters presented in Module 3.2.S.2.2. 
Further experimental details can be found in Module 3.2.S.2.6. Based on the process 
knowledge and the experimentally established proven acceptable ranges (PARs) or design 
spaces certain non-critical parameters were omitted in the submitted Module 3.2.S.2.2 process 
descriptions.
For the process steps after the final intermediate Gd-GlyMe-DOTA, i.e. steps 4a, 4b, 4c and 
4d where potential impact of each parameter may be increased compared with the earlier 
process steps, it has been demonstrated that non-critical process parameters have no impact on 
quality attributes even if they are varied in a broad range and thus, they can be omitted in the 
manufacturing process description. The respective process parameter understanding studies 
are added to S.2.6.01 including variation of amounts for the following solvents and reagents:
• Process step 4a: variation of amounts of acetonitrile and water used as work-up 
solvents (Subchapters of 5.1.5.1: “Input quantity acetonitrile for dilution after 
reaction” and “Input quantity water for dilution after reaction”)
• Process step 4a: variation of amount of acetonitrile used for washing isolated Gd-
Glydonip (Subchapter of 5.1.5.1: “Input quantity acetonitrile for washing of Gd-
Glydonip”)
• Process step 4b: variation of amount of water and aqueous sodium hydroxide within 
aqueous basic work-up (Subchapters of 5.1.5.2: “Quantity of water added for dilution 
before basic treatment” and “DoE on basic treatment”)
• Process step 4b: variation of amount of t-butyl methyl ether used for washing the 
neutralized aqueous phase (Subchapter of 5.1.5.2: “Washing quantities t-butyl methyl 
ether”)
• Process step 4b: variation of amounts of ethanol and acetone used for crystallization of 
gadoquatrane crude after defined distillation endpoint is reached (Subchapters of 
5.1.5.2: “Quantity ethanol added to distillation residue” and “Quantity acetone added 
to distillation residue”)
• Process step 4b: variation of amount of acetone used for washing isolated 
gadoquatrane crude (Subchapter of 5.1.5.2: “Quantity acetone used for washing”)
• Process step 4c (for the diafiltration-/ultrafiltration process, the introductory passage
of chapter 5.1.5.3 in S.2.6.01 already contained the following information): Being a 
physical separation method of solubilized components as opposed to a chemical 
reaction, the key parameter relevant for quality of step 4c is the number of diafiltration 
cycles, as other parameters (variation of water used for gadoquatrane crude 
dissolution, temperature, membrane surface area) only influence the time one cycle 
takes, not the product quality
• Process step 4d: variation of amount of activated charcoal used before final 
crystallization of gadoquatrane drug substance (Subchapter of 5.1.5.4: “Quantity of 
activated charcoal”)
The results of those studies demonstrate that constancy of quality of gadoquatrane is ensured 
within a broad parameter range justifying not to define setpoints for those non-critical process 
parameters.
Although demonstrated that the washing amount of ethanol in the final step 4d has no impact 
on the quality of Gadoquatrane drug substance in a broad range, Bayer agrees to amend the 
manufacturing process description by adding the respective washing amount of ethanol to 
further ensure the constancy of quality. Consequently, a subchapter to 5.1.5.4 in S.2.6.01 
(“Quantity of ethanol used for washing”) is added well.
Considering the number of steps towards the drug substance and additional control of 
intermediates, washing amounts and solvent amounts required for simple dissolution 
procedures or pH adjustments used in earlier synthesis steps have no impact on the quality of 
Gadoquatrane drug substance and therefore are not included in the manufacturing process 
descriptions. Furthermore, several in-process controls (IPCs) are implemented in the early 
steps before the final intermediate (Gd-GlyMe-DOTA intermediate) to monitor the degree of 
conversion and level of impurities fulfilling the requirements of Notification No. 0210001 by 
ensuring the constancy of quality by additional control measures:
Steps 1a+1b: 3 IPCs plus control of Glyptac intermediate based on appropriate release 
specification (S.2.4.03 Glyptac intermediate)
Steps 1c+1d: 3 IPCs plus control of Glyptac intermediate based on appropriate release 
specification (S.2.4.03 Glyptac intermediate)
Steps 2a+2b: 4 IPCs plus control of Gd-GlyMe-DOTA crude intermediate based on 
appropriate release specification (S.2.4.03 Gd-GlyMe-DOTA crude intermediate)
Step 3: 1 IPC plus control of Gd-GlyMe-DOTA intermediate based on appropriate release 
specification (S.2.4.03 Gd-GlyMe-DOTA intermediate)
In conclusion, Bayer does not agree that the manufacturing process descriptions should 
provide more detailed information for process parameters which have no impact on the 
quality of Gadoquatrane drug substance but agrees to add washing amounts of ethanol used in 
the last synthesis step. Control of intermediates and in-process controls justify that such 
detailed process descriptions are generally not required for all manufacturing process steps.
The amount of ethanol used for washing the drug substance after final crystallization has been 
included in the manufacturing description (S.2.2.02 Manufacturing Process – Description / 
Gadoquatrane drug substance):
Before change:
After stirring, the mixture is cooled to『20 °C』, solids are isolated by filtration and washed 
with ethanol.
After change:
After stirring, the mixture is cooled to『20 °C』, solids are isolated by filtration and washed 
with 『2-fold w/w』ethanol with respect to gadoquatrane.
In accordance with the instruction, we will adjust the description in the approval application 
form to clarify that either double or five times the weight of ethanol will be added to the 
weight of Gadoquatrane.

Question:
Question 2
Reply to the following inquiries regarding there are two manufacturing methods for DO3A 
route (Step 1a, Step 1b) and Cyglyp route (Step 1c, Step 1d).
1. 
The equivalence/homogeneity of the drug substance obtained from DO3A and Cyglyp
routes is explained based on the compliance with the control for the intermediates Glyptac 
and Gd-GlyMe-DOTA and the specifications for the drug substance obtained from both 
routes (S.2.6.01, chapter 5.1.1). Provide information on impurity profiles (e.g., 
chromatograms) including the related substances that were not specified in the control of 
intermediates and specifications of drug substance, and explain that the differences in 
manufacturing procedure do not affect the efficacy and safety.
2. 
Based on the answer to 1 above, explain again the appropriateness of setting the retest
period for the drug substance produced by DO3A route based on the results of the stability 
studies, etc., of the drug substance produced by Cyglyp route.
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 2 (3.2.S.2, 3.2.S.7):
Bayer confirms that the differences in manufacturing procedure do not affect efficacy and 
safety. The quality of Gadoquatrane drug substance remains consistent, regardless of whether 
it is produced via Cyglyp route or DO3A route. The drug product Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 
mmol Gd/mL for injection is unaffected, maintaining the same quality, efficacy and safety. 
Further details are provided below.
Response to Question Q2-1:
The synthesis of Gadoquatrane drug substance includes two different routes of synthesis 
towards the first intermediate Glyptac. Both synthesis routes (DO3A route and Cyglyp route) 
are compared in detail in section 5.1.1 of S.2.6.01. The comparison includes the organic and 
inorganic impurity profile, as well as solvents and potential mutagenic impurities in the 
intermediates Glyptac and Gd-GlyMe-DOTA and in the final drug substance. Based on this 
data it is shown that the drug substance produced via DO3A route or Cyglyp route is of equal 
quality.
An additional comparison of the non-specified impurities in intermediates and in the drug 
substance is requested and is therefore provided in the following.
Organic impurities in Gadoquatrane drug substance:
In Gadoquatrane drug substance the following impurities are relevant in both routes and are 
specified with individual limits: Gd-GlyMe-DOTA (refer to Question 11), Formyl-Tris-Gd-
GlyMe-DOTA Isomer 1, Methyl-Gadoquatrane Isomer 1 and 2 and Desmethyl-Gadoquatrane 
Isomer 1.
Besides those specified impurities no further impurities are detected in Gadoquatrane drug 
substance batches above reporting threshold (RT 0.03%). This is demonstrated by the batch 
data of Gadoquatrane drug substance in Table 1 (result for any unspecified impurity <0.03%) 
and by the chromatograms provided in Figure 1. Thus, there is no difference which has an 
impact on quality in the impurity profile of Gadoquatrane drug substance produced via either 
DO3A or Cyglyp route.
Further organic impurities which can be formed in the final chemical steps 4a to 4b are 
described in section 5.2 of S.2.6.01. None of the discussed impurities are route-specific. The 
potential impurities can occur in both routes of synthesis and are effectively purged, as 
discussed in detail in the respective section.
Figure 1: Chromatograms of Gadoquatrane drug substance from Cyglyp route 
compared to Gadoquatrane drug substance from DO3A route. Testing was performed 
according to Purity Method described in S.4.2.01. RT= Reporting Threshold (0.03%)
HPLC Chromatograms for each batch are provided in the appendix:
Gadoquatrane drug substance, Cyglyp route: Chromatogramme_UN623TE_UN623TG_UN623TI_s.pdf
Gadoquatrane drug substance, DO3A route: Chromatogramme_UN62XIK_UN62XIM_UN62XK7_s.pdf
Organic impurities in Gd-GlyMe-DOTA intermediate:
In Gd-GlyMe-DOTA intermediate the following impurities are specified with individual 
limits (S.2.4.03): Bis(Gd-GlyMe-DOTA) and Gd-Me-DOTA. Bis(Gd-GlyMe-DOTA) and 
Gd-Me-DOTA can be formed in both routes of synthesis and are effectively purged towards 
the final drug substance.
Besides those specified impurities, further impurities which were detected occasionally in 
commercial Gd-GlyMe-DOTA batches are Gd-DO3A, Gd-GlyMe-DOTA-ethyl-ester and 1,4-
Des-Acetyl-Gd-GlyMe-DOTA (=RRT 0.25) (refer to Table 2), as well as free Ligand (= Gd-
GlyMe-DOTA ligand) and 1,7-Des-Acetyl-Gd-GlyMe-DOTA (=RRT 0.23) (below reporting 
threshold, Figure 2). All those impurities are controlled by the limit for any unspecified 
impurities of max. 0.10% in Gd-GlyMe-DOTA intermediate and are effectively purged 
towards the final drug substance, as outlined in detail in section 5.2 of S.2.6.01.
Among those impurities, Gd-DO3A is of specific interest, since this impurity can solely be 
formed in the DO3A route. Fate and Purge experiments have proven that levels of 0.15% Gd-
DO3A are purged to below RT (0.03%) in Gadoquatrane drug substance. Therefore, even 
though this impurity is route-specific, it does not impact on the quality of the final drug 
substance.
Further organic impurities, which can potentially be present in Gd-GlyMe-DOTA are 
described in section 5.2 of S.2.6.01. None of those impurities are route-specific and, as 
outlined in detail in section 5.2 of S.2.6.01, all impurities are effectively purged towards the 
final drug substance. Thus, it is excluded that any of those impurities impacts the quality of 
the final drug substance.
Figure 2: Chromatograms of Gd-GlyMe-DOTA intermediate from Cyglyp route 
compared to Gd-GlyMe-DOTA intermediate from DO3A route. Purity testing has been 
performed by HPLC-CAD (CAD=Charged Aerosol detection; RT= Reporting Threshold, 0.03%).
HPLC Chromatograms of each batch are provided in the appendix.
Organic impurities in Glyptac intermediate:
Glyptac intermediate is the first intermediate in the synthesis of Gadoquatrane drug substance 
and is produced via DO3A or Cyglyp route. Glyptac is an early intermediate and the limit for 
any unspecified impurities is set to max. 0.5%.
In both routes of synthesis, Benzyl alcohol and Glyptac monoacid are relevant impurities and 
are therefore specified (max. 1.0%) in Glyptac intermediate. Both impurities are not route-
specific and are effectively purged in the downstream process as described in detail in section 
5.2 of S.2.6.01. Further potential impurities, which can occur in the Cyglyp route and the 
DO3A route, and which are controlled as any unspecified impurities in Glyptac intermediate, 
are listed in section 5.2 of S.2.6.01.
The impurities which are specific to the DO3A route only, are DO3A-Triester, N-Formyl-1,4-
DO2A-diester (=RRT 1.09), 1,7-and 1,4-DO2A-Diester. These compounds are controlled by 
in-process controls during the synthesis of Glyptac intermediate via DO3A route and are 
effectively purged: Specifically, we refer to in-process controls 1 and 2 in step 1a, as well as 
in-process control 3 in step 1b.
For the DO2A-Diester Isomers, fate and purge studies have shown that spiking of those 
impurities results in a slightly elevated level of Bis(Gd-GlyMe-DOTA), which is a controlled 
impurity in Gd-GlyMe-DOTA intermediate. N-Formyl-1,4-DO2A-diester is already 
effectively purged in the crystallization of Glyptac and is not found in Glyptac batches. 
DO3A-Triester is a route-specific impurity which was found at a maximum level of up to 
0.28% in Glyptac which is within the control level of unspecified impurities. In the 
downstream process the impurity reacts to Gd-DO3A, which is controlled in Gd-GlyMe-
DOTA intermediate at a level which excludes any impact on the quality of the final drug 
substance (see discussion above, control at 0.10% as an unspecified impurity; fate and purge 
studies are outlined in detail in section 5.2 of S.2.6.01). Thus, even though those four potential 
impurities in Glyptac are specific for the DO3A route, they have no impact on the quality of 
the final drug substance.
In the Cyglyp route, the telescoped intermediate Cyglyp is a potential impurity in Glyptac 
intermediate. Residual amounts of Cyglyp are controlled by an in-process control in the 
synthesis towards Glyptac. In Glyptac intermediate, Cyglyp is controlled as any unspecified 
impurity at max. 0.5% and has not been detected in any of the commercial batches produced 
so far. Moreover, it has been ensured by fate and purge studies that this impurity is effectively 
purged during the synthesis and does not affect the quality of the final drug substance (refer to 
5.2 of S.2.6.01).
Batch data of Glyptac intermediate from both routes of synthesis, including the not-specified 
potential impurities Cyglyp and DO3A-Triester are presented in Table 5-1 in S.2.6.01.
In summary, a detailed examination of the impurity profiles of the intermediates Glyptac and 
Gd-GlyMe-DOTA shows that slight, not quality-relevant, differences between both routes of 
synthesis are detectable up to Gd-GlyMe-DOTA, with the route-specific impurity DO3A-
Triester in Glyptac and the downstream impurity Gd-DO3A in Gd-GlyMe-DOTA. Control of 
both compounds is discussed in section 5.2 of S.2.6.01.
Since all impurities are effectively purged, no difference in the organic impurity profile of 
Gadoquatrane drug substance is detectable. In none of the produced commercial batches (31 
produced batches so far) any impurities besides the specified impurities were found (reporting 
threshold 0.03%). Regardless of the synthetic route towards the first intermediate Glyptac, it 
is possible to produce drug substance of equivalent quality. Therefore, the difference in route 
of synthesis (DO3A or Cyglyp) has no impact on the efficacy and safety of the drug 
substance.
Response to Question Q2-2:
Since no differences between the quality of Gadoquatrane drug substance produced via 
Cyglyp or DO3A route are given, the same retest period applies.
The retest period is justified by long-term stability data for Gadoquatrane drug substance 
produced via Cyglyp route. An additional stability study for Gadoquatrane drug substance 
from DO3A route is ongoing (6 months data available, accelerated and long-term conditions, 
see updated S.7.1.01-04 and S.7.3.01-04) and shows no signs of degradation and no difference 
compared to the stability batches of Gadoquatrane drug substance produced via Cyglyp route.
Chromatograms of representative Gadoquatrane drug substance stability batches from Cyglyp 
and DO3A can be found in Figure 3. For a good comparison, the 6 months data after storage 
under forced conditions (40 °C, 75% relative humidity, packaging AL/PP) have been chosen.
Figure 3: Chromatograms of Gadoquatrane drug substance from Cyglyp route 
compared to Gadoquatrane drug substance from DO3A route after storage at 40 °C, 
75% relative humidity for 6 months (packaging AL/PP). Testing has been performed 
according to Purity Method described in S.4.2.01. (RT= Reporting Threshold, 0.03%)

Question:
Question 3:
Reply to the following inquiries regarding the control of raw materials.
1. 
Explain the principles of the test method for the following control.
• 
Step 2a Hydrochloric acid concentrated: Iron: 20ppm or less (visual inspection)
• 
Step 2a Sulfuric acid: Chloride: 10ppm or less (visual inspection)
• 
Step 4b Hydrochloric acid concentrated: Chlorine: 0.0004% or less (visual inspection)
and Iron: 0.0001% or less (visual inspection)
2. 
Explain the acceptance criteria and the principle of the test method the following
control.
• 
Step 4b t-butyl methyl ether, Step 4b/4d Denatured ethanol and Step 4b Acetone:
Acidity or alkalinity: must comply (visual and titration)
• 
Step 4d Activated charcoal: Acidity or alkalinity: must comply (visual)
Answer:
Bayer Response to Question 3 (3.2.S.2):
Response to Question 3-1.:
The method for all of these tests has been classified as “visual inspection”, as the final 
judgement of colorized or turbid solutions has to be done visually. Please find here the 
descriptions of the principle of the methods for the requested tests.
Step 2a Hydrochloric acid concentrated: Iron: 20 ppm or less (color reaction)
An aqueous dilution of the test substance is reacted with ammonium persulphate and 
potassium thiocyanate solution containing butanol. In parallel, the same reaction is carried out 
with a standard iron solution.
The test solution meets the requirement if the intensity of the color produced in the butanol 
layers (due to Fe(SCN)3) is less intense than that produced by standard iron solution (20 
ppm).
Step 2a Sulfuric acid: Chloride: 10 ppm or less (precipitation reaction)
An aqueous dilution of the test substance is treated with nitric acid and silver nitrate. In 
parallel, the same reaction is carried out with a standard chloride solution.
The turbidity in the sample solution, produced by precipitated AgCl, is less than in the 
reference solution.
Step 4b Hydrochloric acid concentrated: Chlorine: 0.0004% or less (color reaction)
An aqueous dilution of the test substance is treated with potassium iodide and starch solution.
Any blue coloration (due to iodine produced) must disappear when adding max. 0.2 mL 
sodium thiosulfate solution 0.01 M.
Step 4b Hydrochloric acid concentrated: Iron: 0.0001% or less (color reaction)
An aqueous dilution of the test substance is treated with citric acid monohydrate and 
thioglycolic acid. In parallel, the same reaction is carried out with a standard iron solution.
After 5 minutes the sample solution is max. as pink as the reference solution. The pink 
coloration is due to the ferric thioglycolate produced.
Accordingly we will modify the approval application form to clarify the principles of these 
testing methods. We will also make similar changes to the relevant sections of CTD 2.3.S.
Response to Question 3-2.:
Please find the principles of the test methods and the respective acceptance criteria for the 
requested tests below.
Step 4a Acetonitril, Step 4b t-butyl methyl ether, Step 4b/4d Denatured ethanol and Step 
4b Acetone: Acidity or alkalinity: must comply (neutral litmus paper and titration)
The test substance mixed with water is tested with red and blue litmus paper.
The litmus paper shows neutral reaction.
If the litmus test is weakly alkaline or acidic, carry out a titration.
Test for alkaline substances: 50 mL of the test substance is titrated to color change from blue 
to yellow against bromophenol blue indicator.
The volume of hydrochloric acid 0.1 mol/L consumed must not exceed 0.3 mL.
Test for acidic substances: 50 mL of the test substance is titrated to color change from 
colorless to pink against phenolphthalein indicator.
The volume of sodium hydroxide solution 0.1 mol/L consumed must not exceed 0.3 mL.
Step 4d Activated charcoal: Acidity or alkalinity: must comply (neutral litmus paper)
The test substance is heated in water. After cooling to room temperature, the suspension is 
filtered, the filtrate has to be neutral against litmus paper.
Accordingly we will modify the approval application form to clarify the principles of these 
testing methods. We will also make similar changes to the relevant sections of CTD 2.3.S.
In addition, we have standardized the descriptions for "acidity or alkalinity" in Step 4a 
acetonitrile, which has the same principle of testing method as "acidity or alkalinity" in Step 
4b t-butyl methyl ether, Step 4b/4d denatured ethanol, and Step 4b acetone, and we have also 
made corresponding adjustments to the approval application form.
